title: Former congressmember and winemaker joins HillStaffer
body_text:
HILLSTAFFER ADDS RADANOVICH: HillStaffer has hired former Rep. George Radanovich , adding the eight-term member and one-time winemaker as a senior adviser at the firm.

— During his 16 years representing California’s 19th district, Radanovich served on the Budget, Foreign Relations and Energy & Commerce committees, in addition to chairing multiple subcommittees under the Natural Resources committee. He announced his retirement in 2009.

— The Republican has been an active consultant in California politics since leaving Congress and previously spent three years as president of the California Fresh Fruit Association , representing fruit growers and shippers in Sacramento and Washington.

— His “deep understanding of multi-level government relations enhances our expertise in manufacturing & chemicals, agriculture, healthcare and financial services,” HillStaffer president Thomas Rosenfield said in a statement.

— Radanovich also had the distinction of being the first winemaker to serve in Congress since Thomas Jefferson, co-founding the Congressional Wine Caucus in 1999. Radanovich Winery opened in 1986 and remained in operation following Radanovich’s election to Congress. He closed the winery in 2003, citing poor economic conditions for California winegrowers.

ANONYMOUS PENTAGON DONOR: The Pentagon confirmed today that it has accepted a $130 million gift from a private donor intended to help cover military paychecks during the government shutdown, POLITICO’s Leo Shane III , Paul McLeary and Jack Detsch report .

— President Trump announced the gift yesterday during an event at the White House, saying that a “friend” who wished to remain anonymous had donated the money out of a sense of patriotism.

— “White House officials said that covering the cost of military pay for the first half of October totaled about $6.5 billion. Todd Harrison , a defense budget analyst at the American Enterprise Institute, said that based on that figure, the new donation will cover about one-third of one day’s pay for the force.”

Happy Friday and welcome to PI. Do you know who gave the Pentagon $130 million? Let us know at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

BIG BEAUTIFUL BALLROOM: Lobbyists with close ties to the president are steering clients to donate cash to Trump’s White House ballroom project, Gabe Kaminsky reports for The Free Press .

— Lobbyists and consultants like Brian Ballard , Jeff Miller and Kellyanne Conway have all connected clients with Meredith O’Rourke , Trump’s 2024 campaign finance director who is in charge of raising money for the ballroom project that is estimated to cost $300 million.

— Two Ballard clients, Amazon and Reynolds American , donated after his firm connected them with fundraisers, according to the report. Ballard and Miller represent several other ballroom contributors including Apple , Booz Allen Hamilton , Comcast , Micron , Palantir , Ripple Labs , T-Mobile and Tether .

TRUMP INDUSTRIAL COMPLEX: A drone company that touts Donald Trump Jr. as an adviser has obtained its largest ever Pentagon contract, Joe Miller , Alex Rogers, Steff Chávez , and George Steer report for the Financial Times .

— Florida-based Unusual Machines has been contracted by the U.S. Army to build 3,500 drone motors and other parts with an additional 20,000 components to be ordered next year, according to the report. The company declined to state the value of the contract.

— Trump Jr. was brought on as an adviser in November 2024 and currently holds a roughly $4 million stake in the company. A spokesperson for Trump Jr. and the CEO of Unusual Machines both deny him having any involvement in the acquisition of the contract.

WOULD YOU LIKE FRIES WITH THAT: The International Franchise Association has enlisted some reality TV starpower for its “Franchise Means Local” campaign that launched earlier this month.

— Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star Angie Katsanevas ,founder of franchised chain Lunatic Fringe Salon , features in a new ad from the association capitalizing on her recent barb towards a fellow Housewife: “ You do french fries, I do franchise. ”

— IFA’s $5 million campaign consists of social media, digital and streaming TV ads and is intended to highlight local franchise owners and operators across the country.

title: Cuban exile hires ex-Florida mayor to lobby for pardon
body_text:
PARDON ME: Pardon lobbying work on K Street doesn’t appear to be slowing down, even as the White House seeks to clamp down on the lucrative line of business for D.C.’s influence peddlers.

— The most prominent illustration of that came last week when President Donald Trump pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao , who had lined up an array of paid advocates to help him secure clemency from Trump.

— Earlier this month, Miami developer and Cuban exile Santiago Alvarez retained Florida-based Corcoran Partners to advocate for a presidential pardon, according to disclosures filed over the weekend.

— Alvarez served over two years in prison in the late 2000s after pleading guilty to criminal conspiracy and obstruction of justice in order to avoid more serious weapons charges . Federal authorities had recovered machine guns, ammunition and live grenades from an apartment complex Alvarez owned. The obstruction charge came after Alvarez refused to testify against anti-Castro Cuban militant Luis Posada Carriles in a different case.

— Alvarez was later accused by the Cuban government of plotting a coup with other exiles, allegations he has denied, and had to fight deportation following his earlier case.

— Steve Bovo , who joined Corcoran Partners this spring after stepping down as mayor of Alvarez’s hometown of Hialeah, Florida, began lobbying for a pardon on Alvarez’s behalf on Oct. 1, according to lobbying disclosures.

— Bovo won his mayoral race in 2021 with Trump’s endorsement, and is a longtime ally of now-Secretary of State Marco Rubio , who has employed Bovo’s wife as an adviser for years. Rubio has also supported Bovo’s political career, according to the Miami Herald , including endorsing Bovo and even swearing Bovo and Bovo’s son into various local offices.

— Bovo’s former deputy chief of staff Carlos San Jose will work on the account as well.

— Alvarez’s pardon lobbying campaign comes as the White House moved to tighten the reins on the presidential clemency process. Top White House officials including chief of staff Susie Wiles began to chafe at reports of White House outsiders touting access and dangling exorbitant fees in exchange for help securing pardons, NBC News reported last weekend. Wiles reportedly led the charge to impose a pause on issuing pardons.

— But pardons have resumed for the first time since May. A few weeks ago, the president granted clemency to disgraced former congressman George Santos , who had just begun serving a seven-year sentence for charges of wire fraud and identity theft.

— Last week came Trump’s pardon of Zhao, who pleaded guilty in 2023 to failing to comply with anti-money laundering laws and whose crypto exchange has embarked on several joint ventures with the Trump family’s crypto business.

— Several other potential pardons may be in the offing as well, according to NBC, including for Fugees rapper Pras Michel , who was convicted in 2023 on foreign agent and campaign finance charges.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. As we approach week four of the shutdown, how are you advising clients? Let us know. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

TILTING AT WINDMILLS: As offshore wind developers fight for survival against the Trump administration’s attacks on the sector, a handful of top wind developers have enlisted lobbyists with ties to the White House, per E&E News’ Benjamin Storrow .

— “The Norwegian oil giant Equinor retained former Interior Secretary David Bernhardt ‘s new lobbying firm after its 54-turbine project off Long Island was halted temporarily earlier this year by the department Bernhardt used to run.”

— “ Ørsted , the Danish wind developer whose $6 billion project off New England was stopped for a month,” recently tapped Trump fundraiser and BGR Group lobbyist Nick Iarossi , while Avangrid “turned to Carlos Trujillo , the founder of Continental Strategy who served as Trump’s ambassador to the Organization of American States during the president’s firm term.”

RFK JR. DRIVES A WEDGE BETWEEN GOP, DOCTORS GROUPS: “ Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s tenure as health secretary is straining Republicans’ relationship with the medical establishment to what’s looking like a breaking point,” POLITICO ’s Simon J. Levien reports.

— “Doctors and their professional associations, such as the American Medical Association and American Academy of Pediatrics, have clashed with the GOP over health policy changes, but Kennedy has given them a leftward shove by deriding them as pharma flunkeys and progressive ideologues.”

— “In recent months, Kennedy has sparred with the groups over vaccine guidance, transgender care, the handling of the pandemic and whether pregnant women are putting their children at risk of autism if they take Tylenol.”

— “The groups have long been considered nonpartisan and have many conservative members. But Republicans in Congress are piling on, potentially risking the medical profession’s evolution into a Democratic-leaning interest group” and shrinking doctors’ influence while Republicans are in power. But “some GOP lawmakers say it’s the doctors that lost them as they moved left.”

MAHA ALLIES LEAN ON ROLLINS: Farmers and advocacy groups supportive of Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement want to see more action on MAHA’s food priorities from Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins , as farmers struggle to cope with Trump’s trade wars, inflation, consolidation and funding cuts.

— “We urge USDA to turn the MAHA vision into tangible results,” advocates wrote in a letter to Rollins sent on Friday, which they argued requires a more concerted effort to put the department’s money where its mouth is.

— More than 100 signatories highlighted how the Trump administration’s cuts to key programs supporting local food and infrastructure procurement programs — as well as programs focused on conservation, research and technical assistance for farmers — can hinder MAHA goals to root out chronic disease and corporate influence. USDA, the letter says, should promote smaller, independent farmers over conglomerates in its procurement and assistance programs, which in turn increases access to healthy foods over ultra-processed ones.

— While the MAHA movement has secured several big wins on issues like vaccine policy, food companies and the agriculture industry have avoided stringent restrictions on the use of pesticides or new mandates on certain food ingredients — irking some MAHA allies.

MYSTERY SOLVED: “ Timothy Mellon , a reclusive billionaire and a major financial backer of President Trump, is the anonymous private donor who gave $130 million to the U.S. government to help pay troops during the shutdown,” two people familiar with the matter tell The New York Times’ Tyler Pager .

— When Trump announced the donation last week, “he declined to name the person who provided the funds, only calling him a ‘patriot’ and a friend. But the two people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the donation was private, identified him as Mr. Mellon.”

— “Mr. Mellon, a wealthy banking heir and railroad magnate, is a longtime backer of Mr. Trump and gave tens of millions of dollars to groups supporting the president’s campaign. Last year, he made a $50 million donation to a super PAC supporting Mr. Trump, which was one of the largest single contributions ever disclosed.”

HEMP ON THE HILL: More than three dozen attorneys general from across the country are pleading for Congress to close what they say is a loophole from the 2018 farm bill that legalized hemp and inadvertently gave way to a flourishing market for intoxicating synthetic hemp products.

— “Through use of highly advanced chemical processes … not contemplated by Congress when it enacted the 2018 Farm Bill,” some in the industry “have nefariously misinterpreted” that measure as allowing them to “produce and sell various synthetic cannabinoids regardless of the chemicals’ potency and psychoactive effects,” the state AGs warned in a letter to top congressional appropriators on Friday.

— “In this way, legal, nonintoxicating hemp is used to make Frankenstein THC products that get adults high and harm and even kill children,” they warned. The letter was signed by attorneys general from 37 states along with AGs from Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

— Lawmakers including Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) have been pushing for the inclusion of a hemp crackdown as the GOP tries to push through several minibus spending bills during the shutdown. But Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) is blocking the package from moving forward over the hemp language, per POLITICO ’s Grace Yarrow , arguing that the proposals he’s seen would decimate the Kentucky-centric hemp industry.

PARDON ME: Pardon lobbying work on K Street doesn’t appear to be slowing down, even as the White House seeks to clamp down on the lucrative line of business for D.C.’s influence peddlers.

— The most prominent illustration of that came last week when President Donald Trump pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who had lined up an array of paid advocates to help him secure clemency from Trump.

— Earlier this month, Miami developer and Cuban exile Santiago Alvarez retained Florida-based Corcoran Partners to advocate for a presidential pardon, according to disclosures filed over the weekend.

— Alvarez served over two years in prison in the late 2000s after pleading guilty to criminal conspiracy and obstruction of justice in order to avoid more serious weapons charges. Federal authorities had recovered machine guns, ammunition and live grenades from an apartment complex Alvarez owned. The obstruction charge came after Alvarez refused to testify against anti-Castro Cuban militant Luis Posada Carriles in a different case.

— Alvarez was later accused by the Cuban government of plotting a coup with other exiles, allegations he has denied, and had to fight deportation following his earlier case.

— Steve Bovo, who joined Corcoran Partners this spring after stepping down as mayor of Alvarez’s hometown of Hialeah, Florida, began lobbying for a pardon on Alvarez’s behalf on Oct. 1, according to lobbying disclosures.

— Bovo won his mayoral race in 2021 with Trump’s endorsement, and is a longtime ally of now-Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has employed Bovo’s wife as an adviser for years. Rubio has also supported Bovo’s political career, according to the Miami Herald, including endorsing Bovo and even swearing Bovo and Bovo’s son into various local offices.

— Bovo’s former deputy chief of staff Carlos San Jose will work on the account as well.

— Alvarez’s pardon lobbying campaign comes as the White House moved to tighten the reins on the presidential clemency process. Top White House officials including chief of staff Susie Wiles began to chafe at reports of White House outsiders touting access and dangling exorbitant fees in exchange for help securing pardons, NBC News reported last weekend. Wiles reportedly led the charge to impose a pause on issuing pardons.

— But pardons have resumed for the first time since May. A few weeks ago, the president granted clemency to disgraced former congressman George Santos, who had just begun serving a seven-year sentence for charges of wire fraud and identity theft.

— Last week came Trump’s pardon of Zhao, who pleaded guilty in 2023 to failing to comply with anti-money laundering laws and whose crypto exchange has embarked on several joint ventures with the Trump family’s crypto business.

— Several other potential pardons may be in the offing as well, according to NBC, including for Fugees rapper Pras Michel, who was convicted in 2023 on foreign agent and campaign finance charges.

title: Travel industry warns of Thanksgiving devastation
body_text:
GROUNDED: The domestic travel industry is ratcheting up its pleas to end the shutdown, warning there would be “economically devastating” consequences if it were to drag on into the busy Thanksgiving travel period.

— “Travel spending during the holiday generates billions of dollars in economic activity, supporting jobs, local tax bases, and small businesses nationwide,” a coalition of more than 500 national and local travel and tourism organizations wrote in a letter to congressional leadership today.

— “Congress must act without delay to pass a clean continuing resolution to reopen the government immediately and ensure full federal operations are restored in advance of the Thanksgiving travel period,” they added.

— The National Air Traffic Controllers Association for the first time last week urged lawmakers to pass a clean spending stopgap, and the shutdown has already cost the travel economy more than $4 billion, according to the U.S. Travel Association .

— As staffing shortages drive up delays at airports across the country, the industry coalition warned that “a continued shutdown is likely to significantly suppress travel demand and spending, creating a real threat to American workers, businesses, and the overall economy.”

A GLIMMER OF HOPE?: We’re on track to blow past the previous record for longest shutdown, but former Sen. Richard Burr , who’s now a lobbyist at DLA Piper , said on a webinar this afternoon that there’s reason for optimism. “The intel that we’re getting now leads me to believe that this week there will be a breakthrough,” the North Carolina Republican said on a weekly “office hours” call for clients. Though he added: “I’m not exactly sure what that looks like.”

— Any continuing resolution would likely extend into January, with the potential for a minibus spending bill to move at the same time, Burr predicted. “Then we get to a January date that one has to decide, is it a full year CR, at least until September 30, or do they attempt to pass the additional appropriations bills?” he said, before noting that in the event of a full-year CR, Congress would almost certainly run it past next year’s midterms.

— That “would probably put it sometime in late November, early December, before we saw a need to fund the government again,” which would mean that for industries hoping for a more favorable federal funding landscape in a GOP-controlled Washington — like the defense sector — may be out of luck. “We’re not going to see those new starts unless the administration moves fungible money around,” Burr warned.

— Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters today he is “optimistic” an agreement will be reached this week.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI , where we can’t believe November is here already. Are you seeing the light at the end of the tunnel for this shutdown? Let us know. IT’S NEVER TOO SOON: The 2025 election season will officially conclude tomorrow, formally kicking off the sprint until next year’s midterms. And Andy Blunt , the chief executive at HB Strategies and the son of former Sen. Roy Blunt (R-Mo.), is out with a breakdown of all the redistricting efforts currently underway.

— “Understanding these scenarios is critical for clients navigating the rapidly evolving political environment and planning their federal advocacy strategies for the next Congress,” Blunt writes, though one of the biggest question marks of the cycle will be the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais, the redistricting case heard by the court last month.

— Blunt runs through the best-case scenario for the GOP, in which it would gain 14 House seats through redistricting alone; the best case for Democrats, in which they manage to net five seats thanks to a new map in California; and the most probable outcome, which nets the GOP five red-leaning seats through redistricting before Election Day.

FIRST IN PI: The Business Roundtable has unleashed a new wave of ads as part of a seven-figure campaign urging Congress to enact permitting reforms. The fresh round of spots is popping up at 50 gas stations across the D.C. metro area as well as online and on the radio within the Beltway and in key congressional districts. The ads call on lawmakers to “unlock permitting gridlock” once they return to business as usual, and point viewers to BRT’s “Ready. Set. Let’s Build” campaign hub .

HERITAGE FALLOUT: “ Ryan Neuhaus , who until Friday was chief of staff to Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts , left the conservative think tank in the wake of an uproar over a statement from Roberts last week defending Tucker Carlson after he interviewed antisemitic white nationalist Nick Fuentes ,” The Hill ’s Emily Brooks reports.

— “Neuhaus had angered Heritage staff and other conservative movement allies after he had reposted a number of messages of support for Roberts and his defense of Carlson on social media, including one particularly controversial statement that Heritage employees who were ‘[virtue] signaling’ in wake of the remarks should ‘resign if so outraged,’ and that it ‘would be addition by subtraction for the institution.’”

— Roberts had announced in a staff email on Friday that Neuhaus was being made a senior adviser at the think tank, and that executive vice president Derrick Morgan would take over as acting chief of staff until the end of the year.

— A Heritage spokesperson denied that Neuhaus was fired, telling The Hill that “he offered his resignation, which was accepted.” The spokesperson added that “Ryan is a good man, we appreciate his service, and we have no doubt he will serve the movement in another capacity.”

— “A list released last month by the White House of more than three dozen donors omitted donation amounts, as well as the names of several individuals and companies that collectively have billions of dollars riding on the outcome of administration policy decisions.”

— “Among the donors not disclosed by the White House are a pair of health care companies seeking to protect or expand Medicare reimbursement for their products, as well as the Wall Street powerhouse BlackRock , whose bid to acquire a stake in Panama Canal ports has been supported by Mr. Trump amid opposition from China.”

— “Another is Jeff Yass , a major investor in TikTok ’s parent company who could benefit from a Trump-backed deal to keep the social media app up and running in the United States,” along with chipmaker Nvidia , whose CEO last week said he was “proud to contribute in a small way to what will be a historic and national monument for our country.”

title: What FARA experts are watching in the Linda Sun trial
body_text:
SUN’S UP: The former aide to two New York governors charged with acting as an unregistered Chinese agent heads to federal court in Brooklyn tomorrow for the first big FARA trial of the second Trump administration.

— Linda Sun , who served as a deputy chief of staff to current Gov. Kathy Hochul and worked in Andrew Cuomo ’s administration before that, was indicted last year for allegedly using her job to benefit the Chinese government in exchange for millions in payments to her husband’s business.

— In a sense, it’s notable that Sun’s prosecution has continued at all. Special counsel Robert Mueller brought foreign agent cases against numerous top allies of President Donald Trump during his first term, many of whom he subsequently pardoned. And at the beginning of this year, Trump’s DOJ signaled that it would deprioritize foreign influence campaigns, outlining a pivot in a February memo and dropping foreign agent or corruption charges against politicians including Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) and New York Mayor Eric Adams .

— At the same time, the department has secured a guilty plea from a former CIA agent for FARA violations. And it has stuck with other Biden-era foreign agent cases involving former Rep. David Rivera (R-Fla.) and Korea policy expert Sue Mi Terry , at least for now. Then in September, Trump issued a memo explicitly directing the use of FARA to prosecute nonprofits and NGOs with foreign ties.

— Sun’s case, though it began during the Biden administration, “maps pretty well onto where Bondi said they would continue to focus criminal enforcement,” said Josh Rosenstein , a partner at Sandler Reiff Lamb Rosenstein & Birkenstock , who advises clients on FARA compliance.

— Sun and her husband Chris Hu have pleaded not guilty to a slew of charges, which in addition to the FARA charges against Sun, also include money laundering, tax evasion, visa fraud and more.

— Prosecutors say that Sun’s actions at the behest of the Chinese government include blocking meeting requests from Taiwanese officials to the governor’s office — while organizing meetings for Chinese officials; changing state messaging on issues of importance to China and obtaining state proclamations for representatives of Beijing without authorization.

— In exchange, prosecutors say Chinese officials steered “millions of dollars” toward Hu’s businesses — which helped finance the purchase of a $3.6 million home on Long Island and a $1.9 million high-rise condo in Honolulu and luxury cars including a Ferrari and a Range Rover. They also allege the couple received other perks such as jobs for relatives to Nanjing-style salted ducks prepared by the Chinese consulate’s personal chef.

— Attorneys for Sun have cast doubt on the government’s accusations that Sun undertook the activities in question at the direction of Chinese officials rather than in furtherance of her personal beliefs, or were outside the normal course of her official duties.

— Among the government’s biggest hurdles in the case will be proving that Sun willfully neglected to register as a foreign agent, as well as its assertions that Sun was acting at Beijing’s direction, argued Tom Spulak , a partner at King & Spalding who advises clients on FARA compliance.

— “If you read the indictment carefully, there’s only a few references there to any type of request, or a suggestion of assistance from the [Chinese government],” he said. “Everything seems to be her reporting to them.”

— Matt Sanderson of Caplin & Drysdale told PI that while the defense is likely to “focus more on the mundane nature of the actions” that Sun took, “I think the fundamental question they have to answer is, why should there not be some implication read out from both the receipt of all of these benefits and the actions that were taken by her in her official capacity? Why aren’t those connected?”

— FARA experts pointed to one other element of Sun’s case that bodes well for the government. “What’s present in this case that has not been present in a lot of the [foreign agent] cases that the department lost is … the very sexy fact pattern involving flashy items of value and expensive toys and all of the hallmarks that you would traditionally expect to see in a foreign influence operation,” said Rosenstein.

— He, like others, drew parallels to the successful case against former Sen. Bob Menendez (D-N.J.). “It helps ground the allegations in sort of a very concrete and understandable way for a jury,” Rosenstein argued, while Sanderson noted that the fact pattern can help illustrate that “it wasn’t just a failure to file some forms.”

title: Airlines ask for a shutdown safety net
body_text:
TRUST US: With Congress poised to turn the page on the longest shutdown in history, the airline industry is mobilizing to prevent air travel from being used as a “political football” during future shutdowns. It wants to head off fiascos like the one that led to the cancellation of thousands of U.S. flights over the past five days due to FAA-mandated service cuts.

— “There are long term measures that can be taken to make sure that airlines, hotels, travel, the American public isn’t held hostage every time there’s a tough political debate in Washington,” Airlines for America chief Chris Sununu said during a briefing with reporters today. “This is affecting not just the airlines, but the entire American economy.”

— Sununu, who was joined by American Hotel & Lodging Association President and CEO Rosanna Maietta , said the travel industry will push lawmakers over the next one to two months to allow the FAA to tap its aviation trust fund to continue operations during future shutdowns. Congress, he said, needs to “absolutely get it done.”

— Airlines and passengers help finance the Airport and Airway Trust Fund through excise taxes on purchases of plane tickets or airline miles, air cargo and plane fuel. The funding is used to pay for capital improvements at airports along with other FAA operations, including air traffic control.

— “We’re paying into it as we speak. … Millions of dollars a day are going into this fund designed to pay for FAA costs that cannot or that are just simply not allowed during a shutdown,” Sununu said. By contrast, the Highway Trust Fund is authorized to serve as a stopgap during shutdowns, he noted.

“Why don’t we have this for the FAA? It’s so logical. The only reason you wouldn’t want to do this is if you wanted this to become some sort of political log jam, football every time.”

— Sununu didn’t try to hide his frustration with the current state of affairs in the Capitol. The U.S. aviation system is a private-public partnership, he said, and while airlines “are living up to their end of the bargain spectacularly … it’s the government side that is not.”

FWIW: Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) introduced legislation in March that would allow the FAA to lean on the aviation trust fund’s coffers during a shutdown. There aren’t any listed co-sponsors as of today, while dueling Democratic and GOP versions introduced in the House in September have 100 co-sponsors combined.

title: Scoop: How the left’s dark money behemoth spent its millions
body_text:
FIRST IN PI —SIXTEEN THIRTY FUND SPENDS BIG: The left’s preeminent dark money hub dished out nearly $311 million in 2024 backing progressive causes like abortion and voting rights, climate change and more.

— As detailed in a new tax filing shared with PI, the spending was more than double what the nonprofit Sixteen Thirty Fund steered to liberal groups and causes a year prior. But that was less than its total in 2020, when the group’s all-time high of $410 million in outlays helped sweep Democrats to unified control of Washington.

— Though Democrats suffered “devastating” losses of the White House and Senate in 2024, Sixteen Thirty Fund President Amy Kurtz pointed to last week’s Democratic victories in the off-year elections as affirmation of her group’s work a year earlier.

—This month’s election was a moment of “both validation and motivation,” Kurtz wrote , adding that “progress is built over years, not cycles, and that sustained advocacy, not just electoral wins, drives enduring change.”

— Sixteen Thirty Fund’s massive spending last year was made possible by a fundraising haul of more than $282 million, tax filings show — an increase of over $100 million compared with 2023.

— As a 501(c)4 group, Sixteen Thirty Fund is not required to disclose its donors, though past donors have included the nonprofit led by Swiss billionaire Hansjörg Wyss as well as the philanthropic network started by megadonor George Soros . Even though the group has said it supports reforms — backed by many on the left — that would require more transparency into nonprofits, Sixteen Thirty Fund’s fundraising and spending prowess signals that opaque and deep-pocketed left-leaning political funding hubs aren’t going anywhere.

— More than 60 percent of Sixteen Thirty Fund’s revenues in 2024 came from just five benefactors who cut eight-figure checks to the group, including one who gave $58.9 million and another who gave $51.4 million, according to the filings.

— The fund reported pouring almost $63 million into super PACs and other groups for political purposes, in addition to dropping more than $15 million on Sixteen Thirty Fund’s own direct political spending. That included $6.7 million to Your Community PAC , a super PAC that became a major last-minute spender in support of former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic House and Senate candidates in red states.

— Sixteen Thirty Fund also gave to the main super PACs supporting House and Senate Democrats and the Harris campaign. Roughly another $2 million went to Retire Career Politicians and Civic Truth Action each, super PACs that spent heavily to boost the independent challenger to Nebraska GOP Sen. Deb Fischer as well as third-party presidential candidates that could’ve eaten into President Donald Trump ’s votes.

— The group’s single biggest expenditure by far was a nearly $28 million grant for the liberal voter registration and turnout coalition America Votes . Sixteen Thirty Fund also doled out tens of millions of dollars backing state ballot initiatives, including $14 million for an unsuccessful campaign to expand abortion rights in Florida and $6 million for a failed anti-gerrymandering push in Ohio.

— Other spending by Sixteen Thirty Fund remains unknown, thanks to its model of fiscal sponsorship. It allows the nonprofit to operate as an incubator for new political advocacy groups like Protect Our Care Action , which has pushed back on conservative health care policies; Galvanize Action , which seeks to juice civic engagement among moderate women in the suburbs and rural areas; and Paid Leave for All .

Happy Friday and welcome to PI. Any fun weekend plans? Drop us a line at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

FIRST IN PI — HPE MERGER FIGHT CONTINUES: A bipartisan group of six former state attorneys general has weighed in on the continuing saga of the Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper Networks merger. They sent a letter to Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser , urging him to abandon a multi-state legal effort that seeks to delay or potentially block court approval of the merger.

— “After reviewing the market share and national security facts surrounding the merger, we believe it is clear that the DOJ’s settlement represents a sound and balanced resolution — one that protects consumers and marketplace competition while strengthening the United States’ ability to compete globally,” the former attorneys general write in the letter .

— The letter is signed by three former Democratic AGs ( Andrew Ketterer of Maine, Michael Lilly of Hawaii and Oliver Koppell of New York) and three former Republican AGs ( Sean Reyes of Utah, Curtis Hill of Indiana and Dennis Vacco of New York).

— The Justice Department sued in January to block the $14 billion merger of the two tech companies, saying it would reduce competition in the commercial wireless network market. But in June, DOJ and HPE announced they had reached a settlement to allow the merger to proceed. Soon after, two antitrust division officials were fired and later spoke publicly against the settlement, accusing DOJ leaders of working with Trump-aligned lobbyists hired by HPE to negotiate a favorable settlement on the eve of trial.

— Amid the drama, attorneys general from 12 states plus D.C. submitted a motion to intervene in the case, asking a judge to carefully evaluate the proposed settlement and, if necessary, allow the states to oppose the merger in court. Weiser is leading the states’ effort.

— “Calling for further review of a benign case like this one could inadvertently create a precedent in which merger enforcement becomes politicized or increasingly subject to special-interest influence,” the former AGs caution Weiser in today’s letter. A hearing in the case is scheduled for Tuesday.

MORE MERGER MOVEMENT: Shareholders of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern voted today to approve a proposed $85 billion merger between the two railroads, Josh Funk reports for the Associated Press .

— The proposed merger remains subject to approval by the U.S. Surface Transportation Board, which is not expected to oppose the deal after President Donald Trump fired the only board member who objected to a separate railroad merger two years ago.

— Union Pacific has heavily invested in the success of the merger. The railroad spent more than $1 million on Washington lobbying efforts in Q3 alone and has also donated to Trump’s White House ballroom project. Despite strong initial opposition, the nation’s largest railworkers union blessed the deal earlier this month after securing guarantees that no member would lose their job as a result of the merger.

FAMILY BUSINESS: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s financial services firm, Cantor Fitzgerald , has enjoyed a year of record profitability after its former CEO joined the Trump administration, Todd Gillespie reports for Bloomberg .

— Now controlled by Lutnick’s 27- and 29-year-old sons, Brandon and Kyle, the firm is on track to earn more than $2.5 billion in revenue in 2025. But don’t say it’s because of the firm’s Washington connections, firm leaders tell Gillespie.

— As a 501(c)4 group, Sixteen Thirty Fund is not required to disclose its donors, though past donors have included the nonprofit led by Swiss billionaire Hansjörg Wyss as well as the philanthropic network started by megadonor George Soros. title: Why Big Business is shying away from the tariff legal fight
body_text:
SPOOKED SEASON: Major American companies have arguably the most to lose from President Donald Trump ’s tariffs. But they have largely stayed out of the legal fight challenging the levies , opting instead to quietly lobby against the policy for fear of angering a vindictive White House, your hosts report.

— Tomorrow, the Supreme Court will hear arguments in a case challenging the president’s use of a federal law called the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA, to set the tariffs.

— Small companies have led the way in filing legal challenges to the tariffs. But larger companies like those that populate the Dow Jones haven’t followed suit, blunting the prominence of the legal campaign against the administration, said John Vecchione , senior litigation counsel at the New Civil Liberties Alliance , a libertarian nonprofit that filed the first lawsuit against the tariffs.

— “It has been complete cowardice on the part of industry,” he said. “What about an alternate world where all the importers — all the Amazons, all the Walmarts, all the Targets — what if they had all said, ‘No, we’re not going to take this.’”

— The U.S. Chamber of Commerce opted against bringing its own case against Trump’s tariff powers, but the powerful business lobby filed an amicus brief with the Consumer Technology Association arguing that Trump lacks the power to impose the tariffs — joining a chorus of mostly smaller businesses and other legal or advocacy groups.

— While most business groups have remained on the sidelines of the legal fight, they continue to push back against the tariffs in less headline-grabbing ways. “We haven’t had the type of loud, aggressive lobbying you would have seen in past administrations, or on other issues, for obvious reasons. That doesn’t mean business hasn’t been engaged,” said one person familiar with trade association lobbying efforts on tariffs.

— “I’m trying to think of a more heavily lobbied issue this year, and I don’t know of one,” said Gary Shapiro , CTA’s president. But while Shapiro, whose organization has been among the most vocal critics of Trump’s tariffs from the beginning, said that there are many trade associations of the same mind downtown, “people are concerned about speaking out.”

— “I thought we’d have a lot more people on, who wanted to be on, but they had internal decision-making [and] decided they wouldn’t,” Shapiro said of the effort to recruit more names for the amicus brief. He declined to name any of the other groups who decided not to sign on. “We’ve seen a general quiet of people who generally speak” out on policy issues “since Jan. 20,” he added.

— That doesn’t mean the Trump administration hasn’t been open to hearing groups out. “The White House has been very open to having conversations with industry about tariff relief,” said Samir Kapadia , who leads the trade practice at the lobbying firm Vogel Group . “For those that think that that’s not possible, or happening, I think they’re misinformed.”

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI . Send tips. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

WHO’S BANKROLLING TRUMP’S OTHER TARIFF CRITICS: Though Trump has regularly faced off in court against liberal advocacy organizations, the Supreme Court tariff case “features a very different foe — a legal center funded without public disclosure by some of the country’s wealthiest conservatives ,” per The Washington Post ’s Cat Zakrzewski .

— Liberty Justice Center is a libertarian-leaning nonprofit that “ has previously challenged public-sector unions and sued to prevent the ban on TikTok from taking effect,” and is now helping pay the high-profile lawyers steering small businesses’ challenge to Trump’s tariff authorities.

— The group “does not disclose the names of its donors, but a Washington Post analysis of tax filings found that since 2020, it has received money from Donors Trust , the Walton Family Foundation and the Bradley Foundation , all of which have been prominent conservative donors.”

— Donors Trust in particular is a major conservative donor-advised fund referred to by critics as the “dark money ATM” of the right, and has frequently steered money to groups linked to conservative judicial activist Leonard Leo . “Liberty Justice Center is also listed as a national partner of the State Policy Network , a network of conservative nonprofit organizations with links to Charles and David Koch that also receives funding from Donors Trust,” the Post notes.

WHAT SHAPIRO’S WATCHING AT SCOTUS: Shapiro told PI he plans on trying to attend oral arguments for the tariff case tomorrow, and gave us a rundown of what he’ll be watching for during the proceedings, which he said are “the biggest issue before the court this year.”

— Shapiro is curious to see whether the government offers a “backup” position for why, even if IEEPA does not grant Trump the authority to issue the tariffs, “he somehow has power, has some other way in the Constitution” that gives him that authority. Shapiro will also be watching how the government frames Congress’ inaction on wresting back its authority to impose tariffs.

— “The government may argue there’s a check and balance as part of the law, and Congress has not chosen not to exercise it,” Shapiro said, though he argued that last week’s symbolic Senate votes to rebuke Trump’s tariffs could undermine that rationale. Another tea leaf Shapiro will be looking for is whether the so-called major questions doctrine comes up at all.

— But “the bigger question,” he argued, “because I’m so convinced that we’re going to win this case, is … what happens next?” CTA would like to see the justices stipulate that any tariff money paid by importers be returned “immediately,” with no strings attached or regulatory hoops to jump through.

— “If you’re asking that question at the Supreme Court tomorrow, that means you think there’s a good chance that” the tariffs will be struck down, Shapiro said. “So if there are a lot of questions about that, I’d be pretty excited.”

ALCOHOL GROUPS BACK HEMP FIX: The country’s leading alcohol industry groups are throwing their support behind a congressional fix for a regulatory hemp “loophole” created by the 2018 farm bill.

— “We write to align our respective organizations with 39 state Attorneys General in calling for a federal legislative solution to address the proliferation of unregulated intoxicating hemp products,” the heads of the American Distilled Spirits Alliance , Distilled Spirits Council of the U.S. , the Wine Institute , the Beer Institute and Wine America wrote to congressional leadership today.

— The trade groups bemoaned claims by some entities, “including some within the beverage alcohol space,” that “any effort to rein in the sale of highly intoxicating hemp THC products is tantamount to ‘prohibition’ or a ‘ban’ that will adversely impact industrial hemp farmers or even products that contain non-intoxicating cannabidiol (CBD).”

— They pointed to last month’s letter by state AGs, which the alcohol groups note refuted such assertions. The letter comes as lawmakers have been pushing for the inclusion of a hemp crackdown as the GOP tries to push through several minibus spending bills during the shutdown.

— But Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) has blocked the package from moving forward over the hemp language, arguing that the proposals he’s seen would decimate the Kentucky-centric hemp industry.

SPECIALTY STREAMERS LINK UP: More than a dozen specialty streaming services from around the globe have formed a new advocacy group aimed at giving the sector a voice in global debates about regulation in the streaming era.

— Beyond Mainstream: A Global Streaming Alliance is comprised of streamers like AMC Networks -owned Acorn TV , ALLBLK , HIDIVE , Shudder and Sundance Now ; Crunchyroll , NDM+ , OUTtv , Pure Flix , Rakuten -owned Viki , the Roku Channel , Sony -owned Liv and One ; Fox Corporation -owned Tubi and Zee5 .

— Major streaming platforms like Netflix , Paramount+ , Warner Bros. Discovery ‘s Max , NBC ‘s Peacock and Disney launched their own trade group , along with several smaller streamers, in 2023. They organized amid debates over how and whether to update media regulations to reflect the decline of cable and traditional media and the shift over to streaming.

IN MEMORIAM: The lobbying industry was among those mourning the death of former Vice President Dick Cheney today.

— “‘The Boss’ as we fondly called him was a soft-spoken, decent and good man who had fiercely-held beliefs,” Cesar Conda , a founding principal at Navigators Global who served as Cheney’s chief domestic and economic policy adviser in the White House, wrote on LinkedIn .

Why Big Business is shying away from the tariff legal fight

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

11/04/2025 06:46 PM EST

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

SPOOKED SEASON: Major American companies have arguably the most to lose from President Donald Trump’s tariffs. But they have largely stayed out of the legal fight challenging the levies, opting instead to quietly lobby against the policy for fear of angering a vindictive White House, your hosts report.

— Tomorrow, the Supreme Court will hear arguments in a case challenging the president’s use of a federal law called the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA, to set the tariffs.

— Small companies have led the way in filing legal challenges to the tariffs. But larger companies like those that populate the Dow Jones haven’t followed suit, blunting the prominence of the legal campaign against the administration, said John Vecchione, senior litigation counsel at the New Civil Liberties Alliance, a libertarian nonprofit that filed the first lawsuit against the tariffs.

— “It has been complete cowardice on the part of industry,” he said. “What about an alternate world where all the importers — all the Amazons, all the Walmarts, all the Targets — what if they had all said, ‘No, we’re not going to take this.’”

— The U.S. Chamber of Commerce opted against bringing its own case against Trump’s tariff powers, but the powerful business lobby filed an amicus brief with the Consumer Technology Association arguing that Trump lacks the power to impose the tariffs — joining a chorus of mostly smaller businesses and other legal or advocacy groups.

— While most business groups have remained on the sidelines of the legal fight, they continue to push back against the tariffs in less headline-grabbing ways. “We haven’t had the type of loud, aggressive lobbying you would have seen in past administrations, or on other issues, for obvious reasons. That doesn’t mean business hasn’t been engaged,” said one person familiar with trade association lobbying efforts on tariffs.

— “I’m trying to think of a more heavily lobbied issue this year, and I don’t know of one,” said Gary Shapiro, CTA’s president. But while Shapiro, whose organization has been among the most vocal critics of Trump’s tariffs from the beginning, said that there are many trade associations of the same mind downtown, “people are concerned about speaking out.”

— “I thought we’d have a lot more people on, who wanted to be on, but they had internal decision-making [and] decided they wouldn’t,” Shapiro said of the effort to recruit more names for the amicus brief. He declined to name any of the other groups who decided not to sign on. “We’ve seen a general quiet of people who generally speak” out on policy issues “since Jan. 20,” he added.

— That doesn’t mean the Trump administration hasn’t been open to hearing groups out. “The White House has been very open to having conversations with industry about tariff relief,” said Samir Kapadia, who leads the trade practice at the lobbying firm Vogel Group. “For those that think that that’s not possible, or happening, I think they’re misinformed.”

WHO’S BANKROLLING TRUMP’S OTHER TARIFF CRITICS: Though Trump has regularly faced off in court against liberal advocacy organizations, the Supreme Court tariff case “features a very different foe — a legal center funded without public disclosure by some of the country’s wealthiest conservatives,” per The Washington Post’s Cat Zakrzewski.

— Liberty Justice Center is a libertarian-leaning nonprofit that “has previously challenged public-sector unions and sued to prevent the ban on TikTok from taking effect,” and is now helping pay the high-profile lawyers steering small businesses’ challenge to Trump’s tariff authorities.

— The group “does not disclose the names of its donors, but a Washington Post analysis of tax filings found that since 2020, it has received money from Donors Trust, the Walton Family Foundation and the Bradley Foundation, all of which have been prominent conservative donors.”

— Donors Trust in particular is a major conservative donor-advised fund referred to by critics as the “dark money ATM” of the right, and has frequently steered money to groups linked to conservative judicial activist Leonard Leo. “Liberty Justice Center is also listed as a national partner of the State Policy Network, a network of conservative nonprofit organizations with links to Charles and David Koch that also receives funding from Donors Trust,” the Post notes.

WHAT SHAPIRO’S WATCHING AT SCOTUS: Shapiro told PI he plans on trying to attend oral arguments for the tariff case tomorrow, and gave us a rundown of what he’ll be watching for during the proceedings, which he said are “the biggest issue before the court this year.”

— Shapiro is curious to see whether the government offers a “backup” position for why, even if IEEPA does not grant Trump the authority to issue the tariffs, “he somehow has power, has some other way in the Constitution” that gives him that authority. Shapiro will also be watching how the government frames Congress’ inaction on wresting back its authority to impose tariffs.

— “The government may argue there’s a check and balance as part of the law, and Congress has not chosen not to exercise it,” Shapiro said, though he argued that last week’s symbolic Senate votes to rebuke Trump’s tariffs could undermine that rationale. Another tea leaf Shapiro will be looking for is whether the so-called major questions doctrine comes up at all.

— But “the bigger question,” he argued, “because I’m so convinced that we’re going to win this case, is … what happens next?” CTA would like to see the justices stipulate that any tariff money paid by importers be returned “immediately,” with no strings attached or regulatory hoops to jump through.

— “If you’re asking that question at the Supreme Court tomorrow, that means you think there’s a good chance that” the tariffs will be struck down, Shapiro said. “So if there are a lot of questions about that, I’d be pretty excited.”

ALCOHOL GROUPS BACK HEMP FIX: The country’s leading alcohol industry groups are throwing their support behind a congressional fix for a regulatory hemp “loophole” created by the 2018 farm bill.

— “We write to align our respective organizations with 39 state Attorneys General in calling for a federal legislative solution to address the proliferation of unregulated intoxicating hemp products,” the heads of the American Distilled Spirits Alliance, Distilled Spirits Council of the U.S., the Wine Institute, the Beer Institute and Wine America wrote to congressional leadership today.

— The trade groups bemoaned claims by some entities, “including some within the beverage alcohol space,” that “any effort to rein in the sale of highly intoxicating hemp THC products is tantamount to ‘prohibition’ or a ‘ban’ that will adversely impact industrial hemp farmers or even products that contain non-intoxicating cannabidiol (CBD).”

— They pointed to last month’s letter by state AGs, which the alcohol groups note refuted such assertions. The letter comes as lawmakers have been pushing for the inclusion of a hemp crackdown as the GOP tries to push through several minibus spending bills during the shutdown.

— But Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) has blocked the package from moving forward over the hemp language, arguing that the proposals he’s seen would decimate the Kentucky-centric hemp industry.

SPECIALTY STREAMERS LINK UP: More than a dozen specialty streaming services from around the globe have formed a new advocacy group aimed at giving the sector a voice in global debates about regulation in the streaming era.

— Beyond Mainstream: A Global Streaming Alliance is comprised of streamers like AMC Networks-owned Acorn TV, ALLBLK, HIDIVE, Shudder and Sundance Now; Crunchyroll, NDM+, OUTtv, Pure Flix, Rakuten-owned Viki, the Roku Channel, Sony-owned Liv and One; Fox Corporation-owned Tubi and Zee5.

— Major streaming platforms like Netflix, Paramount+, Warner Bros. Discovery‘s Max, NBC‘s Peacock and Disney launched their own trade group, along with several smaller streamers, in 2023. They organized amid debates over how and whether to update media regulations to reflect the decline of cable and traditional media and the shift over to streaming.

IN MEMORIAM: The lobbying industry was among those mourning the death of former Vice President Dick Cheney today.

— “‘The Boss’ as we fondly called him was a soft-spoken, decent and good man who had fiercely-held beliefs,” Cesar Conda, a founding principal at Navigators Global who served as Cheney’s chief domestic and economic policy adviser in the White House, wrote on LinkedIn.

title: GOP tax hand decamps for K Street
body_text:
BGR SCOOPS UP SMITH TAX AIDE: Kathryn Reed , a top GOP tax aide who helped craft congressional Republicans’ sweeping tax cuts earlier this year, has decamped from the Hill after nearly a decade to join BGR Group as a vice president in the tax, commerce and financial services practices.

— Reed has spent the past four years as a tax adviser to Rep. Jason Smith (R-Mo.), who became chair of the Ways and Means Committee in 2023. Before that, she worked for former Rep. Kevin Brady (R-Texas), Smith’s predecessor on the powerful tax writing panel.

— In a statement provided by the firm, Smith called Reed “integral” to the drafting of the GOP megabill’s tax provisions, which permanently extended a slew of tax cuts prized by the business community while overhauling key safety net programs and winding down clean energy tax incentives.

— Reed worked particularly closely on the bill’s new initiative to set up investment accounts for children as well as its expansion of the Opportunity Zones program and Child Tax Credit, she said in an interview.

— The child investment plan has set off a scramble by lobbyists seeking to shape the new program. Reed noted that other new tax programs in the law, such as no tax on tips, will also require new guidance from regulators — in contrast to tax breaks with existing regulatory guidance that were extended by the law.

— Beyond that, Reed told PI that her position provided insight into the issues and priorities that animate a broad swath of members on the Hill. Having that kind of “insider scoop on where Congress is on policy,” especially when it comes to tax, will be “super helpful and beneficial to BGR,” she predicted.

— Reed is just the latest staffer who worked on the reconciliation bill to head downtown since it became law in July. Brett Horton , who served for the past decade as chief of staff to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise , will start next month as the top lobbyist at the American Hotel & Lodging Association . Andrew Siracuse , a longtime aide and tax adviser for Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), joined Holland & Knight in August.

— Molly Fromm , who served as Ways and Means’ general counsel and parliamentarian under both Smith and Brady, joined the health policy-heavy firm Nickles Group in May, around the same time the GOP megabill cleared the House.

— Vivek Chandrasekhar , who provided guidance on the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill and Democrats’ Inflation Reduction Act while working in Treasury’s Office of Tax Policy, joined the law and lobbying firm Perkins Coie in September as a partner in the tax and environment, energy and resources practices.

FDA ALUM TO LEAD POLICY AT HIMS & HERS: Hims & Hers continues to expand its Washington footprint, tapping former FDA deputy commissioner Deb Autor to be the telehealth company’s first chief policy officer. Autor worked at FDA for 12 years, including serving as deputy commissioner for global regulatory operations and policy during the Obama administration, and also represented the agency as a trial attorney at DOJ.

— Autor went on to serve as a consultant in the private sector, holding public policy roles with drugmakers like AstraZeneca and Mylan .

— She joined the board of Hims & Hers last year, and takes over as head of its global influence operation as the company comes under scrutiny for its advertising practices and readjusts is business model regarding popular weight-loss drugs. Regulators are moving to crack down on sales of cheaper, compounded versions of name brand drugs.

— Hims & Hers has ramped up its influence machine over the last two years, going from $310,000 in federal lobbying expenditures in 2024 to $860,000 through the first three quarters of 2025. The company also launched a PAC last summer, and donated $1 million to President Donald Trump ’s inauguration earlier this year.

GET THE PICTURE?: “For select House of Representatives committee chairs, a decidedly artistic perk for their legislative service is a custom-made portrait, created by an artist of their choosing in coordination with the U.S. Capitol Historical Society . These paintings adorn the walls of congressional hearing rooms and are destined to hang for perpetuity inside the Capitol” — and they’re “also a magnet for lobbyists and special interest money ,” NOTUS ’ Dave Levinthal writes.

— “This decade, corporations, unions, trade associations and individual lobbyists with significant business before Congress have poured more than $600,000 into portrait funds for several current and former federal lawmakers.” The congressional portrait funds are governed by few rules, and the only entities required to disclose their donations are registered lobbyists or the entities that employ them.

— Brady, the former Ways and Means chair, “is among the most popular beneficiaries of lobbyist money directed toward his portrait, painted by the artist Stephen Craighead and unveiled in 2022.” Some $132,500 from companies, trade groups, PACs and individual lobbyists were donated ahead of its unveiling.

— The portrait fund for his Democratic successor, Massachusetts Rep. Richie Neal , has received $128,000 in contributions since 2023 from organizations including MetLife , MGM Resorts , HCA Healthcare , Altria and FedEx — though a spokesperson told NOTUS that Neal “has no idea who donated” to his portrait fund.

INSURANCE POLICY: “Insurers and drug companies facing dire threats to their bottom lines this year from President Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress had to make a choice: Stand and fight, or go to ground and cut some deals. Insurers fought in a bid to kill the threat; drugmakers cut deals to mitigate the damage. The early results are revealing,” per POLITICO ’s Amanda Chu .

— “Trump this month called out the ‘money sucking Insurance Companies’ on Truth Social and pledged to redirect their Obamacare funding to patients. Two days before, he stood with drug companies that’d agreed to cut prices, called the CEOs ‘great talented people’ and friends and said he didn’t begrudge them their profits: ‘They’re entitled to the money because the companies are doing very well.’”

— “Insurers’ prospects of getting what they want – an extension of expiring Obamacare subsidies Democrats supersized during the pandemic – look bleak. Meanwhile, the 100 percent tariffs Trump threatened pharma with are still on hold, pending more deals.”

— “Trump’s diverging take on two of Washington’s most powerful industry rivals was a case study for lobbyists trying to figure out how to handle the mercurial president and his populist approach to politics: Currying favor helps, fighting is risky business.”

HERITAGE TURMOIL AIN’T OVER: Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts ’ video defending Tucker Carlson for his interview with Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes has continued to roil the venerated think tank. Longtime board member Robert P. George is just the latest to announce his resignation over the incident.

— In a Facebook post today, George “said he can no longer remain part of the foundation without a ‘full retraction’ of the video released last month ” by Roberts, POLITICO ’s Cheyanne M. Daniels reports.

— “Although Kevin publicly apologized for some of what he said in the video, he could not offer a full retraction of its content. So, we reached an impasse,” George wrote, one day after Trump defended Carlson to reporters.

— Roberts tried to contain the backlash over his video by downplaying his knowledge of Fuentes and pinning blame on his chief of staff, who has since resigned. At least five members of the think tank’s antisemitism task force have quit in protest of the post , CBS News reported, along with prominent conservative economist Stephen Moore .

CHAMBER OF PROGRESS EYES STATEHOUSES: Liberal-leaning tech lobbying group Chamber of Progress is launching a new influence initiative to shape how Democratic statehouses approach AI regulation.

— The group’s new State AI Leadership Project, or SAIL, is in large part a response to the recent flood of state legislation related to AI — itself a function of the deepening tech-policy paralysis in Washington. “We, just like many other organizations, are supportive of a federal framework, but it’s very clear states are not waiting,” said Koustubh “K.J.” Bagchi , head of U.S. policy and government relations at Chamber of Progress and leader of the new initiative.

— Bagchi said SAIL will push back against AI “doomerism” and “pessimism” by promoting tech-friendly bills in blue states; encouraging AI adoption by state governments; and advancing policies that promote the increased energy production needed to power new data centers.

— Chamber of Progress is funded by AI industry heavyweights like Google , Andreessen Horowitz and Nvidia — companies that have all worked to limit the political influence of individuals and organizations worried about AI risks. The group’s new SAIL initiative aims to extend that work into blue states, where legislators have recently advanced bills that would impose new safety frameworks and other restrictions on the technology.

BGR SCOOPS UP SMITH TAX AIDE: Kathryn Reed, a top GOP tax aide who helped craft congressional Republicans’ sweeping tax cuts earlier this year, has decamped from the Hill after nearly a decade to join BGR Group as a vice president in the tax, commerce and financial services practices.

— Reed has spent the past four years as a tax adviser to Rep. Jason Smith (R-Mo.), who became chair of the Ways and Means Committee in 2023. Before that, she worked for former Rep. Kevin Brady (R-Texas), Smith’s predecessor on the powerful tax writing panel.

— In a statement provided by the firm, Smith called Reed “integral” to the drafting of the GOP megabill’s tax provisions, which permanently extended a slew of tax cuts prized by the business community while overhauling key safety net programs and winding down clean energy tax incentives.

— Reed worked particularly closely on the bill’s new initiative to set up investment accounts for children as well as its expansion of the Opportunity Zones program and Child Tax Credit, she said in an interview.

— The child investment plan has set off a scramble by lobbyists seeking to shape the new program. Reed noted that other new tax programs in the law, such as no tax on tips, will also require new guidance from regulators — in contrast to tax breaks with existing regulatory guidance that were extended by the law.

— Beyond that, Reed told PI that her position provided insight into the issues and priorities that animate a broad swath of members on the Hill. Having that kind of “insider scoop on where Congress is on policy,” especially when it comes to tax, will be “super helpful and beneficial to BGR,” she predicted.

— Reed is just the latest staffer who worked on the reconciliation bill to head downtown since it became law in July. Brett Horton, who served for the past decade as chief of staff to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, will start next month as the top lobbyist at the American Hotel & Lodging Association. Andrew Siracuse, a longtime aide and tax adviser for Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), joined Holland & Knight in August.

— Molly Fromm, who served as Ways and Means’ general counsel and parliamentarian under both Smith and Brady, joined the health policy-heavy firm Nickles Group in May, around the same time the GOP megabill cleared the House.

— Vivek Chandrasekhar, who provided guidance on the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill and Democrats’ Inflation Reduction Act while working in Treasury’s Office of Tax Policy, joined the law and lobbying firm Perkins Coie in September as a partner in the tax and environment, energy and resources practices.

FDA ALUM TO LEAD POLICY AT HIMS & HERS: Hims & Hers continues to expand its Washington footprint, tapping former FDA deputy commissioner Deb Autor to be the telehealth company’s first chief policy officer. Autor worked at FDA for 12 years, including serving as deputy commissioner for global regulatory operations and policy during the Obama administration, and also represented the agency as a trial attorney at DOJ.

— Autor went on to serve as a consultant in the private sector, holding public policy roles with drugmakers like AstraZeneca and Mylan.

— She joined the board of Hims & Hers last year, and takes over as head of its global influence operation as the company comes under scrutiny for its advertising practices and readjusts is business model regarding popular weight-loss drugs. Regulators are moving to crack down on sales of cheaper, compounded versions of name brand drugs.

— Hims & Hers has ramped up its influence machine over the last two years, going from $310,000 in federal lobbying expenditures in 2024 to $860,000 through the first three quarters of 2025. The company also launched a PAC last summer, and donated $1 million to President Donald Trump’s inauguration earlier this year.

GET THE PICTURE?: “For select House of Representatives committee chairs, a decidedly artistic perk for their legislative service is a custom-made portrait, created by an artist of their choosing in coordination with the U.S. Capitol Historical Society. These paintings adorn the walls of congressional hearing rooms and are destined to hang for perpetuity inside the Capitol” — and they’re “also a magnet for lobbyists and special interest money,” NOTUS’ Dave Levinthal writes.

— “This decade, corporations, unions, trade associations and individual lobbyists with significant business before Congress have poured more than $600,000 into portrait funds for several current and former federal lawmakers.” The congressional portrait funds are governed by few rules, and the only entities required to disclose their donations are registered lobbyists or the entities that employ them.

— Brady, the former Ways and Means chair, “is among the most popular beneficiaries of lobbyist money directed toward his portrait, painted by the artist Stephen Craighead and unveiled in 2022.” Some $132,500 from companies, trade groups, PACs and individual lobbyists were donated ahead of its unveiling.

— The portrait fund for his Democratic successor, Massachusetts Rep. Richie Neal, has received $128,000 in contributions since 2023 from organizations including MetLife, MGM Resorts, HCA Healthcare, Altria and FedEx — though a spokesperson told NOTUS that Neal “has no idea who donated” to his portrait fund.

Insurers fought in a bid to kill the threat; drugmakers cut deals to mitigate the damage. The early results are revealing,” per POLITICO’s Amanda Chu.

— “Trump this month called out the ‘money sucking Insurance Companies’ on Truth Social and pledged to redirect their Obamacare funding to patients. Two days before, he stood with drug companies that’d agreed to cut prices, called the CEOs ‘great talented people’ and friends and said he didn’t begrudge them their profits: ‘They’re entitled to the money because the companies are doing very well.’”

— “Insurers’ prospects of getting what they want – an extension of expiring Obamacare subsidies Democrats supersized during the pandemic – look bleak. Meanwhile, the 100 percent tariffs Trump threatened pharma with are still on hold, pending more deals.”

— “Trump’s diverging take on two of Washington’s most powerful industry rivals was a case study for lobbyists trying to figure out how to handle the mercurial president and his populist approach to politics: Currying favor helps, fighting is risky business.”

HERITAGE TURMOIL AIN’T OVER: Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts’ video defending Tucker Carlson for his interview with Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes has continued to roil the venerated think tank. Longtime board member Robert P. George is just the latest to announce his resignation over the incident.

— In a Facebook post today, George “said he can no longer remain part of the foundation without a ‘full retraction’ of the video released last month” by Roberts, POLITICO’s Cheyanne M. Daniels reports.

— “Although Kevin publicly apologized for some of what he said in the video, he could not offer a full retraction of its content. So, we reached an impasse,” George wrote, one day after Trump defended Carlson to reporters.

— Roberts tried to contain the backlash over his video by downplaying his knowledge of Fuentes and pinning blame on his chief of staff, who has since resigned. MAKING MOVES: Paramount Skydance Corporation , the entity formed by one of the most high-profile media acquisitions of the second Trump administration, has made its first outside lobbying hire as the deal faces scrutiny on Capitol Hill. Paramount Skydance retained Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck at the beginning of October to provide work on tax and competition issues, according to a disclosure filing.

— Nadeam Elshami , who isn’t working on the account but who co-leads Brownstein’s lobbying practice, told PI that tax issues could come up as part of a future reconciliation bill. The entertainment industry is also staring down the expiration this year of a prized domestic production tax incentive.

— Among those who are working on the account are Democratic lobbyists Al Mottur , Alice Lugo and Andrew Usyk , Republican Greta Joynes and competition experts Will Moschella and Allen Grunes .

— Last week, a pair of House Democrats accused the new company of “stonewalling congressional oversight” of the $8 billion deal. It was approved by regulators only after Paramount-owned CBS News agreed to pay $16 million to settle a lawsuit filed by President Donald Trump , appoint an ombudsman at the network to eliminate “bias” against the president, and nix diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. Trump also said at the time that the company had agreed to provide millions more in free advertising or PSAs.

— In a letter to Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison Wednesday, House Energy & Commerce ranking member Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) and House Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) rebuked the company’s “inadequate and incomplete response” to an August letter seeking documents about the merger.

— “Given the lack of meaningful responses to our requests, your letter calls into question whether your company intends to cooperate with our investigation,” they wrote.

— Paramount already had a half-dozen outside lobbying firms on retainer before the merger, including FGS Global , Ballard Partners , Capitol Tax Partners and Capitol Counsel . Meanwhile Ellison’s Skydance Media retained Convergence Strategies last year to lobby for the merger’s approval. That contract was terminated last month, disclosures show.

Micah Ketchel , who was most recently a senior adviser in the State Department’s Bureau of International Organization Affairs, is joining the firm as a partner.

— Before moving to State earlier this year, Ketchel was chief of staff to former national security adviser Mike Waltz when Waltz was in the House. Ketchel followed Waltz to the White House, where he served as a senior adviser on the National Security Council.

— At Ballard, he’ll help the firm capitalize on Trump’s interest in striking deals related to the production of critical minerals across the globe — part of an effort to undercut Chinese dominance of the global supply chain for the minerals. In a statement, Brian Ballard called the scramble for critical minerals “one of the most defining national security and economic challenges of our time.”

RETAIL’S OTHER FIGHTS: Tariffs and swipe fees aren’t the only issues dominating the retail industry’s advocacy agenda this year. The National Retail Federation is flying in today with around two dozen tax executives from the grocery, restaurant and retail sectors to press for an extension of the Work Opportunity Tax Credit, which provides incentives to companies that hire people who’ve had trouble finding a job due to things like felony convictions.

— The tax credit, which has bipartisan support, failed to make it into Republicans’ megabill this summer. But it would be an ideal candidate for any end-of-year tax extenders package, its proponents say. NRF’s delegation was expected to meet with Senate Majority Leader John Thune , Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Reps. Blake Moore (R-Utah), Kevin Hern (R-Okla.) and Adrian Smith (R-Neb.), along with senior staff from the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees.

— Nearly 100 business groups and retail and shipping giants, meanwhile, wrote to congressional leadership this morning calling for the passage of legislation to tackle organized retail crime.

— “As we approach peak retail and shipping season, the need for stronger tools to combat ORC remains urgent,” the coalition wrote, arguing that passage of the Combatting Organized Retail Crime Act would provide much-needed coordination between various branches of law enforcement and bolster investigative tools.

The night before, he’d told a ballroom of supporters in West Palm Beach, Florida, that he had held his last political rally—’Can you believe it?’—and was ready to focus on governing. But his message to O’Rourke after the break of dawn was different. ‘I want you to keep going,’ he told her,” The Atlantic ’s Michael Scherer and Ashley Parker report.

— “By August, Trump estimated that he had collected at least $1.5 billion since the election, more than all the money raised to support his 2024 campaign over two years, including funds raised by supportive independent super PACs. The tally is now approaching $2 billion, two people familiar with the effort — who, like others, were not authorized to speak publicly — told us.”
