BALLROOM BLITZ: A trio of Senate Democrats want more information about the lobbyists reportedly helping raise money for President Donald Trump ’s White House ballroom project from corporate America and other donors with business before Trump’s administration.

— In letters to Ballard Partners ’ Brian Ballard , Miller Strategies ’ Jeff Miller and Michael Best Strategies ’ Reince Priebus , the lawmakers request that the Trump-tied lobbyists turn over documents and respond to a slew of questions outlining their role in the ballroom fundraising project. Those include how and when the lobbyists got involved; the donors from whom lobbyists have solicited donations; whether the lobbyists received any guidance about who they should or shouldn’t raise money from; and whether a contribution was intended to be made anonymously.

— Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) demanded to know whether the firms in question “made any representations that the prospective donor would be more likely to secure favorable action from the federal government if it made a donation” or offered anything in exchange for donations or pledges, such as access to administration officials or invites to White House events. The senators posed similar questions to Meredith O’Rourke , Trump’s primary fundraiser.

— The inquiry follows reports that Ballard and Miller —both top Trump fundraisers — and Priebus, Trump’s first White House chief of staff, have been among those heavily involved in fundraising for the ballroom.

— An analysis out today from the watchdog group Public Citizen found that of the known corporate donors to the ballroom project, two-thirds are clients of at least one of the three firms the senators reached out to. Several donors retain two of the three firms, including Palantir (Ballard and Miller) Hard Rock International (Ballard and Michael Best) and Ripple (Ballard and Michael Best).

— Ballard and Priebus declined to comment, while Miller and O’Rourke did not respond to requests for comment.

— Blumenthal, Warren and Schiff also point to an earlier analysis from Public Citizen that found corporate ballroom donors had been awarded $279 billion in government contracts in the last five years. Meanwhile, more than half of the disclosed donors are either currently facing enforcement actions from the federal government or had enforcement actions paused by Trump, according to the analysis.

— The senators requested a response from the lobbyists and O’Rourke by the first week of December.

title: Anthropic’s hiring spree
body_text:
ANTHROPIC LOBBIES UP: The hiring spree kicked off by artificial intelligence startup Anthropic last year isn’t letting up. The maker of the AI chatbot Claude — which has been relatively outspoken about its desire for federal guardrails for the industry and hasn’t shied away from criticizing the Trump administration — has brought on three new outside lobbying firms since the beginning of December, according to newly filed disclosures.

— Thorn Run Partners began lobbying on AI safety initiatives for Anthropic at the start of December, while Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid began working for the company a few weeks later on issues related to the safety, development and use of AI. Avenue Solutions began lobbying for the startup on general AI issues at the beginning of the month, disclosures show.

— Anthropic’s outside lobbying roster has more than tripled in the past year. Since 2023 retained just two outside firms — Aquia Group and Tower 19 . Anthropic registered its first in-house lobbyist in 2024, but the company retained Continental Strategy in April and then Fierce Government Relations in November.

— While Anthropic has yet to disclose its lobbying outlays for the final three months of 2025, the AI firm cracked $1 million in expenditures for the first time in Q3, outstripping ChatGPT maker OpenAI but still lagging other tech giants involved in the AI race such as Meta and Amazon .

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Here’s a few more new registrations that caught our eye in the pre-deadline filing deluge: Indiana federal affairs manager Robert Ordway registered to represent the Hoosier State in D.C. beginning on Dec. 15 — days after GOP legislators there rejected the White House’s redistricting push , defying President Donald Trump and his threats to withhold federal funding for the state. Gov. Mike Braun ’s office previously retained Tillotson Advisors to lobby for the state, but that contract ended in August, disclosures show.

— The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association , which represents pharmacy benefit managers, hired antitrust lobbyist Joseph Gibson of the Gibson Group to work on competition issues related to PBMs. The online prediction market Kalshi retained Matthew McNally and Curtis Doster of Intersection back in November, and conservative cable news company Newsmax brought on David Bockorny last month to lobby on the TV ownership cap.

DEPT. OF ODD BEDFELLOWS: “ Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s demonization of food and pharma has put the Trump administration on the wrong side of its traditional allies in industry — but opened a path to a new alliance with a longtime GOP nemesis: lawyers representing consumers who say they were harmed by companies,” POLITICO ’s Amanda Chu writes.

— “Kennedy’s moves, from his disparagement of Tylenol and ultraprocessed food to his broadsides against vaccines, have lawyers who assemble aggrieved plaintiffs to sue deep-pocketed companies envisioning the sort of cases that turn attorneys into Hollywood heroes and billionaires.”

— “Lawyers behind major settlements against companies told POLITICO that Kennedy’s sweeping anti-corporate agenda targeting food, chemical and pharmaceutical companies, along with rising public skepticism of industry, is creating a tailwind for the tort system to take on corporate power” and setting off a reckoning for business groups that have long leaned on GOP allies to push tort reforms to rein in litigation and cap damages.

DAVOS BEWARE: “The Trump administration’s main event venue in Davos was targeted by scammers who have sold billionaires fraudulent tickets to access USA House,” Bloomberg ’s Jenny Leonard reports. “In a post on the venue’s website, the organizers warned against the purchase of so-called VIP access packages and said the fraudulent sales appear to be widespread this year.”

INVARIANT ADDS TELECOM LOBBYIST: Jason Goldman has joined Invariant as a principal in the firm’s technology and competition practice. Goldman spent the past six years at the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, most recently as the agency’s acting director of congressional affairs.

— Before that, Goldman handled external affairs and stakeholder engagement at the Intelligent Transportation Society of America , and spent more than a decade working on telecom policy at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce .

ANNALS OF THE REVOLVING DOOR: “Environmental Protection Agency ethics officials have interpreted impartiality guidelines in a way that has allowed several former industry insiders to oversee dramatic changes to chemical regulations,” per The Washington Post ’s Amudalat Ajasa .

— “Those ethics decisions have cleared the way for a former agriculture lobbyist to help reinstate a pesticide that had been banned twice by federal courts, as well as for two former chemical industry executives to help reassess the agency’s stance on the dangers of formaldehyde.”

— “Internal emails and documents obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity and shared with The Washington Post show EPA ethics officials determined that Kyle Kunkler ’s recent lobbying on behalf of the American Soybean Association did not require his recusal from pesticide regulation, including decisions about dicamba, a pesticide that soybean farmers have wanted to see reinstated.”

— “According to federal loss-of-impartiality regulations, new government employees are supposed to have a year-long ‘cooling-off period’ on matters that directly involve their previous employer, unless given written authorization by the ethics office.”

GET OUT OF JAIL (NOT SO FREE) CARD: “Convicted armed robber Yener Vahit Belli , the ‘Hoodie Bandit,’ is slated to serve a dozen years more in federal prison to pay off his societal debt for brandishing a firearm and terrorizing patrons while robbing two convenience stores of several hundred dollars, 61 Florida Lottery tickets and a pack of smokes,” per NOTUS ’ Dave Levinthal .

— “But now — taking cues from the likes of corrupt congressmen, felonious rappers, scofflaw CEOs and money laundering cryptocurrency titans — Belli’s family has hired a registered federal lobbyist to help petition President Donald Trump for a pardon.”

— “Some lobbyists have earned five- and six-figure paydays in recent months petitioning Trump’s government for client pardons, creating a presidential pardon influence economy that puts a premium on personal connections and simply didn’t exist until recently.”

— “Belli’s pardon lobbyist, according to a new federal record, is Mike Beltran , an attorney based in Trump’s home state of Florida who previously served as a Republican in the Florida House of Representatives and has attended recent Trump events, including the president’s 2025 inauguration.”

— The Color Pigments Manufacturers Association has tapped Robert F. Helminiak as its next executive director. Helminiak most recently served as vice president of legal and government relations at the Society of Chemical Manufacturers & Affiliates .

Kurland was most recently acting principal deputy assistant secretary for strategic trade and technology security in Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security.

Anthropic’s hiring spree

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

01/20/2026 07:48 PM EST

Presented by

With help from Daniel Lippman

ANTHROPIC LOBBIES UP: The hiring spree kicked off by artificial intelligence startup Anthropic last year isn’t letting up. The maker of the AI chatbot Claude — which has been relatively outspoken about its desire for federal guardrails for the industry and hasn’t shied away from criticizing the Trump administration — has brought on three new outside lobbying firms since the beginning of December, according to newly filed disclosures.

— Thorn Run Partners began lobbying on AI safety initiatives for Anthropic at the start of December, while Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid began working for the company a few weeks later on issues related to the safety, development and use of AI. Avenue Solutions began lobbying for the startup on general AI issues at the beginning of the month, disclosures show.

— Anthropic’s outside lobbying roster has more than tripled in the past year. Since 2023 retained just two outside firms — Aquia Group and Tower 19. Anthropic registered its first in-house lobbyist in 2024, but the company retained Continental Strategy in April and then Fierce Government Relations in November.

— While Anthropic has yet to disclose its lobbying outlays for the final three months of 2025, the AI firm cracked $1 million in expenditures for the first time in Q3, outstripping ChatGPT maker OpenAI but still lagging other tech giants involved in the AI race such as Meta and Amazon.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Here’s a few more new registrations that caught our eye in the pre-deadline filing deluge: Indiana federal affairs manager Robert Ordway registered to represent the Hoosier State in D.C. beginning on Dec. 15 — days after GOP legislators there rejected the White House’s redistricting push, defying President Donald Trump and his threats to withhold federal funding for the state. Gov. Mike Braun’s office previously retained Tillotson Advisors to lobby for the state, but that contract ended in August, disclosures show.

— The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, which represents pharmacy benefit managers, hired antitrust lobbyist Joseph Gibson of the Gibson Group to work on competition issues related to PBMs. The online prediction market Kalshi retained Matthew McNally and Curtis Doster of Intersection back in November, and conservative cable news company Newsmax brought on David Bockorny last month to lobby on the TV ownership cap.

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI. What are you watching for in tonight’s filing deadline? Reach out: You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com. Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com. Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns.

POLITICO Forecast

In a fragmented global landscape, understanding how policy and politics intersect across borders is critical. Forecast synthesizes POLITICO’s global reporting to connect key developments and global convenings, giving readers a clearer view of what’s ahead. Subscribe Now.

DEPT. OF ODD BEDFELLOWS: “Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s demonization of food and pharma has put the Trump administration on the wrong side of its traditional allies in industry — but opened a path to a new alliance with a longtime GOP nemesis: lawyers representing consumers who say they were harmed by companies,” POLITICO’s Amanda Chu writes.

— “Kennedy’s moves, from his disparagement of Tylenol and ultraprocessed food to his broadsides against vaccines, have lawyers who assemble aggrieved plaintiffs to sue deep-pocketed companies envisioning the sort of cases that turn attorneys into Hollywood heroes and billionaires.”

— “Lawyers behind major settlements against companies told POLITICO that Kennedy’s sweeping anti-corporate agenda targeting food, chemical and pharmaceutical companies, along with rising public skepticism of industry, is creating a tailwind for the tort system to take on corporate power” and setting off a reckoning for business groups that have long leaned on GOP allies to push tort reforms to rein in litigation and cap damages.

DAVOS BEWARE: “The Trump administration’s main event venue in Davos was targeted by scammers who have sold billionaires fraudulent tickets to access USA House,” Bloomberg’s Jenny Leonard reports. “In a post on the venue’s website, the organizers warned against the purchase of so-called VIP access packages and said the fraudulent sales appear to be widespread this year.”

INVARIANT ADDS TELECOM LOBBYIST: Jason Goldman has joined Invariant as a principal in the firm’s technology and competition practice. Goldman spent the past six years at the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, most recently as the agency’s acting director of congressional affairs.

— Before that, Goldman handled external affairs and stakeholder engagement at the Intelligent Transportation Society of America, and spent more than a decade working on telecom policy at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

ANNALS OF THE REVOLVING DOOR: “Environmental Protection Agency ethics officials have interpreted impartiality guidelines in a way that has allowed several former industry insiders to oversee dramatic changes to chemical regulations,” per The Washington Post’s Amudalat Ajasa.

— “Those ethics decisions have cleared the way for a former agriculture lobbyist to help reinstate a pesticide that had been banned twice by federal courts, as well as for two former chemical industry executives to help reassess the agency’s stance on the dangers of formaldehyde.”

— “Internal emails and documents obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity and shared with The Washington Post show EPA ethics officials determined that Kyle Kunkler’s recent lobbying on behalf of the American Soybean Association did not require his recusal from pesticide regulation, including decisions about dicamba, a pesticide that soybean farmers have wanted to see reinstated.”

— “According to federal loss-of-impartiality regulations, new government employees are supposed to have a year-long ‘cooling-off period’ on matters that directly involve their previous employer, unless given written authorization by the ethics office.”

GET OUT OF JAIL (NOT SO FREE) CARD: “Convicted armed robber Yener Vahit Belli, the ‘Hoodie Bandit,’ is slated to serve a dozen years more in federal prison to pay off his societal debt for brandishing a firearm and terrorizing patrons while robbing two convenience stores of several hundred dollars, 61 Florida Lottery tickets and a pack of smokes,” per NOTUS’ Dave Levinthal.

WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN: Donald Trump ’s second presidency has ushered in a massive payday for Washington’s top lobbying shops, delivering a revenue boom across K Street in exchange for help navigating the widespread disruption of the first year of Trump’s new term.

— Ballard Partners , which signed more than 200 new clients since the 2024 election, raked in $88.3 million in lobbying fees last year, a 350 percent increase compared to 2024, when the firm reported $19.6 million in lobbying revenues. Ballard reported six contracts during Q4 worth at least half a million dollars and collected six figures from clients including Balkan Energy DMCC , Korea Zinc , Kimberly-Clark , Palantir and UnitedHealthcare , disclosures show.

— K Street’s previous top earner, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck , brought in $73.9 million in lobbying revenues in 2025, up from $67.9 million in 2024. BGR Group rounded out the top three with $71.5 million in revenues, which represents a 58 percent increase from 2024.

— “Every quarter it seems that there are more challenges and opportunities from the administration and Congress,” Nadeam Elshami , who co-leads Brownstein’s lobbying practice, told PI of the deluge of activity on K Street. Uncertainty around artificial intelligence continued to be a major driver of business in 2025, according to Elshami, who said that AI comes up on almost “every single call” with clients, who want advice on everything from how to remain competitive on AI to what the Trump administration will announce next.

— Tariffs were another huge issue on K Street last year. “It’s hard to think of a client that didn’t have questions related to tariffs, even if they weren’t exporters or importers, they were still impacted in one way or another,” said Paul Stimers , who co-leads the lobbying practice at Holland & Knight . Stimers’ firm brought in $54.6 million in lobbying revenues last year, up almost 10 percent from the prior year.

— Lobbyists expect trade to continue dominating Washington in 2026, especially as businesses await the Supreme Court’s decision on the legality of Trump’s so-called reciprocal tariffs. And even as they forecast a slowdown in legislation as the midterms approach, K Streeters said they’ll remain busy with oversight, defense, critical minerals, appropriations, transportation, national security and more — to say nothing of the Trump administration’s foreign policy moves up and down the Western Hemisphere.

— “Frankly, the lesson learned going forward is: Don’t be surprised,” Elshami said when asked about the top takeaways from the first year of Trump 2.0.

THE TRUMP BUMP ON STEROIDS: Of the top 20 earners overall last year, lobbying revenues were up by 10 percent or more at 13 of them compared to 2024, according to a PI analysis of disclosure filings. But while the windfall from Trump’s trade, tax, health care, AI, defense and energy policies boosted the bottom lines of virtually all of K Street’s biggest firms in 2025, the biggest jackpots were reserved for a select number of firms with close ties to Trump or his administration.

— A few of the top Trump-linked firms, including Ballard, Miller Strategies , Mercury Public Affairs , CGCN and Michael Best Strategies , saw even bigger boosts. Miller Strategies brought in $49.1 million, almost quadrupling its lobbying revenues from 2024. Mercury’s lobbying revenues nearly doubled to $22.3 million last year, while CGCN’s shot up by more than 82 percent to $17.6 million.

— Among the upstart firms who cashed in on Trump’s second term were Continental Strategy , which saw its lobbying revenues skyrocket from just $1.8 million in 2024 to more than $27 million in 2025. Checkmate Government Relations , which received $70,000 from just one client in 2024, reported a little over $21 million from more than 80 clients in 2025.

— Even so, Ballard Partners founder Brian Ballard pushed back today on the notion that his firm’s close ties to the Trump administration portend a short-lived success. “We remain doggedly committed to growing a fiercely bipartisan firm that is built to thrive in Washington’s dynamic political environment for decades to come,” he said in a statement on the shop’s 2025 revenues.

FIRST IN PI: More than two dozen conservative advocacy groups and think tanks are urging members of Congress to rebuff Trump’s sudden push to cap credit card interest rates and rein in credit card swipe fees, arguing that “price controls harm consumers and have repeatedly failed to fix the very problem they attempt to solve.”

— “These proposals would reduce consumer credit access, fail to address affordability concerns, and fragment an already dependable, well-functioning payments system,” leaders from Americans for Prosperity , Taxpayers Protection Alliance , Americans for Tax Reform , the Center for a Free Economy , the Competitive Enterprise Institute , R Street and more warn in a letter that will be sent to lawmakers tomorrow morning.

— Top congressional Republicans have already thrown cold water on Trump’s new affordability directives. But the conservative groups’ letter aims to ensure that continues to be the case. “We encourage all members to remain steadfast in their opposition against government overreach via interest rate cap proposals and the [Credit Card Competition Act],” they wrote.

NETCHOICE ASKS GOP TO DROP APP STORE BILL: “Right-leaning tech group NetChoice privately warned House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) earlier this month that an app store age-verification bill advanced in December by an E&C subcommittee would be ‘swiftly struck down’ in court,” POLITICO ’s Brendan Bordelon reports.

— “In a memo obtained by POLITICO , dated Jan. 12 and addressed to Guthrie and others on the committee, NetChoice said the App Store Accountability Act — a GOP-led bill that would require app stores and developers to verify the age of their users and require parental consent for each purchase — ‘suffers from myriad constitutional deficiencies under the First Amendment.’”

LIQUOR STORES TEAM UP ON HEMP: After losing the fight last year to head off new federal hemp regulations, alcohol retailers have launched a new coalition to push for a delay in implementing the new rules.

— The Beverage Alcohol Merchants Coalition , whose members include Total Wine & More , Gopuff and ABC Fine Wine & Spirits , is backing a bill from Rep. Jim Baird (R-Ind.) and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) that would delay the new regulations by two years.

— Hemp farmers and alcohol companies have argued that delaying the compliance deadline for last year’s ban on intoxicating hemp — which supporters of the ban had derided as a loophole — would provide the industry with much-needed certainty while lawmakers hash out a comprehensive regulatory framework.

Jobs report

— Elliott Guffin has joined Brownstein as a policy director. He most recently served as former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin ’s director of federal affairs and point person for the governor’s co-chairmanship of Trump’s council of governors.

— Bryce McNitt is joining RXN as senior vice president of public affairs. McNitt most recently served as chief of staff of the Office of Markets at the CFPB.

— Sydney Redden is now associate director of global external affairs at IP House . She previously worked for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce ’s Global Innovation Policy Center .

— Sarah Swinehart Massey is launching the communications firm Rising Tide Strategies . She previously was at the ONE Campaign .

— Damian Murphy was named as a lecturer in international affairs at George Washington University . He is senior vice president for national security and international policy at the Center for American Progress .

— CFTC Chair Michael Selig has hired Michael Passalacqua and Cal Mitchell as his senior advisers, per Morning Money . Passalacqua comes to the agency from Simpson Thacher & Bartlett , where he worked on crypto issues. Mitchell previously worked at Treasury as a special adviser in the Office of Legislative Affairs.

— Gene Sperling is launching an Economic Dignity Lab at Georgetown ’s McCourt School of Public Policy, per Axios . He’s a former National Economic Council director and Biden White House alum.

— Nancy Moon will be vice president of membership and strategic development at the American Gas Association . She previously worked at the American Council of Life Insurers .

— Yonnick Hammond is joining Cassidy & Associates as a senior vice president in the national security and defense practice. He previously worked at the Missile Defense Agency .

— The States Forum has added Aleigha Cavalier as vice president of content strategy and Priya Singh as vice president of strategy and programs. Cavalier most recently worked at Precision Strategies and is a Biden White House alum. Singh previously worked at the Center for Reproductive Rights and is an Obama and Biden White House alum.

About The Author : Caitlin Oprysko

Caitlin Oprysko covers lobbying for POLITICO and writes the Influence newsletter. She was previously a breaking news reporter for POLITICO, covering the 2018 midterms, 2020 election and everything (seriously) in between. She joined POLITICO Pro in 2016 as a web producer and also worked on Pro’s Legislative Compass team, covering an omnibus spending bill, the farm bill and several appropriations bills from their introduction to the president’s desk.

Before coming to POLITICO, Caitlin worked on the social desk for ABC News’ D.C. Bureau, where she used social media to monitor coverage areas, curated images and videos for broadcasts, pitched and reported out stories and collaborated on breaking news.

Caitlin is originally from the Atlanta area and graduated from the University of Georgia, where she covered state and local news and worked for the student-run newscast Grady Newsource.

WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN: Donald Trump’s second presidency has ushered in a massive payday for Washington’s top lobbying shops, delivering a revenue boom across K Street in exchange for help navigating the widespread disruption of the first year of Trump’s new term.

— Ballard Partners, which signed more than 200 new clients since the 2024 election, raked in $88.3 million in lobbying fees last year, a 350 percent increase compared to 2024, when the firm reported $19.6 million in lobbying revenues. Ballard reported six contracts during Q4 worth at least half a million dollars and collected six figures from clients including Balkan Energy DMCC, Korea Zinc, Kimberly-Clark, Palantir and UnitedHealthcare, disclosures show.

— K Street’s previous top earner, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, brought in $73.9 million in lobbying revenues in 2025, up from $67.9 million in 2024. BGR Group rounded out the top three with $71.5 million in revenues, which represents a 58 percent increase from 2024.

— “Every quarter it seems that there are more challenges and opportunities from the administration and Congress,” Nadeam Elshami, who co-leads Brownstein’s lobbying practice, told PI of the deluge of activity on K Street. Uncertainty around artificial intelligence continued to be a major driver of business in 2025, according to Elshami, who said that AI comes up on almost “every single call” with clients, who want advice on everything from how to remain competitive on AI to what the Trump administration will announce next.

— Tariffs were another huge issue on K Street last year. “It’s hard to think of a client that didn’t have questions related to tariffs, even if they weren’t exporters or importers, they were still impacted in one way or another,” said Paul Stimers, who co-leads the lobbying practice at Holland & Knight. Stimers’ firm brought in $54.6 million in lobbying revenues last year, up almost 10 percent from the prior year.

— Lobbyists expect trade to continue dominating Washington in 2026, especially as businesses await the Supreme Court’s decision on the legality of Trump’s so-called reciprocal tariffs. And even as they forecast a slowdown in legislation as the midterms approach, K Streeters said they’ll remain busy with oversight, defense, critical minerals, appropriations, transportation, national security and more — to say nothing of the Trump administration’s foreign policy moves up and down the Western Hemisphere.

— “Frankly, the lesson learned going forward is: Don’t be surprised,” Elshami said when asked about the top takeaways from the first year of Trump 2.0.

THE TRUMP BUMP ON STEROIDS: Of the top 20 earners overall last year, lobbying revenues were up by 10 percent or more at 13 of them compared to 2024, according to a PI analysis of disclosure filings. But while the windfall from Trump’s trade, tax, health care, AI, defense and energy policies boosted the bottom lines of virtually all of K Street’s biggest firms in 2025, the biggest jackpots were reserved for a select number of firms with close ties to Trump or his administration.

— A few of the top Trump-linked firms, including Ballard, Miller Strategies, Mercury Public Affairs, CGCN and Michael Best Strategies, saw even bigger boosts. Miller Strategies brought in $49.1 million, almost quadrupling its lobbying revenues from 2024. Mercury’s lobbying revenues nearly doubled to $22.3 million last year, while CGCN’s shot up by more than 82 percent to $17.6 million.

— Among the upstart firms who cashed in on Trump’s second term were Continental Strategy, which saw its lobbying revenues skyrocket from just $1.8 million in 2024 to more than $27 million in 2025. Checkmate Government Relations, which received $70,000 from just one client in 2024, reported a little over $21 million from more than 80 clients in 2025.

— Even so, Ballard Partners founder Brian Ballard pushed back today on the notion that his firm’s close ties to the Trump administration portend a short-lived success. “We remain doggedly committed to growing a fiercely bipartisan firm that is built to thrive in Washington’s dynamic political environment for decades to come,” he said in a statement on the shop’s 2025 revenues.

FIRST IN PI: More than two dozen conservative advocacy groups and think tanks are urging members of Congress to rebuff Trump’s sudden push to cap credit card interest rates and rein in credit card swipe fees, arguing that “price controls harm consumers and have repeatedly failed to fix the very problem they attempt to solve.”

— “These proposals would reduce consumer credit access, fail to address affordability concerns, and fragment an already dependable, well-functioning payments system,” leaders from Americans for Prosperity, Taxpayers Protection Alliance, Americans for Tax Reform, the Center for a Free Economy, the Competitive Enterprise Institute, R Street and more warn in a letter that will be sent to lawmakers tomorrow morning.

— Top congressional Republicans have already thrown cold water on Trump’s new affordability directives. But the conservative groups’ letter aims to ensure that continues to be the case. “We encourage all members to remain steadfast in their opposition against government overreach via interest rate cap proposals and the [Credit Card Competition Act],” they wrote.

NETCHOICE ASKS GOP TO DROP APP STORE BILL: “Right-leaning tech group NetChoice privately warned House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) earlier this month that an app store age-verification bill advanced in December by an E&C subcommittee would be ‘swiftly struck down’ in court,” POLITICO’s Brendan Bordelon reports.

— “In a memo obtained by POLITICO, dated Jan. 12 and addressed to Guthrie and others on the committee, NetChoice said the App Store Accountability Act — a GOP-led bill that would require app stores and developers to verify the age of their users and require parental consent for each purchase — ‘suffers from myriad constitutional deficiencies under the First Amendment.’”

LIQUOR STORES TEAM UP ON HEMP: After losing the fight last year to head off new federal hemp regulations, alcohol retailers have launched a new coalition to push for a delay in implementing the new rules.

— The Beverage Alcohol Merchants Coalition, whose members include Total Wine & More, Gopuff and ABC Fine Wine & Spirits, is backing a bill from Rep. Jim Baird (R-Ind.) and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) that would delay the new regulations by two years.

— Hemp farmers and alcohol companies have argued that delaying the compliance deadline for last year’s ban on intoxicating hemp — which supporters of the ban had derided as a loophole — would provide the industry with much-needed certainty while lawmakers hash out a comprehensive regulatory framework.

title: Lutnicks’ firm hires Trump Jr. associate
body_text:
CANTOR FITZGERALD SIGNS CHECKMATE: Wall Street financial services firm Cantor Fitzgerald , which was led by Howard Lutnick until his appointment as Commerce secretary and is currently led by his sons, has hired Checkmate Government Relations , according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— Cantor, which reportedly was on track to its most profitable year ever, hired Checkmate on Dec. 15 and paid the firm $80,000 for slightly more than two weeks of work at the end of 2025, according to a separate Q4 report . That work included lobbying the White House and the Treasury Department on “issues relating to financial services” and “issues relating to fuel, gas, and oil,” according to the report.

— That payment was a late infusion to the more than $21 million Checkmate earned in 2025, a wildly successful year for the North Carolina based firm that didn’t open a Washington office until after Donald Trump’s victory in the 2024 presidential election. The firm and its founder, Ches McDowell , boast strong ties to Trump’s administration and his family .

— McDowell did not respond to questions regarding what specific matters Checkmate is lobbying on, but Cantor has previously identified changes in the energy sector and the growing power needs of AI data centers as “megatrends” that will “reshape the future of our markets.” Cantor declined to comment on the hire.

— In addition to McDowell, the Cantor account will be handled by the firm’s lead financial services lobbyists: Fritz Vaughan , who previously served in Treasury’s legislative affairs office, Usman Rahim , former in-house lobbyist for Bank of America , and Miles Johnson , who most recently served at Treasury as the special adviser to the deputy secretary. Public affairs director Chris LaCivita Jr. is also listed on the filings.

GOING PUBLIC: Public Policy Holding Co. , the parent company of lobbying and public affairs firms like Forbes Tate Partners , Crossroads Strategies , Seven Letter and more, has announced the start of its initial public offering roadshow, a crucial step as the company prepares to be listed on the Nasdaq.

— The company, already listed on the U.K. stock market, is seeking to issue 4.15 million shares of stock at an anticipated price of $13.45 per share. Funds raised from the IPO could potentially be used to expand the company’s portfolio via acquisitions, according to a prospectus filed with the SEC. PPHC has steadily increased its holdings since its founding in 2014, most recently with the July 2025 acquisition of Texas-based Pine Cove Capital .

WINRED WHO?: The Trump Presidential Library is backing PSQ Impact , a competitor digital fundraising platform that threatens WinRed ’s ubiquity in GOP fundraising, selecting it as the library’s fundraising platform of choice, developer PublicSquare announced today.

— Led in part by close Trump ally Alex Bruesewitz , the new platform has promised to take a smaller cut of donations than WinRed and seeks to break the monopoly on Republican online fundraising enjoyed by the older platform, which launched in 2019.

FIRST IN PI — AI ON THE HILL: The National Artificial Intelligence Association will host its inaugural AI Policy Summit on Feb. 10 on Capitol Hill. The AI trade association, founded last year with backing from Oracle , Capital One and a host of other member companies, has largely advocated for federal regulation of the nascent industry as opposed to state-by-state laws.

— Next month’s summit will feature AI product demos for attendees and remarks by United States Nuclear Industry Council President and CEO Bud Albright , quantum computing company Quantinuum ’s director of government relations Ryan McKenney and former HUD Inspector General Rae Oliver Davis . Lawmakers from the House Financial Services Committee, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and House Science, Space and Technology Committee are also expected to attend.

FLYING IN: Members of the Electronic Transactions Association were on Capitol Hill today meeting with member offices to emphasize the results of a new report which found that the payments industry is responsible for more than $350 billion of the country’s GDP in 2024.

— The ETA, which includes major banks, online payment processors and credit card companies, commissioned the report. Electronic payments have been a hot topic since the reintroduction of the Credit Card Competition Act, a bipartisan bill supported by the president that aims to lower so-called “swipe fees” by mandating more competition in the credit card processing market.

BIG TECH SPENDS BIG: Major tech and AI companies spent a combined $109 million on federal lobbying last year, a new record high, according to an analysis by Bloomberg ’s Emily Birnbaum and Maggie Eastland .

— Mark Zuckerberg ’s Meta was the lead spender among all tech companies in Washington, dropping more than $26.3 million on influence efforts in 2025. They were followed by fellow tech giants Amazon ($17.8 million) and Google ($13.1 million).

— One of the largest jumps in tech lobbying spending came from chipmaker Nvidia , which jumped from spending $640,000 on lobbying in 2024 to $4.9 million in 2025. ChatGPT maker OpenAI saw a similar jump in spending, going from spending $1.76 million in 2024 to roughly $3 million last year.

title: GOP opposition research vet now leading America Rising

FIRST IN PI — RISE AND SHINE: One of the leading names in GOP opposition research has concluded its first year under new management and is gearing up for a busy 2026.

— America Rising is now under the stewardship of Matt Wall , who serves as the firm’s owner and president. Wall is a veteran of the NRSC , where he served as deputy executive director during the 2024 election cycle when Republicans gained four seats and flipped control of the chamber. His acquisition of America Rising, which occurred in January 2025, has not been previously reported.

— The firm, founded in 2013 by a group of Mitt Romney and RNC vets, has been a mainstay of Republican opposition research for more than a decade, providing research, candidate tracking and media monitoring to the national party committee as well as individual campaigns.

— “I’ve been in this business for a long time, and seeing the opportunity that America Rising was available and they were looking for new ownership, I decided it would be a perfect fit,” Wall told PI. He declined to comment on what led previous ownership to sell the firm.

— Wall, whose career prior to the NRSC included stints at Fox News and the NRCC , told PI he had been involved with the firm from the client side for “a long time” and was able to “hit the ground running” in 2025 with a focus on business development and hiring new staffers, including former colleagues from the NRSC and NRCC. In addition to Wall, the firm’s current leadership includes chief of staff Mary Mac Cowan , research director Tyler Stark and tracking director Austin Fageol . The firm’s total headcount recently hit 40 employees, and Wall anticipates hiring more trackers and research analysts closer to the 2026 midterms.

— “Something else that we’re really trying to prioritize is investment in new technologies that can help us be faster, more efficient with the research that we’re doing,” Wall said, citing AI as the “future of opposition research.”

— “I don’t think it’s ever going to fully replace the human element that’s required in doing research, but I think it can absolutely assist us, whether it’s automating certain processes like pulling votes, or identifying videos across the entire web,” Wall said. “But you’re still going to need humans to have that political instinct.”

VENABLE LAUNCHES NEW PRACTICE GROUP: Law firm Venable has announced the launch of a new administrative and regulatory litigation practice group, aimed at centralizing the work the firm has already been doing for clients with regulatory matters before federal and state agencies and courts.

— The new group will be chaired by Megan Barbero , former SEC general counsel who joined the firm in March of 2025. Inaugural members of the practice group also include firm newcomers Courtney Dixon , previously a lawyer in the Justice Department’s civil division, and Elizabeth Wilson , who recently completed a clerkship with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

— Part of the goal of the new group will be to “help clients through every step of the regulatory process, from monitoring agency developments, commenting on rule making, weighing in on litigation strategy, depending on how the agency action unfolds, and litigating those cases,” Barbero told PI. “And also we’re seeing an uptick across the board in amicus participation, especially in high-profile litigation involving government regulations.”

— The filing of amicus briefs, submitted by parties that aren’t involved in a particular case but have an interest in the outcome, is up “across the whole range of issues” where the Trump administration is changing policies and agency rules, Barbero said. While such briefs are commonly filed when cases reach the U.S. Supreme Court, “what’s newer … is amici participation in the district court by organizations and associations who have an interest in what’s being litigated,” she added.

— Filing amicus briefs and litigating are just the most public-facing parts of the group’s work, which also includes advising clients under investigation by federal regulators and challenging state-level regulations around the country.

BIG SPENDERS: Pharmaceutical companies reported record amounts of lobbying spending in 2025, our colleagues David Lim and Amanda Chu report for POLITICO Prescription Pulse .

— “Nine of the 13 U.S. drugmakers on the Fortune 500 list, including Bristol - Myers Squibb , Eli Lilly , Johnson & Johnson , Merck & Co. and Zoetis , reported their highest spending in at least a decade. Bristol-Myers Squibb reported the highest jump in annual spending, investing $10 million this year, a 91 percent change from 2024,” they write. PhRMA itself spent nearly $38 million on lobbying, the association’s highest ever annual total .

— “Drugmakers have favored boutique lobbying shops with unique skills and connections, with Tarplin, Downs & Young and Todd Strategy Group among the top firms,” they add.

FUEL FIGHT: Spending big in Washington doesn’t necessarily guarantee successful outcomes. The ethanol industry spent millions last year lobbying Congress to lift limits on the sale of gasoline with higher ethanol levels, only to see their efforts fail despite relatively meager spending by the oil industry on the issue, Shifra Dayak and Anna Kramer report for NOTUS .

— “ The Bayer Corporation spent more than $9 million during 2025 on lobbying the federal government, including on ‘legislative and administrative action related to biofuels, including ethanol,’” they report. Also among the big spenders on the issue “were Koch Companies ’ lobbying arm, which spent more than $9 million in 2025, and ethanol producer Archer Daniels Midland , which spent almost $7 million last year.”

— By comparison, American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers , an oil industry group that has opposed lifting ethanol limits, spent more than $2 million on lobbying in 2025.

HIGHER ED: The Trump administration’s attacks on higher education earlier in 2025 also spurred elevated levels of lobbying spending by universities that faced losing hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funds, Josh Moody reports for Inside Higher Ed .

— Major research universities that make up the Association of American Universities spent more than $37 million on lobbying in 2025, nearly $10 million more than their total lobbying spending in 2024.

— Universities reported their largest spending during Q2 of 2025, when Congress was debating the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Not all universities counted by Inside Higher Ed met the deadline to report their Q4 spending, meaning the actual total for 2025 spending is likely even higher.

— BGR has appointed four new principles from within the firm: Raghav Aggarwal in the health and life sciences practice, Keaghan Ames in the financial services practice, Scott Eisner in the international trade practice, and Syd Terry in the commerce and infrastructure practice.

— Ali Ahmad has joined PLUS Communications as a senior managing director in the firm’s Richmond office. He most recently served as deputy chief of staff for strategy to former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin .

— Larry Calhoun has joined the policy team at Waymo . He most recently served as deputy assistant U.S. trade representative and previously served as a chief of staff to Reps. Ted Yoho (R-Fla.) and Kat Cammack (R- Fla.).

PARAGUAYAN POLITICS: The former Paraguayan vice president and an associate of his who have been banned from entering the United States since 2022 have hired Florida-based Corcoran Partners to lobby on “issues around visas,” according to disclosure reports .

— Hugo Velazquez , who left office in 2023, was accused by State Department officials of attempting to thwart a Paraguayan investigation that threatened his financial interests by offering a $1 million bribe to a public official. The bribe was allegedly offered via an intermediary, Juan Carlos Duarte , a personal friend of Velazquez’s who served as legal counsel for the entity that controls the Yacyreta Dam on the border of Paraguay and Argentina.

— Both men and their families were banned from traveling to the U.S. as a result of the designation. Velazquez was later additionally sanctioned by the Treasury Department under the Magnitsky Act, cutting him off from U.S. banks and prohibiting him from doing business with U.S. companies. The recently filed disclosure report for Velazquez also mentions “issues related to OFAC [Office of Foreign Assets Control] sanctions and removal policies.”

— A third individual, former Paraguayan Minister of Agriculture Rodolfo Max Friedmann , has also hired Corcoran Partners to lobby on visa issues . Friedmann resigned in 2020 after being hit with corruption and money laundering charges related to his time as governor of Paraguay’s Guaira Department. PI could not immediately determine if Friedmann had also been designated as an individual involved in corruption. The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

— On the accounts for Corcoran Partners are Carlos San Jose and Steve Bovo . As PI reported last month , Bovo is a close ally of Secretary of State Marco Rubio from their time in Florida politics. Bovo’s wife, Viviana Bovo , currently works under Rubio at the State Department, according to The Miami Herald .

title: Tech manufacturer hires Lanza amid calls for US ban
body_text:
TO BAN OR NOT TO BAN: A Chinese-founded electronics manufacturer facing bipartisan calls for an investigation into its relationship with the Chinese government has hired former Donald Trump campaign adviser Bryan Lanza of Mercury Public Affairs to lobby Congress and the administration, according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— TP-Link , maker of smart home devices like wireless routers, smart doorbells, security cameras and more, hired Lanza in October to “educate policymakers, federal agencies and Congress” on the company’s U.S. operations and “compliance with U.S. data security and supply chain requirements,” according to the disclosure report. On the account with Lanza are John Lonergan and James Messner .

— Founded by two brothers in China in 1996, TP-Link completed a corporate restructuring last year that spun off its U.S. business, creating a split between China-based TP-Link Technologies and U.S.-based TP-Link Systems. One brother maintains control of the China-based company while the other fully controls the newly-established U.S. company.

— The separation has not assuaged China hawks in Washington. Earlier this year, a group of GOP senators led by Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) sent a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asking him to ban the company’s wireless routers from sale in the U.S. And earlier this month, a bipartisan group of 23 lawmakers sent a letter to Lutnick asking him to investigate, and if necessary, ban sale of TP-Link smart devices like security cameras and baby monitors.

— “Right now, nothing stops CCP-tied companies from spying on Americans through internet-connected cameras in our homes,” the lawmakers wrote. “The Chinese Communist Party can capture and exploit these videos to track, blackmail, or extort U.S. citizens — including top government and military officials.”

— While no official action has been taken on TP-Link, there are signs the administration is taking those concerns seriously. At the end of October, The Washington Post reported that multiple federal agencies had reviewed the matter and backed a proposal to ban TP-Link routers. Separately, Bloomberg reported in April that the Justice Department is conducting a criminal antitrust investigation into the company’s pricing strategies.

— “TP-Link Systems Inc. emphatically objects to any allegation it is tied to the Communist Party of China, dependent on the Chinese government, or otherwise subject to interference under Chinese national security laws,” a company spokesperson told PI. “TP-Link will continue to work with the U.S. Department of Commerce to ensure we understand and can respond to any concerns the government has.”

— “Despite unsourced media reports regarding a Department of Justice antitrust probe, TP-Link has received no inquiries from the DOJ,” the spokesperson added.

— As skepticism of TP-Link rises in Washington, so too has the company’s spending. In the summer of 2024, the company made Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld its first lobbying hire, paying the firm $380,000 that year. In the first three quarters of this year, the company has shelled out nearly $1 million to Akin, Vernonburg Group and Ballard Partners .

Before her time at CGCN, Berg was a senior vice president at Definers Public Affairs .

— Berg told PI she anticipates her background working with corporate clients will “pair well” with the political experience of the firm’s founders, GOP strategists Jason Thielman , Brock Lowrance and Tim Edson .

FIRST IN PI — INVARIANT POACHES HUMANA LOBBYIST: Longtime health care lobbyist Jeff Lungren will join Invariant next week as a principal, leaving his current position as director of government affairs for health insurer Humana .

— Lungren spent more than five years at Humana, where he was also the company’s lead Republican lobbyist. Prior to that he spent a decade as the chief health care and immigration lobbyist for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce .

SWEET TREAT: Lobbyists for Big Sugar and Big Candy reached a hard-fought settlement earlier this year, representing a victory for the confectioners who have, for decades, sought to change government policies that elevate the price of sugar, Emily Birnbaum and Michael Smith report for Bloomberg .

— Early discussions between the sides took place in 2023 at the Georgetown Four Seasons hotel, marking the first time many lobbyists for sugar producers had ever met their counterparts representing the candy industry.

— “The meeting amounted to a strategic pivot from food manufacturers’ decades-long campaign to roll back key parts of the US government sugar program. Confectioners conceded the US sugar program was politically untouchable and scaled back their aims to modest changes.”

— As affordability dominates the political conversation ahead of next year’s midterms, lobbyists for Big Candy tell Bloomberg they’re optimistic that the work done to achieve this compromise could contribute to a larger impact on food costs via a future farm bill.

— “‘If there’s ever a farm bill again,’ [Brian McKeon], the candy lobbyist, said, ‘we’ve changed the muscle memory here in agricultural policy.’”

CON JOB: A former nursing home magnate, sentenced to three years in prison for defrauding the government, was granted a pardon in November, seven months after he paid convicted fraudsters Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl nearly $1 million to lobby the administration for a pardon, Michael Kranish and Aaron Schaffer report for The Washington Post .

— It’s not clear what work Burkman and Wohl did to secure their client’s pardon. A White House official told The Post that the pair didn’t meet with anyone from the White House Counsel’s office or with White House Pardon Czar Alice Johnson.

— Burkman and Wohl were previously “convicted of telecommunications fraud in Ohio in connection with a robocall scheme designed to deter the turnout of minority voters. They also face sentencing next month in Michigan on a similar robocall case and have been subject to millions of dollars in fines in a related case brought by the Federal Communications Commission.”

Tech manufacturer hires Lanza amid calls for US ban

By DANIEL BARNES and CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

11/24/2025 07:32 PM EST

Presented by

With help from Daniel Lippman

TO BAN OR NOT TO BAN: A Chinese-founded electronics manufacturer facing bipartisan calls for an investigation into its relationship with the Chinese government has hired former Donald Trump campaign adviser Bryan Lanza of Mercury Public Affairs to lobby Congress and the administration, according to a newly filed disclosure report.

— TP-Link, maker of smart home devices like wireless routers, smart doorbells, security cameras and more, hired Lanza in October to “educate policymakers, federal agencies and Congress” on the company’s U.S. operations and “compliance with U.S. data security and supply chain requirements,” according to the disclosure report. On the account with Lanza are John Lonergan and James Messner.

— Founded by two brothers in China in 1996, TP-Link completed a corporate restructuring last year that spun off its U.S. business, creating a split between China-based TP-Link Technologies and U.S.-based TP-Link Systems. One brother maintains control of the China-based company while the other fully controls the newly-established U.S. company.

— The separation has not assuaged China hawks in Washington. Earlier this year, a group of GOP senators led by Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) sent a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asking him to ban the company’s wireless routers from sale in the U.S. And earlier this month, a bipartisan group of 23 lawmakers sent a letter to Lutnick asking him to investigate, and if necessary, ban sale of TP-Link smart devices like security cameras and baby monitors.

— “Right now, nothing stops CCP-tied companies from spying on Americans through internet-connected cameras in our homes,” the lawmakers wrote. “The Chinese Communist Party can capture and exploit these videos to track, blackmail, or extort U.S. citizens — including top government and military officials.”

— While no official action has been taken on TP-Link, there are signs the administration is taking those concerns seriously. At the end of October, The Washington Post reported that multiple federal agencies had reviewed the matter and backed a proposal to ban TP-Link routers. Separately, Bloomberg reported in April that the Justice Department is conducting a criminal antitrust investigation into the company’s pricing strategies.

— “TP-Link Systems Inc. emphatically objects to any allegation it is tied to the Communist Party of China, dependent on the Chinese government, or otherwise subject to interference under Chinese national security laws,” a company spokesperson told PI. “TP-Link will continue to work with the U.S. Department of Commerce to ensure we understand and can respond to any concerns the government has.”

— “Despite unsourced media reports regarding a Department of Justice antitrust probe, TP-Link has received no inquiries from the DOJ,” the spokesperson added.

— As skepticism of TP-Link rises in Washington, so too has the company’s spending. In the summer of 2024, the company made Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld its first lobbying hire, paying the firm $380,000 that year. In the first three quarters of this year, the company has shelled out nearly $1 million to Akin, Vernonburg Group and Ballard Partners.

— Berg, who spent the past six years at Republican lobbying powerhouse CGCN, joined S2R this week as a senior vice president to help steer public affairs for the firm’s growing list of clients in industries like telecommunications and health care. Before her time at CGCN, Berg was a senior vice president at Definers Public Affairs.

— Berg told PI she anticipates her background working with corporate clients will “pair well” with the political experience of the firm’s founders, GOP strategists Jason Thielman, Brock Lowrance and Tim Edson.

FIRST IN PI — INVARIANT POACHES HUMANA LOBBYIST: Longtime health care lobbyist Jeff Lungren will join Invariant next week as a principal, leaving his current position as director of government affairs for health insurer Humana.

— Lungren spent more than five years at Humana, where he was also the company’s lead Republican lobbyist. Prior to that he spent a decade as the chief health care and immigration lobbyist for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

SWEET TREAT: Lobbyists for Big Sugar and Big Candy reached a hard-fought settlement earlier this year, representing a victory for the confectioners who have, for decades, sought to change government policies that elevate the price of sugar, Emily Birnbaum and Michael Smith report for Bloomberg.

— Early discussions between the sides took place in 2023 at the Georgetown Four Seasons hotel, marking the first time many lobbyists for sugar producers had ever met their counterparts representing the candy industry.

— “The meeting amounted to a strategic pivot from food manufacturers’ decades-long campaign to roll back key parts of the US government sugar program. Confectioners conceded the US sugar program was politically untouchable and scaled back their aims to modest changes.”

— As affordability dominates the political conversation ahead of next year’s midterms, lobbyists for Big Candy tell Bloomberg they’re optimistic that the work done to achieve this compromise could contribute to a larger impact on food costs via a future farm bill.

title: AI association reveals first advisory board
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — NAIA ANNOUNCES ADVISORY BOARD: One of the newest trade associations in Washington, the National Artificial Intelligence Association , has appointed its inaugural advisory board. It features former government officials as well as representatives from the tech, government services and legal industries.

— Peter Guerra , global vice president for data and AI at Oracle , represents NAIA’s largest member company on the board. Joining him from the tech sector is Ryan McKenney , general counsel for compliance and the director of government relations at quantum computer maker Quantinuum .

— Former government officials on the board include Rae Oliver Davis , the previous inspector general for the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and Eileen Vidrine , former chief data and artificial intelligence officer for the U.S. Air Force. Another appointee is Diane Cullo , former director of USDA’s office of tribal relations and current assistant administrator with the U.S. Small Business Administration .

— Other members are: Jay Lampke , president of Government Acquisitions Inc. , Cleve Adams , CEO of ILS , Joey Lauffer , chief growth officer of BTI360 , Tim Tkacz , CEO of Blue Sky Innovators and Trey White , president and CTO of 540.co .

— “Each advisory board member brings significant expertise to our association as we provide transformative policy solutions to our federal government during a pivotal moment of AI expansion,”NAIA president and CEO Caleb Max said in a statement.

— Officially launched in January, the NAIA has spent much of its first year advocating for federal regulation of the AI industry that would preempt current state laws. In a recent letter to congressional leaders , Max wrote that state-by-state regulation of AI “protects China” and “forces startups to hire more lawyers than engineers.” He urged House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune to include federal AI regulation in the National Defense Authorization Act or in “any available legislative vehicle.”

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI. Hope everyone is enjoying a short week. PI will be off Thursday and Friday for Thanksgiving and will return Monday, Dec. 1. In the meantime, you can still send tips to dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . For turkey pictures, follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

THE MAR-A-LAGO VISA: Pointing to President Donald Trump’s use of seasonal worker visas to staff his properties, the Seasonal Employment Alliance is pushing the administration to expand the program, POLITICO’s Diana Nerozzi reports .

— “SEA spokesperson Gray Delany said in an interview that the group has met with officials at the Department of Homeland Security, the White House’s legislative team, and even made an effort to talk to Eric Trump, the president’s son, and other Trump Org members.”

— H-2B visas, a short term visa sought by employers who need to hire additional support for seasonal work, haven’t drawn MAGA’s anger in the same way as longer-term H-1B visas that allow a path to permanent residency for highly skilled immigrant workers. SEA emphasizes the differences by describing H-2B visas as a “‘workforce visa program’ and not an ‘immigration program.’”

— “In addition, SEA has installed Peter Petrina , who files H-2B visa paperwork for Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property, atop its board of directors. And it has hired Trump ally Caroline Wren to help make inroads in Trump’s network.”

LOBBYING JUSTICE : Lawyers representing companies seeking merger approval from the Justice Department have new advice for their clients: hire a lobbyist.

— “It would be malpractice of me not to tell a client that we do seem to be in an environment where relationships with people at either the Oval Office or the DOJ front office can indeed impact the outcome of a given investigation,” one lawyer told Katie Arcieri of Bloomberg Law .

— Questions have swirled about the impartiality of the Justice Department’s merger review process since earlier this year after a fired official accused department leaders of overruling antitrust division officials to approve a merger between Hewlett-Packard Enterprise (HPE) and Juniper Networks. He said it was done at the behest of politically connected lawyers and lobbyists hired by HPE.

— In this new environment, lawyers counseling clients with business before the antitrust division are advising companies to hire lobbyists who can craft a message that will resonate with the White House.

— “This Justice Department is ‘less independent’ than previous DOJs have been, said an executive in the lobbying industry who agreed to speak on the condition of anonymity. In the past, the executive said, ‘the tail wags the dog’—meaning lawyers in the DOJ antitrust division drove the decision making on proposed deals. ‘In the past, the tail probably had more power. And in this administration, the leadership has more power.’”

ENDANGERED SPECIES: After nearly a decade of losses in court, Greenpeace USA has cut staff and is on the verge of bankruptcy, POLITICO’s Robin Bravender reports .

— The root of Greenpeace’s financial problems is a lawsuit filed against the organization by Texas-based energy company Energy Transfer . Earlier this year a jury found that Greenpeace committed trespassing, conspiracy and defamation while protesting Energy Transfer’s Dakota Access pipeline in 2016 and 2017 and ordered the organization to pay more than $660 million in damages. A judge later reduced the amount of damages the organization is liable for and litigation remains ongoing.

— “This July, Greenpeace USA launched a voluntary separation program that resulted in the departure of nearly 20 percent of its staff. The organization now employs about 91 staffers, said Greenpeace spokesperson Madison Carter.”

SUPER MONDAY: Delivery service Gopuff has launched a nonprofit dedicated to lobbying for the Monday following the Superbowl to be a federal holiday.

— Football legend Tom Brady and comedian Druski will appear in ads promoting the new Super Monday Off Coalition and Gopuff will donate a cut of its proceeds from certain delivery items to the effort from today through the Superbowl.

— In a statement, Gopuff co-founder and co-CEO Yakir Gola called the proposed holiday “the ultimate pro-family, pro-worker, pro-America win” and urged Trump and Congress to “do something truly historic” by creating “a national holiday Americans will celebrate for generations to come.”

Jobs report

— Ziad Ojakli is joining TikTok as the company’s new head of public policy, Americas. He most recently served as the executive vice president of government operations for Boeing .

— Erez Reuveni has joined Democracy Forward as a senior counsel. He is a 15-year Justice Department veteran turned whistleblower who most recently served as acting deputy director in the civil division’s office of immigration litigation. Reuveni litigated the case against Kilmar Abrego Garcia before being fired in April. He was interviewed last month on CBS’ “60 Minutes.”

— Kristina Biyad is now executive director of the American Committee for Middle East Rights . She previously served as senior director for outreach at Foreign Policy for America .

— Lia Palazzo has joined the Health & Fitness Association as manager of public affairs. She most recently served as a digital media strategist for the New Civil Liberties Alliance .

— Kevin Boland is now a senior director with Invariant’s national security practice. He most recently served as executive director for corporate responsibility communications at JPMorgan Chase .

— Windle Jarvis is now executive director at Miles for Military . He most recently served as the chief development officer for Spirit of America .

— The Sports Fans Coalition has added DeMaurice Smith , Chris VanDeHoef and Yosef Getachew to its board of directors. Smith previously served as executive director of the NFL Players Association , VanDeHoef currently serves as CEO of Penn Lincoln Strategies and Getachew currently serves as a senior policy counsel at Reset Tech .

CLIENT LOYALTY: Los Angeles-based Manatt, Phelps & Phillips is signing local government clients by the dozen, a sign that the firm’s decision earlier this year to poach several key lobbyists from Holland & Knight ’s local government advocacy team is paying off.

— Just this month, Manatt signed 10 new local government clients, all of which were previously represented by Holland & Knight and most of which chose to terminate their old contracts in favor of signing Manatt, according to disclosure reports. Notable clients include the cities of San Jose, Seattle and Phoenix. Greensboro, North Carolina, was the lone East Coast representative in this month’s batch of new signings, which also included local government coalitions like the Puget Sound Regional Council and the Southern California Association of Governments .

— Also leaving Holland & Knight for Manatt this month were two education clients: the Los Angeles Community College District and the University of Pittsburgh .

— The wave of new clients comes nearly two months after Manatt announced it was hiring Eve O’Toole , Leslie Pollner , Lisa Barkovic , Joe O’Brien and Adrianna Williams from Holland & Knight. All 13 of the clients Manatt signed this month were previously represented by at least one member of that team at Holland & Knight.

GOING NUCLEAR: Nuclear energy startup Fermi America has hired The Vogel Group ’s trade guru Samir Kapadia to lobby on “issues related to gigawatt scale private electric grid development in Amarillo, Texas,” according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— The company, founded in January by former Energy Secretary Rick Perry along with his son, Griffin Perry , and GOP donor Toby Neugebauer , is part of a new wave of startups founded by executives with little to no experience in nuclear energy that are nevertheless pulling in billions of dollars from investors betting that founders’ close ties to the White House will allow them to leapfrog established competitors in the race to meet the energy demand created by the AI boom, Evan Halper reports today for The Washington Post .

— Fermi went public at the start of October with a valuation of $12.5 billion despite the fact that it has yet to generate any revenue. Later that month, the company announced two deals with South Korean manufacturers that will build equipment for four planned nuclear reactors on Fermi’s Amarillo complex.

— Vogel Group is only Fermi’s second lobbying hire in Washington. In July, the company signed Jeff Miller , Stefan Passantino and Lucas Wallwork of Miller Strategies to lobby on “general issues related to regulatory approval and trade.” Miller, himself close with Trump, reported earning $150,000 from Fermi for his first three months of work.

— Anti-abortion groups have spent months lobbying Congress and the White House to include such limits and are now asking President Donald Trump to take a firm position in favor of new restrictions, POLITICO’s Alice Miranda Ollstein , Jordain Carney and Cheyenne Haslett report .

— Should the White House decline to take a position on new ACA abortion restrictions or advance a subsidy extension plan without those restrictions, that “would ultimately fracture the wide-reaching coalition that got President Trump re-elected,” a spokesperson for Americans United for Life said.

— “But given this difficult landscape, conservative lobbyists are skeptical that passage is possible even if Trump endorsed abortion restrictions,” our colleagues write. “Those in close contact with lawmakers say it’s unlikely an extension of the subsidies could win 60 votes in the Senate — or even 50.”

CEOS FUND TRUMP CRITICS: The Business Roundtable distributed $2.6 million in grants and contributions in 2024, with part of that money going to various organizations that have since criticized the Trump administration and its policies, Taylor Giorno reports for NOTUS .

title: Health lobbyists press for ACA extension
body_text:
— “I don’t think there will be a permanent solution,” former Republican Rep. Charlie Dent predicted during a Monday afternoon webinar hosted by DLA Piper , where he serves as senior policy adviser. “What will happen, I think, is there will be some kind of temporary extension.”

— Dent’s colleague, former Republican Sen. Richard Burr , who heads the firm’s health policy practice, agreed. “We’re either looking at a short-term extension because there’s some deal that’s in the works, probably deals with some income caps, probably deals with a few restrictions on what the money can be used for, or we’re looking at a one-year just clean extension that goes past the midterm election,” Burr said.

— Health insurance providers are lobbying for the subsidies to be extended, citing the increased cost that will fall to consumers if Congress is unable to reach a deal. Insurers plan to continue hammering the consumer impact, emphasizing subsidy extensions as the “most timely” way for lawmakers to support affordability in the individual market, a person familiar with their strategy told PI.

— What sort of language could make it into a bipartisan extension bill is an open question. The Senate is due to vote next week on an extension bill, but details remain sparse and obstacles remain.

— One potential sticking point is abortion coverage. Anti-abortion groups have spent months lobbying Republicans to reject any extension that doesn’t add new abortion restrictions to the ACA. But as our Playbook colleagues reported this morning , Planned Parenthood and Reproductive Freedom for All have now declared their opposition to any bill that includes such restrictions.

— Whatever Congress does, this isn’t the last of the health insurance debate, Burr said.

— “The actions that are taken over the next several weeks or months are going to be very crucial in the makeup and the outcome of the [2026] elections,” he said.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. What outcome do you think is most likely on ACA subsidies? Send tips to dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

THE TRUMP EFFECT: Corporate lobbying in Donald Trump’s Washington looks very different than it has in years past, Isabel Gottlieb reports for Bloomberg Law .

— These days companies are taking extra care with their public statements to avoid angering a vindictive White House. And with Congress largely deferring to Trump on policy questions, appealing directly to the Oval Office is more important than ever, Gottlieb reports.

— Especially important when crafting a message is finding common ground with the administration. “Jason Duva, general counsel at Factorial Energy, which makes electrical vehicle batteries, said he’s adapting by approaching the federal government on issues they’ll be interested in…For example, he’s talking to the government about drones—which fit the administration’s interest in national security, and also run on batteries.”

ICYMI: Last week, the Trump transition team finally revealed the list of 46 individual donors who contributed to the transition effort. The list, reported by Ken Bensinger and David Fahrenthold of The New York Times , includes billionaires like Jeff Yass and Paul Singer and other familiar names who went on to be appointed to administration positions.

— Donors who now serve in the administration include Education Secretary Linda McMahon , Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff , Justice Department official Stanley Woodward and U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio Dominick Gerace.

MAN ON THE INSIDE: White House artificial intelligence and crypto czar David Sacks has used his position to advance policies benefiting Silicon Valley while simultaneously retaining financial interests in many companies that stand to gain from the Trump administration’s position towards tech and AI, Cecilia Kang , Tripp Mickle , Ryan Mac , David Yaffe-Bellany and Theodore Schleifer report for The New York Times .

— Sacks, co-founder of venture capital firm Craft Ventures , “has 708 tech investments, including at least 449 stakes in companies with ties to artificial intelligence that could be aided directly or indirectly by his policies, according to a New York Times analysis of his financial disclosures.”

— In one instance, Sacks planned for his podcast “All-In” to host a July AI summit featuring the president. The original plan involved asking potential sponsors to pay $1 million for access to a private reception with the president. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles ultimately stepped in and prevented “All-In” from serving as the sole host of the event. A spokesperson for Sacks said the “conflict of interest narrative is false” and that he has complied with government and ethics rules.

PEACE PROFITEERING: As the Trump administration seeks an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine, wealthy businessmen in both countries are treating the peace talks as an economic opportunity — a position that seems to be shared by Trump’s negotiators, Drew Hinshaw , Benoit Faucon , Rebecca Ballhaus , Thomas Grove and Joe Parkinson report for The Wall Street Journal .

— Russian billionaires close to Vladimir Putin have sent representatives to meet with American companies interested in rare-earth mining and energy deals, and Exxon Mobil has met with Russia’s largest state energy company, they report.

— “Elsewhere, a cast of businessmen close to the Trump administration have been looking to position themselves as new economic links between the U.S. and Russia. Gentry Beach , a college friend of Donald Trump Jr. and campaign donor to his father, has been in talks to acquire a stake in a Russian Arctic gas project if it is released from sanctions. Another Trump donor, Stephen P. Lynch , paid $600,000 this year to a lobbyist close to Trump Jr. [ Ches McDowell ] who is helping him seek a Treasury Department license to buy the Nord Stream 2 pipeline from a Russian state-owned company.”

ONE TO WATCH: If Netflix is successful in its bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, the streamer may find itself subject to an antitrust review prompted by skeptical White House officials who disapprove of the deal, Charles Gasparino reports for the New York Post .

— Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos and company lobbyists have been making the case in Washington that acquiring the studio that owns HBO , CNN and streaming platform HBO Max wouldn’t violate antitrust laws because “streaming video is now so ubiquitous that it can’t be cornered and price gauged in the traditional sense.”
