Health lobbyists press for ACA extension

By DANIEL BARNES and CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

12/01/2025 07:50 PM EST

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

12 DAYS OF ACA SUBSIDIES: ‘Tis the season in Washington, where lawmakers have returned from Thanksgiving break to answer the burning question of this month: What happens to expiring Affordable Care Act subsidies? Health insurance premiums are set to go up for millions of Americans on New Year’s Day if Congress is unable to reach an agreement to extend the subsidies. With just 12 legislative days to go, health insurers and special interest groups are making sure their voices are part of the conversation.

— “I don’t think there will be a permanent solution,” former Republican Rep. Charlie Dent predicted during a Monday afternoon webinar hosted by DLA Piper, where he serves as senior policy adviser. “What will happen, I think, is there will be some kind of temporary extension.”

— Dent’s colleague, former Republican Sen. Richard Burr, who heads the firm’s health policy practice, agreed. “We’re either looking at a short-term extension because there’s some deal that’s in the works, probably deals with some income caps, probably deals with a few restrictions on what the money can be used for, or we’re looking at a one-year just clean extension that goes past the midterm election,” Burr said.

— Health insurance providers are lobbying for the subsidies to be extended, citing the increased cost that will fall to consumers if Congress is unable to reach a deal. Insurers plan to continue hammering the consumer impact, emphasizing subsidy extensions as the “most timely” way for lawmakers to support affordability in the individual market, a person familiar with their strategy told PI.

— What sort of language could make it into a bipartisan extension bill is an open question. The Senate is due to vote next week on an extension bill, but details remain sparse and obstacles remain.

— One potential sticking point is abortion coverage. Anti-abortion groups have spent months lobbying Republicans to reject any extension that doesn’t add new abortion restrictions to the ACA. But as our Playbook colleagues reported this morning, Planned Parenthood and Reproductive Freedom for All have now declared their opposition to any bill that includes such restrictions.

— Whatever Congress does, this isn’t the last of the health insurance debate, Burr said.

— “The actions that are taken over the next several weeks or months are going to be very crucial in the makeup and the outcome of the [2026] elections,” he said.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. What outcome do you think is most likely on ACA subsidies? Send tips to dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17. And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko.

THE TRUMP EFFECT: Corporate lobbying in Donald Trump’s Washington looks very different than it has in years past, Isabel Gottlieb reports for Bloomberg Law.

— These days companies are taking extra care with their public statements to avoid angering a vindictive White House. And with Congress largely deferring to Trump on policy questions, appealing directly to the Oval Office is more important than ever, Gottlieb reports.

— Especially important when crafting a message is finding common ground with the administration. “Jason Duva, general counsel at Factorial Energy, which makes electrical vehicle batteries, said he’s adapting by approaching the federal government on issues they’ll be interested in…For example, he’s talking to the government about drones—which fit the administration’s interest in national security, and also run on batteries.”

ICYMI: Last week, the Trump transition team finally revealed the list of 46 individual donors who contributed to the transition effort. The list, reported by Ken Bensinger and David Fahrenthold of The New York Times, includes billionaires like Jeff Yass and Paul Singer and other familiar names who went on to be appointed to administration positions.

— Donors who now serve in the administration include Education Secretary Linda McMahon, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, Justice Department official Stanley Woodward and U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio Dominick Gerace.

MAN ON THE INSIDE: White House artificial intelligence and crypto czar David Sacks has used his position to advance policies benefiting Silicon Valley while simultaneously retaining financial interests in many companies that stand to gain from the Trump administration’s position towards tech and AI, Cecilia Kang, Tripp Mickle, Ryan Mac, David Yaffe-Bellany and Theodore Schleifer report for The New York Times.

— Sacks, co-founder of venture capital firm Craft Ventures, “has 708 tech investments, including at least 449 stakes in companies with ties to artificial intelligence that could be aided directly or indirectly by his policies, according to a New York Times analysis of his financial disclosures.”

— In one instance, Sacks planned for his podcast “All-In” to host a July AI summit featuring the president. The original plan involved asking potential sponsors to pay $1 million for access to a private reception with the president. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles ultimately stepped in and prevented “All-In” from serving as the sole host of the event. A spokesperson for Sacks said the “conflict of interest narrative is false” and that he has complied with government and ethics rules.

PEACE PROFITEERING: As the Trump administration seeks an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine, wealthy businessmen in both countries are treating the peace talks as an economic opportunity — a position that seems to be shared by Trump’s negotiators, Drew Hinshaw, Benoit Faucon, Rebecca Ballhaus, Thomas Grove and Joe Parkinson report for The Wall Street Journal.

— Russian billionaires close to Vladimir Putin have sent representatives to meet with American companies interested in rare-earth mining and energy deals, and Exxon Mobil has met with Russia’s largest state energy company, they report.

— “Elsewhere, a cast of businessmen close to the Trump administration have been looking to position themselves as new economic links between the U.S. and Russia. Gentry Beach, a college friend of Donald Trump Jr. and campaign donor to his father, has been in talks to acquire a stake in a Russian Arctic gas project if it is released from sanctions. Another Trump donor, Stephen P. Lynch, paid $600,000 this year to a lobbyist close to Trump Jr. [Ches McDowell] who is helping him seek a Treasury Department license to buy the Nord Stream 2 pipeline from a Russian state-owned company.”

LEA-VING PARAMOUNT: DeDe Lea is stepping down as the top global lobbyist for entertainment giant Paramount after nearly 30 years with the company or its predecessors.

— Lea’s departure in January will come less than six months after the completion of Paramount’s acquisition by Skydance Corporation , and despite signing a new deal last December to stay on as head of global public policy and government of the combined company through the end of 2028, according to The Hollywood Reporter .

— “After an incredible journey of nearly three decades, numerous U.S. administrations, global political change and many iterations of Paramount, it’s time for me to start a new chapter,” Lea wrote in a farewell email to staff this morning obtained by PI.

— Lea first joined the media conglomerate Viacom in 1997 as vice president of government relations. She rose to become the company’s global head of government affairs, and maintained the role of top lobbyist following Viacom’s 2019 merger with CBS Corporation (the merged company later became Paramount Global ).

— Lea’s role, which has spanned major changes to the way people consume movies, TV and news — as well as several high-profile mergers that were not without controversy — placed her on the “front lines of some of the most important moments in politics, media and entertainment,” she wrote in her note to staff.

— “I am particularly proud of the way that we have deepened Paramount’s relationships with political leaders globally, and how we diligently worked to help the company successfully navigate an ever-evolving global political landscape,” she added of her time with the company.

— Lea made no mention of where she may land next or who would succeed her in the role. Makan Delrahim , who previously led DOJ’s antitrust division during the first Trump administration, assumed oversight of Paramount’s lobbying team when he became Paramount’s chief legal officer in October. Lea declined to comment through a spokesperson for Paramount.

ANTHROPIC ADDS ANOTHER OUTSIDE FIRM: Anthropic , the company behind artificial intelligence chatbot Claude , retained Fierce Government Relations last month as part of the AI firm’s D.C. lobbying expansion. The team of lobbyists working on the account includes Patrick Clifton , who served as a special assistant to the president for operations during Donald Trump ’s first presidency.

— The firm began lobbying for Anthropic on Nov. 1 on a slew of policy issues related to AI. They include the White House’s AI roadmap, safety and governance matters, national security, export controls, and energy generation, transmission, permitting and domestic infrastructure investments, according to lobbying disclosures.

— Fierce is the third firm in Anthropic’s stable of outside lobbyists, and the second new outside firm this year after the AI giant hired Continental Strategy in April. Anthropic has been teasing plans to bolster its footprint in Washington, and during the third quarter of the year the company cracked $1 million in quarterly lobbying outlays for the first time.

— The pair, who pleaded guilty in 2022 for their role in a similar scheme in Ohio, “were sentenced to one year of probation by a Wayne County judge Monday. — “The nation’s biggest warehouse club chain is among dozens of companies to file lawsuits in a US trade court since late October challenging President Donald Trump’s use of an economic emergency powers law to impose the levies, according to court records. It’s one of the biggest corporate players to jump into a fight largely driven this year by small businesses and Democratic state officials.”

— “The Supreme Court heard arguments on Trump’s tariffs on Nov. 5. The justices put the fight on a fast-tracked schedule but didn’t say when they intend to rule. In the meantime, businesses of all sizes have brought cases pressing similar legal claims with the goal of avoiding uncertainty about their eligibility for refunds if the court rules against Trump,” including cosmetics giant Revlon and motorcycle manufacturer Kawasaki .

TAKING STOCK: “White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and his immediate family dumped seven-figures’ worth of stock in August — including shares of several defense contractors — to comply with federal conflicts of interest rules and laws,” per NOTUS’ Dave Levinthal .

— “Miller and his wife, Katie Miller , who served as an adviser for DOGE before leaving the White House in May, jettisoned shares of Amazon (up to $515,000), Palantir Technologies Inc. (up to $250,000), GE Aerospace (up to $250,000), Microsoft (up to $50,000) and IonQ (up to $50,000),” according to a government ethics disclosure .

— Miller — a key architect of Trump’s immigration and homeland security agenda — “reported selling these and other stock shares on Aug. 14 — more than nine months after Donald Trump first announced that Miller would serve in the dual White House roles of deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser.”

— “The White House did not answer several specific questions about Miller’s personal finances, including why he invested in and held defense contractor stocks for months after his White House appointment.” He “divested from stock holdings early in the administration per the Office of Government Ethics and White House counsel guidance. There are no conflicts,” White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson told NOTUS.

— Jaarda, who plans on registering to lobby, also has insights about key players on the Hill, especially as it pertains to the way Johnson has managed to navigate Republicans’ razor-thin House majority. “I think understanding that process, and what moves the needle on certain issues, hopefully will be very helpful” to the firm’s clients, he told PI.

A HOUSE DIVIDED: K Street is keeping a close eye on Speaker Mike Johnson as his grip on his conference appears to be weakening — and raising the possibility that the dysfunction in the House could stall their clients’ legislative interests.

— “[Johnson] has been doing a high-wire act since the beginning, and did a remarkable job under the circumstances, but it does seem like something has changed,” one Republican lobbyist granted anonymity to speak candidly told PI.

— A chaotic majority is nothing new for Johnson, who ascended to the speakership in 2023 after former Speaker Kevin McCarthy was ousted in an effort led by fellow Republican Matt Gaetz . Criticism from within his own party has mounted in recent weeks following the longest government shutdown in history and a spate of electoral losses for Republicans. In an interview this week, Rep. Elise Stefanik told the Wall Street Journal Johnson no longer has the votes to remain speaker were a new election to be held.

— “The honeymoon is over,” another GOP lobbyist said. “We’re turning into the end of a very, very tumultuous year with the rough waters of the Trump presidency — the fast pace, the political fallout and ramifications, and the anticipation and anxiety of what might be a difficult election next year. No one could master and weather that perfectly, because it’s incredibly difficult.”

— Any attempt to remove Johnson would eat up valuable legislative time and, if successful, could derail the work of Congress for weeks. It took the House 22 days to select Johnson after McCarthy’s ouster. And time at the start of 2026 will be extra valuable for legislative work before members shift their attention to campaigning for the midterms.

— “Lets face it, Congress isn’t great at getting stuff done under the best of circumstances, so if you take away a lot of time it’s going to be difficult,” the first lobbyist said. “We may have a very tight window in the very beginning of the year to really get in anything related to appropriations or the NDAA or anything like that.”

— Even absent an effort to replace Johnson as speaker, dissatisfied Republican members are hindering leadership’s ability to bring bills to the floor. Yesterday, leadership postponed a scheduled vote on the SCORE Act , a bill supported by the White House that would create new regulations for compensating student athletes.

— Still, chaos in the House is largely business as usual, lobbyists say. And with the way Donald Trump governs, Congress is often not the best route for advancing clients’ goals.

— “More and more, the administration and the agency work is way more important to our clients, and setting up for the moments in a presidency when they do get to do their one priority,” said Sam Geduldig , a Republican lobbyist at CGCN . “You need years to set it up so you can get your provisions included in that big bill, whatever it might be, whoever the administration, whatever party. And that’s why you lobby Congress, to set the frame for when that moment happens.”

title: Warner Bros. megadeal triggers a lobbying bonanza
body_text:
WHO’S WORKING FOR WHO: Lobbying armies are being amassed in real time as the media giants vying to purchase Warner Bros. Discovery — Netflix and Paramount Skydance — game out the Washington landscape in pursuit of their prize.

— Netflix’s nearly $83 billion deal to acquire the legendary Hollywood studio was already facing scrutiny from leaders in Washington before Paramount Skydance upped the ante this morning with a hostile takeover bid of its own .

— While Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos has lobbied President Donald Trump personally to support the streaming giant’s bid for WBD, the president told reporters at the Paramount-hosted Kennedy Center Honors last night that the Netflix deal “could be a problem.” Trump said he’d be involved in the transaction — one of many wrinkles for the army of lobbyists already working for parties involved in or affected by the deal.

— Besides his mid-November meeting with Trump, Sarandos went to the White House again Tuesday, three days before the announcement, according to three people familiar with the visit, including a person who saw him. Clete Willems , Netflix’s chief global affairs officer, accompanied Sarandos to the White House, according to that person.

— A Netflix spokesperson said that Sarandos didn’t meet with Trump last Tuesday. Asked if Trump met with Sarandos during his visit, an official said the White House does not comment “on private meetings that may or may not have happened.”

— Both parties jockeying to buy Warner Bros. Discovery already have serious lobbying firepower. Netflix brought on Willems, a deputy director of the National Economic Council during Trump’s first term, in April. On Monday, Netflix announced another new hire with ties to the White House. Virginia Boney Moore , who served as special assistant to the president in Trump’s first Office of Legislative Affairs, joined the company from Amazon as director for federal affairs.

title: Gowdy joins Miller Strategies
body_text:
MILLER STAFFS UP: Former Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-S.C.) is joining Miller Strategies , the lobbying shop led by top GOP fundraiser Jeff Miller , as of counsel. The former federal prosecutor served four terms in the House, including as chair of the House Oversight Committee and Benghazi Committee, before retiring in 2019.

— Shortly after leaving office, Gowdy rejoined his former law firm, Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough , as a partner in the white collar defense and government investigations practice. He was briefly tapped to be a member of President Donald Trump ’s defense team during his first impeachment, and lobbied the president for a pardon of an entertainment executive over a round of golf last year.

— More recently, Gowdy has been the host of “Sunday Night in America with Trey Gowdy” on Fox News and is one of several political power players who works for the law firm Oberheiden P.C. It’s unclear whether he will register to lobby at Miller Strategies.

— Miller Strategies has also added another Trump White House alum to its roster. Natalie McIntyre , who most recently worked in the White House’s legislative affairs office, has joined the firm as a principal. McIntyre served in Trump’s first term as well, along with her new Miller colleagues George Caram , Ashley Gunn , Jonny Hiler , Stefan Passantino and Luke Wallwork .

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE BREAK: Netflix brought on a prominent GOP antitrust lobbyist last month as the streaming giant works to fend off competition concerns related to its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery ’s studios and streaming assets.

— The Gibson Group ’s Joseph Gibson , who previously worked in DOJ’s Antitrust Division in addition to serving as a top lawyer for the House Judiciary Committee, began working on tech antitrust issues for the streamer on Dec. 12, according to a disclosure filed last week. That was days after reports of the Netflix-WBD merger set off alarm bells across Washington .

— Gibson will join an outside lobbying team for Netflix that includes Monument Advocacy , Miller & Chevalier and Ballard Partners. Ballard is working to help Netflix win regulatory approval despite also being registered to lobby for Paramount Skydance , which has mounted a hostile takeover bid for WBD.

— Netflix’s in-house roster includes Clete Willems , a deputy director of the National Economic Council during Trump’s first term, and Emma Rindels-Hill , a former Kevin McCarthy aide. Virginia Boney Moore , who served as special assistant to the president in Trump’s first Office of Legislative Affairs, also joined Netflix last month.

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

5 YEARS LATER: In the wake of the attack on the Capitol five years ago today, dozens of major corporations announced plans to halt or review their political donations to the 147 Republican lawmakers who voted against certifying Joe Biden ’s victory in the 2020 election.

— Half a decade later, just 10 of those companies have upheld their pledges to stop contributing to congressional election objectors via their corporate PACs, according to Popular Information ’s Judd Legum , Rebecca Crosby and Noel Sims , who have been tracking this issue over the years.

— That group includes Farmers Insurance , Clorox , Whirlpool and Expedia Group , which all said they would suspend all political contributions after the Jan. 6 attack. (Whirlpool shuttered its corporate PAC in 2023.)

— Meanwhile Airbnb , Nike , Lyft , Qurate Retail (now known as QVC ) and Eversource Energy have all upheld their initial pledges to cut off donations specifically to election objectors, per Popular Information. Holland & Hart , the law and lobbying firm that employs former Trump EPA chief Andrew Wheeler , has similarly stuck to its promise not to donate to any of the election objectors.

UNLEASH THE WALL STREET EXECS: Lobbyists for banks and cryptocurrency companies have been brawling for months over a landmark bill that would overhaul how digital assets are regulated. Now, bank CEOs from around the country are about to wade into the fight, per our friends at Morning Money .

— The clash centers on whether crypto exchanges should be allowed to pay an annual percentage yield via rewards programs to customers who hold stablecoins. In a new twist, the American Bankers Association is now trying to harness the political capital of its members by urging bank leaders to press lawmakers for bill language that would ban crypto exchanges from doing so.

— The issue “demands immediate action from every bank leader in the country,” ABA President Rob Nichols wrote in a letter to CEOs . “We need you — along with your staff and, where appropriate, your customers — to contact Congress and make our voices heard.”

— The intensifying lobbying push — and pointed language — is notable coming from the ABA, which represents a huge array of banking institutions that are often at odds with each other over financial policy. The group tends to shy away from taking hardline stances on hot-button issues, and its approach to the yield fight illustrates that there is unity across the banking sector on the matter.

— Digital asset firms, an increasingly powerful force in Washington, are fighting back.

A coalition of crypto companies led by the Blockchain Association wrote in a letter to senators last month that proposals to crack down on exchanges’ rewards programs “would reopen a settled issue, undermine a carefully negotiated compromise, reduce consumer choice, suppress competition, and inject uncertainty into the implementation of a new law before regulations have even been proposed.”

HEADS UP: “Longtime climate advocate Sen. Ed Markey is demanding answers from President Donald Trump over the role that oil companies might have played in his decision to attack Venezuela and arrest its president,” E&E News’ Amelia Davidson reports.

— “In a Monday letter to Trump , Markey urged the White House to ‘cease all hostilities against Venezuela,’ seek approval from Congress for further military actions and inform Congress about how the administration plans to treat the country’s extensive oil resources.”

— The Massachusetts Democrat zeroed in on a pledge from Trump following Nicolás Maduro ’s arrest that American oil companies would “go in, spend billions of dollars, fix the badly broken infrastructure, the oil infrastructure and start making money for the country,” and his later revelations that he’d spoken to U.S. oil companies “before and after” the operation.

— POLITICO reported Monday that Trump officials had been scheduling calls with oil companies to press them to resume oil production in Venezuela.

— “It is especially troubling and unacceptable that, by your own account, domestic oil executives were informed of these plans before Members of Congress,” Markey wrote, accusing the president of “admittedly acting on behalf of private oil companies, to increase their profits.”

Mahoney , formerly a senior legal executive at Microsoft and deputy U.S. trade representative during President Trump’s first term, will join Meta as its new chief legal officer ,” according to an internal note viewed by Axios’ Sara Fischer .

— “Mahoney replaces Jennifer Newstead , who announced late last year that she would be leaving Meta after more than five years to become the general counsel at Apple . MILLER STAFFS UP: Former Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-S.C.) is joining Miller Strategies, the lobbying shop led by top GOP fundraiser Jeff Miller, as of counsel. The former federal prosecutor served four terms in the House, including as chair of the House Oversight Committee and Benghazi Committee, before retiring in 2019.

— Shortly after leaving office, Gowdy rejoined his former law firm, Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough, as a partner in the white collar defense and government investigations practice. He was briefly tapped to be a member of President Donald Trump’s defense team during his first impeachment, and lobbied the president for a pardon of an entertainment executive over a round of golf last year.

— More recently, Gowdy has been the host of “Sunday Night in America with Trey Gowdy” on Fox News and is one of several political power players who works for the law firm Oberheiden P.C. It’s unclear whether he will register to lobby at Miller Strategies.

— Miller Strategies has also added another Trump White House alum to its roster. Natalie McIntyre, who most recently worked in the White House’s legislative affairs office, has joined the firm as a principal. McIntyre served in Trump’s first term as well, along with her new Miller colleagues George Caram, Ashley Gunn, Jonny Hiler, Stefan Passantino and Luke Wallwork.

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE BREAK: Netflix brought on a prominent GOP antitrust lobbyist last month as the streaming giant works to fend off competition concerns related to its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studios and streaming assets.

— The Gibson Group’s Joseph Gibson, who previously worked in DOJ’s Antitrust Division in addition to serving as a top lawyer for the House Judiciary Committee, began working on tech antitrust issues for the streamer on Dec. 12, according to a disclosure filed last week. That was days after reports of the Netflix-WBD merger set off alarm bells across Washington.

— Gibson will join an outside lobbying team for Netflix that includes Monument Advocacy, Miller & Chevalier and Ballard Partners. Ballard is working to help Netflix win regulatory approval despite also being registered to lobby for Paramount Skydance, which has mounted a hostile takeover bid for WBD.

— Netflix’s in-house roster includes Clete Willems, a deputy director of the National Economic Council during Trump’s first term, and Emma Rindels-Hill, a former Kevin McCarthy aide. Virginia Boney Moore, who served as special assistant to the president in Trump’s first Office of Legislative Affairs, also joined Netflix last month.

5 YEARS LATER: In the wake of the attack on the Capitol five years ago today, dozens of major corporations announced plans to halt or review their political donations to the 147 Republican lawmakers who voted against certifying Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election.

— Half a decade later, just 10 of those companies have upheld their pledges to stop contributing to congressional election objectors via their corporate PACs, according to Popular Information’s Judd Legum, Rebecca Crosby and Noel Sims, who have been tracking this issue over the years.

— That group includes Farmers Insurance, Clorox, Whirlpool and Expedia Group, which all said they would suspend all political contributions after the Jan. 6 attack. (Whirlpool shuttered its corporate PAC in 2023.)

— Meanwhile Airbnb, Nike, Lyft, Qurate Retail (now known as QVC) and Eversource Energy have all upheld their initial pledges to cut off donations specifically to election objectors, per Popular Information. Holland & Hart, the law and lobbying firm that employs former Trump EPA chief Andrew Wheeler, has similarly stuck to its promise not to donate to any of the election objectors.

UNLEASH THE WALL STREET EXECS: Lobbyists for banks and cryptocurrency companies have been brawling for months over a landmark bill that would overhaul how digital assets are regulated. Now, bank CEOs from around the country are about to wade into the fight, per our friends at Morning Money.

— The clash centers on whether crypto exchanges should be allowed to pay an annual percentage yield via rewards programs to customers who hold stablecoins. In a new twist, the American Bankers Association is now trying to harness the political capital of its members by urging bank leaders to press lawmakers for bill language that would ban crypto exchanges from doing so.

— The issue “demands immediate action from every bank leader in the country,” ABA President Rob Nichols wrote in a letter to CEOs. “We need you — along with your staff and, where appropriate, your customers — to contact Congress and make our voices heard.”

— The intensifying lobbying push — and pointed language — is notable coming from the ABA, which represents a huge array of banking institutions that are often at odds with each other over financial policy. The group tends to shy away from taking hardline stances on hot-button issues, and its approach to the yield fight illustrates that there is unity across the banking sector on the matter.

— Digital asset firms, an increasingly powerful force in Washington, are fighting back.

A coalition of crypto companies led by the Blockchain Association wrote in a letter to senators last month that proposals to crack down on exchanges’ rewards programs “would reopen a settled issue, undermine a carefully negotiated compromise, reduce consumer choice, suppress competition, and inject uncertainty into the implementation of a new law before regulations have even been proposed.”

— “In a Monday letter to Trump, Markey urged the White House to ‘cease all hostilities against Venezuela,’ seek approval from Congress for further military actions and inform Congress about how the administration plans to treat the country’s extensive oil resources.”

— The Massachusetts Democrat zeroed in on a pledge from Trump following Nicolás Maduro’s arrest that American oil companies would “go in, spend billions of dollars, fix the badly broken infrastructure, the oil infrastructure and start making money for the country,” and his later revelations that he’d spoken to U.S. oil companies “before and after” the operation.

— POLITICO reported Monday that Trump officials had been scheduling calls with oil companies to press them to resume oil production in Venezuela.

— “It is especially troubling and unacceptable that, by your own account, domestic oil executives were informed of these plans before Members of Congress,” Markey wrote, accusing the president of “admittedly acting on behalf of private oil companies, to increase their profits.”

title: Ballard name gets pulled into Mangione case
body_text:
IN THE COURTS: Lawyers for Luigi Mangione, the accused murderer of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, are making a novel argument to get their client’s death penalty case thrown out: They’re claiming that Attorney General Pam Bondi’s previous employment with Ballard Partners has created a conflict of interest.

— Mangione appeared in a New York courtroom today for a hearing where a federal judge set a potential trial date and ruled on an evidentiary issue. But the judge did not address the defense’s tenuous argument that Bondi’s six years at Ballard, which registered to lobby for UnitedHealthcare in 2024, is sufficient grounds to dismiss Mangione’s indictment.

— Ballard signed UnitedHealthcare as a client while Bondi was still working at the firm in August 2024, four months before Thompson’s murder. Citing that timeline, Mangione’s defense team accuses Bondi of having a “personal financial interest” due to a retirement account administered by Ballard, and seeking to “avenge the death of the CEO of her former firm’s client.”

— Prosecutors blasted the defense’s argument in a separate filing this week , calling the description of Bondi’s financial ties to Ballard “incomplete and misleading” and clarifying that the firm has not contributed to her 401(k) since her departure.

— “There is nothing in the Attorney General’s financial disclosure form that suggests receipt

of any ongoing income, distributions, partnership draws, or remuneration from Ballard Partners in any form,” prosecutors wrote. They added that there is “no factual basis” to claim that corporate interests influenced the decision to seek the death penalty and the defense’s “insinuations otherwise rest on an inaccurate financial narrative.”

— Ballard Partners, currently the top lobbying firm in Washington by revenue, declined to comment.

MERGER MOVE: Lobbying firms Covenant Government Affairs and SBL Strategies have merged and will operate under the Covenant name, the newly combined firm announced this week.

— The combined firm will be led by a team of four founding partners: former Rep. Jeff Duncan , who chaired the House Energy Subcommittee, retired Navy Rear Admiral John Roberti , Jeff Loveng and Chad Bradley . Clients include energy companies Constellation Energy , Expand Energy and Southern Gas , as well as American Airlines and public transit and defense systems manufacturer Cubic .

The next chance is on Wednesday when the court will release its next batch of opinions. GRAND OPENING: Two Commerce Department alums have opened a new consulting firm focused on international trade policy and international government relations. Parapet Advisors is led by founders Ashlyn Holeyfield and Emily Gershon , both of whom previously served in the International Trade Administration within Commerce.

— Holeyfield spent more than seven years at the ITA, leaving earlier this year as the deputy director of the office of trade agreements negotiations and compliance. Gershon similarly spent more than six years at the ITA, where she served as a team lead for trade agreements negotiations and compliance.

IN THE COURTS: Lawyers for Luigi Mangione, the accused murderer of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, are making a novel argument to get their client’s death penalty case thrown out: They’re claiming that Attorney General Pam Bondi’s previous employment with Ballard Partners has created a conflict of interest.

— Mangione appeared in a New York courtroom today for a hearing where a federal judge set a potential trial date and ruled on an evidentiary issue. But the judge did not address the defense’s tenuous argument that Bondi’s six years at Ballard, which registered to lobby for UnitedHealthcare in 2024, is sufficient grounds to dismiss Mangione’s indictment.

— Ballard signed UnitedHealthcare as a client while Bondi was still working at the firm in August 2024, four months before Thompson’s murder. Citing that timeline, Mangione’s defense team accuses Bondi of having a “personal financial interest” due to a retirement account administered by Ballard, and seeking to “avenge the death of the CEO of her former firm’s client.”

— Prosecutors blasted the defense’s argument in a separate filing this week, calling the description of Bondi’s financial ties to Ballard “incomplete and misleading” and clarifying that the firm has not contributed to her 401(k) since her departure.

— “There is nothing in the Attorney General’s financial disclosure form that suggests receipt

of any ongoing income, distributions, partnership draws, or remuneration from Ballard Partners in any form,” prosecutors wrote. They added that there is “no factual basis” to claim that corporate interests influenced the decision to seek the death penalty and the defense’s “insinuations otherwise rest on an inaccurate financial narrative.”

— Ballard Partners, currently the top lobbying firm in Washington by revenue, declined to comment.

title: Kalshi opens a DC office
body_text:
FIRST IN PI : Kalshi has opened an office in D.C. as the online betting giant continues to grow its footprint in the nation’s capital. The betting platform has tapped Biden administration and Hill alum John Bivona as its first head of federal government relations.

— Bivona most recently worked for Kalshi’s newest outside lobbying firm, Intersection Government Relations . Before that, he worked at Rasky Partners following a stint as DHS’ White House liaison during the Biden administration and on the Biden campaign. He also served as chief of staff to Antonio Delgado , who served in the House before becoming New York’s lieutenant governor in 2022.

— Kalshi’s expansion in D.C. began during the Biden administration when the platform’s regulator, the CFTC, sought to clamp down on so-called event contracts, which allow prediction markets to take wagers on everything from awards shows to elections and, increasingly, sports. A 2024 court ruling opened the floodgates for prediction markets, and the sector has flourished under President Donald Trump .

— That popularity has sparked a fight with casinos and critics in state and federal government who have sought to challenge the industry’s incursion into sports betting. Late last year, companies including Kalshi, Crypto.com , Coinbase and Robinhood launched the Coalition for Prediction Markets , and earlier this month the coalition hired former Reps. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-N.Y.) and Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) as its president and senior adviser, respectively.

— Kalshi registered its first in-house lobbyist over the summer, and the platform reported dropping $615,000 on federal lobbying last year — down from $670,000 the year before.

FIRST IN PI II — WHAT’S IN A NAME: Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck is revamping its leadership hierarchy to elevate top leaders of the law and lobbying firm’s government relations practice. The firm has named eight of its top lobbyists as principals of public policy, a new title that is the equivalent of an equity shareholder for non-attorneys — though without an ownership stake or fee-sharing arrangement.

— Though the American Bar Association generally bars non-lawyers from holding ownership stakes in a law firm, Brownstein’s lobbying practice brings in “a significant percentage” of the firm’s overall revenues, which firm leaders wanted to recognize, said Will Moschella , who co-leads the federal lobbying practice.

— The new principals — who will take on an expanded role in strategic planning for the firm — include Moschella’s co-leader atop the lobbying practice, Nadeam Elshami . Samantha Carl-Yoder and former Rep. title: Biofuels use Iowa visit to woo Trump
body_text:
ETHANOL FRUSTRATIONS: As President Donald Trump travels to Iowa today to speak about energy and the economy, “ tensions remain high over the future of ethanol sales ” after the collapse last week of an eleventh-hour push to allow year-round sales of E15 as part of Congress’ spending bill, per POLITICO ’s Grace Yarrow .

— “The failed effort left lobbyists feeling betrayed by the White House and farm-state lawmakers feeling frustrated with a key agriculture industry group, according to three people granted anonymity to discuss behind-the-scenes conversations. The National Corn Growers Association rankled Midwestern Republicans on Wednesday when it dismissed the effectiveness” of a new working group set up by House Republicans as a consolation.

— “During a House Agriculture GOP member meeting the following day, several lawmakers said they felt thrown under the bus by NCGA’s reaction to E15 being excluded from the funding package, calling the statement ‘unhinged,’ according to two of the people familiar with the talks.”

— Iowa ethanol advocates appealed directly to the president ahead of his trip today, warning in a letter that corn farmers are at a “breaking point” and that “without immediate policy intervention to create new demand, we are looking at an avoidable decline in Iowa’s rural economy.”

— “Removing the outdated regulatory hurdle for E15 is exactly the type of government efficiency you’ve worked for,” leaders of the Iowa Corn Growers Association and the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association wrote to Trump. The trade groups also took out a full-page ad in today’s Des Moines Register reminding Trump of his previous support for E15 and declaring that “in Iowa, the intersection of economy and energy occurs at a place called E15.” (In what advocates are surely hoping is a good sign, the president slapped his autograph on a copy of the ad, per Reuters’ Jarrett Renshaw .)

— The overtures from the ethanol industry come on the heels of tens of millions of dollars dropped by biofuels advocates last year, in part to win year-round E15 sales. Top biofuel and ethanol producers including Bayer , POET , Koch Industries and Archer Daniels Midland collectively spent almost $28.4 million on federal lobbying last year, disclosures show.

— The National Corn Growers Association spent around $370,000 lobbying Washington in 2025, up from $330,000 a year prior. Ethanol trade group Growth Energy shelled out close to $2.5 million in 2025, compared with $2.3 million the year before, meanwhile fellow biofuel lobby Renewable Fuels Association spent almost $1.1 million — down from nearly $1.6 million in 2024.

‘That’s bad for him to say’: Trump puts Paxton on notice in Texas Senate primary

By DANIEL LIPPMAN , CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES

01/28/2026 06:12 PM EST

Presented by

FIRST IN PI : The debate about banning members of Congress from trading stocks has jumped to the campaign trail. Former Rep. Colin Allred (D-Texas), who is in a heated primary against Rep. Julie Johnson , has bragged about how he never traded any stocks during his six years in Congress, Daniel L. reports.

— His spokesperson said Johnson’s more of a Johnny-come-lately on the issue. “Colin Allred never traded a single stock while serving in Congress — not because anyone required it, but because he believes public service demands putting the people’s interests ahead of personal gain,” Sandhya Raghavan said in a statement. “Meanwhile, Julie Johnson has actively traded stocks throughout her six years in the Texas Legislature and continued to do so as a member of Congress.”

— At a Jan. 14 House Administration Committee markup for congressional stock trading legislation, Johnson said she chose to divest, “not because the law required it, but because earning the trust of my constituents demands it.”

— She continued: “Full divestment is the only way to truly eliminate conflicts of interest, and that is why I took that step myself.”

— But Johnson, who was a successful small business owner and attorney before entering Congress last year, only fully started divesting her holdings in September after a bipartisan group of House lawmakers, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Chip Roy (R-Texas), introduced the Restore Trust in Congress Act , which would ban congressional stock trading. Ocasio-Cortez recently endorsed Johnson .

— Johnson also gained attention last spring for making dozens of stock sales the day before President Donald Trump ’s tariff “Liberation Day” which sent stock markets temporarily reeling. Her office didn’t respond to questions at the time about the sales.

— Her new vocal stance against stock trading in September was a reversal from Johnson’s practice of buying individual stocks the previous month; a spokesperson at the time called it an “ongoing process” to get rid of her holdings. She made almost 350 purchases, sales or exchanges of stock last year, which gave the lawmaker the unwanted distinction of being in the top 2 percent of all congressional traders.

— Johnson said in a statement to PI that her stock holdings are managed by independent third parties and that her divestment began last March and that she fully divested at the end of last year.

— “I came to Congress after years as a small business owner and attorney with complex, pre-existing financial holdings,” she added. “The law did not require me to divest—but I chose to do so because earning the trust of my constituents matters more than personal convenience. Divestment is a process, not a moment, and I completed it fully.”

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips and gossip. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

THE BRITISH ARE COMING: Prominent British strategic advisory firm Hanbury Strategy is planting a flag in D.C. Laura Dooley , the former longtime global lobbying chief for StubHub , will lead the new D.C. office.

— Hanbury was founded a decade ago by former David Cameron aide Ameet Gill and Paul Stephenson , a top spokesperson for the Brexit campaign. The firm is led by CEO Emilie Oldknow , a former executive director of the U.K.’s Labour Party and a former leader with the labor group UNISON . The firm, which has 130 staff across the globe, represents clients such as Blackstone , Coinbase , Epic Games , Workday , Microsoft , Nvidia , Spotify , Samsung and more.

— Though this will be the first outpost in the U.S. for Hanbury Strategy, their sister data and research firm Stack Data Strategy has done work here for years, including for the NRSC during the 2022 and 2024 cycles, according to FEC filings. Stack Data Strategy will continue to support Hanbury’s U.S. offerings.

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING: The network of super PACs funded by the crypto industry “said Wednesday it has grown its war chest to more than $190 million ahead of this fall’s midterm elections, a haul intended to push lawmakers to support industry-friendly legislation that is struggling to advance in the Senate,” POLITICO ’s Jasper Goodman reports.

— The trio of industry-backed super PACs, Fairshake , Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs , pulled in a $25 million contribution from Ripple and $24 million from venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz . “Its $193 million total, set to be reported in federal campaign finance filings that are due at the end of the month, also includes previously reported contributions from the crypto exchange Coinbase that total $50 million since the 2024 election,” per Jasper, marking the latest signal that the PAC network plans to remain a major player in this year’s midterms after funneling tens of millions of dollars into the 2024 election.

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING II : “Just six months ago, most congressional Republicans kept their distance from Elon Musk after the tech mogul’s messy political breakup with President Donald Trump and his feverish attempt to kill their signature megabill. Musk is persona non grata no longer , thanks to his mega checkbook and mega platform — both of which he is now using to influence the future of the GOP,” POLITICO ’s Meredith Lee Hill, Mia McCarthy and Jordain Carney write.

— “Republicans see his recent donation to a Kentucky Senate candidate as an encouraging sign that Musk will make good on his promises to back the GOP, and top House leaders are elated — especially those in charge of defending their razor-thin majority. Musk spent more than $260 million in the last election helping to elect Trump and Republicans.”

SIKE-EDELIC: “People who think psychedelic drugs are the key to treating intractable mental illness could not have been more psyched when Donald Trump named one of their own to lead the government’s health agencies. A year into his tenure, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has yet to expand access to the mind-altering drugs and advocates are starting to lose patience ,” POLITICO ’s Amanda Chu reports.

— “The advocates had every reason to expect quick action. Kennedy once put the drugs at the top of his list of unheralded treatments he planned to promote at the Health and Human Services Department, alongside ‘anything else that advances human health and can’t be patented by Pharma.’”

— “Since, Kennedy has occasionally reiterated his ambition, but hasn’t taken concrete steps to achieve it,” prompting worries among advocates that “their goals have been overshadowed by other Kennedy agenda items, related to food and vaccines, and that a chance to get psychedelic drugs to people who need them could be slipping away.”

NEED FOR SPEED: In the lead-up to last year’s House passage of a bipartisan permitting overhaul, more than 200 companies, associations and other entities reported lobbying on the issue , E&E News’ Timothy Cama reports.

— Lobbyists worked on the issue last quarter on behalf of “oil and gas firms, electric utilities, construction companies, tech interests, renewable energy, labor and green groups. A handful of companies — including Google and natural gas giant Williams Companies , retained new lobbying firms last year to push their cases on permitting. As attention turns toward the Senate, the lobbying is likely to stay at a strong pace — or even increase — as executives and advocates seek to shape a final deal.”

Julie Johnson’s flip-flop on congressional stock trading

By DANIEL LIPPMAN, CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

01/28/2026 06:12 PM EST

Presented by

FIRST IN PI: The debate about banning members of Congress from trading stocks has jumped to the campaign trail. Former Rep. Colin Allred (D-Texas), who is in a heated primary against Rep. Julie Johnson, has bragged about how he never traded any stocks during his six years in Congress, Daniel L. reports.

— His spokesperson said Johnson’s more of a Johnny-come-lately on the issue. “Colin Allred never traded a single stock while serving in Congress — not because anyone required it, but because he believes public service demands putting the people’s interests ahead of personal gain,” Sandhya Raghavan said in a statement. “Meanwhile, Julie Johnson has actively traded stocks throughout her six years in the Texas Legislature and continued to do so as a member of Congress.”

— At a Jan. 14 House Administration Committee markup for congressional stock trading legislation, Johnson said she chose to divest, “not because the law required it, but because earning the trust of my constituents demands it.”

— She continued: “Full divestment is the only way to truly eliminate conflicts of interest, and that is why I took that step myself.”

— But Johnson, who was a successful small business owner and attorney before entering Congress last year, only fully started divesting her holdings in September after a bipartisan group of House lawmakers, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Chip Roy (R-Texas), introduced the Restore Trust in Congress Act, which would ban congressional stock trading. Ocasio-Cortez recently endorsed Johnson.

— Johnson also gained attention last spring for making dozens of stock sales the day before President Donald Trump’s tariff “Liberation Day” which sent stock markets temporarily reeling. Her office didn’t respond to questions at the time about the sales.

— Her new vocal stance against stock trading in September was a reversal from Johnson’s practice of buying individual stocks the previous month; a spokesperson at the time called it an “ongoing process” to get rid of her holdings. She made almost 350 purchases, sales or exchanges of stock last year, which gave the lawmaker the unwanted distinction of being in the top 2 percent of all congressional traders.

— Johnson said in a statement to PI that her stock holdings are managed by independent third parties and that her divestment began last March and that she fully divested at the end of last year.

— “I came to Congress after years as a small business owner and attorney with complex, pre-existing financial holdings,” she added. “The law did not require me to divest—but I chose to do so because earning the trust of my constituents matters more than personal convenience. Divestment is a process, not a moment, and I completed it fully.”

The firm is led by CEO Emilie Oldknow, a former executive director of the U.K.’s Labour Party and a former leader with the labor group UNISON. The firm, which has 130 staff across the globe, represents clients such as Blackstone, Coinbase, Epic Games, Workday, Microsoft, Nvidia, Spotify, Samsung and more.

— Though this will be the first outpost in the U.S. for Hanbury Strategy, their sister data and research firm Stack Data Strategy has done work here for years, including for the NRSC during the 2022 and 2024 cycles, according to FEC filings. Stack Data Strategy will continue to support Hanbury’s U.S. offerings.

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING: The network of super PACs funded by the crypto industry “said Wednesday it has grown its war chest to more than $190 million ahead of this fall’s midterm elections, a haul intended to push lawmakers to support industry-friendly legislation that is struggling to advance in the Senate,” POLITICO’s Jasper Goodman reports.

— The trio of industry-backed super PACs, Fairshake, Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, pulled in a $25 million contribution from Ripple and $24 million from venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. “Its $193 million total, set to be reported in federal campaign finance filings that are due at the end of the month, also includes previously reported contributions from the crypto exchange Coinbase that total $50 million since the 2024 election,” per Jasper, marking the latest signal that the PAC network plans to remain a major player in this year’s midterms after funneling tens of millions of dollars into the 2024 election.

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING II: “Just six months ago, most congressional Republicans kept their distance from Elon Musk after the tech mogul’s messy political breakup with President Donald Trump and his feverish attempt to kill their signature megabill. Musk is persona non grata no longer, thanks to his mega checkbook and mega platform — both of which he is now using to influence the future of the GOP,” POLITICO’s Meredith Lee Hill, Mia McCarthy and Jordain Carney write.

— “Republicans see his recent donation to a Kentucky Senate candidate as an encouraging sign that Musk will make good on his promises to back the GOP, and top House leaders are elated — especially those in charge of defending their razor-thin majority. Musk spent more than $260 million in the last election helping to elect Trump and Republicans.”

SIKE-EDELIC: “People who think psychedelic drugs are the key to treating intractable mental illness could not have been more psyched when Donald Trump named one of their own to lead the government’s health agencies. A year into his tenure, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has yet to expand access to the mind-altering drugs and advocates are starting to lose patience,” POLITICO’s Amanda Chu reports.

— “The advocates had every reason to expect quick action. Kennedy once put the drugs at the top of his list of unheralded treatments he planned to promote at the Health and Human Services Department, alongside ‘anything else that advances human health and can’t be patented by Pharma.’”

— “Since, Kennedy has occasionally reiterated his ambition, but hasn’t taken concrete steps to achieve it,” prompting worries among advocates that “their goals have been overshadowed by other Kennedy agenda items, related to food and vaccines, and that a chance to get psychedelic drugs to people who need them could be slipping away.”

title: Forward Global announces Venezuela task force
body_text:
EYES ON VENEZUELA : Global public affairs and risk advisory firm Forward Global has launched a new advisory group dedicated to helping clients navigate the rapidly changing political and commercial climate in Venezuela, the firm announced today.

— The Venezuela task force brings together firm experts in the fields of international trade, sanctions compliance, government relations and geopolitical intelligence to advise clients with interests in the South American country that was rocked earlier this month when the United States captured longtime President Nicolás Maduro and his wife and transported the pair to New York City to face drug trafficking charges.

— “Venezuela is entering a transformative phase that will have significant implications for regional stability, energy markets, and cross-border commerce,” Forward Global partner Sven Stumbauer said in a statement. “Organizations need sophisticated analysis and strategic counsel to understand the rapidly evolving landscape and position themselves appropriately.”

— Stumbauer will serve as a member of the Venezuela task force leadership which also includes Jose Mallea , Noe Garcia III , Nicholas Fitzgerald , Judith Jacob , Jonathan Bucks and Juan Nino .

— President Donald Trump has said his administration will indefinitely “run” Venezuela, which had been led by Maduro for more than a decade after the 2013 death of the country’s charismatic socialist leader Hugo Chávez . The administration has sought to work with interim President Delcy Rodríguez on the country’s future, but doubts persist about the level of her cooperation with Washington.

— While the energy industry has a natural interest in the historically oil-rich country , a reset in U.S.-Venezuela relations has the potential to open new commercial opportunities for companies with a strong Washington presence. During a Cabinet meeting today, Trump announced the opening of commercial airspace over Venezuela. American Airlines announced that it will soon resume direct flights to the country, the first U.S. airline to do so since they were prohibited by a 2019 order from the first Trump administration.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI . Are you seeing a Venezuela bump? Let us know what’s driving business at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

TO MAHA OR NOT TO MAHA : The American Medical Association is facing internal dissension following a meeting between AMA President Bobby Mukkamala and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , our colleague Simon J. Levien scoops.

— The disagreements among members of the trade group which represents more than 250,000 doctors started after Mukkamala issued a supportive statement about Kennedy’s new dietary guidelines, in regards to targeting ultraprocessed food, sugar and sodium . That positive statement helped Mukkamala secure a long-sought after meeting with Kenendy.

— “Members of the group’s liberal wing messaged AMA Board of Trustees Chair David Aizuss to complain that they weren’t told of the meeting and that Mukkamala’s statement on the dietary guidelines didn’t reflect many physicians’ concerns about the health impacts of eating more red meat, whole milk and other fatty foods,” Simon reports.

LITIGATION FUNDING BILL STALLS: Legislation that would require disclosure of third parties providing financial assistance in civil lawsuits has stalled in the House Judiciary Committee and a path forward for the bill is unclear, our colleague Jordan Williams reports for Pros in a new POLITICO Pro Bill Analysis .

— Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) introduced the Litigation Transparency Act in February 2025, saying it “targets serious and continuing abuses in our litigation system.” Litigation funding is the practice of a third party bankrolling a civil lawsuit, typically by a smaller plaintiff against a wealthier defendant, in exchange for a cut of any settlement or financial judgment. Such arrangements are not currently required to be disclosed in court.

— The bill drew support from Google and the National Association of Manufacturers , but also fierce opposition from conservative legal groups which have said it would require them to publicize the identities of donors supporting litigation related to topics like abortion and religious liberty.

DATA CENTER PR BLITZ: Tech companies like Meta and Amazon are engaged in a nationwide PR campaign aimed at building goodwill towards data centers that form the backbone of new developments in artificial intelligence, Eli Tan reports for The New York Times .

— “ Meta spent $6.4 million to run a series of ads … in the television markets of eight state capitals such as Sacramento, Salt Lake City and Tallahassee, Fla., as well as Washington, D.C., according to data from AdImpact , an analytics firm,” he reports. “ Amazon is helping to fund a similar ad campaign in Virginia, where it operates dozens of data centers. The campaign — focused on job growth and electricity costs — began in December 2024 and is still running, backed by Virginia Connects , a nonprofit created by the Data Center Coalition , an industry trade group.”

— The ads typically focus on the economic benefits data centers can provide to local communities. But the energy needed to power such massive computing power, and community anger about rising electricity costs, has prompted some lawmakers to propose limits on data centers. Trump recently posted that tech companies who build data centers must “pay their own way” on the projects.

— MELANIA’S DEBUT: A new documentary about first lady Melania Trump hits theaters tomorrow, and distributor Amazon has spared no expense on promoting the film, leading some to question whether the company’s $35 million promotional campaign is really an investment in currying favor with the president, Nicole Sperling and Brooks Barnes report for The New York Times .

— Amazon acquired the rights to “Melania,” which is produced by the first lady’s own production company and directed by Brett Ratner , for $40 million, and has spent nearly as much money marketing the documentary. A film producer who helped develop Amazon Studios told the Times the movie is “the most expensive documentary ever made that didn’t involve music licensing” and questioned how it could be seen as anything other than “an outright bribe.”

— “Some employees in Amazon’s entertainment division had similar concerns, according to three sources with knowledge of discussions inside Amazon . They were told that the project was mandated by the company’s leadership and that employees could not opt out of working on the film for political reasons. Andy Jassy , Amazon’s chief executive, and Mike Hopkins , who runs Amazon Studios , attended a private screening of the film at the White House on Saturday,” the Times reports.

— “Amazon, when asked for comment about its promotion of the movie, repeated a statement it had released in the past: ‘We licensed the film for one reason and one reason only — because we think customers are going to love it.’ Representatives for Ms. Trump did not respond to a request for comment.”

MAKING IT RAIN: A cloud-seeding company falsely accused of triggering deadly floods is now spending big in Washington as part of an effort to build a positive image and dispel conspiracy theories, Corbin Hiar reports for E&E News .

— Rainmaker Technology recently spent around $100,000 on an ad campaign targeting Washington Metro stations. And last year the company spent $450,000 on federal lobbying, more than three times its U.S. lobbying spend for 2024. The ads and lobbying campaign are part of a strategy by the company’s CEO, Augustus Doricko , to prebut fears about cloud seeding, a technology that spurs precipitation by dispersing silver iodide into clouds. Following July 2025 floods that killed 135 people in central Texas, some online blamed the company which had been conducting cloud seeding “days earlier and hundreds of miles away.”

— “A top priority for the company is chipping away at support for legislation like the ‘Clear Skies Act,’ which would criminalize the release of chemicals into the atmosphere if they are intended to change the weather, temperature or climate,” Corbin reports.

FARA FRIDAY: Continental Strategy , the firm founded by former Donald Trump campaign adviser Carlos Trujillo , has been hired to represent the government of Kazakhstan, according to FARA registrations filed with the Justice Department last week.

— The contract, valued at $3.3 million for a year of representation, was signed earlier this month and calls for Continental to provide “government relations services … by facilitating meetings and discussions and establish relationships with key stakeholders in the executive and legislative branches.”

— Trujillo and partner Doug MacGillivray will work on the account, according to separate FARA filings.

— In a statement provided to PI, a firm spokesperson said the contract “reflects the continued growth of our international practice and the trust that both commercial and sovereign clients place in our ability to navigate Washington.”

— “President Trump’s leadership on critical minerals, commercial diplomacy, and supply chain security has created extraordinary opportunities for partnership between the United States and resource-rich allies like Kazakhstan,” the statement added.

— Trujillo and MacGillivray will be joined on the account by Manuel Ortiz of Vantage Knight , a prominent Democratic lobbyist whom Continental has hired as an independent contractor to assist with the Kazakhstan representation. Continental will pay Vantage Knight $1.2 million over the course of this year for Ortiz’s work.

— Kazakhstan has pursued closer ties to the United States in recent months. Kazakh President Kassym - Jomart Tokayev , along with other central Asian leaders, visited the White House in November and announced his nation would be the newest signatory to the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel and several Arab countries. Kazakhstan and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding on critical minerals cooperation during the same visit. And last week, Kazakhstan was announced as one of the founding members of Trump’s Board of Peace.

— On Wednesday, Kazakh energy minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said the country has submitted a request to the Treasury Department to be allowed to purchase sanctioned Russian oil assets in Kazakhstan.

LEHMAN TO PARAMOUNT: Paramount Skydance has tapped Ted Lehman to lead its D.C. office amid the entertainment giant’s hostile takeover bid to buy Warner Bros. Discovery , according to a memo sent to staff this morning.

— Lehman was most recently a principal at Todd Strategy Group , where his lobbying clients included Fox Corp. and the cable trade group NCTA , along with health care heavyweights like Eli Lilly , Novo Nordisk , Bayer , AstraZeneca , Amgen , PhRMA , Johnson & Johnson and the American Medical Association .

— In his memo, Paramount chief legal officer Makan Delrahim — who previously led DOJ’s antitrust division during the first Trump administration — said Lehman had been serving as a strategic adviser to the company for the “past few months.”

— Lehman headed downtown in 2022 after more than two decades on the Hill, including serving as chief of staff to Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and working as a top aide for Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee.

— Lehman’s arrival follows the early retirement of the company’s top global lobbyist DeDe Lea . In addition to Paramount’s WBD acquisition push, the company has faced scrutiny from congressional Democrats over CEO David Ellison ’s ties to President Donald Trump and last year’s merger with Skydance. That scrutiny is almost certain to ramp up further after the recent deal to sell TikTok ’s U.S. operations to a group of investors that includes Larry Ellison ’s Oracle .

MORE VENEZUELA: Tower Strategy , the young firm led by retired CIA operations officer Rick de la Torre , is touting its Venezuela bonafides as lobbyists jostle for new business created by the recent U.S. intervention in the South American country.

— This month, the firm hired as a partner Art Estopiñán , who served as chief of staff to then-Rep. Ileana Ros - Lehtinen (R-Fla.) during her time as House Foreign Affairs Committee chair. It also announced Rudolph Atallah , former NSC deputy senior director for counterterrorism; Felipe Garcia Echeverri , former Colombian diplomat; and Tom Naum , president of energy industry supplier REASOL , as strategic partners.

— “Venezuela is not a market you learn from a briefing book,” de la Torre said in a statement. “Our team has dealt with Venezuela as a real-world problem for years, on the ground and inside government. We have worked the policy, security, and energy dimensions under pressure. That experience cannot be improvised, and it matters as the country enters a period of transition.”

— Palantir has been granted substantial government contracts during the second Trump administration, and now earns “roughly half of its revenue” from government sales.

— Jamael Lundy was among the group, which includes former CNN anchor Don Lemon , charged with conspiracy and interfering with a religious service. Lundy is an employee of the county attorney’s office who serves as the prosecutor’s lobbyist to the Minnesota state legislature. He is also a current candidate for the state senate.

title: Travel industry presses to avoid another shutdown travel mess
body_text:
THIS FEELS FAMILIAR: As the House returns to town to squeeze through remaining full-year funding bills and a DHS stopgap, the travel industry — still reeling from last year’s record-breaking shutdown — is pleading with lawmakers to keep the current, partial shutdown as short as possible.

— “When air traffic controllers and TSA officers are forced to work without pay, it strains an already under resourced aviation system and sends ripple effects across the entire travel ecosystem,” the U.S. Travel Association , Airlines for America and the American Hotel & Lodging Association said in a joint statement this morning.

— The groups called on the House to act “with urgency” and pointed out that last fall’s shutdown cost the economy an estimated $6 billion and impacted more than 6 million travelers. “It’s up to the House to pass these measures to prevent significant disruptions, protect travelers, and maintain confidence in the U.S. air travel system,” they said.

— Amid Democratic opposition and efforts from some House Republicans to attach an election citizenship measure to the funding package, an end to the partial shutdown that began over the weekend isn’t likely until tomorrow at the earliest. (President Donald Trump even weighed in on Truth Social this afternoon to urge Democrats and Republicans to support a clean funding package.)

— “Our focus has just been not to try to triage those things or negotiate with unrelated policies, but just to keep focused on the main message,” said Erik Hansen , senior vice president of government relations at U.S. Travel. There are encouraging signs that “Congress has learned the lessons of the damage that it can cause and the havoc that it can create for the economy, but we’re not out of the woods yet,” he told PI.

— The industry has also continued to push for legislation to ensure that FAA employees like air traffic controllers don’t have their pay disrupted by future shutdowns. But though Hansen said there’s been an uptick in interest, others on the Hill haven’t been willing to give up what has become an immense form of leverage in shutdown talks.

— And though we haven’t yet seen the kind of widespread travel disruptions that took place during the last shutdown, Hansen argued that the specter of future shutdowns alone can be a deterrent for hiring crucial aviation workers. “We’re up against a political calculation here, and I don’t think the travel industry should be used as political leverage,” he said.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips and gossip. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

PLACING THEIR BETS: “The two largest online sports gambling companies, DraftKings and FanDuel , have already spent millions of dollars on the 2026 midterm elections,” Popular Information ’s Judd Legum reports, signaling the industry’s shift to federal campaigns following its longtime focus on state political spending.

— “Although the spending is bipartisan, both companies’ giving is tilted toward Republicans,” and includes a $500,000 contribution by DraftKings to the Senate GOP-allied super PAC Senate Leadership Fund , in addition to $2 million to a new PAC formed last year, Win for America .

— “The company was Win For America’s only donor. … [O]n November 21, Win for America donated $500,000 to the American Conservative Fund , a dark money group that works in concert with the SLF to boost Senate Republicans.”

— “Simultaneously, $450,000 was funneled from Win for America to American Future PAC , a new group that was formed days after Win for America. Win for America is the sole source of funding for American Future PAC. Based on the political consultants involved and the messaging of American Future PAC’s nascent website, it appears likely to support Democratic candidates.”

— FanDuel, meanwhile, gave $500,000 to SLF in December and the same amount to the Congressional Leadership Fund , the super PAC allied with House GOP leadership. FanDuel donated the same amounts to its Democratic super PAC counterparts, Senate Majority PAC and House Majority PAC .

RELATED READ: “The Richest 2026 Players: A.I., Crypto, Pro-Israel Groups and Trump,” by The New York Times’ Teddy Schleifer .

MAHA COMES FOR CASSIDY : “ Bill Cassidy seemed aware of the political peril when he decided, a year ago, to challenge Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s skeptical views about vaccines. … Now, as Cassidy seeks a third term, Kennedy’s followers haven’t forgiven the senator for grilling Kennedy at that hearing or for criticizing his efforts as health secretary to cast doubt on vaccine safety,” POLITICO ’s Alice Miranda Ollstein and Simon J. Levien report.

— “Add to that President Donald Trump’s decision last month to endorse challenger Rep. Julia Letlow in the race, and Cassidy is in a fight for his political life. ‘Cassidy, within the MAHA movement, is pretty well despised,’ said Jeff Hutt , a spokesman for the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) super PAC who worked on Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign.”

— Several of Cassidy’s challengers “are now rushing to claim the MAHA mantle as they campaign ahead of the May primary, underscoring the strength of the emerging movement as a national political force ,” and Letlow has even secured a million-dollar pledge of support from a pro-Kennedy dark money group on top of Trump’s endorsement.

THE TIES THAT BIND: “Four days before Donald Trump’s inauguration last year, lieutenants to an Abu Dhabi royal secretly signed a deal with the Trump family to purchase a 49% stake in their fledgling cryptocurrency venture for half a billion dollars, according to company documents and people familiar with the matter,” The Wall Street Journal ’s Sam Kessler , Rebecca Ballhaus , Eliot Brown and Angus Berwick report.

— The blockbuster deal with World Liberty Financial was slated to send $187 million to Trump family entities and another $31 million to entities linked to the family of Trump envoy Steve Witkoff . It also put executives on World Liberty’s board who were from firms backed by the royal, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan , at a time when the sheikh was pressing the U.S. — ultimately, successfully — for access to high-powered AI chips.

— “Trump’s real-estate company has courted deals with foreign companies since his election, and the president has accepted gifts from foreign governments,” WSJ notes. “But the World Liberty deal is the only known case of a foreign government official purchasing a major stake in a Trump company after his election,” even though a company spokesperson said that Trump and Witkoff had no involvement in the deal.

FIRST IN PI : Five conservative former antitrust enforcers are asking DOJ to review the proposed merger of Netflix and Warner Bros. Discovery “based on proven standards that evaluate deals based on their impact on consumer welfare,” rather than through the lens of the “progressive analytic framework fabricated during the prior administration.”

— Ahead of tomorrow’s Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing on the merger, which will feature testimony from Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and WBD executive Bruce Campbell , former FTC officials Asheesh Agarwal , Theodore A. Gebhard , Alden Abbott , Dan Gilman and Neil Chilson urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to eschew the 2023 merger review guidelines put in place by the Biden administration and kept in place by the Trump administration.

— “DOJ should evaluate the merger based on established antitrust jurisprudence, economic learning, and the facts and circumstances presented, not ‘progressive’ wish lists labeled as Guidelines,” the group wrote in its letter to Bondi, adding that DOJ should avoid giving weight to “speculative theories” while considering “tailored” remedies, “[t]o the extent that the Department ultimately harbors some competitive concerns about the merger.”

Jobs report

— Jodie Moxley-Ramos has joined Shumaker Advisors as a vice president of federal affairs. Moxley-Ramos is the founder of Ignite Global Strategies and is a former in-house lobbyist at Ligado Networks and Airbus .

— Christina Gungoll Lepore has joined Constitution Partners as a partner. She was most recently a senior adviser to Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt and led Stitt’s D.C. office.

— Robert Cohen has joined Holtzman Vogel as a partner. He was previously executive director of political risk and compliance at KPMG .

— Andrea Woods is rejoining the American Petroleum Institute as director of external communications. She was most recently acting director of public affairs at the Department of Energy.

— Brian Wanglin is now public affairs regional manager at Google . He most recently was a senior managing director at PLUS Communications .
