title: Turning to K Street to save Christmas
body_text:
DESPERATELY SEEKING SANTA EXEMPTIONS: President Donald Trump ’s move to slap tariffs on imports from around the globe may have been a lump of coal for purveyors of Christmas cheer, but the scramble to roll those tariffs back has been a huge gift for K Street, Caitlin reports .

— Trade groups and companies representing manufacturers and retailers of everything from Christmas trees and decor to toys and spices — like virtually every other sector of the economy — have bolstered their lobbying operations in D.C., dropping massive sums as they jockeyed for tariff relief.

— Lobbying outlays by the Toy Association — which in April warned of devastation for toymakers if an initial 145 percent tariff on Chinese imports were to stand — skyrocketed to $510,000 through the first nine months of the year. That’s up from $40,000 in all of 2024 and the most spent since 2015. In preparation for Trump’s tariffs, the association brought on Ballard Partners last December for guidance on the matter, lobbying disclosures show.

— The association also retained its former top lobbyist Ed Desmond at the beginning of the year, and in February the Toy Association brought on Ridgeline Advocacy Group to work on a number of issues in addition to the tariffs, including consumer protection, sustainability and taxes.

— Detentes between Beijing and Washington gradually lowered tariffs on Chinese toy imports to 20 percent by the end of the year. But toymakers are closely tracking the Supreme Court decision on Trump’s so-called reciprocal tariffs and the prospect of seeing tariff payments refunded.

— Trump’s tariffs have prompted some holiday brands to turn to K Street for the first time. They include the Christmas Trade Group , a coalition of holiday retailers like the ornament and decor purveyors Kurt Adler and Old World Christmas , and artificial tree makers National Tree Company and Puleo . The coalition also includes holiday florists, lighting companies and even one commercial decorator whose portfolio includes the Trump International Hotel in New York.

— The trade group has paid Williams & Jensen $90,000 since March to build ties with the Trump administration and lawmakers on the key congressional committees that oversee trade. It has also lobbied for an exemption on products like Christmas lights similar to the one issued during Trump’s first administration.

— Artificial tree behemoth Balsam Brands , meanwhile, has spent $210,000 on lobbying through the first three quarters of the year — including $110,000 in Q3 alone. That’s less than the $420,000 Balsam Brands spent in 2019, but is the most by far for the company since the end of its three-year lobbying hiatus in 2023.

— Beyond the producers of holiday decor and goods, the retailers that sell those products have been some of the most vocal tariff critics in Washington this year. The National Retail Federation , whose members include Walmart , Target and Macy’s , is on track for its second-highest lobbying expenditures ever. NRF has dropped more than $8.5 million on lobbying so far this year, already more than the $8.3 million spent in all of 2024.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to the final PI of the year . Thank you all for reading and sending tips — we couldn’t have made it through this whirlwind of a year without you. We’ll be back in your inboxes on Jan. 5, but feel free to send us influence tips to chase down in the New Year. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

YOU CAN’T HANDLE THE TRUTH: “K Street’s current playbook for clients avoiding President Donald Trump’s wrath on Truth Social is four words long: ‘Don’t poke the bear.’ That’s how one Democratic lobbyist described their advice to clients,” NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno writes. “Several other lobbyists have told NOTUS — on condition of anonymity so as not to ‘poke the bear’ — that playing defense has become an essential lobbying strategy early in Trump’s second term.”

— “A NOTUS analysis of every Trump Truth Social post since Jan. 20 indicates they have cause for concern. Trump has used the platform — his Trump Media & Technology Group owns it — to call out companies, colleges and other corporations and organizations at least 177 times across at least 129 posts.”

— “Asked where getting called out by Trump on Truth Social falls on a scale ranging from inconvenient to five-alarm fire, one Republican lobbyist told NOTUS it’s a ‘nine out of 10.’”

JANE STREET LANDS ON K STREET: “ Jane Street Group has hired lobbyists for the first time in 20 years, and top executives have been proactively meeting with lawmakers,” per Bloomberg ’s Katherine Doherty , Chiranjivi Chakraborty and Todd Gillespie .

— “In some cases, those appointments have been pitched as simple, get-to-know-Jane-Street conversations, part of an effort to explain how the privately-held firm makes markets and is generating trading hauls greater than many of the world’s largest investment banks in the process.”

— But Jane Street’s decision to enlist Hogan Lovells comes as regulators in India are probing “additional trading strategies Jane Street used, including allegedly manipulating the country’s biggest index to make money with an options strategy commonly known as a ‘short straddle,’ according to people familiar with the investigation.” Jane Street has denied any wrongdoing in India and is appealing a July decision to boot the firm from the country’s financial markets.

— In the U.S., Jane Street has paid Hogan Lovells $160,000 from July to September, and firm representatives have met with officials at Treasury, Commerce and in the Executive Office of the President “to discuss Jane Street’s operations in India, according to the lobbying disclosures and the people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named discussing non-public information. Separately, Jane Street co-founder Rob Granieri has also met with lawmakers, the people said.”

FAMILY MATTERS: The New York Times’ Teddy Schleifer is out today with a look at the tag-team effort by David and Larry Ellison to build out their media empire via the family’s hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery , including Larry Ellison’s overtures to Trump, whose administration would need to green-light any deal.

— “Larry Ellison has taken the lead in making the case to the president for why Paramount and not Netflix, its rival bidder, should win control of Warner Bros., two of the people said. Mr. Trump has pledged to be ‘involved’ in any decision about whether to approve a deal,” per the Times.

— Trump, meanwhile, “has privately said Larry Ellison assured him that he would turn CBS News , which the Ellisons took over when they bought Paramount, into a more conservative outlet, two people with knowledge of the president’s comments said.”

PARDON ME: The new approach to presidential pardons adopted during Trump’s second term “has spawned a pardon-shopping industry where lobbyists say their going rate is $1 million” in order to fast-track their clients’ shot at freedom , The Wall Street Journal ’s Rebecca Ballhaus , Josh Dawsey and C. Ryan Barber

— “Administration officials and lobbyists describe two playbooks that have emerged. There is the official track, which involves pardon czar Alice Johnson , Justice Department pardon attorney Ed Martin and the White House Counsel’s Office.”

— “Applicants usually go through one of the three, and ultimately White House counsel Dave Warrington reviews the application and makes a recommendation to Trump. The two men meet every few weeks to discuss pardons, administration officials said.”

— “The second track is riskier but can be much faster. If an applicant can find Trump at Mar-a-Lago or a White House event and ask for a pardon directly, Trump is often inclined to be helpful, administration officials said—particularly if someone says the magic words: “unjust persecution.”

— “Many of Trump’s most controversial pardons—including for [ Binance founder Changpeng ] Zhao and the Honduran ex-president—have gone through the latter track, which some senior administration officials said worried them. Another senior White House official said the ‘vast majority’ of pardons have gone through the proper channels. Driving up the price for well-connected lobbyists and lawyers is the sense that they can pursue only a few pardons, given the political capital they need to expend to fast-track a case.”

Jobs report

— The Heritage Foundation is adding Stewart Whitson as chief of staff to President Kevin Roberts . He previously worked at the Foundation for Government Accountability and was the GOP nominee in a Virginia special congressional election this year. Peter St. Onge is returning to Heritage as senior economist, and the think tank promoted Jay Richards to vice president of social and domestic policy, Allen Mendenhall to research fellow at the Thomas A. Roe Institute for Economic Policy Studies and Roger Severino to vice president of economic and domestic policy.

New Joint Fundraisers

Cline Victory Committee (Rep. Ben Cline , Conservative Leadership in Elections PAC, NRCC)

Turning to K Street to save Christmas

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

12/24/2025 04:27 PM EST

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

Programming note: We’ll be off for the holidays but will be back to our normal schedule on Monday, Jan. 5, 2026.

DESPERATELY SEEKING SANTA EXEMPTIONS: President Donald Trump’s move to slap tariffs on imports from around the globe may have been a lump of coal for purveyors of Christmas cheer, but the scramble to roll those tariffs back has been a huge gift for K Street, Caitlin reports.

— Trade groups and companies representing manufacturers and retailers of everything from Christmas trees and decor to toys and spices — like virtually every other sector of the economy — have bolstered their lobbying operations in D.C., dropping massive sums as they jockeyed for tariff relief.

— Lobbying outlays by the Toy Association — which in April warned of devastation for toymakers if an initial 145 percent tariff on Chinese imports were to stand — skyrocketed to $510,000 through the first nine months of the year. That’s up from $40,000 in all of 2024 and the most spent since 2015. In preparation for Trump’s tariffs, the association brought on Ballard Partners last December for guidance on the matter, lobbying disclosures show.

— The association also retained its former top lobbyist Ed Desmond at the beginning of the year, and in February the Toy Association brought on Ridgeline Advocacy Group to work on a number of issues in addition to the tariffs, including consumer protection, sustainability and taxes.

— Detentes between Beijing and Washington gradually lowered tariffs on Chinese toy imports to 20 percent by the end of the year. But toymakers are closely tracking the Supreme Court decision on Trump’s so-called reciprocal tariffs and the prospect of seeing tariff payments refunded.

— Trump’s tariffs have prompted some holiday brands to turn to K Street for the first time. They include the Christmas Trade Group, a coalition of holiday retailers like the ornament and decor purveyors Kurt Adler and Old World Christmas, and artificial tree makers National Tree Company and Puleo. The coalition also includes holiday florists, lighting companies and even one commercial decorator whose portfolio includes the Trump International Hotel in New York.

— The trade group has paid Williams & Jensen $90,000 since March to build ties with the Trump administration and lawmakers on the key congressional committees that oversee trade. It has also lobbied for an exemption on products like Christmas lights similar to the one issued during Trump’s first administration.

— Artificial tree behemoth Balsam Brands, meanwhile, has spent $210,000 on lobbying through the first three quarters of the year — including $110,000 in Q3 alone. That’s less than the $420,000 Balsam Brands spent in 2019, but is the most by far for the company since the end of its three-year lobbying hiatus in 2023.

— Beyond the producers of holiday decor and goods, the retailers that sell those products have been some of the most vocal tariff critics in Washington this year. The National Retail Federation, whose members include Walmart, Target and Macy’s, is on track for its second-highest lobbying expenditures ever. NRF has dropped more than $8.5 million on lobbying so far this year, already more than the $8.3 million spent in all of 2024.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to the final PI of the year. Thank you all for reading and sending tips — we couldn’t have made it through this whirlwind of a year without you. We’ll be back in your inboxes on Jan. 5, but feel free to send us influence tips to chase down in the New Year. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com. Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com. Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns.

YOU CAN’T HANDLE THE TRUTH: “K Street’s current playbook for clients avoiding President Donald Trump’s wrath on Truth Social is four words long: ‘Don’t poke the bear.’ That’s how one Democratic lobbyist described their advice to clients,” NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno writes. “Several other lobbyists have told NOTUS — on condition of anonymity so as not to ‘poke the bear’ — that playing defense has become an essential lobbying strategy early in Trump’s second term.”

— “A NOTUS analysis of every Trump Truth Social post since Jan. 20 indicates they have cause for concern. Trump has used the platform — his Trump Media & Technology Group owns it — to call out companies, colleges and other corporations and organizations at least 177 times across at least 129 posts.”

— “Asked where getting called out by Trump on Truth Social falls on a scale ranging from inconvenient to five-alarm fire, one Republican lobbyist told NOTUS it’s a ‘nine out of 10.’”

JANE STREET LANDS ON K STREET: “Jane Street Group has hired lobbyists for the first time in 20 years, and top executives have been proactively meeting with lawmakers,” per Bloomberg’s Katherine Doherty, Chiranjivi Chakraborty and Todd Gillespie.

— “In some cases, those appointments have been pitched as simple, get-to-know-Jane-Street conversations, part of an effort to explain how the privately-held firm makes markets and is generating trading hauls greater than many of the world’s largest investment banks in the process.”

— But Jane Street’s decision to enlist Hogan Lovells comes as regulators in India are probing “additional trading strategies Jane Street used, including allegedly manipulating the country’s biggest index to make money with an options strategy commonly known as a ‘short straddle,’ according to people familiar with the investigation.” Jane Street has denied any wrongdoing in India and is appealing a July decision to boot the firm from the country’s financial markets.

— In the U.S., Jane Street has paid Hogan Lovells $160,000 from July to September, and firm representatives have met with officials at Treasury, Commerce and in the Executive Office of the President “to discuss Jane Street’s operations in India, according to the lobbying disclosures and the people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named discussing non-public information. Separately, Jane Street co-founder Rob Granieri has also met with lawmakers, the people said.”

FAMILY MATTERS: The New York Times’ Teddy Schleifer is out today with a look at the tag-team effort by David and Larry Ellison to build out their media empire via the family’s hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, including Larry Ellison’s overtures to Trump, whose administration would need to green-light any deal.

— “Larry Ellison has taken the lead in making the case to the president for why Paramount and not Netflix, its rival bidder, should win control of Warner Bros., two of the people said. Mr. Trump has pledged to be ‘involved’ in any decision about whether to approve a deal,” per the Times.

— Trump, meanwhile, “has privately said Larry Ellison assured him that he would turn CBS News, which the Ellisons took over when they bought Paramount, into a more conservative outlet, two people with knowledge of the president’s comments said.”

PARDON ME: The new approach to presidential pardons adopted during Trump’s second term “has spawned a pardon-shopping industry where lobbyists say their going rate is $1 million” in order to fast-track their clients’ shot at freedom, The Wall Street Journal’s Rebecca Ballhaus, Josh Dawsey and C. Ryan Barber

— “Administration officials and lobbyists describe two playbooks that have emerged. There is the official track, which involves pardon czar Alice Johnson, Justice Department pardon attorney Ed Martin and the White House Counsel’s Office.”

— “Applicants usually go through one of the three, and ultimately White House counsel Dave Warrington reviews the application and makes a recommendation to Trump. The two men meet every few weeks to discuss pardons, administration officials said.”

— “The second track is riskier but can be much faster. If an applicant can find Trump at Mar-a-Lago or a White House event and ask for a pardon directly, Trump is often inclined to be helpful, administration officials said—particularly if someone says the magic words: “unjust persecution.”

— “Many of Trump’s most controversial pardons—including for [Binance founder Changpeng] Zhao and the Honduran ex-president—have gone through the latter track, which some senior administration officials said worried them. Another senior White House official said the ‘vast majority’ of pardons have gone through the proper channels. Driving up the price for well-connected lobbyists and lawyers is the sense that they can pursue only a few pardons, given the political capital they need to expend to fast-track a case.”

title: Vance-linked firm sets up shop in DC
body_text:
FIRST IN PI: New Jersey-based government affairs shop MAD Global Strategy is expanding to D.C. The firm, which was founded in 2021 by GOP operative Mike DuHaime and has offices in Ohio, New York and West Virginia, has tapped veteran energy and transportation lobbyist Mimi Braniff to steer its new outpost. It will serve as a full-service extension of work the firm has already been doing at the state level and for its existing national clients.

— Braniff has spent the past four years with Exxon Mobil , where she was most recently head of federal government and regulatory affairs. Before that, she was an in-house lobbyist for Delta Air Lines , an aide to Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and a lobbyist for NRG Energy .

— In an interview, Braniff said the new office is currently a one-woman operation and that while she expects an initial heavy focus on energy and transportation policy issues given her background, MAD Global’s D.C. shop will eventually expand into other policy arenas. Braniff plans on registering to lobby for the firm as part of her new role.

— The firm has close ties to Vice President JD Vance . Jai Chabria , an Ohio-based partner at MAD Global, is a longtime Vance adviser who served as the chief strategist for Vance’s 2022 Senate campaign. (Chabria is also helping choreograph Vivek Ramaswamy ’s Ohio gubernatorial bid and ran Patrick Morrissey ’s successful West Virginia gubernatorial campaign in 2024.) Taylor Van Kirk , a longtime Vance spokesperson who joined him at the White House, is a MAD Global alum.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

But now he is starting to feel the squeeze ” after a social media post ribbing billionaires who were threatening to flee California over a proposed one-time wealth tax in the state, according to The New York Times ’ Teddy Schleifer .

— “Some of those wealthy Californians are now quietly mobilizing on WhatsApp chats and conference calls to try to put together a well-funded but long-shot bid to oust Mr. Khanna, according to half a dozen people close to the effort who spoke on the condition of anonymity to disclose private conversations.”

— Khanna “easily won re-election in 2024 and has loyal support from his district’s South Asian community. He sits on almost $15 million in campaign cash that even a candidate backed by wealthy tech donors would struggle to compete against. But the anger toward him … reflects the tense relationship between Silicon Valley and the Democratic Party, particularly its progressive wing.”

FLYING IN: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce hit the Hill today with more than 50 business and association leaders to try to regain momentum for a permitting overhaul after the House passed a package of reforms before skipping town last year.

— A policy forum this morning featured remarks from Senate Environment and Public Works Chair Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), House Natural Resources Chair Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.), Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) and Emily Domenech , who chairs the Trump administration’s permitting council. Participants then headed to meetings across the Hill to emphasize the urgency of passing permitting reform as bipartisan negotiations teeter .

— The event included leaders from individual energy and infrastructure companies as well as from the American Road & Transportation Builders Association , the Data Center Coalition , American Electric Power , the National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association , the American Cement Association , the American Gas Association , the Association of American Railroads , the American Chemistry Council , the Bipartisan Policy Center , the National Mining Association and more.

TRUMP SETS UP SHOWDOWN WITH PRIVATE EQUITY: “President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he will move to ban large investors from acquiring more single-family homes and called on Congress to back the initiative, in a bid to bring down the cost of housing,” POLITICO ’s Victoria Guida , Sam Sutton and Katherine Hapgood report.

— “I am immediately taking steps to ban large institutional investors from buying more single-family homes, and I will be calling on Congress to codify it,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, adding that he would elaborate on the proposal at the World Economic Forum in Davos later this month.

— “The president’s broadside against institutional investors echoes previous Democratic-led efforts to restrict the private equity industry’s involvement in the housing market, and it’s likely to face considerable pushback from an industry that has a long history of beating back Washington-led efforts to rein in its activities,” Victoria, Sam and Katherine note.

— “But the public’s fury over the cost of housing and rising consumer prices has positioned the ‘affordability crisis’ as a central theme of the upcoming midterm elections,” and it comes as Vance “has been sharply critical of the asset management world’s growing role in housing.”

CRUZIN’ FOR A BRUISIN’: “Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) on Tuesday said Ford CEO Jim Farley was scared to testify before Congress, a day after Cruz postponed the hearing due to Farley’s refusal to appear,” POLITICO ’s Chris Marquette reports.

— “Cruz popped off on Farley, whose reluctance to appear delayed what was set to be a marquee hearing with the leaders of the Big Three Detroit automakers and a top engineer at Tesla . Cruz also bashed Farley on a since-scrapped plan by the automaker that would have let dealers continue to offer the $7,500 electric vehicle tax credit on leases, even after the benefit expired.”

— Cruz, who demurred on whether he would issue a subpoena to compel Farley to testify, pledged to hold a hearing focused on affordability and the upcoming surface transportation reauthorization with or without Ford’s input. A spokesperson for the automaker said Ford was “committed to appropriately engaging on issues that impact our company, our employees and the industry and we look forward to continuing to work with leaders such as Senator Cruz.”

— The Consumer Bankers Association has promoted David Pommerehn to executive vice president, general counsel and head of regulatory affairs; Kevin O’Connor to executive vice president, membership and sponsorship; and Jake Letterie to assistant vice president and government relations director.

— Martijn Rasser has been promoted to vice president at the Special Competitive Studies Project , Morning Defense reports. He previously was a special adviser there.

Abboud most recently served as political director at the Independent Insurance Agents and Brokers of America and is an NRSC alum, and Ricchetti most recently served as deputy special representative for city and state diplomacy at the State Department.

SWEET HOME ALABAMA: Public affairs firm Seven Letter is expanding nationwide, opening new offices in Los Angeles, New York City and Huntsville, Alabama, the firm announced today . The move is the firm’s largest expansion to date, raising its total number of offices to five from its current two locations in Washington and Boston.

— The decision to open an office in Huntsville, an area which has become a major hub for the aerospace industry and hosts a variety of Defense Department, Justice Department and NASA components at the Army’s Redstone Arsenal base, is reflective of the firm’s existing client base in the national security sector, CEO Erik Smith told PI.

— “In the aerospace and national security spheres, if people know we have a presence in Huntsville, and a significant one, that shows them we understand their business and we understand where the business is going,” he said.

— Firm veteran Holly Jackson will lead the Huntsville office. She will partner with Blair Taylor , an alum of former Alabama Sen. Richard Shelby’s office and the former communications director for the Senate Appropriations Committee. Also boosting the firm’s work for national security clients is recent hire Sabrina Singh , who served as deputy press secretary at the Pentagon during the Biden administration.

— Helming the Los Angeles office will be new hire Brandon Shaw , who previously worked as a vice president for Disney and Hulu and led his own firm B. Shaw Communications , which has been acquired by Seven Letter. Casey Hernandez , currently a partner in the firm’s Washington office, will move to Los Angeles to assist in launching the new office.

— Previous fellow at the firm Marley Hambourger is returning as a director to launch the New York office located in Manhattan. In addition to the new locations, the firm has hired Camille Cherney to serve as a content specialist in the Boston office.

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE TO MERCURY: Special Assistant to the President and Deputy Director of the White House Office of Public Liaison Brette Powell has left the West Wing to join Mercury Public Affairs , the firm announced today. She will serve as a managing director in the firm’s government relations team.

— Powell’s White House career started with a 2018 internship that led to subsequent positions during the first Trump administration. At the time Trump left office in 2021, she was serving as the president’s lead press advance representative. Following a stint in the private sector, she joined the Trump campaign in 2022 as director of external affairs.

— Powell is the latest in a string of White House aides who have decamped to K Street during the first year of the second Trump administration. Trump staffers Harrison Fields , Trent Morse and May Davis Mailman all exited the administration for K Street gigs in 2025. It is unclear if Powell will register to lobby.

— Mitchell focused on public health issues throughout his communications career, working on matters related to disease prevention, tobacco control and traffic and childhood safety. He retired from the firm he helped co-found in 2016 after being diagnosed with cancer — but his work did not stop. Mitchell launched Patients For Affordable Drugs , a nonprofit aimed at reducing drug costs for patients that is credited with securing a provision of the Inflation Reduction Act allowing Medicare to negotiate prices for certain high-priced drugs.

title: Ballard launches Western Hemisphere practice
body_text:
WILD WILD WEST: Ballard Partners has launched a new practice group dedicated to helping clients navigate the geopolitical upheaval under way across the Western Hemisphere, along with a dedicated working group focused on Venezuela specifically following the Trump administration’s military operation to depose Nicolás Maduro.

— Both groups will include Micah Ketchel and Thomas Boodry , both of whom have worked for the National Security Council under President Donald Trump as well as for top national security officials like Mike Waltz or Marco Rubio ; and Tracie Pough , the longtime former chief of staff to Rep. Debbie Wasserman-Schultz (D-Fla.), whose district includes the highest concentration of Venezuelans living in the U.S.

— Jose Felix Diaz , a former Florida legislator and attorney with extensive experience in international trade issues; Scott Wagner , an attorney specializing in business, maritime and aviation law; and Tucker Knott , who previously served as chief of staff to Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.), will also work with the new practice groups, which will provide clients with strategic advice related to Latin America, Mexico, Canada and Greenland.

— Ballard already represents Chevron , which is the only U.S. oil company licensed to operate in Venezuela after the Trump administration reinstated the company’s permission to do so last year. And though other U.S. oil giants have expressed varying degrees of skepticism about diving headfirst into Venezuela, Ballard has recently registered to lobby for Maha Capital , a Swedish company with rights to another Venezuelan oil project that is seeking U.S. approval for partnerships.

— While K Street has been fielding questions from clients about potential business opportunities in Venezuela in the wake of Maduro’s ouster, lobbyists have cautioned that there are still many unknowns. Trump’s new Western-focused foreign policy agenda “will create plentiful opportunities for clients in the Hemisphere, but they require immediate and strategic engagement in a manner that is aligned with U.S. national interests,” Ballard’s Justin Sayfie told PI.

— The firm’s new offerings are aimed at “ensuring our clients have access to the deep regional expertise and bipartisan institutional knowledge required to succeed in these critical markets,” founder Brian Ballard said in a statement.

FIRST IN PI — AMAZON LOBBYIST JOINS ATLAS: Atlas Crossing has hired Bobby Parmiter as a principal. Parmiter has spent the past three years at Amazon , where he represented the e-commerce giant before Congress on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and data privacy to tax and trade policy. He also chaired the government relations committee and PAC board of the industry group Security Industry Association .

— Before that, Parmiter spent more than a decade on the Hill, serving as general counsel for the House Intelligence Committee under chairs Devin Nunes (R-Calif.) and Mike Turner (R-Ohio). He’s also a House Judiciary, Doug Collins and DOJ alum.

MERCURY ADDS ANOTHER TRUMP ALUM: Brian Hughes , who most recently served as chief of staff at NASA, has joined Mercury Public Affairs as a partner leading the firm’s Tallahassee office. — Before joining NASA last year, Hughes was a deputy national security adviser for strategic communications at the White House and was a senior adviser and Florida campaign director for Trump’s 2024 campaign.

— Hughes also has extensive political experience in the Sunshine State, having served in then-Gov. Rick Scott ’s administration and as chief administrative officer for the city of Jacksonville and chief of staff to former Mayor Lenny Curry . WHAT THE EPC IS READING: “President Donald Trump is taking on Wall Street as he pushes his message of making life more affordable for Americans. Capitol Hill Republicans may be his biggest obstacle ,” POLITICO ’s Aiden Reiter , Katherine Hapgood and Jordain Carney report.

— “On Friday, the president called for a one-year 10-percent cap on credit card interest rates, and early Tuesday morning he endorsed the Credit Card Competition Act, a bill that would subject credit card companies to more oversight and could lower costs for merchants who accept cards.”

— “Both proposals have drawn sharp opposition from the financial sector. And both would likely require action in Congress, where Republicans have stymied similar efforts in the past, even as they have been championed by Democrats. That sets up an election-year clash between Trump and other Republicans over the president’s new populist policy agenda.”

BET ON IT: The newly launched alliance of online prediction markets has landed a pair of high-ranking former congressmembers to help the industry navigate Washington. The Coalition for Prediction Markets , whose members include Kalshi , Crypto.com , Robinhood , Coinbase and Underdog , has tapped former Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-N.Y.) as its president and CEO, while former Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) will join the group as a senior adviser.

— Maloney lost reelection in 2022 after five terms in office, which included a stint leading House Democrats’ campaign arm. McHenry, meanwhile, retired last year after two decades in the House, during which he served as chair of the powerful House Financial Services Committee as well as chief deputy whip and even, briefly, speaker pro tempore. Since leaving office, McHenry has also joined the crypto arm of venture capital firm a16z — a Kalshi investor — as a senior adviser.

— The hires come as prediction markets face increasing scrutiny from both sides of the aisle in Washington, where critics have called for additional guardrails to stem concerns about potential insider trading as well as the industry’s foray into sports betting.

WHAT TECH COMPANIES SAID ABOUT THEIR BALLROOM CHECKS: Congressional Democrats on Monday released responses from half a dozen tech companies to their questions about the tech giants’ donations to the project to erect a White House ballroom.

— The replies from Meta , Microsoft , Nvidia , Amazon , Apple and Comcast , which were shared by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Rep. Dave Min (D-Calif.), varied in length — Meta’s response , for instance, was just a single paragraph — but some did shed new light on the ballroom fundraising process, which Warren, Min and nine other Democrats have sought to frame as potential quid-pro-quo arrangements.

— Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld ’s Karen Elizabeth Christian , responding to the Democratic inquiry on behalf of Microsoft, told lawmakers that the company was contacted last fall by an unnamed fundraiser for the ballroom project and confirmed a donation to the nonpartisan nonprofit Trust for the National Mall in September.

— “Microsoft’s donation was offered without any intent to influence or affect any issue, proceeding or business Microsoft has before the federal government,” Christian wrote, adding that “the benefits of this project will redound not only to this presidency, but presidencies to come, as they welcome guests to the White House on behalf of the American people.”

— Comcast told lawmakers that its donation was made with no restrictions or conditions on how it was to be used and echoed the responses of Apple and Amazon in emphasizing the company’s “extensive history of philanthropic efforts” around D.C. Nvidia noted that D.C. landmarks such as the Washington Monument, Lincoln Memorial, Jefferson Memorial and more were all funded by private donations.

— “On Friday, the president called for a one-year 10-percent cap on credit card interest rates, and early Tuesday morning he endorsed the Credit Card Competition Act, a bill that would subject credit card companies to more oversight and could lower costs for merchants who accept cards.”

— “Both proposals have drawn sharp opposition from the financial sector. And both would likely require action in Congress, where Republicans have stymied similar efforts in the past, even as they have been championed by Democrats. That sets up an election-year clash between Trump and other Republicans over the president’s new populist policy agenda.”

BET ON IT: The newly launched alliance of online prediction markets has landed a pair of high-ranking former congressmembers to help the industry navigate Washington. The Coalition for Prediction Markets, whose members include Kalshi, Crypto.com, Robinhood, Coinbase and Underdog, has tapped former Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-N.Y.) as its president and CEO, while former Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) will join the group as a senior adviser.

— Maloney lost reelection in 2022 after five terms in office, which included a stint leading House Democrats’ campaign arm. McHenry, meanwhile, retired last year after two decades in the House, during which he served as chair of the powerful House Financial Services Committee as well as chief deputy whip and even, briefly, speaker pro tempore. Since leaving office, McHenry has also joined the crypto arm of venture capital firm a16z — a Kalshi investor — as a senior adviser.

— The hires come as prediction markets face increasing scrutiny from both sides of the aisle in Washington, where critics have called for additional guardrails to stem concerns about potential insider trading as well as the industry’s foray into sports betting.

WHAT TECH COMPANIES SAID ABOUT THEIR BALLROOM CHECKS: Congressional Democrats on Monday released responses from half a dozen tech companies to their questions about the tech giants’ donations to the project to erect a White House ballroom.

— The replies from Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, Apple and Comcast, which were shared by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Rep. Dave Min (D-Calif.), varied in length — Meta’s response, for instance, was just a single paragraph — but some did shed new light on the ballroom fundraising process, which Warren, Min and nine other Democrats have sought to frame as potential quid-pro-quo arrangements.

— Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld’s Karen Elizabeth Christian, responding to the Democratic inquiry on behalf of Microsoft, told lawmakers that the company was contacted last fall by an unnamed fundraiser for the ballroom project and confirmed a donation to the nonpartisan nonprofit Trust for the National Mall in September.

— “Microsoft’s donation was offered without any intent to influence or affect any issue, proceeding or business Microsoft has before the federal government,” Christian wrote, adding that “the benefits of this project will redound not only to this presidency, but presidencies to come, as they welcome guests to the White House on behalf of the American people.”

— Comcast told lawmakers that its donation was made with no restrictions or conditions on how it was to be used and echoed the responses of Apple and Amazon in emphasizing the company’s “extensive history of philanthropic efforts” around D.C. Nvidia noted that D.C. landmarks such as the Washington Monument, Lincoln Memorial, Jefferson Memorial and more were all funded by private donations.

title: Iceland lobbies up after ‘52nd state’ crack
body_text:
FARA FRIDAY: The Icelandic government has hired Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck to represent the island in Washington, less than a month after a quip from President Donald Trump ’s pick for ambassador about annexing the country sparked a brief diplomatic frenzy.

— Iceland retained Brownstein beginning this week to provide “strategic advice on navigating engagements” with U.S. officials, according to documents filed with the Justice Department. The six-month contract comes with a monthly retainer of $25,000.

— Their work will include helping Iceland make inroads with the federal government by brokering introductions and meetings with key stakeholders, developing strategies and tactics for its engagement with Washington. Brownstein will also serve as “a consultive [sic] resource and provide constructive feedback on emerging priorities for the Government of Iceland,” filings show.

— Former diplomat Samantha Carl-Yoder will work on the account for Brownstein along with Brandt Anderson , a former national security adviser to Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.); Brady Howell , an alum of the first Trump administration and former staffer on the House Foreign Affairs Committee; Tom Wotka , a former State Department energy official; and Jason Buckner , a former top lobbyist for the mining company BHP .

— Tensions between the U.S. and Iceland flared last month when Billy Long , the former Missouri representative and IRS chief and Trump’s nominee as ambassador to Iceland, joked to former colleagues on the House floor that the NATO ally would become the 52nd U.S. state — and Long, its governor.

— The comment, which Long apologized for a day later , set off a panic in Reykjavík, particularly given Trump’s escalating rhetoric at the time about taking over Greenland (by force if necessary). Icelanders started a petition demanding that the government reject Long as envoy.

— According to a Jan. 23 cable obtained by POLITICO ’s Nahal Toosi , Paul McLeary and Victor Jack , “Iceland’s Permanent Secretary of State Martin Eyjólfsson summoned U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Erin Sawyer to demand a high-level U.S. apology and tell her that such talk ‘has no place in international discourse.’”

DOJ MOVES TO QUASH WILES SUBPOENA: Federal prosecutors in Miami and Washington last night formally moved to quash an effort by former Rep. David Rivera to compel testimony by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles in Rivera’s trial next month on foreign agent charges.

— Defense attorneys for the former Florida Congress member and his co-defendant, political consultant Esther Nuhfer , moved to subpoena Wiles for her testimony back in December, explaining that they wanted to question Wiles about her “extensive communications” related to her lobbying work at Ballard Partners for a Venezuelan businessman who prosecutors say was involved in Rivera’s work as an unregistered agent of the Venezuelan government. Rivera and Nuhfer are also seeking testimony from Secretary of State Marco Rubio .

— But in a filing last night , the lead prosecutors on the case as well as an attorney from DOJ’s National Security Division in Washington sought to have the subpoena thrown out “due to the fact that, based on the government’s investigation in this matter, Ms. Wiles appears to have played no role in any of the relevant events.”

— At the very least, prosecutors asked District Court Judge Melissa Damian to put Wiles’ subpoena on hold “pending a more extensive factual record to be developed at trial … to better assess the potential relevance (or lack thereof) of her testimony based on the actual defense the defendants pursue at trial.”

— Prosecutors argued that Wiles’ lack of involvement is illustrated by the fact that investigators never even interviewed her. Ballard’s work for the Venezuelan TV network Globovision was not central to the core allegations of the case, they added, questioning how additional context about the firm’s work might exculpate Rivera and Nuhfer in the case.

AIPAC WHIFFS: “The American Israel Public Affairs Committee uncorked $2 million to try to sink a mainstream Democrat in a multi-candidate special House election primary in New Jersey — and it’s infuriating mainstream Democrats and some of the pro-Israel lobby’s supporters,” POLITICO ’s Elena Schneider writes.

— “The organization spent heavily through its super PAC, Unite Democracy Project , to attack former Rep. Tom Malinowski (D-N.J.), a pro-Israel moderate who would not support unconditional aid to Israel. In doing so, it provided an opening to Analilia Mejia , a progressive organizer backed by Bernie Sanders who has said Israel committed genocide in Gaza” and who’s leading Malinowski by roughly 500 votes to fill the seat vacated by new Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill .

— “The first test of the group’s muscle ahead of the 2026 primary season, when they are expected to spend millions on Democratic primaries across the country,” AIPAC’s “first foray of 2026 backfired spectacularly.”

COUPANG’S COUP: “A closed-door congressional meeting this week with South Korea’s top trade official was dominated by one topic: Coupang Inc. , the Seattle-headquartered e-commerce platform best known as the ‘ Amazon of South Korea,’” which is facing an intense probe in the country over a massive data breach there last year, per Bloomberg ’s Emily Birnbaum.

— The grilling “comes amid an intense lobbying push by Coupang, which employs just 1,000 people in the US but has ties that go as high as Kevin Warsh ,” Trump’s Fed chair nominee. The company has poured at least $5.5 million into its lobbying blitz over the last two years, winning defenders as ideologically diverse as Vice President JD Vance and Virginia Democratic Rep. Don Beyer .

— “The e-commerce platform has also opened a new Pennsylvania Avenue office just blocks from the White House and the US Capitol and partnered with Washington’s beloved Capitals hockey team. Warsh has been a Coupang board member since 2019 and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has ties to early Coupang investor Stanley Druckenmiller ” — a remarkably “high visibility for a company that is little known to most US consumers.”

BALLARD’S FOREIGN CASH BONANZA: Ballard Partners “has drawn a surge of high-paying clients with foreign interests seeking access to the administration and federal agencies,” Sludge ’s David Moore reports.

— “Many of its biggest spenders in 2025 were foreign companies or clients with significant foreign business interests. Ballard reported millions of dollars in payments from clients including oil and gas company Balkan Energy , based in Albania; TotalEnergies , for its liquified natural gas project in Mozambique; critical minerals company Korea Zinc ; and TikTok , as its Chinese owner ByteDance negotiated new U.S. ownership.”

— “Several more of Ballard’s top lobbying clients have foreign ties: one is the New Era Fund … a defense and aerospace investment fund for ventures with Saudi Arabia. A second is the holding company of Bancrédito , a Puerto Rican bank in liquidation after a bribery scandal. A third is the former fugitive and cryptocurrency billionaire Roger Ver , who cut a deal with the Department of Justice (DOJ) over tax evasion charges after living in Mallorca.”

— “Nearly all of these clients hired Ballard Partners after Trump’s election win—quickly becoming among the firm’s top lobbying spenders. … And nearly all have benefited directly from Trump administration actions. Altogether, these seven clients paid the firm more than $7 million for lobbying during Trump’s first year back in office, and three of them were its top spenders.”

title: Netflix hires another antitrust lobbyist
body_text:
NETFLIX HIRES APELBAUM: Netflix added yet another antitrust lobbyist at the start of the year, according to a newly filed disclosure, as details of the streaming giant’s growing army of lobbyists continue to trickle out. Kressin Powers’ Perry Apelbaum , a longtime top Democratic lawyer on the House Judiciary Committee, began lobbying for Netflix last month on antitrust issues in the tech industry.

— After 30 years with the Judiciary Committee, Apelbaum in 2021 joined the Justice Department as a senior counsel in the antitrust division; he also served as deputy assistant attorney general in the legislative affairs office. He joined Kressin Powers (formerly known as Kressin Meador Powers ) last spring following former partner Mark Meador ’s nomination to join the FTC.

— As PI has previously noted , Netflix has been scooping up veteran antitrust lobbyists left and right since announcing its plans to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery and the ensuing torrent of concern from official Washington and the entertainment industry.

S-3 GROUP ADDS DEM FINANCE AIDE: Chris Arneson , one of the top Democratic aides on the powerful Senate Finance Committee, is leaving the Hill after nearly a decade and a half to join S-3 Group as a principal. Arneson was most recently economic policy director for ranking member Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), helping oversee outreach to the business community and other stakeholders and managing the committee’s strategic initiatives and policy coordination.

— Over the years, he’s also served as the panel’s chief budget and economic adviser, senior tax policy adviser and research assistant over the years — giving Arneson a front row seat to some of the pivotal legislative fights including last year’s GOP reconciliation bill and the party’s 2017 tax overhaul, the 2023 debt ceiling fight and the 2022 Democratic reconciliation package.

— At S-3 Group, Arneson told PI that he expects to work on many of those same issues, especially as tax, trade and health care continue to dominate policy conversations, with an expected Supreme Court ruling on tariffs; a potential second, health care-focused reconciliation bill or tax package on the Hill; and implementation of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act continuing in the executive branch.

— “I have great relationships after 15 years … on the Finance Committee, as well as with our down-dais members” on both sides of the aisle, he said in an interview, “so hoping that I’ll get to keep doing the same issues I’ve been doing, just from a different approach.” Arneson plans on registering to lobby.

— Though S-3 Group is home to several top former aides to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and saw its annual lobbying revenues surge 63 percent last year under full GOP control of Washington, the firm also employs a number of Democratic lobbyists, including former aides to House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), former Senate Approps Chair Pat Leahy (D-Vt.), former Senate HELP Chair Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the DNC .

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips and gossip. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

FLYING IN: Hundreds of nurse practitioners are in town this week as part of a fly-in organized by the American Association of Nurse Practitioners . They’ll hit the Hill tomorrow with a focus on rallying opposition to a rule proposed by the Trump administration that would remove nurse practitioner programs from the definition of “professional degree” for purposes of federal student loan eligibility, which AANP has said the rule would be “disastrous” for the industry.

WHAT PARSCALE IS DOING FOR ISRAEL: “Since November, an unspecified number of Americans have been receiving text messages from unknown numbers claiming to be from organizations called ‘Friends for Peace’ and ‘Partners in Peace’ asking their views on Israel, promoting Israel as a U.S. ally, and pushing links to websites and videos created by Clock Tower X ,” the firm founded by former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale that inked a $9 million contract with the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs last year, according to new details of the campaign unearthed by Responsible Statecraft ’s Nick Cleveland-Stout .

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING: “President Trump’s allies are offering access to him and other perks to donors who give at least $1 million to a new group supporting flashy initiatives he is planning around the nation’s 250th birthday,” per The New York Times’ Ken Vogel , Lisa Friedman and David A. Fahrenthold .

— “The group, Freedom 250 , is threatening to overshadow years of plans meant to reach the broadest cross section of Americans for semiquincentennial celebrations. They are now taking on a Trumpian flare, replete with marble and machismo.”

— “But Freedom 250 has also emerged as another vehicle, akin to the White House ballroom project , through which people and companies with interests before the Trump administration can make tax-deductible donations to gain access to, and seek favor with, a president who has maintained a keen interest in fund-raising, and a willingness to use the levers of government power to reward financial supporters.”

OURA’S AURA: “ Oura rings are on fingers from the Pentagon to Capitol Hill, tracking everything from sleep quality to fertility. Their Finnish maker’s success stems from design savvy and good timing, but also shrewd attention to the way politics works in the capital,” POLITICO ’s Amanda Chu reports.

— “The company in the last year has hired top lobbying shops with links to the administration and Republican lawmakers in Congress, boosting its lobbying spend from $40,000 in 2024 to more than $1 million a year. … [I]t’s got a message that resonates: The rings are a solution to systemic health care challenges no one has been able to fix, ranging from physician shortages to ballooning federal spending.”

— “It’s paying off. The Defense Department, Oura’s largest customer, now provides rings to certain soldiers and civil servants as an employee benefit. … Besides buying the rings, lawmakers have gone to bat to protect Oura from Chinese and Indian competitors. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has made wearables like the Oura ring part of his Make America Healthy Again movement.”

TAKING STOCK: “At least nine senators reported stock purchases or sales last year involving companies in industries overseen by the committees they serve on,” according to CNN ’s Annie Grayer and Marshall Cohen , a trend worrying watchdogs as an effort to ban the practice loses steam on the Hill.

— “Most of the nine senators who invested in stocks that overlap with their committee assignments over the last year have comprehensive financial portfolios, not all of which raise potential conflict-of-interest issues. … But the more than a dozen trades from this small group of well-connected senators provide a window into why the phenomenon of lawmaker stock-trading has led to public outrage – and a major push to ban the practice.”

NAM KICKS OFF SURFACE TRANSPORTATION PUSH: The National Association of Manufacturers is pumping six figures into a lobbying blitz aimed at getting a surface transportation reauthorization bill and permitting reform across the finish line by the time the current authorization bill lapses Sept. 30.

— NAM’s Building to Win campaign reprises the trade group’s earlier pushes for infrastructure investment beginning a decade ago, culminating in 2021’s bipartisan infrastructure bill and last year’s House passage of permitting reforms. In addition to a nationwide ad campaign, NAM is also circulating a graphic mapping out the nation’s 25 worst freight bottlenecks and how that congestion near transportation hubs can cost the manufacturing industry billions annually.

CHANGING OF THE GUARD: The Consumer Technology Association ’s Gary Shapiro is stepping down as CEO of the trade group after 35 years at the helm. Kinsey Fabrizio , who’s been with CTA group for nearly two decades and became its president in 2024, will add chief executive to that title beginning in May. Shapiro will stay on as executive chair.

— Fabrizio joined CTA in 2008 as a manager of member programs, before working her way up to senior vice president of membership and head of CES — the trade group’s massive annual tech trade show.

— She’ll take the helm of CTA at a crucial time for the tech industry, as tech products and artificial intelligence continue to infiltrate every aspect of life across the globe, even absent a federal regulatory framework for the technology in the U.S.

— Shapiro and CTA have also been among the most vocal opponents of President Donald Trump ’s tariffs, and CTA was one of the only major business groups to lend its voice in support of the Supreme Court case challenging the duties. “There is a time for everything, and I’m pleased with the new opportunities for CTA and for my next chapter,” Shapiro said in a statement, calling the transition long-planned.

— CTA’s members include Amazon , Google , Sony , Samsung , Best Buy , Microsoft , Meta and AMD . And though the association’s lobbying outlays pale in comparison to many of its most prominent members and fellow tech organizations, CTA ranks among the largest trade groups in Washington with nearly $154 million in revenue in 2024, tax filings show. That’s a tenfold expansion from when Shapiro took the helm, according to CTA.

title: America First Policy Institute buys $20M DC building
body_text:
FIRST IN PI: The Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute bought the historic Colorado Building at 14th and G NW — massively expanding its footprint in Washington just steps away from the White House.

— AFPI finalized the sale in January and paid $20 million for the building, which sits near the Treasury Building and the soon-to-be new East Wing of the White House. The group was behind much of the Trump team transition planning and is filled with Trump loyalists. It was co-founded by now-Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, and now-Education Secretary Linda McMahon was the group’s chair before she left for the Trump transition team.

— “The America First Policy Institute was launched to carry forward President Trump’s America First agenda and serve as the permanent home for the America First movement. By strengthening our presence in Washington, we are better positioned to relentlessly advance President Trump’s proven policies and ensure these principles become a lasting, unbreakable legacy that shapes our nation for generations to come,” Greg Sindelar, interim president of AFPI, said in a statement.

— AFPI was founded in 2021, and its rise to prominence in Washington, both in influence and now in footprint, was swift. The Heritage Foundation, which was behind the Project 2025 initiative, created its institutional presence in Washington in 1973 and is headquartered on Capitol Hill. Last year, Heritage caused a clash among conservatives over the embrace of Tucker Carlson after he interviewed Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, and over a dozen staffers left the group in December to join a nonprofit led by former Vice President Mike Pence.

NARRATIVE ADDS EX-TREASURY, COMMERCE STAFFER : Narrative Strategies hired Jessica Stallone , who worked in the Treasury and Commerce Department during the Joe Biden administration, as a senior director in the New York Office. Stallone was a senior spokesperson for Treasury and director of public affairs for the Bureau of Industry and Security for Commerce. Prior to those roles, she was deputy chief of staff at the Anti-Defamation League .

— Narrative also hired Christina Cameron , former director of media operations for then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.), as senior director in the New York office. She most recently was a director at maslansky+partners .

— Narrative CEO and founding partner Ken Spain said the firm is focused on expanding its New York footprint after the new office launched in September.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. I’m Alex Gangitano, happy to be filling in for Caitlin. Also pinch hitting this week is Marcia Brown , who will fill in on Thursday, and Daniel Lippman , who will take the reins Friday.

Say hello and send influence tips to Marcia at marciabrown@politico.com and Daniel L. at dlippman@politico.com . And be sure to follow us all on X at @AlexGangitano , @Marcia_Brown9 and @dlippman .

OSBORN CANCELS FUNDRAISER AMID EPSTEIN BACKLASH : Nebraska Senate candidate Dan Osborn abruptly canceled a fundraiser that was set to be co-hosted Tuesday by Dana Chasin , a Democratic operative who was mentioned in the recently released Jeffrey Epstein files, our Daniel scooped. Chasin, a Rockefeller heir who advised Hillary Clinton ’s 2016 presidential campaign as well as former Sens. Tim Johnson (D-S.D.) and Jon Tester (D-Mont.), was mentioned for allegedly transporting young girls for Epstein.

— Osborn is running as an independent against incumbent GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts . The campaign, in an email, said the event was canceled and that “anyone who hurt kids or engaged in other illegal activity needs to be arrested and prosecuted.”

— In a statement sent Wednesday, after publication, Chasin said he had never met Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell or other prominent men mentioned in the emails or had any relationship with them. “I stand with the victims of Jeffrey Epstein and their pursuit of justice and accountability,” he said in an email.

— Chasin also donated $3,300 to Osborn’s 2024 failed Senate campaign. The campaign has donated the money to a “nonprofit organization in Nebraska whose mission is to end child abuse and trafficking.”

— The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee took $82,600 in this cycle from Chasin, Daniel writes in. The DSCC has no plans to refund or transfer the donation. “Every single Democratic senator voted to release the Epstein files to seek justice for the victims and ensure anyone involved in the abhorrent crimes is held accountable. CRITICAL LOBBYING : Ramping up critical minerals production in the U.S. involves a heady cocktail of domestic permitting reform, international infrastructure development and price floors — and that’s where lobbying giant Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck is stepping in.

— Brownstein’s new critical minerals practice, reported first in PI, will be led by co-chairs former foreign service officer Samantha Carl-Yoder and Obama alum Jason Buckner . The firm already has a significant number of critical mineral clients, but the formalization of the practice will enable more specialization for what the industry could need, Carl-Yoder told your host in an interview.

— The Trump administration is eager to dethrone China as top dog in the fight for critical minerals, but it’s easier said than done. Just last week, the administration called on more than 50 countries to join a trading bloc to counter China’s dominance in both mining and processing — but only 11 countries signed on to the nonbinding agreement. That could be partly due to the administration’s aggressive foreign policy positions and punitive tariff regime of the past year, as my colleagues previously reported.

— Navigating President Donald Trump ’s mercurial foreign policy will likely be a key challenge. “A lot of the underlining scope is, how do you improve U.S. resilience? How do you address supply chain issues? How do you make sure you’re working with allied partners?” said Carl-Yoder, who spoke to your host from the Mining Indaba conference in Cape Town, South Africa. “Sometimes that works better than it does other times.”

— Domestically, Buckner told your host he’s already working with clients on permitting reform, capital access and navigating the National Environmental Policy Act process.

— Some of Brownstein’s clients include: Ivanhoe Mines , Ivanhoe Atlantic , Ivanhoe Electric , Boston Metal , Heeney Capital and Albemarle .

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. I’m your host, Marcia Brown, happy to be here while Caitlin is off. Daniel Lippman will be writing tomorrow. Add me on Signal at marciagbrown.68 or email me at marciabrown@politico.com .

Say hello and send influence tips to Daniel L. at dlippman@politico.com . And be sure to follow us all on X at @AlexGangitano , @Marcia_Brown9 and @dlippman .

Programming note: We’ll be off this Monday but back in your inboxes on Tuesday.

ICYMI — KENNEDY CENTER SAGA : Trump “has brought in his top fundraiser to shore up giving at the Kennedy Center after a series of stumbles by its development leader, a former TV host close to Kari Lake , according to six people familiar with the matter,” our Daniel Lippman scooped last night.

— “Trump intervened in January and tapped his longtime supporter Meredith O’Rourke to stabilize the Kennedy Center’s fundraising operation, in a move that effectively sidelined senior vice president Lisa Dale , according to three current and one former employee.”

— “O’Rourke is also in charge of fundraising for the new White House ballroom and helped raise the money to replace the Rose Garden with a paved patio.”

MIDTERM MONEY : “Artificial intelligence startup Anthropic announced Thursday that it is donating $20 million to Public First Action , a political action committee set up to support candidates who favor AI regulations in the midterm elections,” our Brendon Bordelon reported Thursday.

— “Anthropic’s $20-million infusion into Public First, a 501(c)(4), comes days after an AI industry super PAC, Leading the Future , announced it has so far raised $125 million. Leading the Future aims to support AI-industry friendly candidates, and its donors include venture capitalist firm Andreessen Horowitz , OpenAI President Greg Brockman and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale .”

FOREIGN DONATIONS: American colleges and universities have so far reported receiving more than $5.2 billion in foreign gifts and contracts last year, the Trump administration disclosed Wednesday as it presses ahead with investigations into four schools’ foreign ties, our Juan Perez Jr. reports in Morning Education .

The latest available numbers in the Education Department’s new foreign funding reporting portal now reflect approximately $67.6 billion in total foreign funding that institutions have reported receiving since 1986, Juan adds.

THE BLUE ZONE — Washingtonian’s Jessica Sidman reports that Rhonda Foxx , who served as national women’s engagement director for both the Biden and Harris campaigns, has opened Civic, a cafe and bar — a “Butterworth’s for like-minded individuals,” Foxx said, referencing the MAGA locale . (H/t POLITICO Playbook)

— But, but but: D.C. is already a deep-blue city. “‘Why don’t we have a lib Butterworth’s?’ Er... you mean like every other restaurant and coffee shop in DC?” White House deputy press secretary Abigail Jackson said on X .

MARRIAGE BOOTCAMP : The Heritage Foundation is drawing online criticism, per USA Today’s Kate Perez , for a policy proposal to boost birthrates that would involve marriage bootcamps.

— “The online report, titled ‘Saving America by Saving the Family: A Foundation for the Next 250 Years,’ published Jan. 8 by The Heritage Foundation, lays out ways the group says the United States can ‘restore the family home,’ including through monetarily incentivizing couples to have children and stay married, among other efforts,” Perez reports.

— The marriage bootcamps would “cover topics like communication, money management and conflict resolution for ‘cohabiting couples with children.’”

— “The successful completion of the program would conclude with couples ‘ready to walk down the aisle at a communal wedding,’ the report states, and a potential $5,000 monetary incentive − funded by foundations or private donors − for couples to get married. Additionally, newlyweds would leave with a mentor couple to guide them through marriage following the wedding.”

Members will meet with congressional offices to urge changes to the Water Resources Development Act and more investments in the Port Infrastructure Development Program among other issues.

The firm already has a significant number of critical mineral clients, but the formalization of the practice will enable more specialization for what the industry could need, Carl-Yoder told your host in an interview.

— The Trump administration is eager to dethrone China as top dog in the fight for critical minerals, but it’s easier said than done. Just last week, the administration called on more than 50 countries to join a trading bloc to counter China’s dominance in both mining and processing — but only 11 countries signed on to the nonbinding agreement. That could be partly due to the administration’s aggressive foreign policy positions and punitive tariff regime of the past year, as my colleagues previously reported.

— Navigating President Donald Trump’s mercurial foreign policy will likely be a key challenge. “A lot of the underlining scope is, how do you improve U.S. resilience? How do you address supply chain issues? How do you make sure you’re working with allied partners?” said Carl-Yoder, who spoke to your host from the Mining Indaba conference in Cape Town, South Africa. “Sometimes that works better than it does other times.”

title: Swiss billionaire’s nonprofit funding at issue in Nebraska House race
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — CORNHUSKER CONSULTING CASH: Allegations of foreign influence have entered the crowded Nebraska race to replace retiring GOP centrist Rep. Don Bacon — a crucial pickup opportunity for Democrats as they look to retake the House.

— The state’s Republican attorney general is suing five nonprofit groups backing liberal causes including abortion rights and public school funding, claiming they receive support from Swiss billionaire Hansjörg Wyss .

— Democratic operative Denise Powell , one of five Democrats in the race and the top fundraiser , received at least $10,000 in consulting fees from some of the nonprofits at the center of the action by Nebraska AG Mike Hilgers, according to her personal financial disclosure .

— The groups, including the Sixteen Thirty Fund and New Venture Fund , backed two ballot referendums in 2024. One would have enshrined the right to an abortion up to the second trimester in the state constitution but failed. Another one passed that kept public money out of private schools.

— Those two funds that Powell worked for were among the groups sued by Hilgers.

— Powell campaign manager Ryan Longenecker said she is not involved in the lawsuit or fundraising for these entities and instead had worked on organizing and communications for the ballot measures.

— “Denise was proud to help lead efforts to fight back against MAGA attempts to defund Nebraska public schools and pass a statewide abortion ban,” he said in a statement to PI. “This lawsuit is nothing but another desperate, authoritarian attempt by the MAGA movement to attack the ability of Nebraskans to stand up for good schools and healthcare access — following Donald Trump’s efforts to misuse the Justice Department to persecute political opponents.”

— The lawsuit came as the Trump administration and House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) also started to probe some liberal nonprofit groups across the country, with Comer particularly focusing on Wyss-linked groups.

— Hilgers alleged in the suit that Wyss had routed the money through two nonprofits, the Wyss Foundation and Berger Action Fund , which then contributed to two other nonprofits, the New Venture Fund and the Sixteen Thirty Fund. Hilgers claimed that New Venture Fund and the Sixteen Thirty Fund then gave money to other groups, some of which Powell also consulted for. Nebraska law says it’s illegal for “a foreign national, directly or indirectly, to make a contribution to a ballot question committee.”

— The next hearing in the case is scheduled for March.

— “Nebraskans are under an unprecedented assault of foreign money, flowing unlawfully into our state’s elections, which seeks to radically remake Nebraska’s laws and constitution,” Hilgers said in a statement announcing the suit in November. “This billionaire and his dark-money allies have flaunted the law in Nebraska, and we filed suit to put a stop to these groups who seek to violate Nebraska law while pushing their radical agenda on the people.”

— The Wyss Foundation and Berger Action Fund are fighting the lawsuit saying the AG’s allegations are “false” and that they are “confident the facts will demonstrate that the Wyss Foundation and Berger Action Fund have always complied with the law.” The Sixteen Thirty Fund also called the lawsuit “baseless” and “politically motivated” and said the group and state partners it works with comply with Nebraska law.

— Asked if he is also investigating conservative donor networks, Hilgers said he’s seen “no evidence” of wrongdoing by groups on the right. Hilgers said that he’s not accusing the local Nebraska groups of breaking the law.

— The winner of the May 12 Democratic primary will face Republican Omaha City Councilmember Brinker Harding .

CASH CRUNCH AT NELP — A budget crisis at the National Employment Law Project has the workers’ rights organization at odds with its staff , my colleague Nick Niedzwiadek scoops.

— “NELP leadership has initiated buyouts in recent weeks, and the organization is weighing layoffs that staffers fear could cut their ranks by more than half,” Nick writes. “The cutbacks have come after a major grant that the organization had been courting for more than a year fell through in late January, according to four people familiar with the matter who were granted anonymity to discuss the situation.”

Happy Friday the 13th and welcome to PI. Hope everyone has fun Valentine’s Day plans! I’m your host, Daniel Lippman, happy to be here while Caitlin is off. Send K Street tips to daniel@politico.com and follow me on X @dlippman .

RUEMMLER TO RESIGN FROM GOLDMAN — “Goldman Sachs general counsel Kathryn Ruemmler will step down after the Jeffrey Epstein files showed she had remained a close ally of the convicted sex offender through his 2019 arrest,” the Wall Street Journal ’s AnnaMaria Andriotis reports.

— “Ruemmler had risen to the top ranks of Wall Street and become a key adviser to Goldman Chief Executive David Solomon after a storied legal career. … She was picked as White House counsel by former President Barack Obama and was once considered a candidate to be U.S. attorney general. The Wall Street Journal revealed Ruemmler’s relationship with Epstein in 2023 when it reported she was among the powerful people regularly meeting with him in the years after he pleaded guilty to soliciting a minor for prostitution.”

BIG TECH BREATHES A SIGH OF RELIEF — “The departure of Gail Slater , the Department of Justice’s antitrust chief, is sparking fears that President Donald Trump is abandoning the populist antitrust movement that helped propel him to the White House,” my colleagues Katherine Long and Aaron Mak write in Morning Tech.

— “Big Tech has eagerly wined and dined Trump in the hopes he will treat them favorably by enacting pro-tech policies and dropping federal investigations into their companies. And Slater’s exit only exacerbates fears that these cases, which often are directed at industry leaders, will be used as bargaining tools between Big Tech and the administration as the White House exerts its political control of the division.”

— Said William Kovacic , chair of the Federal Trade Commission under President George W. Bush : “If you’re an antitrust division careerist, how do you go about doing your job now when you just watched your boss walk the plank?”

CRYPTO GOES AFTER GREEN — Crypto is officially opening its wallets for the midterms, starting with a challenge to Rep. Al Green (D-Texas).

— A crypto-backed super PAC that’s part of the “industry’s main political organization, Fairshake , said it would spend $1.5 million to try to defeat Mr. Green in his Democratic primary race next month,” the New York Times ’ Theodore Schleifer and Shane Goldmacher report. “The effort is the opening salvo of what is expected to be heavy spending by the crypto industry in the midterms. Fairshake, which began the year armed with $193 million, is making a new push after its 2024 spending helped elect a more pro-crypto Congress, which has passed crypto-friendly legislation that President Trump signed.”

INFLUENCE AD WATCH — Former Rep. Colin Allred is going negative against Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas) in his primary bid, accusing her in a new ad of “making thousands from the company ICE uses to track and detain our neighbors.” (h/t Morning Score)

SAUNDERS TO HANG UP HIS HAT — Lee Saunders , the longtime head of the largest union of state and municipal government workers, plans to retire later this year, Morning Shift reports. Saunders has led the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees for 14 years and will step down after his successor is elected at the union’s convention in August. He was the first African American elected to the position.

ACCF ADDS PERSONNEL — As it marks its 50th anniversary, the American Council for Capital Formation — a bipartisan business advocacy group and affiliated think tank whose boards include Obama’s former chief economist, Jason Furman , and previously included President Trump’s chief economist, Kevin Hassett — has announced a slate of personnel changes.

— George David Banks is now president and CEO of the group, taking over from Mark Bloomfield , who stepped down to become chair of the ACCF board of directors. Michael Zehr has joined as senior fellow for mining and supply chain security, and Timothy Fitzgerald as senior fellow for energy economics. John Dabbar , Maya MacGuineas , Ed Goeas and former Reps. Earl Blumenauer (D-Ore.) and Garret Graves (R-La.) have joined its board of advisers. Tomas Philipson has joined ACCF’s board of scholars.

Jobs report

— David Ogden is now senior counsel at Democracy Defenders Fund , Playbook reports. He most recently worked at WilmerHale and is a longtime DOJ alum.

— Loretta Polk , vice president and deputy general counsel for legal and regulatory affairs at NCTA , is retiring this month, per Morning Tech.

— Ziya Smallens started this week as TD Bank ’s senior speechwriter. He most recently was chief speechwriter and senior adviser to former New Jersey Gov. Phil Murphy , and is also an alum of Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.).

— FanDuel has added Meg McGaughey as senior director of federal government affairs and Rob Mejia as director of federal government affairs. McGaughey previously worked for House Majority Leader Steve Scalise . Mejia previously worked at FGS Global .

— Luisana Pérez Fernández has launched Horizonte Strategies , a bilingual comms firm focused on media and narrative strategy, especially for Latino audiences. She previously worked in the Biden White House, and is an HHS and Biden campaign alum.

— The Herald Group has promoted Cameron Smith to VP, EC Wheatley and Colin Hensel to senior directors, Brooke Ainslie to director, Sallie Sorenson , Wyatt Hamilton , Caitlin Burns , Malyia Kelley and Andrew Thomas to account managers and Tess Cohen-Dumani and Madi Fike to senior associates.

— Kat Skiles is joining Reproductive Freedom for All as SVP of comms and digital strategy. She previously led Narrative and is a DNC and Nancy Pelosi alum.

— Minna Jung is now senior director at Rally . She is an Earthjustice and Environmental Defense Fund alum.

— Retired Col. Peter Boone has taken over as government affairs manager for Air National Guard programs at the National Guard Association of the United States , per National Security Daily. Boone’s final military tour was serving as the National Guard Bureau Legislative Liaison Division Chief.
