MEDIA MOVES: A pair of prominent media outlets have new leaders for their government relations shops in D.C. TelevisaUnivision has tapped Bernadette Carrillo to lead its D.C. office as senior vice president of government relations, filling a role that had been vacant for nearly two years following the departure of Steve Haro in 2024.

— Carrillo was most recently a managing director at the New York consultancy Tusk Strategies , where she helped launch its Washington office and stood up a CHIPS Act practice and Latino outreach practice at the firm. She previously served as director of intergovernmental affairs for former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo and in the White House Office of Presidential Personnel under former President Joe Biden .

— Meanwhile, Versant , the new parent company of MS NOW , CNBC , E! , USA Network and more, has hired Jonathan Kott as senior vice president of government affairs, where he will oversee the company’s public policy efforts. Kott was most recently a partner at Capitol Counsel , and before that he wore a number of different hats on the Hill, including simultaneously working for former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.).

AV STAKEHOLDERS LOBBY UP: A handful of autonomous vehicle stakeholders have added new lobbying muscle since the beginning of the year, according to newly filed disclosures. AV trade group the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association retained Mehlman Consulting last month to work on issues related to the industry as well as “access to critical technologies,” ahead of a Feb. 4 Senate hearing featuring industry leaders and the trade group’s chief executive.

— Meanwhile BlackSea Technologies , which manufactures unmanned boats, brought on American Defense International to lobby on federal “unmanned surface vehicle programs and industrial base,” according to a disclosure. And autonomous submarine manufacturer Albacore hired Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck earlier this month — the company’s second lobbying hire since retaining Crossroads Strategies last summer.

Kevin Yoder (R-Kan.), who will lobby for the aviation giant on a host of issues, including quality and safety, supply chains, commercial aviation and commercial and aftermarket operations.

— “The sum is the biggest election investment by Meta, which owns Facebook , Instagram and WhatsApp ” and which “was previously cautious about campaign engagements. … Now Meta is betting bigger on politics, driven by concerns over the regulatory threat to the artificial intelligence industry as it aims to beat back legislation in states that it fears could inhibit A.I. development.”

— “To do that, Meta is quietly starting two new super PACs, according to federal filings surfaced by The New York Times. One group, Forge the Future Project , is backing Republicans. Another, Making Our Tomorrow , is backing Democrats. The new PACs join two others already started by Meta, one of which is focused on California while the other is an umbrella organization that finances the company’s spending in other states.”

— “Meta’s spending is set to start this week in Illinois and Texas, where the company generally favors backing Democratic and Republican incumbents or engaging in open races rather than deposing existing officials.”

DE MINIMIS FOES PUSH BACK ON COMEBACK BID: A coalition of labor groups, domestic manufacturers, business groups and law enforcement organizations is urging House leadership to reject a bipartisan effort to mirror the so-called de minimis exemption that President Donald Trump moved to end last year.

— A new bill from Reps. Carol Miller (R-W.Va.) and Don Beyer (D-Va.) would create a new channel aimed at streamlining the shipment of low-cost goods of $600 or less using express carriers, which the lawmakers said would address “the growing backlog of goods at America’s express ports” caused by the end of de minimis.

— White House trade adviser Peter Navarro slammed the bill in an op-ed in The Hill earlier this month. And today, more than two dozen members of the Coalition to Close the De Minimis Loophole , including the AFL-CIO , the National Association of Police Organizations , the National Council of Textile Organizations and Families Against Fentanyl urged House Speaker Mike Johnson and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries to block the measure , arguing it would “resurrect the underlying problems associated with the de minimis trade loophole our coalition worked so hard to close.”

WHAT AIPAC’S UP TO: Democrats running in heated congressional primaries in Illinois are accusing AIPAC of “masking its involvement” in their races amid a reexamination in the party of politicians’ support for Israel, The Washington Post ’s Matthew Choi writes.

— “Amid this shift, AIPAC has become a prominent antagonist for many Democrats , particularly those in the progressive wing of the party. Republicans have largely maintained a good relationship with the organization, and it is for that reason that candidates in Illinois say AIPAC, now unable to influence Democratic campaigns as it once did, is attempting to affect results through new groups.”

— “Democrats in the state say they have seen an influx of ads focusing on issues ranging from immigration to health care by groups named Elect Chicago Women and Affordable Chicago Now . None of the ads mention Israel, and none of the groups are publicly affiliated with AIPAC. But the ads benefit candidates favored by AIPAC donors.”

WHO’S FUNDING SCHIFF’S LEGAL DEFENSE: “Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff ’s nascent legal defense fund — created to parry legal threats from President Donald Trump — is already a million-dollar operation ,” NOTUS’ Dave Levinthal reports, having pulled in $1.2 million from around 400 PACs and individual donors through the end of 2025.

— “The influx of cash arrived as Trump publicly accused Schiff of corruption and illegal behavior and the Department of Justice investigated the California lawmaker for mortgage fraud. Schiff denies wrongdoing and hasn’t been indicted.”

— “Schiff’s fund supporters include almost two dozen leadership political action committees, including those led by Sens. Mark Kelly of Arizona, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Alex Padilla of California, Jack Reed of Rhode Island, Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin and Reps. Nancy Pelosi of California, Eric Swalwell of California and Tim Kennedy of New York.”

— “Other contributors include the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians ($10,000), Pulitzer Prize-winning presidential biographer Ron Chernow ($2,500) and movie director Rob Reiner , who donated $1,000 in November, the month before he and his wife were killed.”

title: Crypto optimistic for compromise with banks

CRYPTO DENTENTE: Cryptocurrency companies and big banks may finally be approaching a compromise on stablecoin yield payments that could clear the way for a crypto regulation bill currently stalled in the Senate.

— The crypto industry and banks have fought for months on the issue of stablecoin yields, a practice where crypto exchanges pay stablecoin holders interest via rewards programs. Banks strongly oppose the practice, which competes with traditional interest-paying accounts, and have previously called for Congress to close a loophole in the GENIUS Act that makes such payments possible.

— The back and forth has stalled progress on what would be a landmark crypto regulation bill, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act , currently before the Senate Banking Committee. Brian Armstrong , CEO of crypto exchange Coinbase and one of the industry’s biggest proponents for stablecoin interest payments, publicly denounced a draft version of the bill last month. Now, he’s changing his tune.

— “There’s now a path forward where we can get a win-win-win outcome here,” Armstrong told CNBC yesterday . “Win for the crypto industry, a win for the banks and a win for the American consumer to get President Trump’s crypto agenda through to the finish line so we can make America the crypto capital of the world.”

— “There’s a small list of remaining open items and I think that if a compromise can be found this will get to the president’s desk for a signature in a few months,” he added. In the same interview, Banking Committee member Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) predicted passage “hopefully by April.”

— The apparent progress comes a week after a White House meeting between the two sides. During that meeting, banks proposed an outright ban on stablecoin yield payments. That’s a suggestion the crypto industry is unlikely to acquiesce to, and based on Amrstrong’s latest optimism, may no longer be on the table.

TA-TA TO TARIFFS: President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs are no longer in effect after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled today that the emergency economic powers law cited by the White House last year doesn’t actually permit the president to impose tariffs.

— Trade associations across Washington quickly praised the ruling and cast the decision as an opportunity for the president to work with businesses that have been shaken by volatile trade policies during the first year of the administration.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce , one of the few major business groups to file legal briefs opposing the tariffs, called the decision “welcome news for business and consumers.”

— “We encourage the administration to use this opportunity to reset overall tariff policy in a manner that will lead to greater economic growth, larger wage gains for workers, and lower costs for families,” Neil Bradley , the chamber’s chief policy officer, said in a statement.

— The administration doesn’t appear to share the associations’ desire for a reset. Hours after the court released its opinion, Trump announced a new 10 percent global tariff, instituted under a different authority than the one evaluated by the justices. This new tariff will remain in effect for 150 days, unless extended by Congress.

— The question of whether the government will be required to refund businesses that already paid the now-illegal tariffs also remains unsettled . That question was not addressed by the justices, likely leaving the matter up to lower courts to decide.

Alford is barred in D.C. and Florida.

— Alford is scheduled to be deposed Monday in the HPE case. Other former DOJ officials are currently fighting subpoenas for their depositions, including Chad Mizelle , the attorney general’s former chief of staff. Individuals who lobbied for the merger settlement, including Mike Davis , Will Levi and Arthur Schwartz , are also set to be deposed in the coming weeks.

title: K Street’s tariff work is far from over
body_text:
IT NEVER ENDS: President Donald Trump ’s tariffs may be no longer , but that doesn’t mean K Street’s cash cow is going to fade away after last week’s Supreme Court ruling. There’s still immense interest from the business community about where trade policy goes from here, as evidenced by a webinar on the ruling hosted by the trade team at Squire Patton Boggs this morning, which drew more than 400 attendees.

— “We’re fielding calls from clients opposed to tariffs who are acting like it’s V-E day,” said Hunter Morgen , a trade lobbyist at Ballard Partners , adding that he’s advised clients this is “a short blip.”

— Clients across K Street are clamoring for intel on what the refund process will look like . There are also questions about the fate of the country-specific trade deals already struck by the Trump administration and the alternative tariff authorities the Trump administration plans to lean on to try and recreate the duties struck down by the court Friday. ( Mehlman Consulting ’s Bruce Mehlman has a helpful graphic on his Substack illustrating how many different avenues the administration still has in its toolbox.)

— That includes Section 232 tariffs that have already been levied on products like aluminum, steel and auto parts, with pending investigations focused on everything from critical minerals to pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, as well as Section 301 tariffs on goods from China.

— “If you’re a company, this decision is very problematic, because now there is no predictability into how the layering of other authorities can impact supply chain strategy,” said Samir Kapadia , who leads the trade practice at The Vogel Group . Some clients, he said, may have been happier with Trump’s International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariff regime “because it’s clean, it’s understandable. … Now I’ve got to worry about three different authorities and how they all work together. Pain in the butt, that’s what companies are saying.”

— On the other hand, “the fact that [tariffs] can’t just be dropped on some of these guys just out of nowhere and there’s a defined process is a little more comforting for those in the business community,” Morgen said.

— Lobbyists are already gaming out how to approach this process, which arguably has much higher stakes. “Those programs are super durable, and frankly, once they’re put into place, they’re very hard to roll back,” Kapadia said of trade authorities like Section 301 and 232.

— “If you don’t raise objections then the investigation may not take into account your [or] consider your particular situation, so being on the record is important,” Everett Eissenstat , a trade lobbyist at Squire Patton Boggs, cautioned during today’s webinar.

— Morgen said that his firm “has engagement ideas and engagement strategies based on every possible option or opportunity that the administration can put forward,” But, he added, “we have to see the details surrounding the executive actions before we can really turn the key on anything.”

title: Downtown has some ideas for Trump on affordability
body_text:
WHAT’S IN A NAME: When President Donald Trump takes the stage tonight for the first State of the Union address of his second term , there are a slew of issues the business community will be looking to hear from him on — which has many groups couching their pet policy priorities in language that the president will surely recognize.

— “We’ll be watching to see whether the President connects economic affordability with America’s leadership in financial innovation,” Blockchain Association chief Summer Mersinger told PI in a statement.

— Mersinger touted digital assets as a tool to help with “reducing costs, expanding economic access, and giving Americans more control over their financial lives” and arguing that “the right regulatory framework can protect consumers while ensuring these technologies are developed and scaled here in the United States, not overseas.”

— The U.S. Chamber of Commerce , meanwhile, is hoping that Trump will use his bully pulpit to talk about “how we take on frivolous lawsuits,” Chamber president and CEO Suzanne Clark told CNBC this morning. “We’ve got trial lawyers clogging up the courts and costing American families $4,200 a year,” she said. “States that have tackled it are seeing decreasing insurance costs and housing costs. We’d like to hear the president go after it too.”

— Also on the Chamber’s wishlist is the implementation of a federal regulatory framework for artificial intelligence and passage of a surface transportation reauthorization ahead of its expiration in September.

— And multiple industry groups — including the Business Roundtable , the National Association of Manufacturers , the American Petroleum Institute , the American Chemistry Council and the Chamber — want to hear Trump beat the drum on permitting reforms, which Clark noted would help Trump build on last summer’s tax cuts and his administration’s broader deregulation push.

— “American oil and natural gas production is at record levels, and energy is critical to affordability and economic growth,” API President and CEO Mike Sommers said in a statement, adding that “the challenge before us is not supply but the infrastructure to deliver it.”

— Business groups are also anxiously awaiting Trump’s next moves on tariffs in the wake of last week’s Supreme Court decision. Austen Jensen , senior executive vice president of public affairs at the Retail Industry Leaders Association , said in a statement that “the time is optimal for President Trump and Congress to work together to chart a trade policy that will achieve the administration’s goals to grow the economy, create jobs and protect our national security.”

— Beyond trade policy, retailers want to hear Trump nudge Congress on the contentious swipe fee legislation that the president endorsed last month as part of a midterm-focused affordability push. “By bringing more stability to the trade landscape and ensuring competition in the payments system, Congress and the president can deliver solutions that will help Americans,” Jensen argued.

— Clark echoed RILA’s emphasis on Congress’ role in implementing tariffs, which she suggested would go a long way toward improving much-needed certainty for businesses. BRT’s Joshua Bolten , meanwhile, stressed that an extension of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement along with “duty-free North American trade” would be a huge boon for “domestic manufacturing, supporting American farmers and workers, and keeping costs down for families.”

— On the health care front, drugmakers will be listening to see how Trump proposes building on the pharmacy benefit manager reforms he signed into law this month, “particularly steps to rein in insurer and PBM consolidation, curb excessive coverage denials, and bring more transparency and accountability to the 340B program,” said PhRMA spokesperson Chanse Jones . The trade group is also reiterating the importance of policies that help maintain U.S. leadership in drug development.

DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

FIRST IN PI: Adam Suess is returning to K Street, joining Squire Patton Boggs as a principal following a yearlong stint working for Interior Secretary Doug Burgum . — “While polling suggests the data center debate is far from being a top-tier midterm subject, the issue is bubbling up as a wedge for lesser-known candidates looking to differentiate themselves from the pack,” especially as more high-profile Democrats shift their positions on the issue.

— Still, “it’s unclear how much traction the data center discussion will give underdog candidates. Despite deep concern in certain communities, voters’ views about data centers appear far from settled.”

title: Another White House aide heads downtown
body_text:
ANOTHER ONE: Taylor LaJoie has left the White House, where he most recently served in the legislative affairs office, to join Alpine Group as a vice president. LaJoie has been serving as a special assistant to President Donald Trump as well as one of the West Wing’s liaisons to the Senate, where he previously worked for Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and now-Vice President JD Vance .

— LaJoie is also an alum of the Tax Foundation , and worked on the 2017 GOP tax cuts under Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah). More recently, he was a key intermediary for the Trump administration on last year’s reconciliation bill, placing him among a growing crowd of new K Streeters who worked on the GOP megabill.

— He’s also the latest White House aide to cash in on their time in the administration with a new gig downtown, a group that includes fellow leg affairs alum Natalie McIntyre , now at Miller Strategies , former spokesperson Harrison Fields , now at CGCN Group ; former economic adviser Robin Colwell , now at Intel ; Brette Powell and Brian Hughes , now at Mercury Public Affairs ; former national security advisers Micah Ketchel and Thomas Boodry , now at Ballard Partners ; and May Davis Mailman and Trent Morse , who started their own firms.

REVIEWS ARE IN: Hats off to all of you who stayed up for all of last night’s record-breaking stem-winder , which shed a little more light on what Trump plans to do next on tariffs, but has left lobbyists scrambling for more details about the pledge tech companies are set to sign at the White House next week aimed at forcing Silicon Valley to shoulder more of the financial burden of AI data centers.

— While the speech was “heavy on patriotism, party divide, pageantry, and performance,” it was not “a call to action for a refreshed policy agenda,” the team at Invariant noted in its breakdown of everything the president did (and didn’t) touch on during his address. (POLITICO is a client of Invariant.)

— “On the issues, even the ‘controversial’ items for K street were cursory and shallow,” said John Stanford , a partner and CEO of the consulting firm Novel Strategies .

— One other thing Trump’s speech was shockingly light on? Corporate callouts. “This is the SOTU that corporate PR pros dreamt of: no name checking of the Fortune 100,” Stanford noted. “That’s a big departure from the past and a key objective of their teams in Washington,” he added. Generally speaking though, “that’s as much calm [as] K Street can hope for,” he said.

‘That’s bad for him to say’: Trump puts Paxton on notice in Texas Senate primary

By DANIEL LIPPMAN , DANIEL BARNES and CAITLIN OPRYSKO

02/26/2026 08:09 PM EST

Presented by

FIRST IN PI — Republicans are poised to make the Democratic mayor of Scranton, Pennsylvania’s support for a local bank a top issue in one of the nation’s most competitive House races, Daniel L. reports.

— While Mayor Paige Cognetti has hit her opponent Rep. Rob Bresnahan over his stock trading while in office, she is now facing scrutiny for helping secure a multimillion-dollar state grant for a new Fidelity Bank headquarters at the same time her uncle-in-law sat on the board of the company.

— She also received $14,600 in campaign contributions from Fidelity board members months before getting the city to purchase Fidelity’s old Scranton branch building last year.

— “By the end of the campaign, each and every voter in Northeast Pennsylvania will be acutely aware that Paige is an unelectable, corrupt, poll-constructed fraud,” Reilly Richardson , a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement to PI when asked about the reporting.

— Cognetti, whom the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee on Monday put on its “Red to Blue” list , is running against Bresnahan, one of Democrats’ primary targets this cycle.

— “Mayor Paige Cognetti’s record of delivering for Scranton is unimpeachable,” a Cognetti spokesperson said in a statement when asked about her dealings with Fidelity.

— Cognetti has served as mayor since 2020 and in her 2019 campaign, she ran on fighting political corruption within the local Democratic apparatus, using the campaign slogan “Paige Against the Machine.” One of her top issues she’s using against Bresnahan is his many Wall Street transactions of last year, including the sale of Pennsylvania health care-related bonds and stock in Medicaid providers around the time he voted on Medicaid cuts. Bresnahan’s team has said his financial adviser did all the trading without his prior knowledge, but he has since suspended the activity.

— In 2022, Fidelity Bank, which has been in the region for more than a century, announced it had bought the historic Electric Building in downtown Scranton but left it vacant because it needed extensive renovations. In 2024, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro gave Fidelity a $5 million grant to help renovate the building, which is expected to eventually house 165 Fidelity employees. In 2022, after they purchased the building and were counting on state government support for a renovation, Fidelity thanked Cognetti for her support for the project , calling it “vital to making the Bank’s vision a reality.”

— The next year, on April 29, 2025, all nine members of Fidelity’s board of directors at the time, including her uncle-in-law and Fidelity board secretary John Cognetti , gave $1,500 each to Cognetti’s mayoral campaign, according to Pennsylvania campaign finance records.

— John Cognetti didn’t respond to a request for comment. Bresnahan spokesperson Peter Brath did not respond when asked if Bresnahan supported the new Fidelity Bank headquarters renovation project.

— Seven months later after the donations, council members learned that Cognetti had added an item to the budget requesting the city purchase Fidelity’s old headquarters to convert it into an extension of City Hall, despite a recent costly renovation. Cognetti’s advocacy for the project came after the CEO of Fidelity said the city was interested in buying the building. The extension will be used for public safety purposes including a Police Department real-time crime center facility; Scranton’s police chief called the project “a gold mine for us” because of its potential to improve public safety.

— Two members of the City Council expressed major opposition to the purchase, with Mark McAndrew saying : “If I was to vote yes, then I would vote yes to a conflict and a behavior that I am uncomfortable with.” Council member Thomas Schuster raised questions about the fiscal responsibility of the purchase, asking about the loss of tax revenue from the building, a possible pricey renovation and uncertain operating costs. Incoming City Council member Sean McAndrew also voiced concerns about the purchase. The city ended up purchasing the building for slightly lower than the assessed value . The proposal to buy the building ultimately passed the City Council by only a 3-2 margin.

— The Cognetti spokesperson defended her actions in the matter by touting her mayoral tenure. “She has breathed new life into the city by creating good-paying union jobs, upgrading Scranton’s credit rating to A- level status, and investing millions of dollars in policing,” the spokesperson said. “Every decision Paige has made as mayor has been with the goal of benefiting the people – never herself.” The spokesperson pointed out that there are 186 Cognettis in the region and many of them have donated to her.

— DCCC spokesperson Eli Cousin also hit back against Republicans raising concerns about Cognetti’s Fidelity dealings by saying in a statement “they are resorting to desperate, laughable lies.”

— Bresnahan, who owns between $15,001 and $50,000 in Fidelity stock, has also praised the bank’s presence in Scranton, saying in 2022 , “I love having Fidelity there.” (In April 2024, Bresnahan also received a $3,300 donation from James Clemente , who joined the Fidelity Bank board last month. Clemente didn’t respond to a request for comment.) In recent months, Bresnahan has tried to make crime an issue in the race although Brath, his spokesperson, did not respond to a question when asked whether he supports the new police facility. But Brath said Bresnahan “is a steadfast supporter of our brave police” and had recently secured a half million grant for officer safety in Scranton.

— Fidelity spokesperson Tara Smith said in a statement that the restoration of the Scranton Electric Building was supported by numerous leaders at the government level and that it was grateful for the support of Cognetti and other elected officials for the project.

— “As for individual campaign contributions, Fidelity Bank does not direct or coordinate political giving,” Smith said. “Board members, like any private citizens, may support candidates of their choosing in their personal capacity. … Our focus remains on strengthening the communities we serve and continuing to invest in the economic vitality of Scranton and the region.”

REFUND FIGHT : The Trump administration is working overtime to come up with a strategy that would allow the government to keep billions of dollars in tariff revenue collected before the Supreme Court struck down the president’s IEEPA tariffs last week, our colleagues Megan Messerly and Daniel Desrochers report . But officials are likely to run into a wall of opposition from Big Business, which is eager for refunds following the court’s ruling.

— Business groups across Washington publicly called for the administration to begin issuing refunds last week and at least one major company, FedEx , has filed a lawsuit demanding its money back. Bresnahan’s team has said his financial adviser did all the trading without his prior knowledge, but he has since suspended the activity.

title: CAA hires Brownstein
body_text:
BIG PICKUP FOR BROWNSTEIN: Hollywood talent giant Creative Artists Agency has retained Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck to lobby on issues related to the entertainment industry and artificial intelligence, according to a disclosure filing. It’s the first time CAA has had federal outside lobbyists on retainer, disclosure filings show, though Tyrone Bland served as the talent agency’s head of global government affairs from 2020 to 2023.

— The hire comes as the entertainment and media industries grapple with myriad challenges posed by AI, including its use of copyrighted materials and the unauthorized use of AI-generated images, voices and likenesses.

— Though many of the entertainment industry’s top stakeholders — from movie studios and recording labels to sports leagues and unions — have reported monitoring Washington’s efforts to set guardrails for AI, the major individual talent agencies have minimal lobbying footprints in the nation’s capital.

— Endeavor , the parent company of sports and media talent agency WME , briefly retained I Street Advocates last year to work on NIL issues for college athletes and issues related to AI deepfakes. Endeavor also retained ACG Advocacy during President Donald Trump ’s first term, disclosure filings show. The firm continues to work for another Endeavor-owned property, United Fighting Championship , on AI issues, among other things.

— Though CAA didn’t previously have any D.C. lobbying firms on its roster, that’s not to say the agency lacked connections in Washington. CAA has long represented Higher Ground, the production company started by Barack and Michelle Obama . And in February, the agency picked up two more big political clients : former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris .

Happy Monday and welcome to PI . Send K Street scoops and feedback. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X : @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

FOOD FIGHT: The beverage and packaged goods industries have formed a new coalition focused on promoting ingredient transparency. It’s an effort to tamp down growing skepticism of ultra-processed foods and additives fueled by the Make America Healthy Again movement.

— The coalition, Americans for Ingredient Transparency , is a project of the American Beverage Association and the Consumer Brands Association and it is working with the food and ag lobbying firm Russell Group , according to a disclosure filing.

— The initiative builds on separate pushes by ABA, CBA and their member companies to stave off ingredient bans at the hands of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Both ABA and CBA rolled out initiatives earlier this year aimed at providing more information about ingredients in processed foods.

SPEAKING OF: Kennedy “has a reputation for bashing powerful corporate interests in his quest to ‘Make America Healthy Again.’ But one industry has eked out a win under Kennedy’s MAHA agenda: Big Agriculture,” WaPo ’s Amudalat Ajasa and Rachel Roubein write.

— “In May, the Trump administration’s MAHA commission released a report raising questions about the health effects of two commonly used pesticides, glyphosate and atrazine. The report’s rhetoric frustrated powerful agriculture groups such as CropLife America and the American Soybean Association , prompting them to launch a concerted lobbying blitz to promote the chemicals farmers rely on to produce large crops, according to interviews with industry officials.”

— “Their efforts seemingly paid off. The Trump administration’s MAHA strategy document released last month did not call for restrictions on pesticides and instead said the EPA would work to ensure the public is aware of its ‘robust’ review procedures, a marked shift from Kennedy’s past criticism of chemicals as contaminating the nation’s food supply.”

ANNALS OF POSITIVE REINFORCEMENT: Nearly three dozen national trade associations representing a broad cross-section of industry implored the White House today to “resist pressures” to let up on antitrust enforcement in Trump’s second term and to “reaffirm its commitment” to an aggressive antitrust posture.

— After a series of developments that have spooked competition hawks,the groups wrote in a letter to the president , that he should “press forward with the full slate of pending cases currently being advanced by the FTC and DOJ” and avoid relenting to pressure for adopting a “more hands-off approach” to antitrust.

— “We encourage you to stand with those committed to implementing the bold vision you’ve articulated when you announced your Administration’s antitrust enforcers,” the groups added, lauding antitrust appointees like Gail Slater at DOJ and Andrew Ferguson and Mark Meador at the FTC.

— The plea comes on the heels of several big losses for antitrust hawks in recent months. They include a settlement between the FTC and Amazon, and DOJ settling its challenge to a proposed software merger. The latter case has cast a spotlight on internal divisions over antitrust policy and debate over the influence of politically connected lobbyists in antitrust cases.

— The letter comes in the midst of antitrust proceedings involving companies like Google and Ticketmaster . Its signatories include the Coalition for App Fairness , Energy Marketers of America , the National Community Pharmacists Association , the National Grocers Association , the News Media Alliance and the Small Business Majority , as well as dozens of state and local business groups and businesses.

DOWNBALLOT DOWNLOAD: “ Everytown for Gun Safety , the country’s largest gun control group, has contributed $200,000 to Jay Jones ’ campaign for Virginia attorney general and hailed the Democrat as an ‘advocate for safer communities.’ But now, as Jones is embroiled in scandal over text messages in which he fantasized about shooting a Republican state leader, Everytown is sitting on the sidelines ,” the Washington Free Beacon ’s Chuck Ross reports.

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE WEEKEND: “The lines between business and geopolitics have blurred in the second Trump presidency,” The Wall Street Journal ’s Rebecca Ballhaus , Drew Hinshaw and Joe Parkinson report. And “ zigzagging between them is” Gentry Beach , an investor with ties to Donald Trump Jr. “who just weeks into the new administration launched a new company that echoes Trump’s trademark slogan: America First Global .”

— “Since November’s election, he has traveled to 20 countries to meet presidents, prime ministers and foreign ministers, pursuing deals he says are worth billions of dollars. His targets align with a key Trump foreign policy plank: The president wants to resolve wars and geopolitical disputes by placing American companies in the potentially lucrative center.”

— “Beach expects his investment firm to be one of those companies. He has no official title or State Department designation, and said he has never invoked the Trump family or the Trump administration in his business dealings. Instead, he says he represents a new model of diplomacy to help foreign governments strengthen ties with Washington.”

— Still, “Trump Jr., who declined to comment, has privately told people he is frustrated with his old friend.”

BIG PICKUP FOR BROWNSTEIN: Hollywood talent giant Creative Artists Agency has retained Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck to lobby on issues related to the entertainment industry and artificial intelligence, according to a disclosure filing. It’s the first time CAA has had federal outside lobbyists on retainer, disclosure filings show, though Tyrone Bland served as the talent agency’s head of global government affairs from 2020 to 2023.

— The hire comes as the entertainment and media industries grapple with myriad challenges posed by AI, including its use of copyrighted materials and the unauthorized use of AI-generated images, voices and likenesses.

— Though many of the entertainment industry’s top stakeholders — from movie studios and recording labels to sports leagues and unions — have reported monitoring Washington’s efforts to set guardrails for AI, the major individual talent agencies have minimal lobbying footprints in the nation’s capital.

— Endeavor, the parent company of sports and media talent agency WME, briefly retained I Street Advocates last year to work on NIL issues for college athletes and issues related to AI deepfakes. Endeavor also retained ACG Advocacy during President Donald Trump’s first term, disclosure filings show. The firm continues to work for another Endeavor-owned property, United Fighting Championship, on AI issues, among other things.

— Though CAA didn’t previously have any D.C. lobbying firms on its roster, that’s not to say the agency lacked connections in Washington. CAA has long represented Higher Ground, the production company started by Barack and Michelle Obama. And in February, the agency picked up two more big political clients: former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. Send K Street scoops and feedback. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com. Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com. Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns.

FOOD FIGHT: The beverage and packaged goods industries have formed a new coalition focused on promoting ingredient transparency. It’s an effort to tamp down growing skepticism of ultra-processed foods and additives fueled by the Make America Healthy Again movement.

— The coalition, Americans for Ingredient Transparency, is a project of the American Beverage Association and the Consumer Brands Association and it is working with the food and ag lobbying firm Russell Group, according to a disclosure filing.

— The initiative builds on separate pushes by ABA, CBA and their member companies to stave off ingredient bans at the hands of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Both ABA and CBA rolled out initiatives earlier this year aimed at providing more information about ingredients in processed foods.

SPEAKING OF: Kennedy “has a reputation for bashing powerful corporate interests in his quest to ‘Make America Healthy Again.’ But one industry has eked out a win under Kennedy’s MAHA agenda: Big Agriculture,” WaPo’s Amudalat Ajasa and Rachel Roubein write.

— “In May, the Trump administration’s MAHA commission released a report raising questions about the health effects of two commonly used pesticides, glyphosate and atrazine. The report’s rhetoric frustrated powerful agriculture groups such as CropLife America and the American Soybean Association, prompting them to launch a concerted lobbying blitz to promote the chemicals farmers rely on to produce large crops, according to interviews with industry officials.”

— “Their efforts seemingly paid off. The Trump administration’s MAHA strategy document released last month did not call for restrictions on pesticides and instead said the EPA would work to ensure the public is aware of its ‘robust’ review procedures, a marked shift from Kennedy’s past criticism of chemicals as contaminating the nation’s food supply.”

ANNALS OF POSITIVE REINFORCEMENT: Nearly three dozen national trade associations representing a broad cross-section of industry implored the White House today to “resist pressures” to let up on antitrust enforcement in Trump’s second term and to “reaffirm its commitment” to an aggressive antitrust posture.

— After a series of developments that have spooked competition hawks,the groups wrote in a letter to the president, that he should “press forward with the full slate of pending cases currently being advanced by the FTC and DOJ” and avoid relenting to pressure for adopting a “more hands-off approach” to antitrust.

— “We encourage you to stand with those committed to implementing the bold vision you’ve articulated when you announced your Administration’s antitrust enforcers,” the groups added, lauding antitrust appointees like Gail Slater at DOJ and Andrew Ferguson and Mark Meador at the FTC.

— The plea comes on the heels of several big losses for antitrust hawks in recent months. They include a settlement between the FTC and Amazon, and DOJ settling its challenge to a proposed software merger. The latter case has cast a spotlight on internal divisions over antitrust policy and debate over the influence of politically connected lobbyists in antitrust cases.

— The letter comes in the midst of antitrust proceedings involving companies like Google and Ticketmaster. Its signatories include the Coalition for App Fairness, Energy Marketers of America, the National Community Pharmacists Association, the National Grocers Association, the News Media Alliance and the Small Business Majority, as well as dozens of state and local business groups and businesses.

DOWNBALLOT DOWNLOAD: “Everytown for Gun Safety, the country’s largest gun control group, has contributed $200,000 to Jay Jones’ campaign for Virginia attorney general and hailed the Democrat as an ‘advocate for safer communities.’ But now, as Jones is embroiled in scandal over text messages in which he fantasized about shooting a Republican state leader, Everytown is sitting on the sidelines,” the Washington Free Beacon’s Chuck Ross reports.

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE WEEKEND: “The lines between business and geopolitics have blurred in the second Trump presidency,” The Wall Street Journal’s Rebecca Ballhaus, Drew Hinshaw and Joe Parkinson report. And “zigzagging between them is” Gentry Beach, an investor with ties to Donald Trump Jr. “who just weeks into the new administration launched a new company that echoes Trump’s trademark slogan: America First Global.”

— “Since November’s election, he has traveled to 20 countries to meet presidents, prime ministers and foreign ministers, pursuing deals he says are worth billions of dollars. His targets align with a key Trump foreign policy plank: The president wants to resolve wars and geopolitical disputes by placing American companies in the potentially lucrative center.”

— “Beach expects his investment firm to be one of those companies. He has no official title or State Department designation, and said he has never invoked the Trump family or the Trump administration in his business dealings. Instead, he says he represents a new model of diplomacy to help foreign governments strengthen ties with Washington.”

body_text:
BONDI DODGES ON DOJ LOBBYING QUESTIONS: Attorney General Pam Bondi spent her morning sparring with Senate Judiciary Committee Democrats, deflecting questions on Jeffrey Epstein and decrying former special counsel Jack Smith ’s subpoenaing of phone records from various GOP senators during his investigation into President Donald Trump ’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election results.

— Bondi, who lobbied for Qatar when she was in private practice, got only one question about her role in approving Qatar’s donation of a Boeing 747 for use as the new Air Force One. But she faced questions from several senators about reported attempts to lobby the Justice Department by companies in the crosshairs of the antitrust division.

— Earlier this summer , the Justice Department fired two senior antitrust officials after they disagreed with a decision by higher-ups to overrule the antitrust division and settle a lawsuit that sought to block a merger between Hewlett Packard Enterprise and fellow tech company Juniper Networks . One of the fired officials, Roger Alford , later publicly accused department leaders of cutting a deal with MAGA-friendly lobbyists who had been hired to represent Hewlett Packard.

— “I have full faith in Gail Slater ,” Bondi said in regards to the assistant attorney general in charge of the DOJ’s antitrust division. She otherwise declined to answer questions about ongoing antitrust matters, including the department’s lawsuit against LiveNation and Ticketmaster .

— Bondi got more combative when Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) brought up her former boss Brian Ballard’s connection to a separate dropped antitrust lawsuit involving American Express Global Business Travel and CWT Holdings .

— “I understand that Brian Ballard , longtime backer and head of the [lobbying] firm where you worked, was instrumental in lobbying the Justice Department to drop that lawsuit,” Blumenthal asked. “What conversation did you have with Mr. Ballard?”

— “Senator Blumenthal, I cannot believe that you would accuse me of impropriety when you lied about your military service,” Bondi said, referencing accusations that Blumenthal had inflated his service record during his first Senate campaign. “You lied. You admitted you lied to be elected a U.S. senator. You lied. How dare you? I’m a career prosecutor, don’t you ever challenge my integrity. I have abided by every ethics standard. Do not question my ability to be fair and impartial as attorney general in anything [inaudible] my former firm Ballard Partners.”

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI. Have you had success lobbying the Justice Department? Send us your tips at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

FIRST IN PI — CAP6 LANDS HILL VETERAN: Capitol 6 Advisors has hired Kristin Richmond Clarkson , a nearly 15-year veteran of Capitol Hill who spent the last decade working in various staff roles for the House Appropriations Committee and its subcommittees, as vice president. She most recently served as staff director and majority clerk for the subcommittee on interior and environment.

— Clarkson will take her appropriations expertise to the small firm founded in 2019 by Chris Cox , former chief lobbyist for the National Rifle Association . Cap6 has signed 13 new clients since the start of 2025 — an eclectic group that includes firearms manufacturer Sig Sauer , Taser manufacturer Axon Enterprise , the U.S. Park Police union, preservation non-profit The Everglades Trust and canned soup maker The Campbell’s Company .

MANATT POACHES TEAM FROM HOLLAND & KNIGHT: Los Angeles-based Manatt, Phelps & Phillips has poached several key members of Holland & Knight’s local government advocacy team. They have brought with them numerous local government clients, such as the cities of Philadelphia, San Francisco, Cleveland, San Diego and the port of Los Angeles. Termination reports filed by Holland & Knight in recent days suggest that as many as 30 clients could follow the team to Manatt.

— Eve O’Toole , Leslie Pollner , Lisa Barkovic , Joe O’Brien and Adrianna Williams have all decamped to Manatt’s growing government advocacy and contracting practice. They will bulk up the Washington presence of a team largely based in California. O’Toole and Pollner join as managing directors, Barkovic as a senior legislative advisor and O’Brien and Williams as legislative advisors.

INTERNATIONAL FRANCHISE ASSOCIATION LAUNCHES $5 MILLION AD CAMPAIGN: Seeking to spread the word that franchises are more than just faceless chain stores, the International Franchise Association is launching a $5 million ad campaign aimed at highlighting local franchise owners and operators.

— The “Franchise Means Local” campaign is the largest ever run by the IFA and will consist of social media, digital and streaming TV ads featuring franchisees across the country discussing their store’s ties to local communities.

FLYING IN: The government may be shut down but the fly-ins continue. Since the shutdown started last week, members of the National Star Route Mail Contractors Association went to Capitol Hill to meet with Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Jim Lankford (R-Okla.), Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) and Reps. Nikki Budinski (D-Ill.), James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) and Emily Randall (D-Wash.).

Jessica Blakemore also joins as principal deputy general counsel. She most recently served as special assistant to the president and senior associate counsel in the Biden White House Counsel’s Office.

— Katie Barr has been promoted to CEO of Glen Echo Group . She has been with the firm for 14 years, serving as president since last September.

— Bondi, who lobbied for Qatar when she was in private practice, got only one question about her role in approving Qatar’s donation of a Boeing 747 for use as the new Air Force One. But she faced questions from several senators about reported attempts to lobby the Justice Department by companies in the crosshairs of the antitrust division.

— Earlier this summer, the Justice Department fired two senior antitrust officials after they disagreed with a decision by higher-ups to overrule the antitrust division and settle a lawsuit that sought to block a merger between Hewlett Packard Enterprise and fellow tech company Juniper Networks. One of the fired officials, Roger Alford, later publicly accused department leaders of cutting a deal with MAGA-friendly lobbyists who had been hired to represent Hewlett Packard.

— “I have full faith in Gail Slater,” Bondi said in regards to the assistant attorney general in charge of the DOJ’s antitrust division. She otherwise declined to answer questions about ongoing antitrust matters, including the department’s lawsuit against LiveNation and Ticketmaster.

— Bondi got more combative when Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) brought up her former boss Brian Ballard’s connection to a separate dropped antitrust lawsuit involving American Express Global Business Travel and CWT Holdings.

— “I understand that Brian Ballard, longtime backer and head of the [lobbying] firm where you worked, was instrumental in lobbying the Justice Department to drop that lawsuit,” Blumenthal asked. “What conversation did you have with Mr. Ballard?”

— “Senator Blumenthal, I cannot believe that you would accuse me of impropriety when you lied about your military service,” Bondi said, referencing accusations that Blumenthal had inflated his service record during his first Senate campaign. “You lied. You admitted you lied to be elected a U.S. senator. You lied. How dare you? I’m a career prosecutor, don’t you ever challenge my integrity. I have abided by every ethics standard. title: A new strategy for Tesla
body_text:
TESLA HIRES CONTINENTAL: Elon Musk’s Tesla has hired Continental Strategy , according to a disclosure filing, the latest sign that the electric car manufacturer is seeking to rebuild its standing in Donald Trump’s Washington.

— As PI reported last year , Tesla lost several members of its public policy staff and cut ties with multiple outside lobbying firms amid Musk’s political realignment and vociferous support for then-candidate Trump. Tesla’s September 2024 signing of Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld was an early sign that the company was seeking to reenergize its lobbying efforts but the firm appears to have done little work for Tesla since then, reporting no activity in 2025.

— What work Continental will perform for Tesla is unclear. The disclosure lists a start date of Monday this week and says the firm will lobby on “mobility and transportation” issues. On the account for Continental are Paul Calkins , Alex Garcia and Tim Costa.

— The hiring of Continental also marks the first time Tesla has gone with an explicitly pro-Trump firm — perhaps notable given the public deterioration of Musk and Trump’s relationship since the start of the administration. Continental founder Carlos Trujillo is a longtime Trump adviser and campaign surrogate who helped mobilize Latino voters for Trump in 2024. The other firms on Tesla’s payroll — Akin, Rich Feuer Anderson and Cassidy & Associates — are all bipartisan shops.

FIRST IN PI — RIDGELINE ADDS GOP NATSEC VET : Ridgeline Advocacy Group , the firm started earlier this year by a trio of former lobbyists at FTI Consulting , has added a new partner and practice group focused on defense tech and international investment.

— Josh Hodges , a former national security adviser to House Speaker Mike Johnson and an alum of the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, will lead the new practice group.

— Hodges most recently worked in corporate affairs and as a senior adviser at telecom and digital services company VEON , and he currently serves in a handful of other national security-focused roles, including as a member of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission and Anthropic ’s National Security and Public Sector Advisory Council.

— He also worked for the Inter-American Development Bank during Trump’s first term — all of which Hodges argues give him unique insights for those looking to take advantage of the direction the Trump administration is headed on key foreign policy issues.

— “The current administration recognizes that the status quo was not working and [that the] Pentagon was falling behind,” Hodges told PI, which “presents a generational opportunity for companies that are pushing innovative technology, speed, and delivering results on a wide range of issues from weapons sales to better leveraging AI, and new defense tech.”

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. The government has now been shut down for a full week. Let us know your thoughts at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

FAMILY BUSINESS: An online prescription drug delivery company that boasts Donald Trump Jr. as a board member will host a gathering of pharmaceutical executives and Trump administration regulators at the Four Seasons in Georgetown this December, Annie Linskey and Josh Dawsey report for The Wall Street Journal .

— The company, BlinkRx , operates a service that helps drug companies set up direct-to-patient sales like the type that have recently been pushed by Trump. Last week, the president announced the upcoming launch of a new website ( TrumpRx.gov ) that will direct consumers to a platform selling Pfizer drugs at reduced prices.

— An invite to the December event lists meeting opportunities with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr ., Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz and Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Marty Makary , according to the report. Companies invited include Pfizer , Eli Lilly and Amgen .

SPEAKING OF SONS: Hunter Biden was involved in the potential sale of land surrounding the U.S. embassy in Romania to a group that included a Chinese company while simultaneously serving as the personal lawyer for the Romanian developer who owned the land, Ken Vogel reports for The New York Times .

— Biden’s work for the Romanian developer, Gabriel Popoviciu, was referenced last year by prosecutors in Biden’s tax evasion case. Biden and others on Popoviciu’s legal team were hired to defeat a corruption case against the developer and reached out to U.S. officials to urge intervention on Popoviciu’s behalf, according to prosecutors. Biden was never charged with FARA violations, but prosecutors said they intended to introduce evidence at trial showing how Popoviciu’s payments to Biden and his associates were structured to avoid meeting registration requirements.

HACKERS INFILTRATE WILLIAMS & CONNOLLY: Chinese hackers have accessed computer systems at Williams & Connolly and are suspected of accessing more than a dozen other law firms and tech companies, Michael Schmidt reports for The New York Times .

— “In recent days, the firm has sought to reassure clients by telling them that to the best of its knowledge the hackers are not looking to make the information they took public or sell it. It told clients that some of the email accounts for its lawyers had been breached and that the hackers may have gained access to some client emails.”

— In a statement provided to the Times, Williams & Connolly said there is “no evidence that confidential client data was extracted from any other part of our I.T. system, including from databases where client files are stored.”

ZIP IT UP: A coalition made up of dozens of municipalities across the country has turned to K Street as part of a fight to update the nation’s zip codes. The National ZIP Code Advocacy Coalition , which was started by the Southern California city of Eastvale, retained Van Scoyoc Associates at the beginning of the month to advance the coalition’s goals.

— Harry Glenn , Jim Crum , Rodney Emery , Will Smith and Maggie McGrane will work on the account for Van Scoyoc, according to disclosure filings.

— Eastvale, like dozens of other cities in the coalition, comprises two different ZIP codes, which it shares with neighboring jurisdictions. Cities and towns say that sharing ZIP codes has hampered everything from sales tax revenue and insurance rates to mail delivery and emergency response times, and lawmakers have introduced several legislative fixes that would assign unique ZIP codes to select municipalities.

— In July, the House passed a bipartisan bill led by Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) that would designate dozens of towns and cities to receive unique ZIP codes, while a separate bill also passed by the House in July would call for unique ZIP codes for a smaller number of communities. The Senate has yet to take up either of the measures.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: The American Chemistry Council has hired Ballard Partners to work on issues related to cargo and transportation safety and efficiency, according to a disclosure filing.

— Brian Ballard and Dan McFaul began lobbying for the trade group at the beginning of October, amid a push by the chemicals industry for the Trump administration to reject the proposed merger between rail giants Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern . Last month, more than three dozen executives of ACC member companies urged President Donald Trump to oppose the merger , warning that combining two of the country’s largest freight railroads would subject American manufacturers to higher costs and service disruptions.

— Meanwhile anti-abortion group Students for Life of America has enlisted outside lobbyists for the first time as part of a push for the Trump administration to investigate ways to identify traces of abortion pills in the water supply. Michael Eging of Acuity Strategic Partners began working this week on issues related to “clean water in American cities,” on behalf of Students for Life, according to a disclosure filing.

— The New York Times reported last month that Students for Life was behind a June letter sent from 25 Republican lawmakers that asked EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to look into the matter, which the agency reportedly did.

— As abortion pills like mifepristone have emerged as a new focal point in the fight over abortion rights, anti-abortion advocates have sought to raise environmental concerns about the use of the pills, which sometimes result in fetal remains being flushed down the toilet. Experts have dismissed the claim that abortion pills might contaminate the water supply.

— “Stardust is developing an integrated system to produce reflective particles, distribute them in the stratosphere and monitor their effectiveness. The startup and its investors are hoping the U.S. or a coalition of other governments will eventually decide to pay for the use of its technology.”

title: Lobbyist faces disturbing charges
body_text:
A TROUBLING CASE: A Republican lobbyist who worked for Donald Trump ’s 2016 presidential campaign and his first transition has been indicted on charges of possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material.

— Scott Mason , 61, is accused of distributing the material — some of which was generated using artificial intelligence — “approximately 50 times between March 28, 2025, and May 1, 2025” using the online messaging platform Kik , according to documents filed in federal court in Charlotte, North Carolina, last week.

— Mason turned himself in to authorities Oct. 27 and pleaded not guilty to one charge of distribution of child sexual abuse material and one charge of possession and access with intent to view child sexual abuse material, according to court filings. He was released on bond with unspecified conditions the same day, and his trial was set for January.

— If convicted, Mason faces a mandatory minimum sentence of five years in prison, prosecutors say. Mason declined to comment, and his attorneys did not respond to requests for comment.

— Mason most recently was a lobbyist in the D.C.-based government relations practice of Holland & Knight, a major law and lobbying firm. He joined the firm in 2017 after serving as a congressional liaison for Trump’s first transition team and on his 2016 campaign. Before that, Mason spent nearly a decade as an in-house lobbyist for Lowe’s .

— Lobbying disclosures filed ahead of October’s third quarter reporting deadline show Mason de-registered from all of his more than two dozen federal lobbying clients.

— Holland & Knight spokesperson Darrin Schlegel told PI that Mason was terminated from the firm prior to his indictment. “The charges filed in this case are shocking and profoundly disturbing,” he said in a statement, adding that “our thoughts are with those affected and the Firm is cooperating fully with law enforcement authorities.”

— Authorities first began investigating Mason in May after Kik’s parent company reported an account on the platform to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children for uploading suspected child sexual abuse material, prosecutors said. An email address and IP address linked to the account in question were registered to Mason, according to prosecutors.

— After obtaining Mason’s alleged chat records, the FBI executed a search warrant at Mason’s Mooresville, North Carolina, home July 14, where they seized 11 electronic devices, prosecutors say. Investigators interviewed Mason the same day, during which he agreed to turn over his iPhone and password.

— He “denied intentionally downloading or distributing CSAM [child sexual abuse materials]” but “admitted to using Kik for sexual-related conversations, which he called, ‘entertainment,’” according to court filings.

— “He acknowledged that he engaged in sexually explicit conversations about minor females, which he claimed to be a fantasy and an outlet. He further acknowledged that he received CSAM ‘to continue the fantasy,’ although he claimed he ‘never solicited’ the material,” the filings continue.

— Prosecutors shed light on details of the case as part of a dispute with Mason’s attorneys over their plans for reviewing the contents of his seized devices.

— Though Mason is not a lawyer — his title at Holland & Knight was senior policy adviser — his attorneys have claimed attorney-client privilege and work product protection over all of the devices and are pushing for a special master to conduct a forensic analysis of them, prosecutors said in court records. The government has argued that is not necessary.

PAY UP: Cornell University announced this afternoon it reached a deal to pay the Trump administration a $30 million fine to settle ongoing federal investigations into alleged antisemitic incidents on campus, POLITICO’s Bianca Quilantan reports . The agreement will restore hundreds of millions of dollars in federal grants that had been frozen since earlier this year. Cornell also agreed to invest an additional $30 million in agricultural research.

title: Kimberly-Clark hires Ballard
body_text:
KIMBERLY-CLARK LOBBIES UP: Kimberly-Clark , the consumer goods conglomerate that owns brands including Kleenex and Huggies , boosted its outside lobbying roster last month ahead of an announcement that it plans to purchase Tylenol parent company Kenvue . Ballard Partners began lobbying for Kimberly-Clark on Oct. 15 on “issues related to corporate transactions, regulatory compliance, and general business matters,” according to disclosure filings.

— Kimberly-Clark revealed last week it would spend $40 billion on its acquisition of Kenvue, the company formed in 2023 when Johnson & Johnson broke off its consumer products division. Kenvue had already been struggling before the Trump administration began openly linking the active ingredient in Tylenol, acetaminophen, to autism, The New York Times reported, and had been talking to potential buyers since the summer.

— Both companies have minimal lobbying operations in Washington. Kenvue has been slowly building out its roster of outside lobbyists, bringing on the Vogel Group , Barnes & Thornburg and Washington Tax & Public Policy Group in recent years.

— The more established Kimberly-Clark has just two other outside firms on retainer besides Ballard: Prime Policy Group and Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld . The company has dropped $1 million on lobbying Washington so far this year, according to disclosure filings, compared with $240,000 for Kenvue.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI . What are your clients prioritizing once the government reopens? Let us know. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

WHAT TO EXPECT WHEN YOU’RE EXPECTING: The longest shutdown in history is on track to end this week , setting up myriad legislative fights for lawmakers to try to tackle during the dwindling 2025 legislative calendar.

— “The House hasn’t been in session now for over 50 days. The Senate’s been here, but it’s been largely just voting on funding bills. So all the conversations that we saw happening before Oct. 1, whether it was about permitting reform, a potential end-of-year health care package, a lot of the debates that you’re seeing within the financial services industry, are going to come back to the forefront,” said Mary Werden , a vice president at public affairs firm Rokk Solutions .

— In a memo last week, Werden advised companies looking to capitalize on the government’s eventual reopening to “think of policymakers’ top priorities as entry points into conversations that are timely and will attract attention from key audiences.”

— With last week’s elections in the rearview, that means there’s a “real need” for clients to retool their messaging accordingly, Werden told PI today. “Now is the time to really think long-term about how to … find a message that’s going to work regardless of whether you’re talking to Republicans and Democrats,” she said. “And that is affordability. It’s talking about job growth, and it’s talking about how you’re helping people in their own backyards.”

— There likely isn’t enough time left for measures like permitting reform or health care to make it across the finish line by 2026. But Werden expects crucial groundwork to be laid in the coming weeks — especially with Affordable Care Act subsidies remaining a live issue and another funding deadline coming up at the end of January, assuming the Senate deal passes.

RIGHT ON CUE: The name brand drug lobby PhRMA , which is hoping to see a crackdown on pharmacy benefit managers passed by the end of the year, is out with a new ad blaming PBMs and the 340B hospital drug discount program for higher drug costs.

— “America is the only country in the world where middlemen take nearly 50 cents of every dollar spent on medicine,” the 30-second spot says , before going on to highlight drugmakers’ commitments — under pressure from Trump — to offer direct-to-consumer discounts for certain medicines and to invest in domestic manufacturing. The ad will run within the Beltway through the end of the year.

COMING ATTRACTIONS: “Sen. Bernie Sanders (I., Vt.) and a group of Democratic senators are demanding the White House answer for higher electric bills they blamed in part on the artificial-intelligence boom driving one of the most expensive infrastructure build-outs in U.S. history,” The Wall Street Journal ’s David Uberti reports.

— “In a letter to the White House and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , the group took aim at Meta , OpenAI , Alphabet , Oracle and other firms behind a data-center build-out stretching from the Washington suburbs to rural Oregon. President Trump’s push to fast-track these projects is forcing Americans into ‘bidding wars with trillion-dollar companies to keep the lights on at home,’ they wrote.”

— “The missive is the latest sign of pushback against the AI boom buoying the U.S. economy and markets while straining power producers’ ability to keep up. Local activists in many areas have begun organizing against data centers that receive sizable tax breaks and require huge amounts of power,” and “concerns around increasing electric bills helped fuel Democratic victories last week in New Jersey’s gubernatorial election and down-ballot races in Virginia and Georgia.”

ANNALS OF ETHICS: Housing finance chief Bill Pulte “fired internal watchdogs at Fannie Mae who were looking into multiple complaints against a high-ranking company officer close to him,” The Washington Post ’s Rachel Siegel reports.

— “Pulte said last month he had fired dozens of Fannie Mae employees in what he said included a bid to end diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives at the mortgage giant. Yet six people familiar with the matter said those firings effectively cleared out the company’s internal watchdogs, charged with ensuring Fannie and its officials follow the law.”

— “The ethics team — including its chief, Suzanne Libby — was fired shortly after Fannie management directed investigators to cease looking into the Pulte ally, said a couple of the people familiar with the situation.”

FLYING IN: More than 300 members of the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association will descend on the Hill on Wednesday for the group’s annual fly-in and conference. Participants are slated to meet with hundreds of House and Senate offices to push for the restoration of Medicare telehealth authority for audiologists and speech-language pathologists and for lawmakers to support a bipartisan bill to extend the expiring ACA subsidies.

— They’ll also urge lawmakers to prevent the firing of federal workers who administer programs that facilitate hearing screenings for newborns and who help school-based professionals support students with disabilities.

SASSOON’S NEW GIG: Danielle Sassoon , the former federal prosecutor who quit rather than drop corruption charges against New York Mayor Eric Adams , has joined boutique conservative law firm Clement & Murphy as a partner in its Supreme Court and appellate practice. Sassoon resigned in February as interim U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York when she was asked to dismiss the charges against Adams. Two other top DOJ attorneys joined Sassoon in quitting over the order.

AL-SHARAA’S SHERPAS: Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa made his first trip to the White House today, a visit preceded by “a flurry of activity in Washington , as lawmakers tried to make sense of a country that one day was considered a rogue nation locked in protracted civil war and the next was viewed as a free state on the path to stability,” according to Jewish Insider ’s Gabby Deutch .

— “Two people in particular have become fixtures on Capitol Hill, pushing the message that Washington should lift sanctions on Damascus and build stronger ties with Syria: Jasmine Naamou and Tarek Naemo , a married couple who live in Daytona Beach, Fla., with a knack for social media self-promotion and a willingness to strike up a conversation with anyone.”

— “They first came to Capitol Hill this year as activists with the Syrian American Alliance for Peace and Prosperity , a nonprofit that emerged early this year to advocate for closer ties between the U.S. and Syria, though Naamou said she doesn’t work directly with them anymore.”

— “The organization arranged meetings for Syria’s foreign minister in New York this year, and in April it brought two members of Congress — Reps. Cory Mills (R-FL) and Marlin Stutzman (R-IN) — to Syria for the first visit by U.S. officials in years. Naamou and Naemo were on the trip with them.”
