Kimberly-Clark hires Ballard

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

11/10/2025 06:10 PM EST

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

KIMBERLY-CLARK LOBBIES UP: Kimberly-Clark, the consumer goods conglomerate that owns brands including Kleenex and Huggies, boosted its outside lobbying roster last month ahead of an announcement that it plans to purchase Tylenol parent company Kenvue. Ballard Partners began lobbying for Kimberly-Clark on Oct. 15 on “issues related to corporate transactions, regulatory compliance, and general business matters,” according to disclosure filings.

— Kimberly-Clark revealed last week it would spend $40 billion on its acquisition of Kenvue, the company formed in 2023 when Johnson & Johnson broke off its consumer products division. Kenvue had already been struggling before the Trump administration began openly linking the active ingredient in Tylenol, acetaminophen, to autism, The New York Times reported, and had been talking to potential buyers since the summer.

— Both companies have minimal lobbying operations in Washington. Kenvue has been slowly building out its roster of outside lobbyists, bringing on the Vogel Group, Barnes & Thornburg and Washington Tax & Public Policy Group in recent years.

— The more established Kimberly-Clark has just two other outside firms on retainer besides Ballard: Prime Policy Group and Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld. The company has dropped $1 million on lobbying Washington so far this year, according to disclosure filings, compared with $240,000 for Kenvue.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. What are your clients prioritizing once the government reopens? Let us know. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com. Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com. Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns.

WHAT TO EXPECT WHEN YOU’RE EXPECTING: The longest shutdown in history is on track to end this week, setting up myriad legislative fights for lawmakers to try to tackle during the dwindling 2025 legislative calendar.

— “The House hasn’t been in session now for over 50 days. The Senate’s been here, but it’s been largely just voting on funding bills. So all the conversations that we saw happening before Oct. 1, whether it was about permitting reform, a potential end-of-year health care package, a lot of the debates that you’re seeing within the financial services industry, are going to come back to the forefront,” said Mary Werden, a vice president at public affairs firm Rokk Solutions.

— In a memo last week, Werden advised companies looking to capitalize on the government’s eventual reopening to “think of policymakers’ top priorities as entry points into conversations that are timely and will attract attention from key audiences.”

— With last week’s elections in the rearview, that means there’s a “real need” for clients to retool their messaging accordingly, Werden told PI today. “Now is the time to really think long-term about how to … find a message that’s going to work regardless of whether you’re talking to Republicans and Democrats,” she said. “And that is affordability. It’s talking about job growth, and it’s talking about how you’re helping people in their own backyards.”

— There likely isn’t enough time left for measures like permitting reform or health care to make it across the finish line by 2026. But Werden expects crucial groundwork to be laid in the coming weeks — especially with Affordable Care Act subsidies remaining a live issue and another funding deadline coming up at the end of January, assuming the Senate deal passes.

RIGHT ON CUE: The name brand drug lobby PhRMA, which is hoping to see a crackdown on pharmacy benefit managers passed by the end of the year, is out with a new ad blaming PBMs and the 340B hospital drug discount program for higher drug costs.

— “America is the only country in the world where middlemen take nearly 50 cents of every dollar spent on medicine,” the 30-second spot says, before going on to highlight drugmakers’ commitments — under pressure from Trump — to offer direct-to-consumer discounts for certain medicines and to invest in domestic manufacturing. The ad will run within the Beltway through the end of the year.

COMING ATTRACTIONS: “Sen. Bernie Sanders (I., Vt.) and a group of Democratic senators are demanding the White House answer for higher electric bills they blamed in part on the artificial-intelligence boom driving one of the most expensive infrastructure build-outs in U.S. history,” The Wall Street Journal’s David Uberti reports.

— “In a letter to the White House and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, the group took aim at Meta, OpenAI, Alphabet, Oracle and other firms behind a data-center build-out stretching from the Washington suburbs to rural Oregon. President Trump’s push to fast-track these projects is forcing Americans into ‘bidding wars with trillion-dollar companies to keep the lights on at home,’ they wrote.”

— “The missive is the latest sign of pushback against the AI boom buoying the U.S. economy and markets while straining power producers’ ability to keep up. Local activists in many areas have begun organizing against data centers that receive sizable tax breaks and require huge amounts of power,” and “concerns around increasing electric bills helped fuel Democratic victories last week in New Jersey’s gubernatorial election and down-ballot races in Virginia and Georgia.”

ANNALS OF ETHICS: Housing finance chief Bill Pulte “fired internal watchdogs at Fannie Mae who were looking into multiple complaints against a high-ranking company officer close to him,” The Washington Post’s Rachel Siegel reports.

— “Pulte said last month he had fired dozens of Fannie Mae employees in what he said included a bid to end diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives at the mortgage giant. Yet six people familiar with the matter said those firings effectively cleared out the company’s internal watchdogs, charged with ensuring Fannie and its officials follow the law.”

— “The ethics team — including its chief, Suzanne Libby — was fired shortly after Fannie management directed investigators to cease looking into the Pulte ally, said a couple of the people familiar with the situation.”

FLYING IN: More than 300 members of the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association will descend on the Hill on Wednesday for the group’s annual fly-in and conference. Participants are slated to meet with hundreds of House and Senate offices to push for the restoration of Medicare telehealth authority for audiologists and speech-language pathologists and for lawmakers to support a bipartisan bill to extend the expiring ACA subsidies.

— They’ll also urge lawmakers to prevent the firing of federal workers who administer programs that facilitate hearing screenings for newborns and who help school-based professionals support students with disabilities.

SASSOON’S NEW GIG: Danielle Sassoon, the former federal prosecutor who quit rather than drop corruption charges against New York Mayor Eric Adams, has joined boutique conservative law firm Clement & Murphy as a partner in its Supreme Court and appellate practice. Sassoon resigned in February as interim U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York when she was asked to dismiss the charges against Adams. Two other top DOJ attorneys joined Sassoon in quitting over the order.

AL-SHARAA’S SHERPAS: Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa made his first trip to the White House today, a visit preceded by “a flurry of activity in Washington, as lawmakers tried to make sense of a country that one day was considered a rogue nation locked in protracted civil war and the next was viewed as a free state on the path to stability,” according to Jewish Insider’s Gabby Deutch.

— “Two people in particular have become fixtures on Capitol Hill, pushing the message that Washington should lift sanctions on Damascus and build stronger ties with Syria: Jasmine Naamou and Tarek Naemo, a married couple who live in Daytona Beach, Fla., with a knack for social media self-promotion and a willingness to strike up a conversation with anyone.”

— “They first came to Capitol Hill this year as activists with the Syrian American Alliance for Peace and Prosperity, a nonprofit that emerged early this year to advocate for closer ties between the U.S. and Syria, though Naamou said she doesn’t work directly with them anymore.”

— “The organization arranged meetings for Syria’s foreign minister in New York this year, and in April it brought two members of Congress — Reps. Cory Mills (R-FL) and Marlin Stutzman (R-IN) — to Syria for the first visit by U.S. officials in years. Naamou and Naemo were on the trip with them.”

title: Fugees star sentenced to 14 years in FARA case
body_text:
KILLING HIM SOFTLY: Pras Michel, founding member of 90s hip-hop trio The Fugees, was sentenced to 14 years in prison today following a conviction on charges that he acted as an unregistered foreign agent of China, made illegal campaign contributions using foreign money and later tried to cover it up.

— Jurors convicted Michel, 52, in 2023 on 10 felony counts related to two schemes hatched by Michel and a Malaysian businessman, Jho Low , who is separately accused of embezzling billions of dollars from that country’s sovereign wealth fund.

— Michel’s trial was punctuated by testimony from star witnesses Leonardo DiCaprio , Jeff Sessions and Michel himself. Jurors heard details of the schemes, carried out by Michel and others and funded by Low, who used the billions he allegedly stole from Malaysia’s 1MDB fund to lead a glamorous lifestyle, praying with celebrities around the globe. Low used some of the money he allegedly stole to fund Hollywood films, including DiCaprio’s Wolf of Wall Street.

— The first scheme involved an attempt to secure a meeting between Low and President Barack Obama so Low could get a picture of himself shaking the president’s hand. Michel, using money obtained from Low, donated nearly $2 million to a super PAC supporting Obama’s 2012 reelection campaign and hid the source of the money using a network of straw donors.

— The second scheme involved efforts by Michel, Republican fundraiser Elliott Broidy and others to lobby the first Trump Justice Department to drop an ongoing investigation into Low related to the 1MDB scandal. Low was indicted along with Michel but remains a fugitive in China.

— In addition to pushing for the DOJ to drop its investigation of Low, Michel and Broidy also took money from Low to lobby the Trump administration on behalf of China, pushing for officials to extradite a Chinese dissident living in New York. That dissident, Guo Wengui , was later arrested and convicted in his own fraud case. He has not yet been sentenced.

— “The sentence reflects the gravity of the defendant’s efforts to manipulate decision-making at the highest levels of our government, for profit and on behalf of foreign interests,” said John Keller , a former prosecutor on the case who resigned in February when he was ordered to dismiss the case against New York Mayor Eric Adams.

— Erica Dumas , a spokesperson for Michel, told PI “this is not the end of [Michel’s] story. He appreciates the outpouring of support as he approaches the next chapter.”

— In delivering the sentence, U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly said that Michel was “dishonest in some of his answers” when he testified in his own defense during trial and that his demeanor “came across as arrogant.”

— Michel’s defense pushed for a lower sentence, arguing that the Trump administration’s current position on FARA enforcement should be applied to this case.

— “If this case, these facts, were presented to the government today, they would not be pursuing a FARA case against Mr. Michel,” defense lawyer Peter Zeidenberg argued.

— Prosecutors pushed back on Zeidenberg’s characterization of current FARA enforcement.

— “One thing on which I think the defense is mistaken is the conclusion that the department does not bring FARA cases anymore,” prosecutor Sean Mulryne said, pointing at the ongoing FARA trial of former New York political aide Linda Sun .

— In addition to his prison sentence, Michel must also forfeit nearly $65 million he earned from Low.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. Any thoughts on what’s next for FARA enforcement? Send your thoughts to dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or ping us on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

ANOTHER FARA SENTENCE: Meanwhile, across the river in Alexandria, a former CIA operative who pleaded guilty earlier this year to FARA violations connected to contracting work he did for BGR has been sentenced to a year and one day in prison.

— Dale Bendler , a three-time CIA station chief who remained a CIA contractor following his retirement from the agency, will report to prison in January and must also pay a fine of $25,000.

— In belated FARA filings submitted after his guilty plea, Bendler detailed work he did for foreign principals in Venezuela, Lebanon, Angola and France as a BGR contractor, earning $6,000 per job, plus travel reimbursements.

— “Mr. Bendler believed that his employer, a major lobbying and communications firm in Washington, D.C. had completed the required paperwork for Mr. Bendler under FARA,” his defense team wrote in a pre-sentencing filing , adding that Bendler reported his lobbying income on his taxes and received CIA approval to take on private sector clients.

BGR responded in a statement: “Dale Bendler, who was a BGR independent contractor years ago, agreed in writing to abide by all applicable laws including the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Bendler did not consult with BGR about registration and recently – after he was indicted and pled guilty to a variety of offenses including misuse of secret documents – registered retroactively. BGR fully cooperated with investigators as a witness in the case.”

— Bendler’s lawyer, Jesse Binnall , said that for decades, “Dale Bendler served this nation with honor, first as a United States Marine and later as a CIA officer. He has sacrificed for his country throughout his entire career and that record of service matters. Mr. Bendler’s story is not over.”

FIRST IN PI — SIGNAL GROUP HIRES TESTER ALUM: After 12 years on the Hill, most recently as former Sen. Jon Tester’s (D-Mont.) communications director, Sarah Feldman is heading to Signal Group .

— Feldman joins the firm as a senior vice president in its public affairs practice. She started her Senate career as deputy press secretary for the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) before moving to former Sen. Claire McCaskill’s (D-Mo.) office, followed by Tester’s office, where she also advised his 2024 Senate reelection campaign.

— Feldman, who will not register to lobby, told PI she plans on stressing to clients the importance of consensus building and staying nimble — skills she learned shaping messaging for red-state Democrats.

— “It’s understanding that the traditional ways of doing things don’t always work anymore,” Feldman said. “How can we get creative, how can we be relentless? Sometimes it’s finding strategic, proactive ways to get your message across. Sometimes it’s defending against reputational risk. Often it’s both.”

— Her experience could come into play soon if Democrats are able to regain control of the House or Senate in next year’s midterms. During her time on the Hill, Feldman says she “worked in every configuration of divided government.”

E.X.P.E.R.T.S: Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) yesterday introduced a bill (the Experts Protect Effective Rules, Transparency and Stability Act) aimed at minimizing the impact of industry lobbyists in the federal rulemaking process.

— “At a time when corporations and CEOs have outsized power, it is critical that we ensure that public interest is protected,” Jayapal said in a statement.

— Among other things, the bill would require full disclosure of the funding behind “scientific, economic and technical studies submitted to agencies during the rulemaking process” and require a public explanation when an agency withdraws a rule.

TRADING FLOOR: Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) sold $130,000 worth of stock in companies that manage nearly half of all Medicaid enrolled health care providers before voting to cut Medicaid funding as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill, Melanie Zanona reports for NBC News .

— Bresnahan, a first-term member who owns a real estate development company in Pennsylvania, sold stock in Centene , Elevance Health , UnitedHealth and CVS on May 15, exactly a week before the House first voted on the mega bill.

— “In a statement to NBC News, Bresnahan said he ‘never instructed my financial advisors on what to buy, sell, or hold. It is no secret that I built a successful career before serving, and I am beholden to no lobbyist or special interest,’ he said.”

KILLING HIM SOFTLY: Pras Michel, founding member of 90s hip-hop trio The Fugees, was sentenced to 14 years in prison today following a conviction on charges that he acted as an unregistered foreign agent of China, made illegal campaign contributions using foreign money and later tried to cover it up.

— Jurors convicted Michel, 52, in 2023 on 10 felony counts related to two schemes hatched by Michel and a Malaysian businessman, Jho Low, who is separately accused of embezzling billions of dollars from that country’s sovereign wealth fund.

— Michel’s trial was punctuated by testimony from star witnesses Leonardo DiCaprio, Jeff Sessions and Michel himself. Jurors heard details of the schemes, carried out by Michel and others and funded by Low, who used the billions he allegedly stole from Malaysia’s 1MDB fund to lead a glamorous lifestyle, praying with celebrities around the globe. Low used some of the money he allegedly stole to fund Hollywood films, including DiCaprio’s Wolf of Wall Street.

— The first scheme involved an attempt to secure a meeting between Low and President Barack Obama so Low could get a picture of himself shaking the president’s hand. Michel, using money obtained from Low, donated nearly $2 million to a super PAC supporting Obama’s 2012 reelection campaign and hid the source of the money using a network of straw donors.

— The second scheme involved efforts by Michel, Republican fundraiser Elliott Broidy and others to lobby the first Trump Justice Department to drop an ongoing investigation into Low related to the 1MDB scandal. Low was indicted along with Michel but remains a fugitive in China.

— In addition to pushing for the DOJ to drop its investigation of Low, Michel and Broidy also took money from Low to lobby the Trump administration on behalf of China, pushing for officials to extradite a Chinese dissident living in New York. That dissident, Guo Wengui, was later arrested and convicted in his own fraud case. He has not yet been sentenced.

— “The sentence reflects the gravity of the defendant’s efforts to manipulate decision-making at the highest levels of our government, for profit and on behalf of foreign interests,” said John Keller, a former prosecutor on the case who resigned in February when he was ordered to dismiss the case against New York Mayor Eric Adams.

— Erica Dumas, a spokesperson for Michel, told PI “this is not the end of [Michel’s] story. He appreciates the outpouring of support as he approaches the next chapter.”

— In delivering the sentence, U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly said that Michel was “dishonest in some of his answers” when he testified in his own defense during trial and that his demeanor “came across as arrogant.”

— Michel’s defense pushed for a lower sentence, arguing that the Trump administration’s current position on FARA enforcement should be applied to this case.

— “If this case, these facts, were presented to the government today, they would not be pursuing a FARA case against Mr. Michel,” defense lawyer Peter Zeidenberg argued.

— Prosecutors pushed back on Zeidenberg’s characterization of current FARA enforcement.

— “One thing on which I think the defense is mistaken is the conclusion that the department does not bring FARA cases anymore,” prosecutor Sean Mulryne said, pointing at the ongoing FARA trial of former New York political aide Linda Sun.

— In addition to his prison sentence, Michel must also forfeit nearly $65 million he earned from Low.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. Any thoughts on what’s next for FARA enforcement? Send your thoughts to dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or ping us on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17. And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko.

ANOTHER FARA SENTENCE: Meanwhile, across the river in Alexandria, a former CIA operative who pleaded guilty earlier this year to FARA violations connected to contracting work he did for BGR has been sentenced to a year and one day in prison.


— Dale Bendler, a three-time CIA station chief who remained a CIA contractor following his retirement from the agency, will report to prison in January and must also pay a fine of $25,000.

— In belated FARA filings submitted after his guilty plea, Bendler detailed work he did for foreign principals in Venezuela, Lebanon, Angola and France as a BGR contractor, earning $6,000 per job, plus travel reimbursements.

— “Mr. Bendler believed that his employer, a major lobbying and communications firm in Washington, D.C. had completed the required paperwork for Mr. Bendler under FARA,” his defense team wrote in a pre-sentencing filing, adding that Bendler reported his lobbying income on his taxes and received CIA approval to take on private sector clients.

BGR responded in a statement: “Dale Bendler, who was a BGR independent contractor years ago, agreed in writing to abide by all applicable laws including the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Bendler did not consult with BGR about registration and recently – after he was indicted and pled guilty to a variety of offenses including misuse of secret documents – registered retroactively. BGR fully cooperated with investigators as a witness in the case.”

— Bendler’s lawyer, Jesse Binnall, said that for decades, “Dale Bendler served this nation with honor, first as a United States Marine and later as a CIA officer. He has sacrificed for his country throughout his entire career and that record of service matters. Mr. Bendler’s story is not over.”


FIRST IN PI — SIGNAL GROUP HIRES TESTER ALUM: After 12 years on the Hill, most recently as former Sen. Jon Tester’s (D-Mont.) communications director, Sarah Feldman is heading to Signal Group.

— Feldman joins the firm as a senior vice president in its public affairs practice. She started her Senate career as deputy press secretary for the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) before moving to former Sen. Claire McCaskill’s (D-Mo.) office, followed by Tester’s office, where she also advised his 2024 Senate reelection campaign.

— Feldman, who will not register to lobby, told PI she plans on stressing to clients the importance of consensus building and staying nimble — skills she learned shaping messaging for red-state Democrats.

— “It’s understanding that the traditional ways of doing things don’t always work anymore,” Feldman said. “How can we get creative, how can we be relentless? Sometimes it’s finding strategic, proactive ways to get your message across. Sometimes it’s defending against reputational risk. Often it’s both.”

— Her experience could come into play soon if Democrats are able to regain control of the House or Senate in next year’s midterms. During her time on the Hill, Feldman says she “worked in every configuration of divided government.”

E.X.P.E.R.T.S: Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) yesterday introduced a bill (the Experts Protect Effective Rules, Transparency and Stability Act) aimed at minimizing the impact of industry lobbyists in the federal rulemaking process.

— “At a time when corporations and CEOs have outsized power, it is critical that we ensure that public interest is protected,” Jayapal said in a statement.

— Among other things, the bill would require full disclosure of the funding behind “scientific, economic and technical studies submitted to agencies during the rulemaking process” and require a public explanation when an agency withdraws a rule.

TRADING FLOOR: Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) sold $130,000 worth of stock in companies that manage nearly half of all Medicaid enrolled health care providers before voting to cut Medicaid funding as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill, Melanie Zanona reports for NBC News.

— Bresnahan, a first-term member who owns a real estate development company in Pennsylvania, sold stock in Centene, Elevance Health, UnitedHealth and CVS on May 15, exactly a week before the House first voted on the mega bill.

— “In a statement to NBC News, Bresnahan said he ‘never instructed my financial advisors on what to buy, sell, or hold. It is no secret that I built a successful career before serving, and I am beholden to no lobbyist or special interest,’ he said.”

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman and Amanda Chu

HIGH TIMES: Donald Trump’s executive order to ease restrictions on marijuana is the culmination of more than a yearlong campaign by the cannabis industry to persuade the president to embrace a cause the GOP has historically opposed, Caitlin and Natalie Fertig report tonight .

— The effort included not only traditional levers of influence such as lobbying and political donations, but encompassed opinion polling and one-on-one conversations with friends of the famously sober president.

— “I’ve never been inundated by so many people as I have about” reclassifying marijuana, Trump said during a signing ceremony in the Oval Office on Thursday.

— High on that list of people was Howard Kessler , a Florida financial services executive and longtime friend of Trump’s who attended the future president’s wedding to Melania Trump in 2005. Kessler pushed and prodded Trump to sign the executive order, according to multiple cannabis industry and administration officials with knowledge of how it came about. He was also a champion for one of the other policy changes Trump announced Thursday: a pilot program that would allow Medicare to cover treatments involving CBD for seniors.

— Also instrumental was Kim Rivers , CEO of Florida’s largest medical marijuana company Trulieve . It was she who convinced the president to include reclassifying marijuana in Thursday’s executive order, according to two people briefed on the conversations granted anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly.

— Rivers met Trump in early 2024 at his golf course in Bedminster, New Jersey, to discuss a ballot measure campaign to legalize recreational marijuana in Florida that year. Trump eventually backed the state legalization effort — which fell short of the supermajority it needed to pass. Once Trump took office, Rivers traveled to the White House to discuss marijuana policy, including for an Oval Office meeting last week.

— “There hasn’t been a single time that I’ve had the privilege to be with the president where we talked about medical cannabis and research, where he wasn’t supportive,” Rivers said in an interview, recalling multiple interactions over the past year and a half. Thursday’s executive order, she said, was the result of many months of work and did not come as a sudden decision on Trump’s part.

— Beyond her personal relationship with Trump, Rivers’ company has spent heavily on influence efforts and retains a slate of lobbyists with close ties to the president. Trulieve’s first lobbying firm in D.C. was Florida heavyweight Ballard Partners in 2018. And the company has hired two more firms this year with Florida ties: Advocus Partners , which is home to Trump-linked lobbyist Nick Iarossi , and Rubin, Turnbull and Associates , which counts Caroline Wiles , daughter of Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles , among its leadership.

— “The Chief of Staff’s daughter is not a lobbyist and had nothing to do with the President’s decision to sign this executive order,” White House spokesman Kush Desai told POLITICO Thursday. “As he himself stated in the Oval Office, President Trump made this decision after hearing from many friends and supporters, including Howard Kessler and various veterans groups.”

— Trulieve also contributed $750,000 to Trump’s inaugural committee, according to campaign finance disclosures. Trulieve donated another $250,000 to American Rights and Reform , an industry-funded super PAC that has given $1 million to Trump’s super PAC.

— POLITICO tracked at least 26 lobbying registrations related to cannabis this year, up more than 60 percent from last year and more than double the number of registrations in 2017, the first year of Trump’s first term in office.

— These registrations include WeedMaps , which also hired Rubin, Turnbull this year. Jemmstone hired Ballard Partners, while Verano Holdings hired Trump campaign adviser David Urban’s firm, BGR Group .

— Meanwhile Team Hemp , an industry nonprofit, has hired three lobbying firms – more than any other player — including Frontline Government Relations ’ lobbyist, John Pence , a former Trump advisor, and Martin Obst and Robert Goad at MO Strategies , who have also worked with the president.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. Send tips to dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

The resulting firm will instantly become one of the largest in the world, with an expected annual revenue of more than $3.6 billion and more than 3,000 lawyers working in offices across the globe.

Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) sent a letter to Attorney General Pam Bondi yesterday asking her to recuse herself from the Justice Department’s review of the competing bids to acquire Warner Bros . Discovery , citing her previous job at Ballard Partners and POLITICO’s reporting that the firm lobbies for both Netflix and Paramount Skydance .

— “In line with our anti-corruption oversight and legislative priorities, and given the cloud of corruption surrounding this merger and your former employer Ballard’s potential role in this merger, we ask that you recuse yourself from the review of this purchase,” the senators write.

— Bondi has long denied engaging in any impropriety related to her former employer. During a Senate Judiciary committee hearing in October, she grew angry when Blumenthal questioned if she had spoken to firm leader Brian Ballard regarding a separate antitrust matter.

— “Do not question my ability to be fair and impartial as attorney general in anything [inaudible] my former firm Ballard Partners,” she said at the time .

— “We have proudly represented many of the world’s top entertainment companies, and we represent all our clients with absolute and unyielding integrity, complying with every ethical restriction,” the firm said in a statement. “We have never once communicated with the U.S. Attorney General about any Department of Justice matter or any other matter before the U.S. government. Period. Full stop. End of story. These blindly partisan attacks on Attorney General Bondi’s integrity are utterly clownish and beneath the offices held by the letter’s authors.”

FIRST IN PI — CHAMBER’S DAVIS JOINS PSA BOARD : Rodney Davis , head of government affairs for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce , has joined the advisory board of the Public Service Alliance , a social enterprise aimed at helping public servants protect themselves from political violence.

— Davis, a former five-term Republican representative from Illinois, was himself a victim of political violence before joining the Chamber. In 2017, he was part of a group of House Republicans attacked while practicing for the Congressional Baseball Game. Four people, including Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), were injured in the shooting.

— “Having experienced political violence up close, I refuse to accept it as the new normal,” Davis said in a statement. “PSA is the first organization of its kind, and it would have been an invaluable resource in the aftermath of the 2017 Congressional Baseball shooting.”

— Also joining PSA’s advisory board alongside Davis are: James Murray , vice president of global security and resilience at CoreWave and former director of the U.S. Secret Service; Lawrence Norden , vice president of elections and government programs at the Brennan Center ; and Cecilia Young , responsible innovation lead and director of portfolio management at General Catalyst .

CRYPTO CALI PUSH: Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase is attempting to activate its more than 800,000 California users, sending push alerts this week urging recipients to email a state agency head in an effort to restore the company’s “staking” service in the Golden State, our colleagues Tyler Katzenberger , Christine Mui and Juliann Ventura scooped for Pros in California Decoded .

— Coinbase’s staking program, which refers to the practice of cryptocurrency owners locking down crypto assets to help secure the exchange’s network in exchange for rewards, is currently banned in California and three other states. Users have sent more than 1,500 emails as a result of the push notification, Coinbase told Decoded.

— “The tactic of mobilizing one’s own app users has been tested by other tech platforms — most notably, by TikTok to fight off a ban from Congress. In that instance, it backfired: lawmakers bristled at the flood of calls, and the display reinforced concerns about the app’s influence.”

The association lobbies in Washington on a variety of issues affecting the tech industry, including trade, autonomous vehicles, renewable energy, cyber security and more.

It was she who convinced the president to include reclassifying marijuana in Thursday’s executive order, according to two people briefed on the conversations granted anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly.

— Rivers met Trump in early 2024 at his golf course in Bedminster, New Jersey, to discuss a ballot measure campaign to legalize recreational marijuana in Florida that year. Trump eventually backed the state legalization effort — which fell short of the supermajority it needed to pass. Once Trump took office, Rivers traveled to the White House to discuss marijuana policy, including for an Oval Office meeting last week.

— “There hasn’t been a single time that I’ve had the privilege to be with the president where we talked about medical cannabis and research, where he wasn’t supportive,” Rivers said in an interview, recalling multiple interactions over the past year and a half. Thursday’s executive order, she said, was the result of many months of work and did not come as a sudden decision on Trump’s part.

— Beyond her personal relationship with Trump, Rivers’ company has spent heavily on influence efforts and retains a slate of lobbyists with close ties to the president. Trulieve’s first lobbying firm in D.C. was Florida heavyweight Ballard Partners in 2018. And the company has hired two more firms this year with Florida ties: Advocus Partners, which is home to Trump-linked lobbyist Nick Iarossi, and Rubin, Turnbull and Associates, which counts Caroline Wiles, daughter of Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles, among its leadership.

— “The Chief of Staff’s daughter is not a lobbyist and had nothing to do with the President’s decision to sign this executive order,” White House spokesman Kush Desai told POLITICO Thursday. “As he himself stated in the Oval Office, President Trump made this decision after hearing from many friends and supporters, including Howard Kessler and various veterans groups.”

— Trulieve also contributed $750,000 to Trump’s inaugural committee, according to campaign finance disclosures. Trulieve donated another $250,000 to American Rights and Reform, an industry-funded super PAC that has given $1 million to Trump’s super PAC.

— POLITICO tracked at least 26 lobbying registrations related to cannabis this year, up more than 60 percent from last year and more than double the number of registrations in 2017, the first year of Trump’s first term in office.

— These registrations include WeedMaps, which also hired Rubin, Turnbull this year. Jemmstone hired Ballard Partners, while Verano Holdings hired Trump campaign adviser David Urban’s firm, BGR Group.

— Meanwhile Team Hemp, an industry nonprofit, has hired three lobbying firms – more than any other player — including Frontline Government Relations’ lobbyist, John Pence, a former Trump advisor, and Martin Obst and Robert Goad at MO Strategies, who have also worked with the president.

title: What K Street is watching for in 2026
body_text:
— “We’re still going through a massive disruptive period, and when you’re disrupting literally everything from how the government works to how the private sector operates, to how markets work to how trade works, it creates a very busy environment with a lot of demand for clear messaging and advocacy,” Nahigian Strategies ’ Ken Nahigian told PI.

— Or, as Mehlman Consulting co-founder Bruce Mehlman put it in this weekend’s slide deck previewing the year: “If you were expecting a calm and predictable year in politics & policy, you’ve come to the wrong place. 2026 is a six-ring circus, so buckle up.”

Here’s a snapshot of some of the big issues expected to dominate this year:

— Government funding and health care: Lawmakers have until the end of the month to agree on a funding deal that can pass both chambers or they risk another shutdown. Downtown expects the issue — which was caused by a bitter partisan battle over health care — to dominate the first half of 2026.

— “It’s going to be a busier year on the health care side than what we saw this last year,” said Vogel Group CEO Alex Vogel . But exactly what health care provisions can be approved by the slim Republican majorities in the House and Senate remains to be seen.

— “I think the Republican polling numbers are going to make them want to deal with it — even more so because they’re now starting to agree that health care is actually an affordability issue,” said Jeff Forbes of Forbes Tate Partners .

— But K Streeters cautioned PI not to expect Republicans and Democrats to suddenly join forces on any health care bill, given the politics at play in a midterm year. That means the GOP may have to turn to reconciliation again, despite mixed opinions throughout D.C. as to whether that’s possible.

— “I know House leadership thinks it’s gonna be hard to get through,” Firehouse Strategies ’ Alex Conant said of the prospect for any reconciliation bill. “I think Trump’s gonna want it, and I think House members are gonna want it when they’re facing their reelections. … If they want to have additional policies to run on next fall, reconciliation may be the only option.”

— Crypto: The crypto industry, one of the ascendant political forces in Washington, is “laser focused on getting market structure legislation completed in Q1,” said Tommy Andrews , a lobbyist at Squire Patton Boggs who worked in the White House during Trump’s first term.

— There are also a number of outstanding tax provisions that the industry is seeking clarification for, as well as brewing policy fights between the crypto and decentralized finance sectors on one side, and traditional financial heavyweights on Wall Street on the other.

— Trade: Uncertainty on trade issues, spurred by Trump’s tariff regime and the ensuing court fight over the policy, drove massive lobbying spending in 2025. The Supreme Court will rule by summer on the legality of Trump’s use of an emergency power to impose the duties, but K Street expects trade questions to linger regardless of the outcome.

— “The president has people around him that have their own views on trade, and the president himself has his own view on trade. So I think that has been difficult too, to try to determine for each industry, who is the controlling decision maker,” said Stacy McBride , executive vice president of federal government affairs for HB Strategies . “Is it Commerce? Is it the [U.S. Trade Representative]? Is it the White House?”

— The MAHA agenda: That confusion over exactly whom to lobby on trade also applies to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his Make America Healthy Again agenda, some lobbyists say. But Kennedy’s embrace of the fringe of medical science and his antagonism towards the mainstream pharmaceutical industry has created new opportunities for pharmaceutical companies that haven’t previously invested heavily in Washington lobbying.

— “Making sure the MAHA agenda gets passed through federal agency action and Secretary Kennedy is something that many clients are excited about,” said John Pence , CEO of Frontline Government Relations and a Kennedy supporter. “Change at HHS presents a lot of opportunities for companies that have not historically been in the mix in Washington.”

— Pardons: Trump’s willingness to use his pardon power early in his second term shows no sign of abating. While presidents typically wait until they are about to leave office to issue pardons to supporters or other controversial individuals, Trump granted more than 1,000 pardons in 2025, mostly to people convicted for participating in the Jan. 6 riot.

— Is hiring a lobbyist with a personal connection to Trump the only way to get a pardon? “Not necessarily,” said one lawyer who has lobbied Justice Department pardon officials on behalf of clients.

— “There are high-profile cases that go that way for sure, so they may get more attention. But in terms of the numbers, my guess is that DOJ has still got their fingerprints on a higher number,” said the lawyer, granted anonymity to speak candidly.

— “[Trump] isn’t worried about the optics in general,” the lawyer added. “I think he’s going to continue to grant pardons, it’s just a matter of getting his attention.”

Andrew Elliott has joined the trade group as vice president and content policy counsel, where he will work with MPA member studios to shape state and federal laws regulating their work and content distribution.

Now, many of its alumni run this town ,” POLITICO ’s Megan Messerly and Diana Nerozzi write in a look at the rising think tank.

— According to a POLITICO analysis, “at least 70 participants in Claremont’s small suite of fellowships over the last decade hold or have held posts” in the second Trump administration, including budget director Russ Vought , White House legislative director James Braid , Secretary of State Marco Rubio ’s adviser Michael Needham and CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis .

OIL’S ULTIMATUM: “American oil companies have long hoped to recover the assets that Venezuela’s authoritarian regime ripped from them decades ago. Now the Trump administration is offering to help them achieve that aim — with one major condition,” POLITICO ’s Ben Lefebvre , Zack Colman and James Bikales reported over the weekend following the administration’s ouster of Nicolás Maduro .

— “Administration officials have told oil executives in recent weeks that if they want compensation for their rigs, pipelines and other seized property, then they must be prepared to go back into Venezuela now and invest heavily in reviving its shattered petroleum industry, two people familiar with the administration’s outreach told POLITICO on Saturday.”

— “But people in the industry said the administration’s message has left them still leery about the difficulty of rebuilding decayed oil fields in a country where it’s not even clear who will lead the country for the foreseeable future.”

Franco succeeds Bernie Friedman , who will remain an active shareholder at the firm and continue to represent clients before local governments in Florida.

— Franco joined Becker in 2011 to help open Becker’s federal lobbying shop, which represents clients including Disney , Paramount , Bacardi North America , iHeartMedia , Johnson & Johnson , the Society for Human Resources Management and Florida’s Palm Beach County.

ICYMI: Trump’s super PAC pulled in more than $100 million in the second half of 2025, “with much of the money coming from wealthy people and corporations with issues before the administration,” The New York Times ’ Ken Vogel and Karen Yourish write.

— “The haul by MAGA Inc. , detailed in a campaign finance report filed on Thursday night, reveals how aggressive fund-raising has continued for a political operation that revolves around Mr. Trump, giving the organization over $300 million ahead of this year’s midterms, it said.”

— “The biggest donations were $12.5 million each from Greg Brockman , a co-founder of the artificial intelligence firm OpenAI , and his wife, Anna Brockman ; and contributions totaling $20 million from the parent company of Crypto.com , a cryptocurrency trading platform that has lobbied the administration.”

— “Other donors included a nursing home entrepreneur seeking an ambassadorship, a vape-maker, a pro-cannabis group and a woman whose father was seeking a deal from prosecutors to settle charges that in 2020 he bribed Puerto Rico’s governor at the time.”

TAKING STOCK: FAA chief Bryan Bedford has disclosed a Sept. 12 sale of up to $100,000 in CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. stock, our friends at Morning Transportation report . CrowdStrike was behind the botched software update in July 2024 that sparked a global technology disruption, including a wave of flight cancellations and delays, with Delta Air Lines hit especially hard .

— Bedford in a prior ethics agreement had pledged to divest from CrowdStrike. Officials like him must report significant sales made on behalf of themselves, their spouse or their dependent children.

What K Street is watching for in 2026

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

01/05/2026 07:19 PM EST

Presented by

With help from Daniel Lippman

WELCOME TO 2026: As the capital jolts back to life after a much-needed break, the city’s lobbyist class is preparing for a 2026 that promises to be just as tumultuous as last year. That’s saying a lot after Donald Trump’s trade war and upending of the federal bureaucracy, to name just a few of 2025’s shockwaves.

— “We’re still going through a massive disruptive period, and when you’re disrupting literally everything from how the government works to how the private sector operates, to how markets work to how trade works, it creates a very busy environment with a lot of demand for clear messaging and advocacy,” Nahigian Strategies’ Ken Nahigian told PI.

— Or, as Mehlman Consulting co-founder Bruce Mehlman put it in this weekend’s slide deck previewing the year: “If you were expecting a calm and predictable year in politics & policy, you’ve come to the wrong place. 2026 is a six-ring circus, so buckle up.”

Here’s a snapshot of some of the big issues expected to dominate this year:

— Government funding and health care: Lawmakers have until the end of the month to agree on a funding deal that can pass both chambers or they risk another shutdown. Downtown expects the issue — which was caused by a bitter partisan battle over health care — to dominate the first half of 2026.

— “It’s going to be a busier year on the health care side than what we saw this last year,” said Vogel Group CEO Alex Vogel. But exactly what health care provisions can be approved by the slim Republican majorities in the House and Senate remains to be seen.

— “I think the Republican polling numbers are going to make them want to deal with it — even more so because they’re now starting to agree that health care is actually an affordability issue,” said Jeff Forbes of Forbes Tate Partners.

— But K Streeters cautioned PI not to expect Republicans and Democrats to suddenly join forces on any health care bill, given the politics at play in a midterm year. That means the GOP may have to turn to reconciliation again, despite mixed opinions throughout D.C. as to whether that’s possible.

— “I know House leadership thinks it’s gonna be hard to get through,” Firehouse Strategies’ Alex Conant said of the prospect for any reconciliation bill. “I think Trump’s gonna want it, and I think House members are gonna want it when they’re facing their reelections. … If they want to have additional policies to run on next fall, reconciliation may be the only option.”

— Crypto: The crypto industry, one of the ascendant political forces in Washington, is “laser focused on getting market structure legislation completed in Q1,” said Tommy Andrews, a lobbyist at Squire Patton Boggs who worked in the White House during Trump’s first term.

— There are also a number of outstanding tax provisions that the industry is seeking clarification for, as well as brewing policy fights between the crypto and decentralized finance sectors on one side, and traditional financial heavyweights on Wall Street on the other.

— Trade: Uncertainty on trade issues, spurred by Trump’s tariff regime and the ensuing court fight over the policy, drove massive lobbying spending in 2025. The Supreme Court will rule by summer on the legality of Trump’s use of an emergency power to impose the duties, but K Street expects trade questions to linger regardless of the outcome.

— “The president has people around him that have their own views on trade, and the president himself has his own view on trade. So I think that has been difficult too, to try to determine for each industry, who is the controlling decision maker,” said Stacy McBride, executive vice president of federal government affairs for HB Strategies. “Is it Commerce? Is it the [U.S. Trade Representative]? Is it the White House?”

— The MAHA agenda: That confusion over exactly whom to lobby on trade also applies to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his Make America Healthy Again agenda, some lobbyists say. But Kennedy’s embrace of the fringe of medical science and his antagonism towards the mainstream pharmaceutical industry has created new opportunities for pharmaceutical companies that haven’t previously invested heavily in Washington lobbying.

— “Making sure the MAHA agenda gets passed through federal agency action and Secretary Kennedy is something that many clients are excited about,” said John Pence, CEO of Frontline Government Relations and a Kennedy supporter. “Change at HHS presents a lot of opportunities for companies that have not historically been in the mix in Washington.”

— Pardons: Trump’s willingness to use his pardon power early in his second term shows no sign of abating. While presidents typically wait until they are about to leave office to issue pardons to supporters or other controversial individuals, Trump granted more than 1,000 pardons in 2025, mostly to people convicted for participating in the Jan. 6 riot.

— Is hiring a lobbyist with a personal connection to Trump the only way to get a pardon? “Not necessarily,” said one lawyer who has lobbied Justice Department pardon officials on behalf of clients.

— “There are high-profile cases that go that way for sure, so they may get more attention. But in terms of the numbers, my guess is that DOJ has still got their fingerprints on a higher number,” said the lawyer, granted anonymity to speak candidly.

— “[Trump] isn’t worried about the optics in general,” the lawyer added. “I think he’s going to continue to grant pardons, it’s just a matter of getting his attention.”

MORE LOBBYING FIREPOWER FOR AAM, BIO: The Association for Accessible Medicines , which represents generic drugmakers, is expanding its roster of hired guns, bringing on White House-linked Florida lobbying heavyweight Rubin, Turnbull & Associates .

— Firm founders Bill Rubin and Heather Turnbull began lobbying for the trade group last month on issues related to medication, pharmaceuticals and health care, according to a disclosure filing. Michael Burley , who joined Rubin Turnbull last month after serving as deputy assistant to President Donald Trump and deputy director of the White House Office of Presidential Personnel, is also working on the account.

— AAM, which also retains Squire Patton Boggs , Capitol Hill Consulting Group , Foley & Lardner , Fierce Government Relations and the Gibson Group , spent nearly $2 million during the first nine months of 2025 — investments that appear to have paid off with an expected carveout for generic drugs from Trump’s tariffs.

— Meanwhile the Biotechnology Innovation Organization , which represents manufacturers of biopharmaceuticals and biotech firms, added its fourth new outside firm in less than a year. The Nickles Group ’s Greg D’Angelo , who served as the health care lead in OMB during Trump’s first term, and fellow former GOP Hill aides Brett Baker , Molly Fromm , Mary Beth Savary Taylor and Rachel Jones Hensler , began working on tax and trade issues for BIO at the beginning of the month.

— In addition to the Nickles Group, since April, BIO has added the likes of former Sen. Richard Burr (R-N.C.), former John Thune chief of staff Doug Schwartz and former Trump aide Matt Mowers to the trade group’s stable of outside lobbyists. Even so, BIO was on track for its lowest annual lobbying expenditures in nearly two decades, according to a PI analysis of disclosures.

IS THE GOP ON A PRO LABOR STREAK? “Republicans will likely table a bill that would tighten the standard for determining joint employment a day after the party’s pro-labor flank tanked separate legislation to ease overtime rules,” three people familiar with the situation told POLITICO ’s Meredith Lee Hill and Lawrence Ukenye .

— “The Save Local Business Act was part of a package of labor bills that cleared the House Rules Committee on Monday. But it never reached the floor after six Republicans j oined Democrats to block the Flexibility for Workers Education Act over concerns that bill would disadvantage workers.”

— “The legislation would narrow the federal ‘joint employer’ standard, allowing a company to be considered a joint employer of another firm’s workers only if it directly and immediately controls key terms of their job — like hiring, pay, schedules and discipline,” handing the franchise industry a major victory after aggressively fighting the Biden administration’s joint employer standards .

ICYMI — DEMS LEAN ON BIG TECH TO REVIVE PERMITTING TALKS: “Senate Democrats hope the White House’s quest to win the artificial intelligence race with China will blunt President Donald Trump’s unrelenting hatred of offshore wind turbines and help restart talks on a permitting deal,” E&E News’ Kelsey Brugger writes.

— “The administration’s decision in December to halt the construction of five offshore wind projects prompted Democrats to pause bipartisan permitting negotiations on Capitol Hill at a time when some of the nation’s most powerful lobby groups are increasing pressure on Congress to ease project approvals. They said continued attacks on wind and solar means the president can’t be trusted to treat all projects fairly.”

— “Now, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Environment and Public Works Committee, is calling on technology companies involved in artificial intelligence and energy-hungry data centers to intercede with the president.”

— “The artificial intelligence folks, the crypto folks, the data system folks who need massive amounts of electrons — you all need to start showing up and letting people know that you actually want permitting reform, and you actually want an administrative and regulatory process in which electrons are treated fairly, irrespective of source, so you can get the power that you need,” Whitehouse said from the Senate floor on Wednesday.

Generic, biotech lobbies add new outside firms

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

01/14/2026 07:11 PM EST

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

MORE LOBBYING FIREPOWER FOR AAM, BIO: The Association for Accessible Medicines, which represents generic drugmakers, is expanding its roster of hired guns, bringing on White House-linked Florida lobbying heavyweight Rubin, Turnbull & Associates.

— Firm founders Bill Rubin and Heather Turnbull began lobbying for the trade group last month on issues related to medication, pharmaceuticals and health care, according to a disclosure filing. Michael Burley, who joined Rubin Turnbull last month after serving as deputy assistant to President Donald Trump and deputy director of the White House Office of Presidential Personnel, is also working on the account.

— AAM, which also retains Squire Patton Boggs, Capitol Hill Consulting Group, Foley & Lardner, Fierce Government Relations and the Gibson Group, spent nearly $2 million during the first nine months of 2025 — investments that appear to have paid off with an expected carveout for generic drugs from Trump’s tariffs.

— Meanwhile the Biotechnology Innovation Organization, which represents manufacturers of biopharmaceuticals and biotech firms, added its fourth new outside firm in less than a year. The Nickles Group’s Greg D’Angelo, who served as the health care lead in OMB during Trump’s first term, and fellow former GOP Hill aides Brett Baker, Molly Fromm, Mary Beth Savary Taylor and Rachel Jones Hensler, began working on tax and trade issues for BIO at the beginning of the month.

— In addition to the Nickles Group, since April, BIO has added the likes of former Sen. Richard Burr (R-N.C.), former John Thune chief of staff Doug Schwartz and former Trump aide Matt Mowers to the trade group’s stable of outside lobbyists. Even so, BIO was on track for its lowest annual lobbying expenditures in nearly two decades, according to a PI analysis of disclosures.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com. Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com. Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Rubin Turnbull, whose massive expansion into Washington over the past year has been led by Caroline Wiles, the daughter of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, has registered to lobby for a half-dozen other new clients this week, disclosures show.

— They include the hearing aid manufacturer Starkey, the Port of Houston, Consumer Reports, decontamination company Aeroclave, Orlando real estate developer Avalon Park Group and gas station chain Pilot Travel Centers.

— And the Los Angeles County government has retained Tamar Magarik Haro and Steve Haro of Haro Solutions to monitor health care policy on the Hill and lobby against cuts to Medicaid and other public health programs. Tamar Haro is a former staff director for the Senate HELP Subcommittee on Children and Families, while Steve Haro worked for the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) and for Rep. Xavier Becerra (D-Calif.) before Becerra’s time as Biden HHS Secretary.

IS THE GOP ON A PRO LABOR STREAK? “Republicans will likely table a bill that would tighten the standard for determining joint employment a day after the party’s pro-labor flank tanked separate legislation to ease overtime rules,” three people familiar with the situation told POLITICO’s Meredith Lee Hill and Lawrence Ukenye.

— “The Save Local Business Act was part of a package of labor bills that cleared the House Rules Committee on Monday. But it never reached the floor after six Republicans j oined Democrats to block the Flexibility for Workers Education Act over concerns that bill would disadvantage workers.”

— “The legislation would narrow the federal ‘joint employer’ standard, allowing a company to be considered a joint employer of another firm’s workers only if it directly and immediately controls key terms of their job — like hiring, pay, schedules and discipline,” handing the franchise industry a major victory after aggressively fighting the Biden administration’s joint employer standards.

ICYMI — DEMS LEAN ON BIG TECH TO REVIVE PERMITTING TALKS: “Senate Democrats hope the White House’s quest to win the artificial intelligence race with China will blunt President Donald Trump’s unrelenting hatred of offshore wind turbines and help restart talks on a permitting deal,” E&E News’ Kelsey Brugger writes.

— “The administration’s decision in December to halt the construction of five offshore wind projects prompted Democrats to pause bipartisan permitting negotiations on Capitol Hill at a time when some of the nation’s most powerful lobby groups are increasing pressure on Congress to ease project approvals. They said continued attacks on wind and solar means the president can’t be trusted to treat all projects fairly.”

— “Now, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Environment and Public Works Committee, is calling on technology companies involved in artificial intelligence and energy-hungry data centers to intercede with the president.”

— “The artificial intelligence folks, the crypto folks, the data system folks who need massive amounts of electrons — you all need to start showing up and letting people know that you actually want permitting reform, and you actually want an administrative and regulatory process in which electrons are treated fairly, irrespective of source, so you can get the power that you need,” Whitehouse said from the Senate floor on Wednesday.

— But his insinuation that the tech industry had been absent from the fight was met with pushback from lobbyists. “This isn’t like a new policy priority for us,” Cy McNeill, senior director of federal affairs at the Data Center Coalition, told Kelsey.

title: Here’s where K Street sent its money in the Texas Dem Senate primary
body_text:
DEEP IN THE HEART: Today’s primary elections in Texas feature a number of heated races, but the marquee contests revolve around the fight for the Senate. While both of the Texas Senate primaries have attracted a gusher of outside spending bankrolled by industry titans, they’ve also, naturally, drawn interest from Washington’s influence industry.

— On the Democratic side of the ticket, where state Rep. James Talarico is facing off against U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett , Talarico pulled in the larger checks of the two from K Street, according to a PI analysis of FEC filings. That includes a max donation of $7,000 from Cornerstone Government Affairs managing principal Michael Smith . Democratic strategist Guy Cecil , the former head of the marquee super PAC Priorities USA , kicked in around $7,000 as well.

— Anthony Harrington of Albright Stonebridge Group and Mary Stanton of Invariant both donated $3,500 to Talarico, while Airbnb global policy chief Laura Spanjian and Cornerstone principal Todd Webster cut him checks for $2,500, and the Daschle Group ’s Tom Daschle kicked in $2,000. (POLITICO is a client of Invariant.)

— Talarico’s K Street haul also included $1,000 from Allyson Baker of Paul Hastings , David Pore of Hance Scarborough , Estefania Rodriguez of theGROUP , Chris Coffey of Tusk Strategies , Richard Carbo of Cornerstone and David Perry of Jake Perry + Partners .

— Crockett, meanwhile, brought in $2,500 from Jennifer Stewart of Stewart Strategies & Solutions and ShaShrina Thomas of Reynolds American , along with $2,750 from Ervin Policy Group managing director Frank Ervin . Crockett also took in four-figure checks from Invariant ’s Nicole Venable and Justin Gray of Gray Global Advisors .

— Even more K Streeters made smaller contributions in the race. Talarico got $500 from Edward Ayoob of Barnes & Thornburg , Ted Dean of DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group , Tim Wolfmeyer of Cornerstone, John Gonzalez of Tiber Creek Group and Oscar Ramirez of Fulcrum Public Affairs .

— Crockett received $500 from nearly a dozen lobbyists, including Christopher Davis of Capitol Hill Consulting , John Mason of Altria , Keenan Austin Reed of the Alpine Group , Alane Dent of TruStage , Colette Honorable of Exelon , Megan Moore of FGS Global , Ebony Simpson of Stewart Strategies, Alexander Washington of Entergy and Kimberly Afoakwah of Home Depot .

DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

WALKING BACK THE WALKBACK: The Justice Department told a federal appeals court Tuesday that the administration intends to continue defending President Donald Trump ’s executive orders targeting law firms — a surprising reversal less than 24 hours after the department informed the same court it no longer wished to defend the orders, Daniel B. and Josh Gerstein write.

— DOJ lawyers did not provide an explanation for their change in posture, which came via a short Tuesday filing . DOJ declined to comment on the reversal.

— Judges in four cases last year struck down as unconstitutional Trump’s executive orders seeking to punish law firms affiliated with his political opponents. The Justice Department appealed those losses in June and was set to deliver its opening brief to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit on Friday. But in a Monday evening filing, the department declared it no longer wished to pursue the appeal and moved to voluntarily dismiss it.

— “Under no circumstances should the government’s unexplained about-face provide a basis for an extension of its brief,” lawyers representing the targeted firms — Perkins Coie , Jenner & Block , WilmerHale and Susman Godfrey — stated in their filing.

THE AI GOLD RUSH: “Disrupting jobs, fueling a data center boom, even killing off this em dash—artificial intelligence is the conversation policymakers, and the rest of us, just can’t escape. That’s especially the case in Washington, where spending on federal AI influence hit an all-time high last year,” Bloomberg ’s Kate Ackley , John Woolley and Ava Mandoli report.

— “Lobbying firms reported a record $37.2 million in earnings from AI-related influence peddling in the fourth quarter alone, a 38% jump from a year earlier, according to a Bloomberg Government analysis.”

— “For the full year, Washington lobbyists received almost $130 million for work related to AI, as Microsoft Corp. , Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc. ’s Google led the spending blitz. Some of the biggest jumps came from frontier labs OpenAI Inc. and Anthropic PBC , two of the highest valued startups in history vying to shape the AI industry’s future and most recently engulfed in a dispute over its use within the US military.”

BROWNSTEIN ADDS A DEFENSE APPROPS LOBBYIST: John Lucio is joining Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck as of counsel, expanding the firm’s defense and national security practices with quite perfect timing. Lucio was most recently an in-house lobbyist with defense contractor BWX Technologies , and before that he was a senior vice president at Ervin Graves Strategy Group .

— Lucio also spent more than half a decade on the Hill, where he was a professional staff member on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee that oversees defense spending. That process will take on even more importance given everything happening in the Middle East.

— “There’s enough emerging efforts going on right now that how you figure out what the new priorities might or might not be over the next several months” will be lobbyists’ latest challenge, Lucio told PI.

THE ROOM WHERE IT HAPPENED: Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) and Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and California Democratic Rep. Sam Liccardo want Attorney General Pam Bondi and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to spill the details of their meeting with Netflix boss Ted Sarandos last week.

— The meetings were intended to help assuage antitrust concerns holding up Netflix’s bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery . But instead, the streaming giant walked away from the deal, leaving Paramount Skydance one step closer to victory in its hostile takeover bid.

— “Your conversations with Mr. Sarandos taint the Warner Bros. bidding process by raising suspicions that the Trump administration’s DOJ is making merger review decisions based on politicized favoritism rather than the law or the facts,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Bondi and Wiles on Monday.

— The reported meetings “look even more disturbing because the meetings occurred just days after the politicized ouster of Antitrust Division Chief Gail Slater and amidst increasing lobbyist influence over DOJ’s antitrust work,” the Democrats added, nodding to the uptick in antitrust lobbying work flooding into administration-aligned firms like Ballard Partners , which lobbies for both Netflix and Paramount and which previously employed both Bondi and Wiles.

— Blumenthal, Warren and Liccardo — whose district includes Netflix’s Los Gatos headquarters — asked Bondi and Wiles to respond to a series of questions about last week’s meetings about the deal or any other conversations involving Netflix, Paramount or Ballard representatives.

— Sandgren was previously chief of staff to the late Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-Utah) and served as a senior counsel on the Senate Judiciary Committee, of which Hatch was a former chair.

BIG BELTWAY TIE-UP: Democratic public affairs powerhouse Precision Strategies has acquired the strategic comms shop Firehouse Strategies , bringing the senior leaders of multiple presidential campaigns — on both sides of the aisle — together under one roof.

— Precision was started in 2013 by Obama campaign alumni Stephanie Cutter , Teddy Goff and Jen O’Malley Dillon , while Firehouse was started three years later by leaders of Marco Rubio ’s 2016 presidential campaign, Alex Conant , Terry Sullivan and Will Holley .

— Cutter will be acting CEO of the combined firm, with Goff serving as chief growth officer, Conant serving as senior partner and Democrat Ray Glendening serving as partner. Though Firehouse will be integrated into Precision, it will retain the Firehouse brand as a conflict subsidiary.

— The merger will bring new bipartisan heft to Precision. “I think we’ve seen very consistently, no matter who’s in power … our clients, corporate clients, nonprofit clients, even our advocacy clients want to have a bipartisan perspective, understand that they need to be speaking with and trying to engage and persuade both voters and electeds from both parties if they want to get anything done,” Goff told PI.

— Precision will also be able to tap into Firehouse’s “unrivaled” 50-state network of bipartisan operatives that can be deployed for state-level campaigns, Goff noted. Firehouse’s clients, meanwhile, will now have access to Precision’s “great creative, paid, digital and research services that we don’t have in house,” Conant told PI.

FIRST IN PI — FRENCH HANGS A SHINGLE: GOP lobbyist Towner French has decamped from Cozen O’Connor Public Strategies , where he served as head of the firm’s federal lobbying shop, to launch his own firm. Three more Cozen alums — Meagan Foster , Bryce Matthews and Margaret Edsey — are joining French at the new firm, Potomac Strategic Consulting .

— French joined Cozen in 2021 after spending more than half a decade with Capitol Counsel . Before that, he was on the Hill for 15 years, including serving as deputy staff director of the powerful House Rules Committee and chief of staff to Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas).

— Foster is a former top aide to Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) and is a Tom Udall , Mark Begich and U.S. Telecom alum, while Matthews is a former staffer for Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas). Edsey joined Cozen in 2023 after graduating from Georgetown University .

— In an interview, French said the decision to open his own shop stemmed from the desire to remain involved in day-to-day lobbying activities and strategic planning rather than sticking solely to the management track. He added that the firm doesn’t plan on specializing in any one policy area at the moment.

— “That’s sort of how I’ve always been with my experience over the years at Rules Committee,” he said. “So we’re a little bit all over the board — but in a good way, leaning on that process expertise and ability to design a lobbying plan effectively for clients.” More than a dozen clients are following French to the new firm, including medical imaging company RadNet , AT&T , Discount Tire , Habitat for Humanity and shipping company Pasha Group — several of which date back to his time at Capitol Counsel.

ABOUT THAT POST: “President Donald Trump met privately on Tuesday with Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong before publicly backing the company’s position in an ongoing lobbying clash with banks that has derailed a major cryptocurrency bill,” POLITICO ’s Jasper Goodman reports.

title: Trump DOE vet heads downtown
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — TRUMP DOE OFFICIAL HEADS DOWNTOWN: A veteran of both Trump Energy Departments has left the administration to join S2R , the public affairs firm founded last year by a trio of former NRSC strategists.

— Shawn Affolter has joined the firm as a senior vice president where he will register to lobby, initially on behalf of the firm’s energy-sector clients. Until last month, Affolter was the principal deputy assistant secretary for congressional and intergovernmental affairs at DOE, where he helped manage the department’s interactions with Congress as well as state, local and tribal partners. During his first tour of duty at DOE, Affolter served for more than two years as the deputy assistant secretary for Senate affairs. Previous to that, Affolter worked for Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.), who sits on the Senate Energy Committee.

— Affolter’s departure comes at a critical time in the energy sector, which has endeavored to find sufficient methods of energy generation to power data centers central to President Donald Trump ’s vision of American AI dominance.

“Demonstrating American energy affordability, reliability, and security will continue to be the lens in which policymakers and the public measure results,” Affolter wrote in an email to PI regarding the administration’s approach to energy policy. “The confluence of re-industrialization, AI data centers, advanced manufacturing, upgrading aging infrastructure, and geopolitics make this a defining time. These are big, weighty topics, but there remains a through line back to the kitchen table affordability concerns of everyday Americans.”

— War in Iran has contributed to rising oil prices, which has become a major concern at the White House, our colleague Ben Lefebvre reported today . Affolter expects to see a heightened focus going forward on how energy policy relates to national security, particularly when it comes to supply chain security, he said.

— “Identifying ongoing vulnerabilities, closing those gaps, accelerating investments, and scaling up our domestic capabilities in partnership with our allies will continue to be the name of the game,” he wrote.

— Affolter is just the latest addition to S2R, which opened its doors in Alexandria last year. Founders Jason Thielman , Tim Edson and Brock Lowrance started the firm after helping to make the Senate red in the 2024 elections.

title: Marijuana company hires Ballard for patent dispute
body_text:
BALLARD’S NEW BUSINESS: California-based marijauna company Stiiizy has hired Washington lobbyists for the first time, turning to Ballard Partners for help with an ongoing patent dispute that threatens the company’s ability to import certain vape devices, according to a newly filed disclosure report.

— Ballard signed the new client on Feb. 9, according to the disclosure, nearly three weeks after the U.S. International Trade Commission issued a final determination finding Stiiizy had imported vapes that infringe on patents held by domestic vape manufacturer PAX Labs . As part of its final determination, the ITC issued a cease and desist order to Stiiizy.

— Now, Stiiizy has hired Ballard to provide “advocacy regarding patent and trademark issues” and “relief for an exclusion order following a patent infringement action,” according to the disclosure. Firm leader Brian Ballard will handle the account along with Hunter Morgen and Michael Rubino .

MORE NEW BUSINESS: The Vogel Group registered seven new clients today across various industries. Cement manufacturer Sathi and commodities trader Javelin Global Commodities hired the firm to work on trade issues. In the housing space, developer Champion Homes hired the firm to work on “D.C. housing issues” and “lobbying on housing issues,” respectively. Defense startup Aermetric Technology Group , mineral exploration company Tsodilo Resources Limited , conservancy group Friends of the Mississippi River and sustainability nonprofit CERES round out the list.

— Capital One added Crossroads Strategies to its list of hired guns in January, according to a newly filed registration. The team, led by firm CEO Matthew Lapinski , will lobby on “legislative and regulatory issues affecting the banking industry; issues related to consumer data privacy; and issues related to payment networks.”

— The hire makes Crossroads the third new firm the bank has engaged since the start of 2026. Capital One previously hired Venable and Federal Hall Policy Advisors to lobby on similar issues.

title: Meet the new TikTok, same as the old TikTok
