UNDER NEW MANAGEMENT: The new American-owned version of TikTok has registered to lobby and appears to be continuing to focus on the same issues as its former parent company ByteDance , according to a new filing .

— TikTok USDS Joint Venture , as the new U.S. entity is known, submitted its registration on Jan. 22, the same date the company was formed to comply with the bi-partisan law requiring Chinese-owned ByteDance to divest itself of the app’s U.S. operations or face a ban. The new company is owned by a consortium of investors led by Silver Lake , Oracle and MGX , each of whom hold 15 percent of the company. ByteDance retains a 19.9 percent stake.

— The joint venture will lobby on “issues related to internet technology and learning-enabled content platforms, including data protection and privacy, algorithm security and integrity, content moderation, software assurance, online safety, interoperability of global platforms, and small business and the economic impact of TikTok,” according to the registration.

— Another constant appears to be TikTok’s public policy and government affairs staff, nearly all of whom previously appeared on ByteDance filings. Mac Abrams , Michael Bloom , Albert Calamug and Derrick Dockery , will continue lobbying under the new joint venture.

— There is one new addition to the team: Nicole Nason , former head of the Federal Highway Administration, has been appointed as the joint venture’s head of public policy, according to her LinkedIn . TikTok USDS did not respond to a request for comment on Nason’s appointment or the new registration.

— It’s too soon to know how much the new TikTok is prepared to spend in Washington, but Nason’s hiring and the many similarities between this registration and previous ByteDance disclosure reports suggests it could be a similar amount. ByteDance reported spending $8.3 million on in-house lobbying alone last year.

Happy Friday and welcome to PI . Enjoy the nice weather this weekend and send tips to dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or message us on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

ANTHROPIC OUT: All federal agencies have been directed to completely cease using Anthropic products and the company has been designated a supply-chain risk to national security following a breakdown in talks between the company and the Pentagon about the military’s use of Anthropic’s AI model, our colleague Brendan Bordelon reports .

— “The Leftwing nut jobs at Anthropic have made a DISASTROUS MISTAKE trying to STRONG-ARM the Department of War, and force them to obey their Terms of Service instead of our Constitution,” President Donald Trump posted this afternoon , warning of “major civil and criminal consequences” for the company if it is not “helpful” during a six month “phase out period.”

— That was followed by a post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announcing that “no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic.” The announcement marks a major change to Anthropic’s relationship with the federal government, which just last year awarded the company a $200 million Pentagon contract . Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment from Politico.

PARAMOUNT WINS: Paramount Skydance has emerged as the victor in its battle against Netflix to acquire WarnerBros Discovery , leaving regulator approval as the final hurdle to creating what would be a massive media empire controlled by a strong ally of the president.

— Netflix’s decision yesterday to pull out of the race came hours after its CEO met with Attorney General Pam Bondi and Trump, seeking facetime with the officials who would’ve needed to approve the streamer’s acquisition of Warner Bros and assurances that government review of the prospective deal would be handled fairly, our colleagues Yasmin Khorram and Sophia Cai reported .

— But despite receiving such assurances, Netflix chief Ted Sarandos announced his company would not seek to match Paramount’s latest offer, ceding its attempt to acquire the HBO Max streaming service and Warner Bros. studios. Paramount’s deal to acquire Warner Bros. includes all of the company’s properties, including CNN .

MAKING SOLAR GREAT AGAIN : Yesterday, PI told you about the questions that had been raised by Katie Miller’s sudden and mysterious push for solar energy. Thanks to POLITICO’s Kelsey Brugger , Zack Colman and Pavan Acharya , that mystery has been solved .

— Miller’s pro-solar posts are the result of an initiative by the American Clean Power Association to engage conservative influencers to promote solar energy, according to a strategy memo obtained by our colleagues. The “American Energy First” campaign plans to expand in the coming weeks and will include polling data gathered by Kellyanne Conway’s firm, paid media partnerships with podcasts and paid content placed in right-leaning publications.

— Miller has denied being paid by ACP for her solar posts. “I do not have a paid partnership with them,” she said in a statement. ACP declined to comment on whether it paid or partnered with Miller.

— The memo says the campaign is “not directly associated with ACP’s multi-technology brand,” and in a statement, the trade group’s spokesperson, Artealia Gilliard , said “American Energy First is supported and led by a small number of ACP member companies that deploy utility scale solar across the U.S.”

AIPAC’S NEXT TEST : The upcoming Illinois primary will be closely watched by those wondering how much sway the American Israel Public Affairs Committee still has in modern Democratic politics, Leah Askarinam , Maya Sweedler and Matt Brown report for the Associated Press .

— The leading pro-Israel advocacy group has invested at least $1.9 million in political ads in the race to replace retiring Rep. Danny Davis (D-Ill.). “Other organizations that critics believe are tied to AIPAC are also spending heavily in Illinois, a source of bitterness and recriminations in a state already known for its bare knuckled brand of politics,” they report.

— This comes after AIPAC invested nearly $2 million on attacking moderate Democrat Tom Malinowski in the recent Democratic primary for New Jersey’s upcoming special election, which resulted in the victory of an even harsher Israel critic, Analilia Mejia .

— AIPAC appears unbothered. “We expect to be involved in dozens of races both in primaries and general elections this cycle,” Patrick Dorton , a spokesperson for AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC, the United Democracy Project, told the AP.

By DANIEL BARNES and CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

02/27/2026 08:09 PM EST

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

UNDER NEW MANAGEMENT: The new American-owned version of TikTok has registered to lobby and appears to be continuing to focus on the same issues as its former parent company ByteDance, according to a new filing.

— TikTok USDS Joint Venture, as the new U.S. entity is known, submitted its registration on Jan. 22, the same date the company was formed to comply with the bi-partisan law requiring Chinese-owned ByteDance to divest itself of the app’s U.S. operations or face a ban. The new company is owned by a consortium of investors led by Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX, each of whom hold 15 percent of the company. ByteDance retains a 19.9 percent stake.

— The joint venture will lobby on “issues related to internet technology and learning-enabled content platforms, including data protection and privacy, algorithm security and integrity, content moderation, software assurance, online safety, interoperability of global platforms, and small business and the economic impact of TikTok,” according to the registration.

— Another constant appears to be TikTok’s public policy and government affairs staff, nearly all of whom previously appeared on ByteDance filings. Mac Abrams, Michael Bloom, Albert Calamug and Derrick Dockery, will continue lobbying under the new joint venture.

— There is one new addition to the team: Nicole Nason, former head of the Federal Highway Administration, has been appointed as the joint venture’s head of public policy, according to her LinkedIn. TikTok USDS did not respond to a request for comment on Nason’s appointment or the new registration.

— It’s too soon to know how much the new TikTok is prepared to spend in Washington, but Nason’s hiring and the many similarities between this registration and previous ByteDance disclosure reports suggests it could be a similar amount. ByteDance reported spending $8.3 million on in-house lobbying alone last year.

Happy Friday and welcome to PI. Enjoy the nice weather this weekend and send tips to dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or message us on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17. And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko.

ANTHROPIC OUT: All federal agencies have been directed to completely cease using Anthropic products and the company has been designated a supply-chain risk to national security following a breakdown in talks between the company and the Pentagon about the military’s use of Anthropic’s AI model, our colleague Brendan Bordelon reports.

— “The Leftwing nut jobs at Anthropic have made a DISASTROUS MISTAKE trying to STRONG-ARM the Department of War, and force them to obey their Terms of Service instead of our Constitution,” President Donald Trump posted this afternoon, warning of “major civil and criminal consequences” for the company if it is not “helpful” during a six month “phase out period.”

— That was followed by a post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announcing that “no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic.” The announcement marks a major change to Anthropic’s relationship with the federal government, which just last year awarded the company a $200 million Pentagon contract. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment from Politico.

PARAMOUNT WINS: Paramount Skydance has emerged as the victor in its battle against Netflix to acquire WarnerBros Discovery, leaving regulator approval as the final hurdle to creating what would be a massive media empire controlled by a strong ally of the president.

— Netflix’s decision yesterday to pull out of the race came hours after its CEO met with Attorney General Pam Bondi and Trump, seeking facetime with the officials who would’ve needed to approve the streamer’s acquisition of Warner Bros and assurances that government review of the prospective deal would be handled fairly, our colleagues Yasmin Khorram and Sophia Cai reported.

— But despite receiving such assurances, Netflix chief Ted Sarandos announced his company would not seek to match Paramount’s latest offer, ceding its attempt to acquire the HBO Max streaming service and Warner Bros. studios. Paramount’s deal to acquire Warner Bros. includes all of the company’s properties, including CNN.

MAKING SOLAR GREAT AGAIN: Yesterday, PI told you about the questions that had been raised by Katie Miller’s sudden and mysterious push for solar energy. Thanks to POLITICO’s Kelsey Brugger, Zack Colman and Pavan Acharya, that mystery has been solved.

— Miller’s pro-solar posts are the result of an initiative by the American Clean Power Association to engage conservative influencers to promote solar energy, according to a strategy memo obtained by our colleagues. The “American Energy First” campaign plans to expand in the coming weeks and will include polling data gathered by Kellyanne Conway’s firm, paid media partnerships with podcasts and paid content placed in right-leaning publications.

— Miller has denied being paid by ACP for her solar posts. “I do not have a paid partnership with them,” she said in a statement. ACP declined to comment on whether it paid or partnered with Miller.

— The memo says the campaign is “not directly associated with ACP’s multi-technology brand,” and in a statement, the trade group’s spokesperson, Artealia Gilliard, said “American Energy First is supported and led by a small number of ACP member companies that deploy utility scale solar across the U.S.”

AIPAC’S NEXT TEST: The upcoming Illinois primary will be closely watched by those wondering how much sway the American Israel Public Affairs Committee still has in modern Democratic politics, Leah Askarinam, Maya Sweedler and Matt Brown report for the Associated Press.

— The leading pro-Israel advocacy group has invested at least $1.9 million in political ads in the race to replace retiring Rep. Danny Davis (D-Ill.). “Other organizations that critics believe are tied to AIPAC are also spending heavily in Illinois, a source of bitterness and recriminations in a state already known for its bare knuckled brand of politics,” they report.

— This comes after AIPAC invested nearly $2 million on attacking moderate Democrat Tom Malinowski in the recent Democratic primary for New Jersey’s upcoming special election, which resulted in the victory of an even harsher Israel critic, Analilia Mejia.

— AIPAC appears unbothered. “We expect to be involved in dozens of races both in primaries and general elections this cycle,” Patrick Dorton, a spokesperson for AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC, the United Democracy Project, told the AP.

IT’S NICE TO HAVE A FRIEND: No one in Washington has prepared for this moment as long as the Mojahedin-e-Khalq , an organization of Iranian exiles who have been fighting for decades to turn their homeland into a democracy.

— While supporters of Reza Pahlavi , the son of the deposed shah who hopes to return to Iran as its next leader, have assembled a broad network of enthusiastic exiles, the MEK has focused on an inside game in Western capitals. It recruited some of the most prominent figures in American politics, including former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and former Democratic National Committee chair Howard Dean , initially with the goal of getting the State Department to shed the MEK’s longstanding designation as a terrorist group .

— Now the MEK, which has been accused by critics of operating like a cult, sees an opening it has never had before. After this weekend’s killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei by Israeli and U.S. airstrikes, France-based MEK leader Maryam Rajavi announced the formation of a secular provisional government.

— Rajavi’s announcement was celebrated by a ready-made echo chamber of American political figures, including several with close ties to the Trump administration. Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo declared that “Iran’s democratic opposition is ready to step up and lead.” Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani spent the weekend attacking Pahlavi, a longtime MEK rival, as “destabilizing” and “a formula for disaster.”

— “The only way to see an end to the threat of the Iran regime is to end the role of the dictatorship in Iran, and that’s, of course, the responsibility of the people of Iran,” said Alireza Jafarzadeh , deputy director of the U.S. branch of MEK’s political arm, the National Council of Resistance of Iran .

— Since MEK won removal of the terrorist designation in 2012, the council has paid more than $2.7 million to a lobbying firm run by former Sen. Robert Torricelli (D-N.J.), according to records filed with the Justice Department. Rosemont Associates worked to set up meetings with U.S. diplomats and lawmakers about various issues affecting Iranian refugees abroad, as well as promoting media appearances and signing onto letters or penning op-eds defending MEK and its leadership.

— Others registered to represent NCRI under FARA include Robert Joseph , a former undersecretary of State for arms control and international security, and former Attorney General Michael Mukasey , who have touted MEK talking points in op-eds and media interviews. The group also retains the booking agency Special Guests , DOJ filings show.

— MEK shows its political muscle during its annual “Free Iran” conferences in Washington and other global summits it has put on in locations across Europe. Pompeo addressed the group’s most recent summit in November alongside former U.S. Ambassador to Denmark Carla Sands , conservative commentator Guy Benson , and former Rep. Patrick Kennedy (D-R.I.). John Bercow , the former speaker of the British House of Commons, also participated.

— Many of the speakers are paid lavishly for their participation. Former Vice President Mike Pence received more than $400,000 in speaking fees from NCRI and affiliate groups after leaving office in 2021, according to financial disclosures filed during a subsequent presidential campaign.

— The events attract hordes of sitting elected officials, too. Of the more than 30 U.S. lawmakers who spoke to the group at its 2021 gathering were then-Senate Foreign Relations Chair Bob Menendez (D-N.J.), future House Speaker Kevin McCarthy and future House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , according to a recap posted by the group.

— In the wake of this weekend’s military action, NCRI maintains that its requests of U.S. policymakers haven’t changed. “We’re not asking for boots on the ground. We’re not asking for appropriation of money. We’re not asking for arms, none of that,” Jafarzadeh told POLITICO.

— “Don’t give concessions to the Iranian regime, hold them accountable for their crimes and terrorism and recognize the right of the people of Iran to overthrow this regime,” he said. “Recognize the right of the resistance units, those forces on the ground who have been fighting the regime, recognize the right to confront the Revolutionary Guards, to fight them and to end the regime. That’s all that is really needed and asked for.”

MLB LOBBIES UP: Major League Baseball has added some more depth to its bullpen of outside help in Washington. The league retained Forbes Tate Partners and Cornerstone Government Affairs beginning yesterday to lobby on a slew of issues including taxes, game broadcasts, drones and stadium security and visas for athletes, disclosure filings show.

— More than a dozen lobbyists between the two firms are set to work on the accounts, including Jeff Forbes and Zach Williams of Forbes Tate and David Planning , Chris Hodgson and Mike Smith of Cornerstone.

— Cornerstone and Forbes Tate are the second and third additions to the MLB’s bench this year. In January, MLB brought on PhronesisDC , the firm started by veteran GOP tax lobbyist Brendan Dunn , to work on tax issues ahead of Republicans’ reconciliation push.

— The league has four other outside firms — Ballard Partners , Hogan Lovells , the Duberstein Group and Washington Council Ernst & Young — on retainer, but MLB’s lobbying hires this year were its first since 2019, disclosure filings show.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Bayer added new lobbying heft last month prior to a series of significant wins in the form of a watered-down MAHA Commission report from HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the inclusion of a prized liability shield in a GOP spending bill.

— According to a newly filed disclosure, Bayer brought on Mercury Public Affairs’ Bryan Lanza and John Lonergan at the beginning of September to lobby on “issues related to the importance of crop protection tools and related supply chains for U.S. agricultural production.”

— Meanwhile sports betting giant FanDuel has retained Mehlman Consulting to lobby on sports gambling and tax issues. The hire came amid the gaming industry’s push for a legislative fix to language in the GOP reconciliation package that advocates said would hike taxes on gamblers.

— And embattled Chinese drone company DJI Technologies brought on new lobbying help as the company stares down threats to its U.S. business from across the federal government. The drone giant hired MO Strategies’ Marty Obst , a longtime adviser to former Vice President Mike Pence , and Robert Goad , who served as DHS’ liaison to Congress and as a special assistant to the president during Trump’s first term, to “facilitate discussions on border security and technology” at the beginning of September, per a disclosure filing.

— A provision in last year’s defense authorization bill called for an automatic FCC ban on Chinese drone companies like DJI beginning in December unless cleared by a national security review. DJI has sought to rally its users ahead of the deadline. Adding to the pressure, a federal judge last week rejected DJI’s bid for removal from a Pentagon blacklist of companies with alleged ties to the Chinese military.

title: Manatt picks up another batch of Holland & Knight clients

MANATT SIGNS MORE HOLLAND & KNIGHT CLIENTS: Manatt, Phelps & Phillips has registered to lobby for a half-dozen local government clients previously represented by lobbyists who decamped for the firm from Holland & Knight last year. They include Florida’s Jacksonville Transportation Authority , the government of Des Moines, Iowa, and the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority .

— Several other new clients signed with Manatt as subcontractors of Holland & Knight, such as Florida’s Hillsborough Area Regional Transit Authority , California’s Orange County Fire Authority , the Orlando Housing Authority and the North Tampa Housing Development Authority .

— Eve O’Toole , Leslie Pollner , Lisa Barkovic , Joe O’Brien and Adrianna Williams , all members of Holland & Knight’s local governments lobbying group, left the firm in October to join Los Angeles-based Manatt. In all, Manatt has registered to lobby for nearly three dozen current or former Holland & Knight clients in the last year, according to a PI analysis of disclosures.

NO CAP: Wall Street doesn’t know how President Donald Trump ’s proposed temporary 10 percent cap on credit card interest rates would work, but banks and credit card companies are coming out forcefully against the idea floated Friday in a social media post.

— The Electronic Payments Coalition , which includes top banks and credit card issuers like Visa and Mastercard , pushed out a study Monday criticizing a bill from Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) that would cap credit card rates at 10 percent indefinitely. It said that anywhere from 82 percent to 88 percent of open credit card accounts would “lose their credit card as they know it today,” either through account closures or having their credit limits rolled back.

— “In essence, the credit card would become a very nice bookmark,” EPC executive director Richard Hunt said on a press call Monday, maintaining that an interest rate cap would simply create too much risk for many credit card issuers.

— “I understand the president is trying to make sure Americans can afford to make ends meet, and we support that,” he said. “This study is to show them the draconian effects that would happen to his voters and to the Senate and the House members’ constituents. This is serious stuff. This isn’t campaign rhetoric.”

— Hunt said he wasn’t aware of where Trump’s 10 percent number came from — or Trump’s vow for the interest rate cap to last only a year. And he added that he didn’t believe there was any mechanism for Trump to impose such a cap without congressional action, which appears unlikely. But the industry rushed to condemn the idea regardless.

— Trump’s proposal would be “devastating for millions of American families and small business owners who rely on and value their credit cards, the very consumers this proposal intends to help,” the Consumer Bankers Association , Bank Policy Institute , American Bankers Association , Financial Services Forum and Independent Community Bankers of America said in a joint statement Friday night. They pledged to work with Trump but warned that a cap “would only drive consumers toward less regulated, more costly alternatives.”

THE OTHER KIND OF INFLUENCER: “Trump’s return to the White House has transformed the federal government and upended the business of lobbying, creating a new class of Washington operatives that blur the lines between consulting, advocacy and journalism,” the Wall Street Journal ’s Maggie Severns , Natalie Andrews , Josh Dawsey and Eliza Collins write.

— “Corporate and foreign interests that used to rely primarily on paid lobbyists to pitch their case to lawmakers and administration officials are instead pouring money into trying to get their cause promoted by a group of young, conservative influencers known to be close to Trump’s staff.”

— “A camera-ready pack of Gen-Z social-media natives — many of whom were too young to vote when Trump announced his first run for office — are reaping the rewards. They don’t work for traditional news outlets and are thus unshackled from newsroom ethics rules, such as the typical ban on accepting gifts worth more than $25.”

— “They don’t have to follow the disclosure laws that apply to big-money super PACs or lobbyists. And they have large followings eager to hear pro-Trump views, a gold mine for those looking to sway both Washington and the public.”

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

DRONE LOBBYIST: Holland & Knight is boosting its expertise at the intersection of transportation, aviation and technology as the Trump administration vows to “unleash American drone dominance.” Matthew Satterley , the former head of global policy for Alphabet -owned drone delivery company Wing , has joined Holland & Knight as a senior policy adviser in the firm’s public policy and regulation practice group.

— Before joining Wing in 2019, Satterley was head of federal policy and government affairs for the shuttered drone traffic management company AirMap . He previously served as legislative director for former Rep. Frank LoBiondo (R-N.J.), who chaired the House Transportation & Infrastructure Aviation Subcommittee.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Battery maker Duracell retained ArentFox Schiff in late November to lobby on federal funding for domestic battery materials processing and battery production, according to a newly filed disclosure.

— The hire came a little over a month after the Energy Department canceled more than $700 million in grants for advanced battery manufacturing projects issued by the Biden administration with funds from the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law.

— And Capital One has brought on Venable , the credit card company’s first new outside firm since 2024. Venable previously lobbied for Discover Financial Services , which completed its merger with Capital One in May.

— Venable’s Thomas Boyd , Sarah Donovan , Josh Raymond , Chris Scribner and Timothy Ursprung began working for the card issuer at the beginning of the year on general banking policy, including issues related to data privacy and payment networks, disclosures show.

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE WEEKEND: Americans for Prosperity said on Friday that it will yank support for Republican lawmakers who voted in favor of restoring expired Affordable Care Act subsidies, POLITICO ’s Amanda Chu reports.

— “First on the group’s blacklist are the 17 House Republicans who broke from the party Thursday to join Democrats in passing legislation that would revive and extend the Obamacare subsidies for three years. … AFP said it was pausing current and future grassroots activity in those 17 districts, as well as advertisements in them promoting the domestic policy package that Republicans enacted in July and that is their foremost legislative achievement.”

TAKING STOCK: “GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan last year bought stock in a major supplier for data centers that subsequently boomed in value — at the same time he was encouraging data centers to be built in his Pennsylvania district,” Daniel L. reports.

— “In June, Bresnahan bought between $1,001 and $15,000 of stock in Credo Technology , a company that provides electric cables and chips for data centers, according to a House report he filed in July. Bresnahan spokesperson Hannah Pope said the purchase totaled $1,454. Since then, the share price of Credo stock has risen about 109 percent — joining the set of AI companies ballooning in value.”

— “The trade, which has not been previously reported, comes as data centers have become an increasingly hot-button political issue and his Democratic opponent has sought to make Bresnahan’s stock trading a top issue in the campaign.”

META GETS TRUMPIER: “ Meta named former Trump adviser Dina Powell McCormick to serve as president and vice chair Monday, further cementing the company’s growing ties to Republicans” and the White House, POLITICO ’s Brendan Bordelon writes.

— “In addition to a long career on Wall Street, Powell McCormick served as Trump’s deputy national security adviser during his first term. She was also a member of the George W. Bush administration,” and is married to Sen. David McCormick (R-Pa.).

— Powell McCormick has served on Meta’s board since last April, as “part of a broader play by the social media and artificial intelligence giant to hire Republicans following Trump’s election,” Brendan notes. That push has included elevating Republican Joel Kaplan to serve as its head of global affairs and adding former Republican FCC Chair Kevin Martin as Kaplan’s deputy.

— Right on cue, Trump praised the move in a post on Truth Social on Monday that praised Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg for making a “great choice.” The president called Powell McCormick “a fantastic, and very talented, person, who served the Trump Administration with strength and distinction!”

— Charlie Andrews is joining Nvidia ’s policy comms team in D.C. He previously worked at Weber Shandwick and is a Commerce Department and Patty Murray alum.

He previously served as a senior research fellow at The Heritage Foundation . Bill Hansen is joining DFI’s board of directors. Hansen is currently the CEO of Building Hope Holdings .

FOREIGN INFLUENCE: The Senate Judiciary Committee voted today to advance a bill that would ban former senior government officials from lobbying for foreign “countries of concern” like Russia and China.

— The bipartisan Conflict-free Leaving Employment and Activity Restrictions, or CLEAR, Path Act seeks to limit the impact of foreign influence in Washington by prohibiting former agency heads, their deputies and other former Senate-confirmed employees from lobbying the federal government on behalf of geopolitical adversaries. “Countries of concern” under the bill would initially include China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba and Syria. Adding or removing a country from that list would require a proposal from the secretary of state and the attorney general plus sign off from Congress.

— “Foreign adversaries with ill intentions should not wield influence on American policymaking, nor should they exploit our own citizens to intercede on their behalf,” said the bill’s sponsor Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

— The bill, which has drawn bipartisan support from co-sponsors Sens. Peter Welch (D-Vt.), James Risch (R-Idaho) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), is just the latest Senate effort to reduce the influence of foreign lobbying. In December, the Senate passed two bills aimed at improving transparency around lobbying efforts with foreign connections that aren’t required to be reported to the Justice Department under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. The House has not taken any action on those measures.

FOCUS ON FRAUD: Jenner & Block has hired former Justice Department fraud chief Glenn Leon as a partner in the firm’s investigations, compliance and defense practice. Leon, who until recently served as the leader of the DOJ criminal division’s fraud section, has spent years investigating and prosecuting major health care fraud, securities and commodities fraud and other similar cases.

— His hiring comes as the Trump administration is telegraphing an enhanced focus on federal fraud prosecutions. Last week, Vice President JD Vance announced the creation of a new assistant attorney general position focused solely on fraud to investigate allegations that federal aid money had been widely misused in Minnesota. The new AAG for fraud would eventually investigate fraud nationwide, Vance said, adding that the new prosecutor would directly report to himself and the president.

— Leon alluded to those developments in a statement to PI, saying his experience would be “particularly valuable to clients navigating the evolving regulatory environment shaped by recent changes to federal enforcement priorities and Executive Orders.”

WICKER MAN HANGS UP A SHINGLE : John Keast , a top aide to Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) for more than 30 years and a central figure in national security legislating, is launching a new firm with RTX as one of his first clients — just as the defense heavyweight finds itself in President Donald Trump’s crosshairs.

— Keast has formed the lobbying and consulting firm Keast Strategic Solutions , and he identified RTX as a client at a farewell reception Wednesday evening hosted by BGR Group . He is expected to file disclosure paperwork on Tuesday.

— The announcement comes as Trump has stepped up public criticism of major defense contractors, including RTX, injecting new uncertainty into the industry’s relationship with the White House even as Congress presses ahead with a $1.5 trillion budget proposal for 2027.

— Trump’s salvo included an executive order directing scrutiny of stock buybacks and executive compensation at defense contractors, all as the administration pushes companies to reinvest more aggressively in expanding U.S. munitions production capacity.

— Keast most recently served as staff director of the Senate Armed Services Committee. He spent more than a decade at Cornerstone Government Affairs before rejoining Wicker’s staff in 2018 as the GOP staff director of the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee.

— Wicker, in a recent floor speech marking Keast’s departure, praised him as a master of Senate process and policy, crediting him with playing a central role in National Defense Authorization Act negotiations, acquisition reform and industrial base issues.

— Wicker called out Keast’s work on the CHIPS and Science Act and credited him with delivering more than $1 billion in infrastructure and broadband funding to Mississippi and nationwide through Commerce Committee work.

ALL EYES ON GREENLAND : President Trump has set his sights on acquiring Greenland, and at least one company with interests in the Danish territory is positioning itself in Washington to seize the moment.

— Eclipse Metals , an Australian mining exploration company with holdings in Greenland, signed BGR Government Affairs in December to lobby on issues related to the company’s efforts to “unleash Greenland’s rare-earths potential in a manner consistent with the state commercial priorities of President Trump and the Administration,” according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— “Eclipse believes its Greenland holdings, licenses and interests can contribute to U.S. and allied resilience against disruptions in minerals critical to defense, advanced manufacturing, and AI-enabling technologies,” the report further states.

— Though Trump has emphasized national security reasons for obtaining the territory in recent weeks, the island’s rich deposits of critical minerals offer an additional explanation for the importance the administration has placed on the matter.

— BGR founding partner Ed Rogers will handle the account, joined by former BP top lobbyist Joe Ellis and former ExxonMobil senior adviser Collin Janich .

NETFLIX NEW HIRE : Netflix has added an additional hired gun to its Washington lobbying roster as it works to close the deal for its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery ’s studios and streaming platforms while fending off Paramount Skydance ’s attempt at a hostile takeover of WBD.

— Avoq registered to lobby for the streamer on Dec. 15, according to a disclosure report , on “issues related to the media and telecommunications industry.” Working on the account will be a bipartisan team of Barry LaSala , Natalie Farr Harrison and Joseph Orlando .

— The team at Avoq joins the growing list of firms hired by Netflix, which currently includes The Gibson Group , Monument Advocacy, Miller & Chevalier and Ballard Partners .

TRUMPCARE: The Trump administration has unveiled a proposed blueprint for health care reform that bashes private industry players that have long been considered GOP allies, POLITICO’s Amanda Chu , David Lim , Robert King and Kelly Hooper reported yesterday.

— “Republicans, on their heels after letting Obamacare premiums spike this month, sounded ready to embrace a plan to drive down costs that puts the blame on private industry,” they write. “Trump’s plan, notably, does not include free-market ideas in a bill House Republicans passed in December. That bill, for example, would have allowed small businesses to band together to drive harder bargains with insurers.”

— While Trump’s plan is scant on details, it marks a clear change in the Republican position on health care that for years has been largely defined by opposition to the Affordable Care Act.

— “The Paul Ryan Republican conference … was repeal and replace, and there was no other plan. … In terms of health care, this Republican Party looks a lot more innovative, a lot more open, and a lot more, quite frankly, forward-looking and aspirational,” Lauren Stewart , senior federal affairs liaison at Americans for Prosperity , told POLITICO.

PARDON ME : The president quietly issued a new slate of pardons this week, including a pardon for a convicted fraudster who had previously received clemency from Trump during his first term, Kenneth Vogel and Suzanne Craig report for The New York Times .

— Also pardoned this week was a man whose daughter donated millions to MAGA Inc. , the Trump-supporting super PAC. The man, a banker convicted on charges that he bribed the former governor of Puerto Rico, was represented by Christopher Kise , one of the president’s former criminal defense lawyers.

— Adriana Camberos , who was granted clemency by Trump in the final days of his first term and later convicted on new fraud charges, received a new pardon after hiring the same lawyers who secured her original commutation: former deputy White House counsel Stefan Passantino and former Rudy Giuliani defense lawyer Adam Katz .

SPENDING ON CIVIL RIGHTS : Civil rights groups upped their spending in Washington in 2025, according to an analysis by Jonathan Salant for OpenSecrets .

— The NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund reported spending $180,000 during the first three quarters of the year, nearly doubling its lobbying spending during the same period of 2024.

— The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights spent nearly $1.7 million during the same time last year. That was a $200,000 increase from the group’s spending during the same time period in 2024.

— “It is an unfortunate reality, the defensive posture every civil rights organization finds itself in at the moment,” Cedric Haynes , vice president, policy & legislative affairs for the NAACP , told Salant.

title: The Qatar lobby takes a victory lap
body_text:
QATAR’S CAUSE TO CELEBRATE: President Donald Trump and his allies are enjoying a victory lap after yesterday’s announcement that a peace deal has been reached to end two years of conflict between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire fulfills a central campaign promise for the president and goes a long way towards boosting his odds of winning a much-desired Nobel Peace Prize. Also celebrating the peace deal: the Qatar lobby, which has worked for years to change the narrative in Washington around the tiny Persian Gulf nation that played a major role in mediating peace talks.

— Among members of the Qatar lobby there is hope that the success of the ceasefire negotiations will establish Qatar’s reputation as a peacemaker in the region and quash accusations that Qatar is responsible for harboring terrorists and boosting anti-Israel sentiment within the United States.

— “I think it’s reasonable to assume that they put a certain amount of pressure on Hamas to accept the deal. That’s what a good negotiator has to do,” said former U.S. Rep. Jim Moran, who has lobbied for Qatar for nearly a decade. “I think the people who look at this objectively are going to give credit to Qatar.”

— A change in Washington’s perception of Qatar is precisely what its small army of lobbyists have been working on for the better part of the last decade. Qatar began heavily investing in lobbying during the first Trump administration when leaders realized their nation was lagging behind regional rivals like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in terms of Washington influence.

— Members of the Qatar lobby had already sought to present the country as a regional peacemaker, a role that will likely be highlighted even more should this peace deal hold. Brokering this deal “would solidify Qatar’s indispensable position as the world’s trusted mediator,” said Todd Webster of Cornerstone Government Affairs , a registered lobbyist for Qatar. “Time and again, the world has seen that when you want to make peace, you call Doha.”

— If Qatar is able to maintain the reputation of a peacemaker, that could open new doors for foreign investment in Qatar and Qatari investment in Western nations, said Ben Freeman , who studies Qatar’s influence for the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft .

— “Frankly, it gets a lot of folks to turn a blind eye to some of the human rights issues that surfaced after the World Cup,” Freeman said. “If you get this mediator image that really trumps some of these other concerns that countries might have.”

— So will all this make the job of the Qatar lobby in Washington easier? “I hope it does,” Moran said.

title: College commissioners push NIL bill
body_text:
D-I COMMISSIONERS MOVE TO TEE UP NIL BILL: The House may be at a standstill, but college athletic commissioners are working to position the federal name, image, likeness bill backed by the NCAA for quick floor action once the shutdown ends.

— In a letter to the bipartisan heads of the House Judiciary, Energy and Commerce and Education and Workforce committees this morning, the heads of all 31 NCAA Division-I conferences called for lawmakers to take up the SCORE Act, an NCAA-backed bill seeking to tame what the college sports world agrees is a Wild West of rules governing NIL compensation for athletes.

— The bill would give the NCAA crucial antitrust protections it has sought, insulating it from future lawsuits challenging its rulemaking authority. It would block colleges from designating student athletes as employees and codify a new revenue-sharing agreement struck by the NCAA and some college sports’ biggest conferences over the summer.

— The bill advanced out of the requisite House committees, mostly on party lines, in July. But it has been awaiting floor action amid concerns it may not have the votes. Wealthy athletic booster Cody Campbell , who was recently tapped by President Donald Trump to lead a commission focused on the future of college sports, has mounted an opposition campaign arguing that the SCORE Act hands the NCAA too much power, while not doing enough to help ensure the survival of so-called non-revenue and women’s sports.

— Senate Democrats introduced their own NIL proposal last month that does not include prohibitions on student athletes’ employment status — clarity the NCAA has demanded in any federal NIL bill.

— But the D-I commissioners sought to put many of those concerns to bed, framing today’s letter as a show of force — and agreement — across a broad swath of varying interests.

— “Collectively our conferences provide opportunities in higher education through sports to nearly 200,000 student-athletes,” the commissioners wrote. “Our campuses are urban, rural, historically Black, and land grant, and include United States service academies, small liberal arts colleges, large flagship state universities, and everything in between.”

— Yet “we believe we are on common ground not just among each other, but with members of both parties in Congress as well as the American public in our desire to have college sports return to a state of stability.”

— To hammer the point home, four of the top D-I conferences will air a new ad calling for passage of the SCORE Act during this weekend’s football games. The spot, which is supported by the Southeastern Conference , Big Ten , Atlantic Coast Conference and Big 12 , touts the conferences’ support of women’s and Olympic sports at the collegiate level. And it calls the SCORE Act a key way to “ensure the continued support” of those sports.

— “It would prevent federal agencies from contracting with unnamed ‘biotechnology companies of concern’ to be designated by the White House. It also would cut off federal contracts from U.S. companies that would use equipment or services from companies of concern in performance of the contract.”

— The language will still need to make it through conference negotiations between the House and Senate to hash out the differences between their defense bills. — The group is set to host U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) in November. AGP was founded by Republican consultants Richard Walters , Garrett Ventry , Jason Thielman , Josh Helton and Jim McCray .

— Mulvaney, who is also a co-chair of the consulting firm Actum , “will chair a new advisory board at the customer data sharing firm SOLO , the startup announced Friday. ‘Their model is fascinating,’ Mulvaney said about the firm during an interview. ‘Their model is essentially cutting out the credit bureaus and allowing you to own your credit data.’”

— “The move comes as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — which Mulvaney led during the first Trump administration — is gearing up to rewrite an ‘open banking’ rule that governs consumer data access. The issue has long pitted Washington’s banking lobby against fintech firms. But Mulvaney said Thursday he doesn’t view the two as necessarily at odds now, calling them ‘competitors but not enemies.’”

title: The ugly fight over ‘litigation finance’
body_text:
FIRST IN PI: In recent months a fight has kicked off in Washington over an effort to crack down on litigation finance — when hedge funds and other wealthy investors fund lawsuits against companies in an exchange for a share of the proceeds if they win, Daniel L. reports.

— It pits the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and insurance companies that want a crackdown on the practice against groups that say they represent consumers, including a Leonard Leo -linked outfit, that argue that it’s a critical tool to hold corporate America accountable for wrongdoing.

— The latest round of the feud has insurance giant Chubb tussling with the Leo-supported Consumers’ Research . title: Hollywood turns to K Street for help against AI threat
body_text:
— But the dizzying pace of new developments coming out of Washington right now, combined with the deeply personal stakes of issues like generative AI and the potential censorship of administration critics, are fueling a heightened interest in deploying influence peddlers to make their stand with the Trump administration and Congress.

— The latest sign of the seriousness came when famed talent agency Creative Artists Agency retained Washington lobbying shop Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck , as PI noted last week .

— In the two years since AI concerns propelled Hollywood actors and screenwriters to go on strike, unions representing directors, writers and crew members have also bolstered their lobbying footprints. So have top production studios and industry groups looking to ensure their perspectives are heard as Washington confronts thorny questions about how to balance the quest for AI dominance and the need for guardrails for safety and to protect intellectual property.

— There’s “no question that the risks and rewards created by AI are prompting more engagement in D.C. than I’ve seen in over a decade,” said Carl Thorsen , a co-founder of the lobbying firm Thorsen French Advocacy , which has represented the Directors Guild of America and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees for a decade and a half.

— In addition to CAA, the issue has brought several other Hollywood newcomers to Washington over the past few years, including the National Association of Voice Actors and the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences .

— But AI anxieties aren’t the only Hollywood concern driving business on K Street. The industry, which took a major hit during the pandemic, is bleeding high-paying jobs as productions flee for cheaper locales overseas. President Donald Trump ’s jawboning of major media companies has been another pressure point for the industry.

— “In terms of what’s happening at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue and within some of the departments and agencies, I just don’t think there was a clear line of sight,” said one consultant for the industry who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the dynamics at play.

— With their K Street hires, agents and other industry interests now have a team that “can help [them] navigate and walk both efficiently and effectively through these times, and be able to have those relationships to transact on.”

(ALARM) BELLS WILL BE RINGING: Hollywood’s relationship with Washington is at a crossroads, and its stars are turning to K Street A-listers for cover, your host reports. Entertainers are no strangers to lending their voices to advocacy fights in Washington. More often than not, those are ad hoc appearances, with studios, unions and industry organizations typically taking the lead.

— But the dizzying pace of new developments coming out of Washington right now, combined with the deeply personal stakes of issues like generative AI and the potential censorship of administration critics, are fueling a heightened interest in deploying influence peddlers to make their stand with the Trump administration and Congress.

— The latest sign of the seriousness came when famed talent agency Creative Artists Agency retained Washington lobbying shop Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, as PI noted last week.

— In the two years since AI concerns propelled Hollywood actors and screenwriters to go on strike, unions representing directors, writers and crew members have also bolstered their lobbying footprints. So have top production studios and industry groups looking to ensure their perspectives are heard as Washington confronts thorny questions about how to balance the quest for AI dominance and the need for guardrails for safety and to protect intellectual property.

— There’s “no question that the risks and rewards created by AI are prompting more engagement in D.C. than I’ve seen in over a decade,” said Carl Thorsen, a co-founder of the lobbying firm Thorsen French Advocacy, which has represented the Directors Guild of America and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees for a decade and a half.

— In addition to CAA, the issue has brought several other Hollywood newcomers to Washington over the past few years, including the National Association of Voice Actors and the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences.

— But AI anxieties aren’t the only Hollywood concern driving business on K Street. The industry, which took a major hit during the pandemic, is bleeding high-paying jobs as productions flee for cheaper locales overseas. President Donald Trump’s jawboning of major media companies has been another pressure point for the industry.

— “In terms of what’s happening at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue and within some of the departments and agencies, I just don’t think there was a clear line of sight,” said one consultant for the industry who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the dynamics at play.

— With their K Street hires, agents and other industry interests now have a team that “can help [them] navigate and walk both efficiently and effectively through these times, and be able to have those relationships to transact on.”

title: ADL switches Ballard from lobbying to advising
body_text:
BALLARD AND ADL ADJUST THEIR RELATIONSHIP: The Anti-Defamation League’s decision to hire Ballard Partners in the wake of last year’s general election raised eyebrows when it was originally disclosed. The Jewish advocacy group had long been antagonistic toward President Donald Trump , but hiring a Trump-connected lobbyist like Brian Ballard indicated a willingness on its part to reset the relationship and strike a friendlier tone with the new administration.

— So it was surprising to see a new disclosure filed today terminating that lobbying relationship less than a year after it started. But while Ballard’s lobbying work for the ADL is ending, a spokesperson for the organization tells PI it is not parting ways with Ballard entirely — rather, it is switching the firm’s role to an advisory capacity.

— The pivot comes after a few hard weeks for the ADL, which has faced an uphill battle to ingratiate itself in Trump’s Washington. The organization and its president, Jonathan Greenblatt , have struggled to overcome years of built-up resentment from some on the right who consider the group unfairly critical of Trump and his supporters.

— That job has gotten even harder in the wake of Charlie Kirk’s killing last month. In the days and weeks following Kirk’s death, far-right commentators on social media discovered that the ADL listed information about Kirk’s Turning Point USA on its website as part of the group’s Glossary of Extremism and Hate. “ADL sells hate,” Elon Musk wrote on X . “Disgraceful,” wrote Donald Trump Jr .

— Two weeks ago, FBI Director Kash Patel ended a partnership between the bureau and the ADL that provided training on hate crimes and antisemitism to all new agents. In a statement to Fox News , Patel referred to the ADL as “an extreme group functioning like a terrorist organization.”

— The ADL, which paid Ballard $130,000 total for its work since last December, is not dependent on outside help. The group is on track to spend more than $1 million on its in-house lobbying team this year and has had at least one outside firm, H&M Strategies , remaining on its payroll. Other than Ballard, the ADL had not hired a new outside firm since H&M Strategies in 2021.

PIRRO SIGNS NEW CLIENTS: Albert Pirro , ex-husband of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro , one-time Trump real estate lawyer and recipient of one of the last pardons of Trump’s first term, has resumed signing lobbying clients, according to new disclosure reports.

— Pirro had lobbied for clients in New York and Washington throughout his career but had not registered a new client in Washington since 2021. Earlier this year, Pirro resumed representing the Greater New York Hospital Association , a longtime client. And this week, he filed disclosures for two new clients: Quantum Worldwide and Topspin Consumer Partners .

— According to the disclosures, Pirro started representing pharmaceutical ingredient producer Quantum in September. His work for private equity investors Topspin started in June and is focused on tariffs.

DINNER PARTY: President Donald Trump hosted a collection of wealthy donors and corporate executives at the White House Wednesday evening for a dinner celebrating their financial contributions toward the new White House ballroom.

— “So many of you have been really, really generous,” Trump said during his remarks, adding that some in attendance had promised up to $25 million donations for the project. Attendees included Trump donors such as Harold Hamm and Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss , according to a guest list reported by The New York Times’ Zolan Kanno-Youngs . Corporate representatives from Amazon , Apple , Booz Allen Hamilton , Comcast , Google , Lockheed Martin , Meta , Microsoft , Palantir , T-Mobile US , Union Pacific Railroad and more were also in attendance.

CHEMISTS AGAINST RAIL-MERGER: CEOs from the American Chemistry Council (ACC) member companies have sent a letter to President Trump detailing their opposition to the proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern railroads, arguing that combining the companies would make American manufacturing less competitive.

— Chemical manufacturers represented by the ACC depend on rail systems for the safe transportation of hazardous materials, a position that leaves them especially susceptible to consolidation in the market. “Past mergers have led to server service disruptions, rising rates, weakened supply chains and a less competitive U.S. industrial base,” the CEOs write. “We have no doubt that combining UP and NS into the nation’s largest railroad will make these problems worse.”

— The CEOs close by urging the president to allow the Surface Transportation Board, which reviews proposed railroad mergers, to do its job and evaluate the merger with a critical eye. In August, Trump fired one of the board’s Democratic appointees without explanation. The fired board member, Robert Primus , is challenging his dismissal.

CHAMBER SUES OVER H-1B VISAS: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce sued the Trump administration today over the imposition of a new $100,000 fee for H-1B visa applications, a rare contribution from the business lobby to the various legal challenges against administration policies.

— Last month’s announcement of the new fee prompted indignation from the business community, particularly among big tech companies who depend on H-1B visas for skilled foreign workers like software engineers. Today’s lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of overstepping its authority by setting a higher fee than the one approved by Congress.

Jobs report

— Joyce Kazadi has joined Coinbase as Democratic policy lead. She is a Kamala Harris and Barbara Lee alum and most recently worked for the 2024 Democratic National Convention Committee.

— Former Rep. Chris Stewart (R-Utah) has been named chair of America First Policy Institute’s AI and emerging technology team. Also joining the newly formed team are Yusuf Mahmood as director, Dean Woodley Ball as senior fellow and Shea Throckmorton as campaign director.

— Former Rep. James Langevin (D-R.I.) has been named chair of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation .

— Matt Corridoni is now communications director for Majority Democrats . He most recently served as vice president of communications for VoteVets and is a Harris alum.

— Sarah Corcoran has launched Corcoran Strategies Group , her own firm specializing in mental health, health and social services policy. She was most recently senior vice president and chief operating officer at Guide Consulting Services .

— Nicole Vele has joined GrayRobinson as a shareholder in the firm’s Washington office. She was most recently of counsel at Holland & Hart and previously served nearly 12 years as a judge advocate general in the U.S. Air Force.

— Trace Scruggs has joined The Herald Group as a vice president. He most recently served as senior director for public affairs at PLUS Communications .

— Maura Rezendes has joined Sidley Austin as a partner in the firm’s global arbitration, trade and advocacy practice. She was most recently a partner at A&O Shearman .

— The Steel Manufacturers Association has added Max Hyman as director of government affairs and Emily Bradshaw as senior manager of government affairs. Hyman was most recently director of transportation, infrastructure, and labor policy for the National Association of Manufacturers. Bradshaw was most recently a public affairs specialist in the office of the under secretary for international trade at the International Trade Administration .

— Marsha Anderson Bomar has been appointed president of the American Society of Civil Engineers . She most recently served as assistant general manager at the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority .

title: United Way hires Burr
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — CHARITY CASE: One of the largest charities in the country, United Way Worldwide (UWW) , has hired former Republican Sen. Richard Burr and the team at DLA Piper to lobby on its behalf as it attempts to make new inroads with Republican lawmakers.

— The move makes DLA Piper only the third outside firm hired by the nonprofit, which last week topped the Chronicle of Philanthropy’s list of America’s Favorite Charities . UWW spent $350,000 on lobbying in the first half of 2025, with the majority of that going to Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid and the remainder to Venn Strategies .

— “I think really what they sought to do in bringing us on board was strengthen their Republican bona fides,” Karina Lynch , chair of DLA Piper’s government affairs and public policy practice, told PI. “I think we’re viewed as having a pretty strong Republican bench and having an ability to help build some of those relationships which are just a matter of necessity in the world we’re in right now.”

— Michael Sorensen rounds out the team on the account with Lynch and Burr, who started registering clients earlier this year after his mandatory two-year lobbying ban expired. The team, which started working for UWW in September, will focus on issue areas such as “disaster relief, housing, healthcare and childcare,” according to a disclosure report.

— A previous lobbying focus for UWW has been passage of a bill to provide states with funding to improve non-criminal emergency 2-1-1 lines. Under previously proposed bills, funds would be provided for states to expand such systems, which aim to provide mental health and other social services to callers reporting non-criminal or non-medical emergencies that would otherwise be handled by police.

— DLA Piper is doing some work educating senators on the 2-1-1 line proposal, Lynch said, but for now the firm is focused on strengthening UWW’s relationship with Republican officials.

IRS AND PAUL RYAN ALUM HANG A SHINGLE: Jorge Castro and Ted McCann have started CM Strategic , a bipartisan firm that launches with a client roster featuring big names the pair has previously worked with. Standouts in the firm’s initial batch of clients include Exxon Mobil , The Carlyle Group , Pinterest and Standard Industries .

— “I think that’s kind of a testament to the fact that they trust us, they know us well, they know that we can do the work,” said Castro, an alum of the Obama IRS who most recently co-led the tax policy practice at law firm Miller & Chevalier .

— McCann represents the Republican half of the firm. He previously served for nearly three years as an assistant to the speaker for policy in Paul Ryan’s office and has spent the last six years operating his own one-man lobbying shop, The Article One Group . Both men spent years working on the Hill for various committees and lawmakers before leaving government for private practice.

— Matt Thrasher has joined Fluet to build out the firm’s cybersecurity practice. He most recently served as senior counsel for international affairs at the Pentagon.

— Trent Wisecup has been named creative director of FP1 Strategies and PLUS Communications . He has been a partner at the sister firms since 2018.

title: Binance pardon lobby pays off
body_text:
TRUMP PARDONS BINANCE FOUNDER: President Donald Trump has pardoned Changpeng Zhao , founder of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance , POLITICO’s Declan Harty reported this afternoon, confirming a scoop first reported by The Wall Street Journal .

FIRST IN PI — X JOINS COALITION FOR APP FAIRNESS: Congress has revived its push to wrest control of mobile app stores away from Apple and Google , and the effort is getting a big boost from X , the Elon Musk -owned social media giant. X is joining the Coalition for App Fairness , an advocacy group representing app developers including Spotify , Epic Games , Match Group and Proton .

— “We believe in a digital future where competition thrives, innovation is rewarded, and users have ultimate control,” X head of global government affairs Romina Khananisho said in a statement, calling the decision “a testament to our commitment to dismantling monopolistic practices and building a mobile ecosystem that truly serves its users and fosters growth for all.”

— This isn’t the first time Musk has weighed in on competition in the mobile app ecosystem. Even before he bought X’s predecessor, Twitter, in 2022, Musk complained online about fees for app developers and expressed support for Epic in its lawsuit against Apple .

— Shortly after acquiring Twitter, as the Open App Markets Act awaited floor action in Congress, Musk accused Apple of threatening to boot the social media site from its app store — though he later called it a misunderstanding .

— This summer, Musk renewed his criticisms, He questioned whether Apple was declining to feature his apps for political reasons or conspiring with rival artificial intelligence companies to prevent Musk’s AI firm from claiming the top spot in the app store. (X’s community notes debunked his latter claim.)

— The new addition to CAF comes as the Hill debate over regulating the mobile app ecosystem heats up. X’s endorsement of an effort to break up the Apple/Google app store duopoly could hold considerable weight with Musk-allied Republicans, particularly following the recent détente between Musk and President Donald Trump .

— The most notable proposal in the mix is the Open App Markets Act, the updated version of a bipartisan 2022 bill that died on the Senate floor. OAMA was reintroduced in June by Sens. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.).

— It aims to allow consumers “to download applications without having to use an official app store, such as Google Play; open the market to third-party app stores and alternative payment systems; prevent app stores from disadvantaging certain developers; and more,” per our friends at Morning Tech .

— But trade groups that count Apple and Google among their members have, predictably, hammered proposed app store legislation as an unnecessary — and potentially unconstitutional — government intervention that will threaten consumer privacy and security.

— “The Coalition for App Fairness is funded by a small group of powerful developers who simply don’t want to pay for the immense value they receive from Apple’s platforms and technologies,” an Apple spokesperson told PI, adding that “they represent only a very small portion of the broader developer community.”

THE BALL’S IN COURT: Congress has increasingly ceded its influence over major policy decisions to the executive branch, and the flood of legal challenges stemming from that activity has given the judiciary an outsize role in deciding federal policies crucial to K Street’s interests.

— “The Trump Administration is currently party to at least 500 lawsuits covering a range of issues,” DB3 , the lobbying firm formerly known as the Daschle Group, said in a recent presentation to clients titled “King of the Courts.”

— The litigation currently pending “concerns some of the most fundamental parts of our democracy, such as the limits to executive power, birthright citizenship, and the rules of Congressional redistricting,” the deck, which was shared with PI, notes.

— “The stakes are higher than with anything that will happen in Congress,” CEO Nathan Daschle told PI. So while the firm’s updates to clients usually center on upcoming elections, which shape the landscape for future policy fights, DB3’s latest presentation dives into six key cases before the courts, breaking down where things currently stand and how the cases could impact clients, ranging from immigration to tariffs.

UNTETHERED: “Stablecoin giant Tether is looking at spending money on US elections as it prepares to open a US entity and is considering options other than the political action committee that has won the support of big US crypto companies,” Bloomberg ’s Anna Irrera reports.

— “The chief executive officer of Tether, Paolo Ardoino , said in an interview with Bloomberg, that ‘everyone is upset with Fairshake ,’ the crypto PAC that rose to prominence during the 2024 election by spending $133 million on pro-crypto candidates,” in part because Ardoino said the PAC was “doing the bidding of one single company.”

— Though he declined to name the company, Fairshake was seeded by nearly $70 million in donations from Coinbase , which “is closely tied to USDC, a stablecoin that is the biggest competitor to Tether’s token.”

— Tether is currently headquartered in El Salvador, which disqualifies it from donating to U.S. campaigns. But Tether plans on setting up shop in the U.S. by the end of the year, in an office that will be led by former White House crypto czar Bo Hines .

DON’T CALL IT A COMEBACK: Less than five years after Trump pardoned him for financial fraud, lobbying violations and witness tampering, Paul Manafort , the president’s former campaign chair, has completed an “unlikely full-circle journey from high-flying global fixer to federal inmate and back,” Ken Vogel writes in a POLITICO Magazine excerpt of his new book, “Devils’ Advocates: The Hidden Story of Rudy Giuliani, Hunter Biden, and the Washington Insiders on the Payrolls of Corrupt Foreign Interests.”

— “In the weeks after Election Day, Manafort, sensing opportunity, began aggressively courting far-right populist interests around the world looking to align themselves with Trump,” Vogel reports.

— Manafort’s clients have included Sali Berisha , a former disgraced president and prime minister of Albania who tried and failed to make a political comeback in a parliamentary election this spring. Manafort has also “consulted with the party of Milorad Dodik , the pro-Russian authoritarian who has served as president of the self-governing Balkan territory of Republika Srpska,” on an upcoming election.

— Manafort has not registered as a foreign agent for any of his recent work. But the veteran fixer, who pleaded guilty to FARA violations stemming from work for a former Kremlin-aligned Ukrainian president, “says he is being careful to avoid anything that could even faintly resemble lobbying.”

— Manafort’s associates in these undertakings have included Trumpworld fixtures like 2024 campaign co-manager Chris LaCivita and longtime pollster Tony Fabrizio . And though “Manafort remains in Trump’s good graces, he is not nearly as close to the inner circle of foreign policy decision-making as he was under Reagan or Bush,” according to Vogel.

— Still, Manafort’s “formula of casting far-flung politicians as pro-Trump populists could be a blueprint for winning favor in Trump’s Washington in much the same way that opposing communism was during the Reagan and Bush administrations,” even if his record thus far has been mixed.

FIRST IN PI — X JOINS COALITION FOR APP FAIRNESS: Congress has revived its push to wrest control of mobile app stores away from Apple and Google, and the effort is getting a big boost from X, the Elon Musk-owned social media giant. X is joining the Coalition for App Fairness, an advocacy group representing app developers including Spotify, Epic Games, Match Group and Proton.

— “We believe in a digital future where competition thrives, innovation is rewarded, and users have ultimate control,” X head of global government affairs Romina Khananisho said in a statement, calling the decision “a testament to our commitment to dismantling monopolistic practices and building a mobile ecosystem that truly serves its users and fosters growth for all.”

— This isn’t the first time Musk has weighed in on competition in the mobile app ecosystem. Even before he bought X’s predecessor, Twitter, in 2022, Musk complained online about fees for app developers and expressed support for Epic in its lawsuit against Apple.

— Shortly after acquiring Twitter, as the Open App Markets Act awaited floor action in Congress, Musk accused Apple of threatening to boot the social media site from its app store — though he later called it a misunderstanding.

— This summer, Musk renewed his criticisms, He questioned whether Apple was declining to feature his apps for political reasons or conspiring with rival artificial intelligence companies to prevent Musk’s AI firm from claiming the top spot in the app store. (X’s community notes debunked his latter claim.)

— The new addition to CAF comes as the Hill debate over regulating the mobile app ecosystem heats up. X’s endorsement of an effort to break up the Apple/Google app store duopoly could hold considerable weight with Musk-allied Republicans, particularly following the recent détente between Musk and President Donald Trump.

— The most notable proposal in the mix is the Open App Markets Act, the updated version of a bipartisan 2022 bill that died on the Senate floor. OAMA was reintroduced in June by Sens. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.).

— It aims to allow consumers “to download applications without having to use an official app store, such as Google Play; open the market to third-party app stores and alternative payment systems; prevent app stores from disadvantaging certain developers; and more,” per our friends at Morning Tech.

— But trade groups that count Apple and Google among their members have, predictably, hammered proposed app store legislation as an unnecessary — and potentially unconstitutional — government intervention that will threaten consumer privacy and security.

— “The Coalition for App Fairness is funded by a small group of powerful developers who simply don’t want to pay for the immense value they receive from Apple’s platforms and technologies,” an Apple spokesperson told PI, adding that “they represent only a very small portion of the broader developer community.”

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com. Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com. Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns.

THE BALL’S IN COURT: Congress has increasingly ceded its influence over major policy decisions to the executive branch, and the flood of legal challenges stemming from that activity has given the judiciary an outsize role in deciding federal policies crucial to K Street’s interests.

— “The Trump Administration is currently party to at least 500 lawsuits covering a range of issues,” DB3, the lobbying firm formerly known as the Daschle Group, said in a recent presentation to clients titled “King of the Courts.”

— The litigation currently pending “concerns some of the most fundamental parts of our democracy, such as the limits to executive power, birthright citizenship, and the rules of Congressional redistricting,” the deck, which was shared with PI, notes.

— “The stakes are higher than with anything that will happen in Congress,” CEO Nathan Daschle told PI. So while the firm’s updates to clients usually center on upcoming elections, which shape the landscape for future policy fights, DB3’s latest presentation dives into six key cases before the courts, breaking down where things currently stand and how the cases could impact clients, ranging from immigration to tariffs.

UNTETHERED: “Stablecoin giant Tether is looking at spending money on US elections as it prepares to open a US entity and is considering options other than the political action committee that has won the support of big US crypto companies,” Bloomberg’s Anna Irrera reports.

— “The chief executive officer of Tether, Paolo Ardoino, said in an interview with Bloomberg, that ‘everyone is upset with Fairshake,’ the crypto PAC that rose to prominence during the 2024 election by spending $133 million on pro-crypto candidates,” in part because Ardoino said the PAC was “doing the bidding of one single company.”

— Though he declined to name the company, Fairshake was seeded by nearly $70 million in donations from Coinbase, which “is closely tied to USDC, a stablecoin that is the biggest competitor to Tether’s token.”

— Tether is currently headquartered in El Salvador, which disqualifies it from donating to U.S. campaigns. But Tether plans on setting up shop in the U.S. by the end of the year, in an office that will be led by former White House crypto czar Bo Hines.

DON’T CALL IT A COMEBACK: Less than five years after Trump pardoned him for financial fraud, lobbying violations and witness tampering, Paul Manafort, the president’s former campaign chair, has completed an “unlikely full-circle journey from high-flying global fixer to federal inmate and back,” Ken Vogel writes in a POLITICO Magazine excerpt of his new book, “Devils’ Advocates: The Hidden Story of Rudy Giuliani, Hunter Biden, and the Washington Insiders on the Payrolls of Corrupt Foreign Interests.”

— “In the weeks after Election Day, Manafort, sensing opportunity, began aggressively courting far-right populist interests around the world looking to align themselves with Trump,” Vogel reports.

— Manafort’s clients have included Sali Berisha, a former disgraced president and prime minister of Albania who tried and failed to make a political comeback in a parliamentary election this spring. Manafort has also “consulted with the party of Milorad Dodik, the pro-Russian authoritarian who has served as president of the self-governing Balkan territory of Republika Srpska,” on an upcoming election.

— Manafort has not registered as a foreign agent for any of his recent work. But the veteran fixer, who pleaded guilty to FARA violations stemming from work for a former Kremlin-aligned Ukrainian president, “says he is being careful to avoid anything that could even faintly resemble lobbying.”

— Manafort’s associates in these undertakings have included Trumpworld fixtures like 2024 campaign co-manager Chris LaCivita and longtime pollster Tony Fabrizio. And though “Manafort remains in Trump’s good graces, he is not nearly as close to the inner circle of foreign policy decision-making as he was under Reagan or Bush,” according to Vogel.
