FRESH WATER: Current Strategies , which launched at the end of September as the only public affairs firm in Washington focused exclusively on water infrastructure and policy, filed its first disclosure reports today, And it revealed a client list of state and local government coalitions, trade associations and one household name in water filtration.

— Water filter manufacturer Brita is Current’s first disclosed client. Firm founder and CEO Mae Stevens is joined on the account by Wendi Wilkes and Theodore Mondloch , both of whom followed Stevens from Banner Public Affairs to launch Current. All three previously represented Brita in their time at Banner, which first signed the water filter maker as a client in May 2024 and has reported being paid $100,000 per quarter since last Fall.

— In fact, all six of Current’s initial clients are registered as Banner clients and have not yet filed termination reports. Others in the initial class of clients include industry associations like the Water Quality Association and the Clean Water Construction Coalition , as well as the National Recreation and Park Association . Rounding out the list are two Washington-area clients: utility WSSC Water and the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments .

IT’S 6 A.M. SOMEWHERE: The newest member of the Stagwell network is SixAM Strategies , a new bipartisan public affairs firm launched today aimed at using on-the-ground partners in all 50 states to produce hyperlocal communications campaigns for clients.

— Running the new operation will be longtime political strategists Maggie FitzGerald and Jessie Andrews Keady . FitzGerald, the GOP half of the firm, will serve as CEO. She most recently worked as an executive vice president at Targeted Victory , running the GOP firm’s hyperlocal practice.

— Keady comes to the new firm after a long career in Democratic politics, spending nearly 10 years in House staff positions before serving as chief of staff to New York Lt. Governor Antonio Delgado. She will serve as COO of the new firm.

— The firm plans to work with others in the Stagwell family, like SKDK and Targeted Victory, and plans to have a full-time staff of 10 employees by the start of next year, Eleanor Hawkins reports for Axios .

STONE ZONE: A small Native American tribe is experiencing a wave of success in Washington after hiring longtime Trump ally Roger Stone to lobby on its behalf, Taylor Giorno reports for NOTUS .

— In the months since the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana hired Stone and announced it would be nominating President Donald Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize, the tribe has secured an Oval Office meeting, reservation visits from federal officials and a $10 million construction contract from the State Department.

— The meeting was part of a new initiative led by the Hamm Institute for American Energy and GOP lobbying firm CGCN Group . Attendees included Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Deputy Secretary Katharine MacGregor.

— “The coalition is focused on four major policy areas, said Michael Catanzaro, a longtime GOP energy policy expert who served as a senior White House aide during the first Trump administration. Those are: permitting reform, regulatory reform, supply-chain resilience and public-private partnerships.”

SACRAMENTO SWAMP: The indictment of California Gov. Gavin Newsom ’s ex-chief of staff has rocked Sacramento, POLITICO ’s Jeremy White and Lindsey Holden report for Pros .

— Prosecutors allege that Dana Williamson worked with prominent Sacramento lobbyist Greg Campbell and former California AG Xavier Becerra ’s chief of staff Sean McCluskie to embezzle hundreds of thousands of dollars from dormant Becerra campaign accounts.

— “The government alleges that Williamson … worked with Campbell and McCluskie to funnel roughly $225,000 from Becerra’s dormant state campaign account to McCluskie. It describes McCluskie saying he took a pay cut when he followed his boss from the California Department of Justice to HHS in 2021 and that he needed the additional funds to pay for airline travel so he wouldn’t have to relocate to Washington. His federal salary at the time was about $183,000.”

title: Longtime hospitals chief is departing

AHA CHIEF RETIRING: Rick Pollack is stepping down as president and CEO of the American Hospital Association after more than four decades with the powerful hospital lobby — including the past 10 years at its helm.

— Pollack first joined the AHA back in 1982, and he spent 24 years as the trade group’s executive vice president for advocacy and public policy before taking over as its leader in 2015. Since then, he’s seen the hospital industry through numerous crises, including the Covid-19 pandemic and GOP attempts to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act.

— AHA, which represents more than 5,000 hospitals across the country, is regularly one of the top lobbying spenders in Washington. Last year, the trade group spent more than $24 million on federal lobbying, and AHA is set to exceed that this year following the industry’s fierce — but unsuccessful — campaign to fend off more than $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts enacted by Republicans as part of their reconciliation bill earlier this summer.

— The AHA has hired the executive search firm WittKieffer to find a new chief executive. Pollack will stay in his role through the transition.

PARAMOUNT WARNING SHOT: Lawmakers continued today to stake out their positions on the competing bids for Warner Bros. Discovery , with a pair of House Democrats warning that a Paramount Skydance triumph could pose “substantial national security consequences.”

— Several Middle East sovereign wealth funds backing Paramount’s bid agreed to give up voting rights in order to help a merger deal avoid scrutiny by the interagency Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S. But in a letter to Warner Bros. board members and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent today, Reps. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) insisted that such a review take place. The headquarters of Paramount’s rival, Netflix , is located in Liccardo’s district.

— To help bankroll the hostile takeover bid launched by Paramount on Monday, the company said it had secured financing from sovereign wealth funds in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, along with Affinity Partners , the investment fund started by presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner that is also backed by Gulf money. Even without governance rights, investors could still gain access to sensitive user data, the lawmakers said.

— Liccardo and Pressley argued that forgoing a CFIUS review of any Paramount-WBD deal would represent “a serious lapse in fiduciary judgment” and could expose the company to regulatory or reputational risk. They warned that a future Congress (presumably one controlled by Democrats) could unwind key parts of the deal upon review.

— “The American public relies on Warner’s platforms for news, entertainment, and vital information,” they wrote. “Allowing foreign-backed investors to obtain influence over this ecosystem without the fullest possible scrutiny would be irresponsible and dangerous.”

— On the flip side, Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah), who chairs a key antitrust panel, told Semafor last night he has “grave doubts” about the ability of a Netflix-Warner Bros. deal to survive federal antitrust scrutiny.

— Cook’s closed-door appearance came ahead of a markup tomorrow morning where the House Energy and Commerce Committee will take up several bills to address kids’ online safety. Cook raised privacy concerns about language in the App Store Accountability Act that would require app stores to verify users’ ages. His trip to the Hill follows a letter from Apple’s global head of privacy last week making the same argument.

— “Republican Representative Gus Bilirakis of Florida, who chairs the panel’s technology subcommittee, said he met with Cook and doesn’t expect major changes to the bill. ‘It would be good if they would work with us, but we are going full speed ahead,’ said Bilirakis, who added the measure has support from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers.”

— “Industry groups are asking Congress to appropriate additional money for specialty crop producers, who have borne the brunt of increased costs for labor, fertilizer, seeds and other needs and international market uncertainty as a result of President Donald Trump ’s trade wars.”

— “The appeal comes after officials announced Monday they will deliver $12 billion in farm aid to U.S. producers by the end of February, with $11 billion of that funding allocated for producers of major row crops like corn and soybeans. Just $1 billion will be reserved for aid for specialty crops, sugar and other commodities.

— “USDA also announced that applications for row crop producers would open in the coming weeks but offered no details for specialty crop producers.”

— “Since Trump returned to the White House, his regulators have moved to withdraw permits for six offshore wind projects along the East Coast and halted construction of two others. … He has also wiped out federal tax credits supporting wind and solar, while his agencies have opened reviews of the wind industry’s national security implications and alleged health hazards and erected barriers to turbine projects on both water and land.”

— “The uprooting of wind projects is especially striking at a time when political leaders from both parties are calling for a massive increase in electricity generation nationwide , citing rising consumer prices and the soaring power demands of data centers.”

— “And the ferocity of the president’s attacks stunned executives who had assumed they could work with him, even after a 2024 campaign in which Trump baselessly alleged that wind power causes cancer and has killed hundreds of whales.”

JOURNEY TO THE MANOSPHERE: The 2024 elections shined a spotlight on the widening political gap between men and women, vaulting terms like “manosphere” into the popular lexicon. And as Democrats have scrambled to find their way out of the political wilderness — in large part by trying to boost the party’s appeal to men — the progressive consultancy Precision Strategies is out with new research it hopes can help.

— In partnership with Tunnl , Precision has developed the “Manosphere Index” to provide campaigns and brands with insight into how to reach men by diving into what is shaping their worldview.

— Post-2024, “there was a lot of data and framing that very narrowly talked about this ‘masculinity crisis,’” said Krishana Davis, who leads Precision’s digital and multicultural engagement efforts. But much of that dialogue was “flattening the conversation, and basically looking at millions of men from a very monolithic view.” Or, she argued, it became “a shorthand of white men, when even white men are not a monolith.”

— Through thousands of interviews, Precision and Tunnl found that economic pressures, more than ideology, are shaping masculinity today. Religion is also playing a major role in men’s lives, especially among Gen Z, Davis said, with many finding a sense of community in faith in addition to platforms like YouTube and various podcasts rather than more traditional media institutions.

— “It’s not that advocacy organizations need to mimic influencers,” Davis said. “But they need to partner with them, work with them, and ensure that they’re also equipping them with these counter narratives, as it makes sense.”

FIRST IN PI – Bryan Lanza , who was a senior adviser on President Donald Trump ’s 2024 campaign, is now a consultant to the international division of Russia oil company Lukoil as it tries to find a buyer for its global assets after it was sanctioned last month, two people familiar with the matter told Daniel L.

— Lanza and his firm Mercury Public Affairs are interfacing with the U.S. government on the transaction and are among the entities that have helped get extensions for the sale from the Treasury Department, according to one of the people. The deadline for Lukoil to sell its non-Russian assets is now Jan. 17. Reuters reported Thursday that American bank Xtellus Partners is the leading bidder for those assets. Lanza started doing the work for Lukoil in the last few weeks.

— Lukoil’s international division, which is based in Austria, has refineries, oil fields and 2,000 gas stations around the world, including more than 200 in the U.S. Because the work is not encompassed by FARA or covered under LDA and involves a commercial transaction, Lanza does not have to register. Lanza also does lobbying work for several major Fortune 500 companies, including Bank of America and Qualcomm .

— Lanza declined to comment. Spokespeople for Mercury and Lukoil didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

MALONEY HEADS TO SPORTS BETTING COALITION: The Sports Betting Alliance , which represents some of the top sports betting and online gaming platforms, has hired Joe Maloney as its next president. Maloney joins the coalition from the American Gaming Association , where he’s served the past two years as senior vice president of strategic communications. Jeremy Kudron , SBA’s current president, will become chair of the alliance.

— Maloney also has experience from the league side of sports betting, having served as vice president of public affairs and strategic comms for the Washington Commanders prior to joining AGA.

— SBA will continue its push for the expansion of legal sports and online gambling under Maloney’s leadership, he told PI. Amid high-profile betting scandals just in the past few months , the industry’s job “is to continue to embrace” the increased scrutiny that has come with its growth, Maloney added..

— “The events of the last several weeks … have demonstrated that our companies, our legal operators, are actually on the front lines in identifying and reporting that activity so that investigation can ensue and bad actors can be brought to justice,” he argued. “And that continues to be a story that we absolutely need to tell.”

— His arrival at SBA also comes amid a fissure between sports betting platforms and the broader gambling industry. FanDuel and DraftKings — both SBA members — left the AGA last month amid the trade group’s campaign against online prediction markets ; Fanatics , another SBA member which launched its own sports prediction market last week, also quit AGA as a result. Maloney said that SBA hasn’t taken a position on prediction markets.

FIRST IN PI — CAPITOL HILL CELEBRATES JENNER & BLOCK: Congressional Republicans and Democrats came together last night for a bipartisan event celebrating the release of “ When Congress Comes Calling ,” a newly updated handbook on congressional investigations published by Jenner & Block and the Project on Government Oversight .

— Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), two of the president’s staunchest allies on Capitol Hill, were part of the crowd at the event, which celebrated the work of the government watchdog group and a law firm President Donald Trump previously accused of abusing its pro-bono practice to “engage in activities that undermine justice and the interests of the United States.”

— Jenner is one of four law firms that sued the Trump administration earlier this year in response to executive orders threatening their ability to do business. The order targeting Jenner accused the firm of engaging in “obvious partisan representations to achieve political ends.” It cited its previous hiring of former federal prosecutor Andrew Weissmann as justification for suspending security clearances held by firm lawyers, reviewing government contracts held by the firm and its clients and limiting the ability of its lawyers to enter government buildings and interact with government personnel.

— A federal judge ruled in May that the order was unconstitutional. The Justice Department is currently appealing that ruling.

— But you wouldn’t detect any of that from the tenor of last night’s event, which brought Johnson and Jordan together with Democrats like Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) and Reps. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.), per a tipster.

— In remarks, Jordan praised the work of lawyers on all sides of congressional investigations, including committee staff and the lawyers who represent witnesses. “You can’t get to the bottom of any of these investigations unless you have staff who are willing to do the work,” he said. “We got staff who are now on the other side [of the table], the counsel who make the process work, the folks at Jenner & Block, and all of you, all of these good folks. … When you bring in the witnesses, you can’t really make the whole process function unless those witnesses have good counsel like we have here.”

— The updated congressional investigations handbook is a 434-page compendium of the laws and processes that govern congressional investigations and is intended as an all-in-one guidebook for staff investigators and private lawyers. The handbook was last updated in 2017, leaving it in desperate need of an update to reflect case law around congressional inquiries developed during the first Trump administration and the Jan. 6 Committee investigation.

— “The work that you’re doing … is very important,” Lofgren, who served on the Jan. 6 Committee, said.

— “This edition of ‘When Congress Comes Calling’ will serve as a go-to guide for congressional investigators for years to come, and we’d like to thank the Project on Government Oversight for entrusting us with the responsibility of updating this seminal publication,” said Ashley Callen , co-chair of Jenner’s congressional investigations practice.

— Callen’s involvement in the project may help explain the bipartisan well wishes. Before joining Jenner in May, she served in the speaker’s office as general counsel, the capstone to more than two decades on the Hill working for Republican members and committees. Callen previously served as the Republican deputy staff director for the House Oversight Committee while Jordan was ranking member.

— “‘President Trump and David Sacks aren’t making policy — they’re running a con,’ said [California Gov. Gavin Newsom], referring to Trump’s AI and crypto czar, a Silicon Valley investor who helped shape the policy and attended the signing. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), said during yesterday’s subcommittee markup hearing.

HOLLAND & HART ADDS COGAR: The top aide to Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) is heading to K Street after nearly three decades on the Hill. Charles Cogar , who has worked for Scott since 2013 — most recently as chief of staff — has joined Holland & Hart as a senior director of federal affairs.

— Cogar’s hire is part of an expansion of the firm’s federal lobbying practice beyond energy, environmental and natural resources issues that have made up the bulk of its portfolio. That expansion is being led by Andrew Wheeler , who served as EPA administrator during President Donald Trump ’s first term.

— “We really see some synergies between what Chuck has focused on the last few years and what the firm is working on,” Wheeler said in an interview. He pointed to issues like banking and cryptocurrency as well as congressional oversight and implementation of this summer’s GOP megabill as areas where Cogar’s experience will be useful.

— Holland & Hart, which is based in the Mountain West, also does work on permitting reform, artificial intelligence and the energy needs of data centers. Those issues are poised to dominate policy debates across Washington in 2026. Wheeler does not lobby, but Cogar told PI he plans on registering to do so (though he is subject to a yearlong cooling-off period barring him from lobbying his former Senate colleagues).

— Wheeler’s hires over the past year and a half haven’t been limited to members of his own party. So far in 2025, the firm has hired former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola to help lead Alaska work, along with several former Democratic Hill aides.

SPEAKING OF PERMITTING: The oil and gas industry is making a late push to shore up GOP support for a permitting overhaul expected to hit the House floor this week. But first it will have to overcome opposition from some House conservatives who say the bill to ease environmental reviews would undermine Trump’s assault on renewable energy, our friends at Morning Energy report .

— The leaders of several oil and gas trade groups are directly urging Trump to “prioritize” passage of the bipartisan SPEED Act this week in a move to counteract an effort from offshore wind foes who have tried to bait the president into opposing the bill.

— In a letter to Trump today , the heads of the National Ocean Industries Association , Energy Workforce & Technology Council , Independent Petroleum Association of America and Western Energy Alliance specifically called out the importance of the most controversial language in the bill that would limit presidential power to revoke permits for projects, a key priority across energy industries fearful of getting their approvals yanked depending on the party in power.

— A similar group of oil and gas leaders sent a letter to Speaker Mike Johnson on Friday that pushes back at House members who “have expressed concerns that the SPEED Act might give preference to other sectors at the expense of” the fossil fuel industry. “We do not share those concerns, and those sentiments do not reflect our position,” the industry leaders wrote.

— Earlier today, House Majority Whip Tom Emmer touted the support of more than 300 organizations for the SPEED Act, including the American Exploration & Production Council , American Gas Association , American Petroleum Institute , Edison Electric Institute , Data Center Coalition , Google , National Association of Manufacturers and National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association .

FIRST IN PI: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s Make America Healthy Again movement has upended the health policy landscape thanks to Kennedy’s ascension to head of HHS, and a new analysis from Democratic consulting and public affairs firm Global Strategy Group aims to help clients navigate the MAHA universe.

— “Health and wellness debates now begin upstream — in creator ecosystems that move faster than hearings, comment periods, or stakeholder processes,” GSG says in the report, shared first with PI.

— The key to understanding this new health information ecosystem is recognizing that it’s fueled by “a high-volume content pipeline that prioritizes emotional punch over accuracy,” the analysis argues. The upshot is that now, stakeholders must “contend with a policy conversation that is already in motion by the time it reaches Washington.”

— GSG advises that groups be proactive in establishing their own credibility early on and anticipating how MAHA figureheads might frame a given issue. Organizations should also be more mindful of not just their messengers — opting for scientists over corporate spokespeople, for example — but their messaging. They should prepare simple and digestible explanations and be prepared to address issues that are percolating online instead of waiting until concerns are raised by officials in D.C., the firm said.

WALL STREET LOBBYIST JUMPS TO EBAY: eBay has hired Dan Martini as head of U.S. federal government relations. — In an interview with POLITICO ’s James Bikales ahead of today’s announcement, “Ash said SAFE is keeping its focus on lessening reliance on foreign supply chains, though its emphasis on energy has shifted since the shale revolution made the U.S. a net oil exporter.”

— “The group is now focused on critical minerals policy and pushing the adoption of technologies with both defense and commercial applications, he said. That includes drones, driverless cars and advanced batteries.”

— “The Tanzanian government’s request for proposals from lobbyists has been circulating around Washington over the last week as the government of President Samia Suluhu Hassan seeks support to bolster its existing relationships on the Hill with a special focus on deploying media expertise as it tries to counter reports of repression and claims of religious oppression , which it has disputed.”

HOUSE PBM PROPOSAL FALLS SHORT: As House Republicans tee up votes on a health care package this week, half a dozen industry groups clamoring for Congress to rein in pharmacy benefit managers want to see lawmakers take a tougher line on the pharmaceutical middlemen.

— “The failure to curb harmful PBM practices is no longer a crisis in the making — it now constitutes a crisis unaddressed,” the National Association of Chain Drug Stores , the American Pharmacists Association , the National Grocers Association and more wrote in a letter to congressional leadership on Friday. They called the issue “a win within reach for patients and for the pharmacies that serve them” that has been marred by “procedural and political delays.”

— The coalition laid out a wishlist of PBM reforms that they wrote “are essential to ensure that a legislative package is effective and can be supported by pharmacies,” including a ban on so-called spread pricing in Medicaid.

— While the health package released by House leaders contains pieces of a bipartisan crackdown on PBMs that was ultimately derailed by Elon Musk a year ago, the provisions are more focused on increased transparency than a sweeping crackdown on the sector.

— “More than six pharmacies in America are closing every single day, depriving Americans of access to affordable care. For this reason, we are eager to see the key provisions of PBM reform — outlined in the letter — swiftly included in legislation by Congress,” NACDS’ Chris Krese said in a statement when asked how the House proposal stacks up.

SIGN OF THE TIMES: “A lawsuit against Instacart alleges that the mobile shopping giant fired a corporate employee for running for Congress , citing fears that some of her Democratic positions could lead to backlash from President Donald Trump and Republicans,” per The Washington Post ’s Dan Merica .

— “The lawsuit from Lisa Vedernikova Khanna , a candidate in Virginia, alleges that the California-based company ‘conditioned’ her employment on her ending her campaign and that an internal Instacart ‘risk assessment’ of her bid stated that the campaign ‘presented risk to the company’ because it could involve criticizing the president and other Republicans.”

FIRST IN PI: The Pharmaceutical Reform Alliance , which crusades against major drugmakers, will take over a portion of the National Mall beginning tomorrow with an installation aimed at spotlighting the high cost of drugs in the U.S. compared to what those medicines cost overseas.

— The installation, which will pop up near the Smithsonian Metro stop through Thursday, will feature giant pill bottles with oversized price tags to argue that “Americans are getting a bad deal on drug prices.” PRA will also be conducting a live poll and collecting stories about drug prices from passersby in order to convince the Trump administration to build on the momentum of policies like Most Favored Nation and its crackdown on direct-to-consumer ads by the industry.

SILICON VALLEY’S DATA CENTER PROBLEM: “Tech companies and lobbyists are investing millions of dollars to tackle a new political problem for the industry : Data centers, the lifeblood of the growing AI economy, are becoming toxic with voters,” POLITICO ’s Gabby Miller writes.

— “Alarmed by elections that candidates won by campaigning against new data centers, the industry is taking out ads and funding campaigns to flip the narrative and put data centers in a positive light — spinning them as job creators and economic drivers rather than resource-hungry land hogs.”

— “The new campaigns mark a sharp change for an industry that has long relied on tech’s image as an engine of growth and development,” and they “signal how concerned the tech sector is becoming about data centers in the 2026 midterm elections.”

Y COMBINATOR FORMS A PAC: Silicon Valley startup accelerator Y Combinator has taken another step to bolster Little Tech’s political maturation in Washington with the launch of its corporate PAC. The new PAC, which is also referred to in FEC filings as Little Tech PAC, comes as the startup community has sought to compete with more entrenched Big Tech interests to shape AI and competition policy in Washington.

— It also follows the launch of a network of super PACs focused specifically on AI policy. One group, Leading the Future , said it has already reached $100 million in commitments from the likes of venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ron Conway , OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale . The super PAC will pour that money into midterm races to support candidates that align with the industry’s AI priorities and to defeat candidates who oppose tough AI regulations.

— Meta has also seeded multiple super PACs to help beat back AI regulations around the country, while former Reps. Chris Stewart (R-Utah) and Brad Carson (D-Okla.) are leading another set of super PACs to counter industry spending in the midterms.

— “Little tech needs a voice, and we’ll support candidates who get that and oppose those who don’t,” Luther Lowe , Y Combinator’s head of public policy, said of the decision to launch a PAC. In a statement, Lowe laid out some of the biggest policy concerns for Little Tech, including the lament that whether in consumer tech, defense or fintech, “incumbents have captured the rules to freeze out better products.”

— “How will consumers enjoy the fruits of AI — all these new apps and services — if they aren’t discoverable?” Lowe added. He also reiterated the tech industry’s preference for a federal AI framework over a patchwork of state laws as well as the need for immigration reforms to make it easier for “brilliant founders from outside the U.S. to obtain O-1 visas and create companies from scratch that go on to employ tens of thousands of Americans.”

— Unlike the industry super PACs — which can raise and spend unlimited funds as long as there is no coordination with candidates — Y Combinator’s corporate PAC will be restricted to donations from employees only. title: Notre Dame adds K St. powerhouse
body_text:
LUCK OF THE IRISH: The University of Notre Dame has added another K Street heavyweight to its bench of outside lobbying firms. The prestigious Catholic university retained Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck at the beginning of November to provide “strategic counsel” and advocacy on education and tax policy issues affecting the school, according to a disclosure filing.

— Notre Dame will face a bigger tax bill beginning in 2027, thanks to the GOP megabill signed into law this summer that hiked taxes on wealthy colleges’ endowments. Instead of paying a 1.4 percent tax rate on its endowment, the university’s endowment tax rate will jump to 4 percent — bringing its tax bill to around $40-50 million from around $12 million in previous years, according to an August post from the school’s executive officers.

— The Notre Dame officers pledged to continue working with other religious universities to lobby for an exemption to the tax for such schools. An exception was included in the House’s version of the reconciliation bill but was dropped from the final version for procedural reasons.

— Among those working on the account for Brownstein are Marc Lampkin and Radha Mohan , both members of the firm’s higher education task force ; Bart Reising , a former top aide to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise ; Brian McGuire , a former Treasury and Mitch McConnell aide; and Harold Hancock , a former tax counsel for the House Ways and Means Committee.

— Notre Dame also retains BGR Group and Cornerstone Government Affairs , and it hired Lewis-Burke Associates in August.

— “ Future Forward USA Action , the so-called dark-money group of the main super PAC backing Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Kamala Harris , took in a staggering $613 million from donors last year, according to a tax filing obtained by The New York Times.” The vast majority of that haul — $515 million — came from just 10 donations, with the biggest check coming in at $97.5 million. The nonprofit flipped around $252 million of that money to its affiliated super PAC, FF PAC .

— “Mr. Trump’s main nonprofit group, Securing American Greatness , collected about $275 million from donors in 2024, according to a separate filing obtained by The Times. Nearly $68 million of that headed to the nonprofit group’s affiliated super PACs.”

— “The filings show starkly how much the main Democratic super PAC leaned on its dark-money group, reflecting one way that the left has raced ahead of the right in campaign finance. Befitting the difference in scale between the two operations, the Democratic nonprofit group’s 2024 tax filing has twice as many pages as its Republican counterpart’s.”

— They also illustrate how 501(c)(4) nonprofits have continued to take on an outsize role in modern political campaigns. Tiffany Muller , head of the money in politics group End Citizens United , estimated to the Times that “only about 25 percent of the money spent by outside groups in elections could now be traced back to its true source.”

MEEKS AIDE HEADS BACK DOWNTOWN: Megan Hannigan is joining FS Vector as a managing principal on its government relations and public policy team. Hannigan was most recently deputy chief of staff for Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), a member of the House Financial Services Committee, and before that, she spent eight years working in PayPal ’s D.C. office.

— “Chastened by the 2008 financial crisis, America’s biggest banks have mostly avoided the limelight in Washington and have tried to work behind the scenes. NICOTINE STARTUP HIRES CHECKMATE: A nicotine pouch startup aiming to compete with Zyn has hired Checkmate Government Relations as its first Washington lobbying firm, according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— Sesh+ , founded in 2020 and based in Austin, Texas, announced in September it had raised more than $40 million in funding as part of a push to take on Philip Morris’s Zyn, the dominant brand in the nicotine pouch market. In addition to support from venture capital firms such as 8VC , the company also boasts celebrity investors like Post Malone , Diplo , Zac Brown , Andrew Schulz and others.

— Checkmate began representing the company in Washington in mid-November, according to the disclosure report. Firm founder Ches McDowell is listed on the account along with Caitlin Koury , Muhammad Rahim and James Johnson . Chris LaCivita Jr. , the son of President Donald Trump’s 2024 co-campaign manager Chris LaCivita , rounds out the team that will be lobbying on “issues relating to the PMTA process.”

— Premarket tobacco product applications (PMTA) are submitted to the FDA as part of the approval process for any new tobacco product. Pouches produced by Sesh+ don’t contain tobacco, according to the company’s website, but are regulated as tobacco products under FDA guidelines.

— In September, Reuters reported that the FDA plans to fast-track review of nicotine pouches from four companies after receiving pressure from the White House. Sesh was not among the manufacturers receiving White House support, according to the report.

ICYMI: Earlier this week the Senate passed two bills aimed at increasing transparency around foreign influence efforts by closing loopholes in the Lobbying Disclosure Act and the Foreign Agent Registration Act.

— The bills would require lobbyists to indicate on disclosures if they are taking advantage of exemptions that allow them to represent foreign individuals without registering under FARA or if foreign governments have any interest, financial or otherwise, in their lobbying efforts. The measures were introduced by Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

— House versions of the bills have languished in the Judiciary Committee since being introduced in March.

LUNAR LOBBYING : The United States is aiming to go back to the moon and commercial space companies are lobbying for NASA to use their rockets, POLITICO’S Audrey Decker reports in POLITICO Pro Space .

— A new proposal by the Commercial Space Federation , a trade group that represents companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin , urges the House to add language to a NASA reauthorization bill. It would allow the space agency to use commercial rockets for moon missions instead of the current Boeing system, which the agency plans to use for upcoming lunar flights.

— “Long-term, there’s consensus in the space industry that NASA needs cheaper commercial rockets to achieve a sustainable presence on the moon — since [the Boeing system] costs billions per launch. But there’s no clear agreement on when exactly that shift should happen,” Decker writes.

— “The Commercial Space Federation says its proposal would simply give NASA additional flexibility to move to commercial spacecraft once it’s ready. And, the provision itself doesn’t specify an exact timeframe to move to commercial,” she adds.

FULL STEAM AHEAD: Union Pacific Railroad Company ’s proposed acquisition of fellow rail-giant Norfolk Southern moved into its next phase today as the railroad filed an official merger application with the Surface Transportation Board, the government body that will have to approve the deal. Union Pacific CEO Jim Vena announced the filing on an investor call this morning, during which he spoke candidly about the impact the merger would have on the market, POLITICO’S Chris Marquette reports for Pros .

— “Now, are we going to win some business from other railroads? Absolutely,” Vena said. “Customers have a choice.”

— But the Rail Customer Coalition , a collection of trade groups representing industries that depend on freight rail, said today’s application fails to show how the merger will improve service or enhance competition among railroads.

— “At a time when the top concern for Americans is the cost of living and inflation, policymakers must stand with consumers and reject any deal that fails to promote competition over monopolies and drives prices even higher,” Chris Jahn , president and CEO of the American Chemistry Council said in a statement. The ACC is a member of the Rail Customers Coalition along with the American Petroleum Institute , the Alliance for Automotive Innovation and more.

GAMIFYING LOBBYING: Toyota has an internal platform where employees can play games and earn rewards in exchange for listening to recordings of company lobbyists and contacting lawmakers to urge action on the automaker’s policy goals, Dharna Noor reports for The Guardian .

— The platform, called Toyota Policy Drivers, gives employees the ability to win points by playing retro-themed games and engaging with company messaging on issues like emissions regulations. Points can be exchanged for physical rewards like stickers, t-shirts and even trips. Calls to action on the platform encourage employees to contact their representatives to support Toyota’s policy positions.

— “On Monster Mansion, a game featuring cozy haunted house motifs, users can earn 100 points for listening to corporate recordings. In one, company lobbyists discuss how the company is affected by trade policy; in another, women Toyota dealers praise a Washington, D.C. company event with lawmakers. A third features Stephen Ciccone – the longtime vice-president of public affairs for Toyota in North America – criticizing environmental measures.”

BREAKING THE BANK: The American Bankers Association , along with bankers associations from all 50 states, D.C. and Puerto Rico, sent a letter to Congress yesterday urging lawmakers to take action on a loophole in the GENIUS Act. They say the loophole has allowed stablecoin issuers and crypto exchanges to offer interest payments to stablecoin holders, threatening banks’ abilities to make loans.

— “The GENIUS Act envisioned payment stablecoins as a payments instrument, not an investment product. Congress barred issuers from paying interest for precisely that reason. Closing the current loophole by clarifying that the prohibition extends to partners and affiliates would restore parity, protect consumers, and align practice with legislative intent,” the associations write.

— The letter from the banks came on the same day as a letter from a collection of crypto associations and companies , led by the Blockchain Association , urging the Senate Banking Committee to leave the GENIUS Act as is and continue allowing crypto exchanges to offer the financial incentives.

— “The push to restrict stablecoin rewards beyond that agreed to in GENIUS is not a technical refinement or a consumer protection fix,” the crypto letter states. “It would prohibit the same types of incentive programs for stablecoin payments that banks have long offered on credit cards and other types of payment services.”

LUNAR LOBBYING: The United States is aiming to go back to the moon and commercial space companies are lobbying for NASA to use their rockets, POLITICO’S Audrey Decker reports in POLITICO Pro Space.

— A new proposal by the Commercial Space Federation, a trade group that represents companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin, urges the House to add language to a NASA reauthorization bill. It would allow the space agency to use commercial rockets for moon missions instead of the current Boeing system, which the agency plans to use for upcoming lunar flights.

— “Long-term, there’s consensus in the space industry that NASA needs cheaper commercial rockets to achieve a sustainable presence on the moon — since [the Boeing system] costs billions per launch. But there’s no clear agreement on when exactly that shift should happen,” Decker writes.

— “The Commercial Space Federation says its proposal would simply give NASA additional flexibility to move to commercial spacecraft once it’s ready. And, the provision itself doesn’t specify an exact timeframe to move to commercial,” she adds.

FULL STEAM AHEAD: Union Pacific Railroad Company’s proposed acquisition of fellow rail-giant Norfolk Southern moved into its next phase today as the railroad filed an official merger application with the Surface Transportation Board, the government body that will have to approve the deal. Union Pacific CEO Jim Vena announced the filing on an investor call this morning, during which he spoke candidly about the impact the merger would have on the market, POLITICO’S Chris Marquette reports for Pros.

— “Now, are we going to win some business from other railroads? Absolutely,” Vena said. “Customers have a choice.”

— But the Rail Customer Coalition, a collection of trade groups representing industries that depend on freight rail, said today’s application fails to show how the merger will improve service or enhance competition among railroads.

— “At a time when the top concern for Americans is the cost of living and inflation, policymakers must stand with consumers and reject any deal that fails to promote competition over monopolies and drives prices even higher,” Chris Jahn, president and CEO of the American Chemistry Council said in a statement. The ACC is a member of the Rail Customers Coalition along with the American Petroleum Institute, the Alliance for Automotive Innovation and more.

GAMIFYING LOBBYING: Toyota has an internal platform where employees can play games and earn rewards in exchange for listening to recordings of company lobbyists and contacting lawmakers to urge action on the automaker’s policy goals, Dharna Noor reports for The Guardian.

— The platform, called Toyota Policy Drivers, gives employees the ability to win points by playing retro-themed games and engaging with company messaging on issues like emissions regulations. Points can be exchanged for physical rewards like stickers, t-shirts and even trips. Calls to action on the platform encourage employees to contact their representatives to support Toyota’s policy positions.

— “On Monster Mansion, a game featuring cozy haunted house motifs, users can earn 100 points for listening to corporate recordings. In one, company lobbyists discuss how the company is affected by trade policy; in another, women Toyota dealers praise a Washington, D.C. company event with lawmakers. A third features Stephen Ciccone – the longtime vice-president of public affairs for Toyota in North America – criticizing environmental measures.”

BREAKING THE BANK: The American Bankers Association, along with bankers associations from all 50 states, D.C. and Puerto Rico, sent a letter to Congress yesterday urging lawmakers to take action on a loophole in the GENIUS Act. They say the loophole has allowed stablecoin issuers and crypto exchanges to offer interest payments to stablecoin holders, threatening banks’ abilities to make loans.

— “The GENIUS Act envisioned payment stablecoins as a payments instrument, not an investment product. Congress barred issuers from paying interest for precisely that reason. Closing the current loophole by clarifying that the prohibition extends to partners and affiliates would restore parity, protect consumers, and align practice with legislative intent,” the associations write.

— The letter from the banks came on the same day as a letter from a collection of crypto associations and companies, led by the Blockchain Association, urging the Senate Banking Committee to leave the GENIUS Act as is and continue allowing crypto exchanges to offer the financial incentives.

— “The push to restrict stablecoin rewards beyond that agreed to in GENIUS is not a technical refinement or a consumer protection fix,” the crypto letter states. “It would prohibit the same types of incentive programs for stablecoin payments that banks have long offered on credit cards and other types of payment services.”

WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN: Some of Washington’s biggest lobbying firms raked in unprecedented amounts of cash last quarter. But it’s the upstart firms with ties to President Donald Trump or his administration that have been drowning in lobbying fees as they lap their more established rivals on K Street and continue to shake up the downtown hierarchy .

— Ballard Partners led the charge in Q3 with more than $25 million in lobbying revenues, shattering the firm’s previous record of $20.7 million last quarter. Ballard’s $25.1 million haul from July to September is more than five times its revenue from the same period a year ago, as clients flock to the firm that once counted White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Attorney General Pam Bondi as employees.

— The flood of lobbying activity last quarter powered BGR Group to the No. 2 spot in the revenue rankings, ahead of former perennial leaders Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck and Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld . BGR Group, which employs Trump adviser David Urban and previously employed Transportation Secretary (and acting NASA Chief) Sean Duffy , reported $19.2 in lobbying revenues in Q3 — up from $17.7 million in Q2 and $11.4 million a year ago.

— “I said to someone the other day that if your lobbyist is telling you that nothing is happening in Washington because of the shutdown or because of gridlock or because of August recess … you are missing the forest from the trees,” Loren Monroe , a principal at BGR Group, told PI.

— Brownstein still brought in a firm record of $18.9 million last quarter, while Akin took in $16.3 million in Q3. Miller Strategies , the firm led by Trump fundraiser Jeff Miller , jumped into the top five with $14.1 million in lobbying revenue last quarter — up from $2.9 million a year ago.

— The top 20 also includes one Trump-linked firm that hadn’t even opened its doors in Washington this time last year. Checkmate Government Relations , which is led by Trump family friend Ches McDowell , hauled in just over $7 million the past three months — up from $4.5 million in Q2. Continental Strategy , which was started in 2021 by former Trump administration official Carlos Trujillo , continued to climb the revenue rankings as well with $8.3 million in lobbying fees in Q3. That’s compared to nearly $400,000 during the same period last year.

— Mercury Public Affairs , Wiles’ most recent K Street home, also reported a strong third quarter haul of $6.8 million. That’s roughly the same as the firm’s Q2 revenues, but it’s more than double Mercury’s revenues from the same time a year ago.

— Lobbyists said that the frenetic pace of activity in the executive branch — on trade in particular — is driving huge business downtown. So are health care issues ranging from Medicaid and rural health care coverage to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s Make America Healthy Again platform and drug pricing.

— Education, energy, defense and artificial intelligence policy also kept K Street busy last quarter, while planning for the end of the shutdown has kept clients engaged during the first few weeks of Q4.

— The shutdown has required some readjustments. “Hearings that we thought were going to happen, they’ve been postponed, or markups have been postponed,” said Will Moschella , who co-leads Brownstein’s lobbying practice.

— “We need to look past the shutdown, because that ultimately is going to resolve itself.” And that will set off a new scramble to beat the legislative clock on funding the government, passing the National Defense Authorization Act and setting up a package of potential tax extenders or teeing up the beginnings of another reconciliation bill, he added.

NONPROFIT CHILL: A chill has come over liberal nonprofit organizations since Trump’s pledge to investigate such groups in the wake of Charlie Kirk ’s killing. Foundations are hiring extra security and lawyers as some foreign donors withhold funds amid concerns that the Trump administration could be taking note of foreign donations to left-leaning nonprofits, Gabe Kaminsky reports for The Free Press .

— Groups that receive money from Democratic megadonor George Soros have questioned whether they will need to make policy changes to avoid being targeted by the administration. And at least one Soros-funded organization is increasing its compliance efforts to make sure it can’t be accused of illegal lobbying, Kaminsky reports.

— Others are taking steps to purge their websites of content that could be considered hostile toward Trump and taking down staff biographical information due to security concerns. “Many other large foundations have enlisted crisis communications and legal consultants to advise their grant recipients about how to prepare for potential government scrutiny, according to one of the consultants involved in the effort.”

INDUSTRY INSIDE EPA: Kyle Kunkler was, until June, the senior director of government affairs for the American Soybean Association . In that role he lobbied regulators on behalf of the soybean industry to keep a weedkiller called dicamba on the market. Now, Kunkler is the EPA’s chief official in charge of pesticide policy and dicamba has been proposed for use on genetically engineered cotton and soybeans, according to Hiroko Tabuchi of The New York Times .

— “Former corporate lobbyists or executives now in leadership roles at EPA include Nancy Beck and Lynn Dekleva , both former directors at the American Chemistry Council , a major trade association. Douglas Troutman , who until recently was head of government affairs at the American Cleaning Institute , which represents makers of cleaning products, is also joining in a senior role.”

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED—OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN: Some of Washington’s biggest lobbying firms raked in unprecedented amounts of cash last quarter. But it’s the upstart firms with ties to President Donald Trump or his administration that have been drowning in lobbying fees as they lap their more established rivals on K Street and continue to shake up the downtown hierarchy.

— Ballard Partners led the charge in Q3 with more than $25 million in lobbying revenues, shattering the firm’s previous record of $20.7 million last quarter. Ballard’s $25.1 million haul from July to September is more than five times its revenue from the same period a year ago, as clients flock to the firm that once counted White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Attorney General Pam Bondi as employees.

— The flood of lobbying activity last quarter powered BGR Group to the No. 2 spot in the revenue rankings, ahead of former perennial leaders Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck and Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld. BGR Group, which employs Trump adviser David Urban and previously employed Transportation Secretary (and acting NASA Chief) Sean Duffy, reported $19.2 in lobbying revenues in Q3 — up from $17.7 million in Q2 and $11.4 million a year ago.

— “I said to someone the other day that if your lobbyist is telling you that nothing is happening in Washington because of the shutdown or because of gridlock or because of August recess … you are missing the forest from the trees,” Loren Monroe, a principal at BGR Group, told PI.

— Brownstein still brought in a firm record of $18.9 million last quarter, while Akin took in $16.3 million in Q3. Miller Strategies, the firm led by Trump fundraiser Jeff Miller, jumped into the top five with $14.1 million in lobbying revenue last quarter — up from $2.9 million a year ago.

— The top 20 also includes one Trump-linked firm that hadn’t even opened its doors in Washington this time last year. Checkmate Government Relations, which is led by Trump family friend Ches McDowell, hauled in just over $7 million the past three months — up from $4.5 million in Q2. Continental Strategy, which was started in 2021 by former Trump administration official Carlos Trujillo, continued to climb the revenue rankings as well with $8.3 million in lobbying fees in Q3. That’s compared to nearly $400,000 during the same period last year.

— Mercury Public Affairs, Wiles’ most recent K Street home, also reported a strong third quarter haul of $6.8 million. That’s roughly the same as the firm’s Q2 revenues, but it’s more than double Mercury’s revenues from the same time a year ago.

— Lobbyists said that the frenetic pace of activity in the executive branch — on trade in particular — is driving huge business downtown. So are health care issues ranging from Medicaid and rural health care coverage to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again platform and drug pricing.

— Education, energy, defense and artificial intelligence policy also kept K Street busy last quarter, while planning for the end of the shutdown has kept clients engaged during the first few weeks of Q4.

— The shutdown has required some readjustments. “Hearings that we thought were going to happen, they’ve been postponed, or markups have been postponed,” said Will Moschella, who co-leads Brownstein’s lobbying practice.

— “We need to look past the shutdown, because that ultimately is going to resolve itself.” And that will set off a new scramble to beat the legislative clock on funding the government, passing the National Defense Authorization Act and setting up a package of potential tax extenders or teeing up the beginnings of another reconciliation bill, he added.

NONPROFIT CHILL: A chill has come over liberal nonprofit organizations since Trump’s pledge to investigate such groups in the wake of Charlie Kirk’s killing. Foundations are hiring extra security and lawyers as some foreign donors withhold funds amid concerns that the Trump administration could be taking note of foreign donations to left-leaning nonprofits, Gabe Kaminsky reports for The Free Press.

— Groups that receive money from Democratic megadonor George Soros have questioned whether they will need to make policy changes to avoid being targeted by the administration. And at least one Soros-funded organization is increasing its compliance efforts to make sure it can’t be accused of illegal lobbying, Kaminsky reports.

— Others are taking steps to purge their websites of content that could be considered hostile toward Trump and taking down staff biographical information due to security concerns. “Many other large foundations have enlisted crisis communications and legal consultants to advise their grant recipients about how to prepare for potential government scrutiny, according to one of the consultants involved in the effort.”

INDUSTRY INSIDE EPA: Kyle Kunkler was, until June, the senior director of government affairs for the American Soybean Association. In that role he lobbied regulators on behalf of the soybean industry to keep a weedkiller called dicamba on the market. Now, Kunkler is the EPA’s chief official in charge of pesticide policy and dicamba has been proposed for use on genetically engineered cotton and soybeans, according to Hiroko Tabuchi of The New York Times.

— “Former corporate lobbyists or executives now in leadership roles at EPA include Nancy Beck and Lynn Dekleva, both former directors at the American Chemistry Council, a major trade association. title: Here’s who else is feeling the Trump bump
body_text:
THE WIDE RADIUS OF THE TRUMP BUMP: Washington’s influence industry is going gangbusters nine months into Donald Trump ’s second presidency. As PI highlighted yesterday ( and dove deeper into this afternoon ), the vast majority of the spoils have been flowing to the handful of Trump-tied firms PI readers have been reading about for months.

— But there’s another, less-discussed tier of boutique lobbying firms who are seeing business soar thanks to their ties to Trump or his inner circle.

— They include The Bernhardt Group , which was launched earlier this year by former Trump Interior secretary — and veteran lobbyist — David Bernhardt . Last quarter, Bernhardt Group hauled in $2.6 million in lobbying fees from nearly four dozen clients like ConocoPhillips and the American Exploration and Production Council . That’s up from $430,000 in the firm’s first quarter of existence.

— The Artemis Group , the firm started after Trump’s election by former NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine , doubled its lobbying revenues to $970,000 between the second and third quarters of the year. The firm’s clients include United Launch Alliance , Voyager Space Holdings and the University of Arizona .

— Valcour , which was started in 2023 by former Trump State Department and White House official Matt Mowers , took in $1.1 million during the third quarter of 2025. That’s down slightly from Q2, but is more than the firm earned in 2023 and 2024 combined.

— There’s also Capitol 6 Advisors , the firm started by the former top lobbyist for the National Rifle Association , which lobbied for just three clients from 2020 through most of 2024. But since the election last November, Capitol 6 has registered to lobby for 14 new clients including the drugmaker Amgen and canned soup titan Campbell’s . Capitol 6 reported $600,000 in lobbying revenues last quarter, up 175 percent from the same time a year ago.

— HillNorth is another boutique government affairs shop experiencing a Trump bump. The firm is led by Doug Schwartz , who served as chief of staff to now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune .

— HillNorth brought in $342,500 in lobbying revenue from nine clients last quarter, according to PI’s analysis of disclosure filings. Five of those clients — which include the National Football League and trade associations representing biopharmaceuticals; name brand drugs; and broadcasters — only retained the firm this year.

— While they’re more established in the lobbying world, heavily Republican firms like Vogel Group and CGCN Group have also seen massive surges in business this year. CGCN, which boasts close ties to numerous congressional GOP leaders but also counts several Trump administration alumni among its staff, brought in close to $5 million lobbying fees in Q3. That’s up from $4.6 million during the second quarter and more than double their revenue during the same time last year.

— Meanwhile the Vogel Group raked in $4.5 million in lobbying revenue during the third quarter. That’s an increase of $2 million compared to the same period a year ago for the firm, which is affiliated with top conservative political law firm Holtzman Vogel and was the former K Street home of White House counsel pick-turned-DOGE lawyer Bill McGinley .

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. What interesting nuggets have you spotted in the Q3 lobbying disclosures? ANTHROPIC, NVIDIA CRACK $1M: A pair of top AI stakeholders have reached a new milestone as the industry continues to build out its presence on K Street: the first seven-figure quarterly lobbying spend. Anthropic , the company behind AI chatbot Claude, just barely cracked the $1 million mark during Q3, according to disclosures filed this week.

— Anthropic’s $1.01 million in spending last quarter — up from $920,000 in Q2 — coincided with the White House’s unveiling of its highly anticipated AI Action Plan (and Anthropic’s offer to sell government access to its chatbot for just $1 per year). title: Google taps KDCR for permitting push

JUST IN: “A federal judge in Brooklyn on Monday declared a mistrial in the case of Linda Sun , a former aide to Democratic governors who was accused of working as an agent of China, after jurors said they could not reach a verdict,” The New York Times’ Santul Nerkar and Anusha Bayya report.

— “Ms. Sun, 42, was accused by federal prosecutors of being an unscrupulous public servant who sold her allegiance to China, which rewarded her handsomely for helping to carry out its global campaign of influence peddling.”

— “She and her husband, Chris Hu , who was also on trial, carried out Beijing’s bidding, prosecutors claimed, including by blocking Taiwanese officials from meeting the governor and by removing references to the Uyghurs, a primarily Muslim ethnic minority that has faced persecution from the Chinese Communist Party, from official speeches. … But the couple’s lawyers argued that she was just doing her job. And jurors seemed unconvinced by the case brought by the Justice Department.”

— Prosecutor Andrew Solomon told Judge Brian Cogan today “that the government wanted to retry the case as soon as possible. Both parties are due back in court on Jan. 26.”

GOOGLE LOBBIES UP FOR PERMITTING PUSH: Google bolstered its lobbying roster ahead of a major congressional push to overhaul federal permitting that advanced out of the House last week, according to a disclosure filing.

— Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid ’s Dave Peluso and Lisa Kountoupes began lobbying for the tech giant on permitting reform last month, disclosures show. Peluso was a top aide to former House Energy & Commerce Chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-Wash.) as well as Florida Rep. Gus Bilirakis , who now chairs the E&C technology subcommittee. Kountoupes was a former staffer to longtime E&C Chair John Dingell .

— Last week, the House passed a bipartisan measure aimed at easing regulatory hurdles for new energy projects, including those that could help meet surging power demands fueled by artificial intelligence data centers . The move came after a push from the energy industry, business lobbies and Silicon Valley.

— KDCR isn’t the only firm that’s lobbied for Google on permitting reform. The Simmons & Russell Group began working on the issue for Google beginning at the end of 2024, while the tech giant’s in-house team of lobbyists first reported working on permitting reforms last summer, according to a PI analysis of disclosure filings.

— Google is also a member of the Data Center Coalition , an alliance of tech giants like Meta , Amazon Web Services and Microsoft , which has also been lobbying Washington on energy issues.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI . There are only a few more days to send your tips for the newsletter this year. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

PENCE GROUP LANDS HERITAGE DEFECTORS: “Former Vice President Mike Pence ’s political group is poaching top officials from the conservative Heritage Foundation amid growing ideological fights within the conservative movement and backlash at the think tank,” The Wall Street Journal ’s Josh Dawsey reports.

— Pence’s nonprofit, Advancing American Freedom , is expected to add 15 former Heritage staffers, including John Malcolm , who led Heritage’s legal and judicial studies center, Kevin Dayaratna , who headed its data analysis center and Richard Stern , who led Heritage’s economic policy studies institute.

— “In an interview, Pence told the Journal he had long admired the Heritage Foundation but sees the group now ‘abandoning its principles.’ He said the foundation had ‘fallen’ because it had embraced elements of isolationism, stopped backing Ukraine in the war with Russia, supported some tariffs and backed Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as Health and Human Services secretary, among other things.”

— “In a statement, Heritage’s chief advancement officer, Andy Olivastro , was critical of some staffers who have decided to leave, accusing them of disloyalty. He said Malcolm and another staffer last week were ‘terminated for conduct inconsistent with Heritage’s mission and standards.’”

VALLEY TALK: Trump’s “aggressive move to block states from regulating artificial intelligence is splitting the tech lobby — and steering its frustration squarely toward David Sacks , the president’s top AI adviser,” according to POLITICO ’s Brendan Bordelon , Gabby Miller and Yasmin Khorram .

— “Sacks, a San Francisco-based investor, largely wrote the executive order Trump signed last week that throws the legal and financial power of the federal government against state AI laws. A controversial move even within the GOP, it was a major win for Sacks, who also acted as its biggest promoter within the White House.”

— But even as tech companies support action to preempt a patchwork of state AI regulations with one federal standard, “more than half a dozen people closely involved with the issue in Washington told POLITICO that Sacks undercut the tech industry’s effort on Capitol Hill to craft a more permanent federal solution on state AI rules, instead ramming through unilateral action that could turn AI law into a national political fight.”

CLICKER: “Since President Trump was elected a second time, he and his allies have raised nearly $2 billion for his favored political causes and passion projects,” per The New York Times’ Karen Yourish , Ken Vogel and Charlie Smart , a sum so massive it “likely eclipses the amount raised to support his 2024 campaign.”

— “The astounding haul hints at a level of transactionalism for which it is difficult to find obvious comparisons in modern American history.” A Times analysis “traced a large portion of the funds raised — more than half a billion dollars’ worth — back to 346 donors who each gave at least $250,000. It also found that more than half of them have benefited, or are involved in an industry that has benefited, from the actions or statements of Mr. Trump, the White House or federal agencies.”

MANGIONE INVOKES BONDI’S LOBBYIST PAST: “ Luigi Mangione ’s lawyers contend that Attorney General Pam Bondi ’s decision to seek the death penalty against him in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson was tainted by her prior work as a lobbyist at a firm that represented the insurer’s parent company,” the Associated Press ’ Michael R. Sisak reports.

— Bondi was never registered to lobby for UnitedHealthcare while working as a partner at Ballard Partners , where UnitedHealthcare has been a client since 2024. title: Tech’s hidden hand in the kids online safety battle
body_text:
FIRST IN PI: Social media platforms have spent the past three years fending off congressional efforts that would force platforms to take a firmer hand in mitigating issues related to mental health, addiction and bullying of kids and teens online.

— Their allies in opposition to the Kids Online Safety Act have included industry-funded trade groups as well as nonprofit advocacy groups across the ideological spectrum . But an analysis of tax filings by Issue One , a money-in-politics group that supports KOSA, reveals that some of those nonprofits fighting the bill have financial ties to the tech industry.

— They include Patriot Voices , a nonprofit started by former Sen. Rick Santorum (R-Pa.) that was one of the leading KOSA critics on the right in 2024. Tax returns filed by both organizations show that of the roughly $738,000 raised by Patriot Voices last year, more than three-quarters came from NetChoice , an industry group whose members include Meta , Google , X and YouTube . NetChoice’s $580,000 grant to Patriot Voices was the largest issued by the trade group last year, according to tax filings.

— A year earlier, NetChoice accounted for all of the funds raised by another 501(c)4 group opposing KOSA, the Stop Child Predators Coalition . The coalition has long pushed for policies to protect children from sexual predators online, but has argued that shifting the responsibility to tech companies would not be as effective as investing more resources in law enforcement to investigate predators.

— The coalition brought in $210,000 in 2023, tax filings show , all of which came from NetChoice . The coalition raised $95,000 in 2024, but the source of those donations is unclear. Nonprofits like Stop Child Predators and Patriot Voices are not required to disclose their donors.

— Stop Child Predators also has a 501(c)3 arm, the Stop Child Predators Partnership , that has received virtually all of its funding in 2023 and 2024 from Meta, tax filings show. The social media giant and major KOSA foe accounted for $75,000 of the $75,047 raised by the partnership in 2024 and all of the group’s $50,410 in revenues in 2023.

— “We support groups for the excellent work they are already doing on this issue,” NetChoice spokesperson Krista Chavez told PI. A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did Stop Child Predators or Patriot Voices.

— Earlier this month, a coalition that includes Issue One launched a pledge calling for nonprofits to disclose any funding they’ve received from tech giants. “Policymakers and the public deserve to know if innocuously named organizations are independent actors or carrying water for special interests,” Michael Beckel , Issue One’s senior research director, said in a statement. He added that “strategically funding advocacy efforts helps create an echo chamber that prevents real accountability.”

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI . Tomorrow will be our last edition of the year, so if there are any juicy tips you’re sitting on … no time like the present. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

HOW THE LUMBEE TRIBE WON RECOGNITION: “President Donald Trump worked the phones. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) threatened to jam up the Senate. And a new player in Washington lobbying blitzed the nation’s capital. That’s all part of how the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina won a decades-long push for full federal recognition ,” Bloomberg ’s Kate Ackley reports.

— “After decades of advocacy without success, lawmakers tucked the Lumbee provision into this year’s annual defense policy bill that sets troop raises and weapons procurement — despite opposition from rival tribes. Now the Lumbee tribe and its K Street firm plan to navigate the executive branch, tapping federal funds available because of the recognition. The tribe also could decide to start a casino business.”

— “Lobbyist Ches McDowell , whose North Carolina firm Checkmate Government Relations came on the Washington scene this year, took up the tribe’s cause at the federal level pro bono. McDowell said there was a multi-pronged strategy of working the Trump team and harnessing support from lawmakers in both chambers, including his brother Rep. Addison McDowell (R-N.C.).”

— The tribe, whose outreach included “dozens of trips to Washington,” including for a fundraiser for Vice President JD Vance , and a letter to Trump noting his daughter Tiffany ’s ancestral ties to the Lumbee .

— “On the other side, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians has paid $270,000 for federal lobbying this year to the firm Integrated Strategy Group , disclosures show. That tribe lobbied against the Lumbee measure,” which Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said stemmed from disputes over gambling businesses.

MAIL CALL: “Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut wants to know who is funding President Trump’s White House ballroom project, how much it is going to cost and what it is going to look like,” The New York Times’ Ken Vogel reports.

— “Mr. Blumenthal, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a raft of letters on Monday seeking information from people who were reportedly invited to a White House dinner for donors to the ballroom project” as well as the architect recently hired to take over the project.

— “As the cost and scale of the project have expanded, so too have concerns about preserving a historically significant building and potential conflicts of interest related to Mr. Trump’s ability to use the levers of government to help the people and corporations who are financing the project.”

— In particular, Blumenthal’s letter to the potential ballroom benefactors “asked whether they had donated and said there were grounds to wonder ‘what promises may have been or may yet be made in exchange for what presumably will be substantial contributions,’” pointing to many of the donors’ “deep financial, business or other personal interests before the administration.”

PARDON ME: Trump has issued more than 1,600 pardons during his second term, with beneficiaries ranging from the billionaire crypto founder Changpeng Zhao to former Honduras President Juan Orlando Hernández and former Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.).

— They also include businessperson Timothy Leiweke , who was indicted this summer on charges of alleged bid rigging, but who was granted a reprieve earlier this month after lobbying by former Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-S.C.), The Free Press ’ Gabe Kaminsky reports in a new look at the pardon-industrial complex under Trump 2.0.

— “Gowdy’s round of golf with the president is just one example of the pardon playbook that is being used to great success by those with wealth, or connections to Trump or people close to him, or both,” per Kaminsky.

— “The strategy sometimes means hiring lawyers who have a history with the president. Other times, it means hiring MAGA lobbyists or sending him flattering letters. It could also mean finding some other leverage to command his attention, whether through party loyalty, past donations, or shared business interests.”

A DECISIVE BLOW: Trump “has taken jabs at offshore wind all year. On Monday, he threw a haymaker that threatens to knock the U.S. industry to the mat ,” POLITICO ’s Benjamin Storrow and Kelsey Tamborrino write of the president’s decision to halt construction of five major offshore wind projects along the East Coast.

— The move “marked an escalation of a yearlong effort to shut down the industry, jolting the political debate surrounding rising electricity prices” and triggering an outcry from Trump’s own allies.

— “In New England, the regional grid operator warned the stoppage could send power prices soaring and threaten the reliability of its six-state electric system. In Virginia, the utility building the country’s largest coastal wind project said the pause hinders its ability to keep up with rising electricity consumption from data centers. And on Capitol Hill, the order threatened to stymie a long-debated bipartisan energy permitting bill winding its way through Congress.”

— Ashling Preston has joined the American Federation for Children as federal affairs director. She previously was associate director of government relations at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops and is a Tim Scott alum.

A DECISIVE BLOW: Trump “has taken jabs at offshore wind all year. On Monday, he threw a haymaker that threatens to knock the U.S. industry to the mat,” POLITICO’s Benjamin Storrow and Kelsey Tamborrino write of the president’s decision to halt construction of five major offshore wind projects along the East Coast.

— The move “marked an escalation of a yearlong effort to shut down the industry, jolting the political debate surrounding rising electricity prices” and triggering an outcry from Trump’s own allies.

— “In New England, the regional grid operator warned the stoppage could send power prices soaring and threaten the reliability of its six-state electric system. In Virginia, the utility building the country’s largest coastal wind project said the pause hinders its ability to keep up with rising electricity consumption from data centers. And on Capitol Hill, the order threatened to stymie a long-debated bipartisan energy permitting bill winding its way through Congress.”
